Chapter 1: What is Docker? (The Container Revolution)

Before diving into commands, let's understand why Docker exists, what problems it solves, and how the container revolution changed software development forever. We'll use our anihpj/jobpost Django app to make every concept concrete.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours📖 Conceptual🎯 Foundation

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why "works on my machine" is a universal problem
  • ✅ How Docker solves dependency hell and environment inconsistency
  • ✅ Containers vs Virtual Machines — the critical architectural difference
  • ✅ Docker's client-daemon-registry architecture
  • ✅ The complete Docker ecosystem and where each tool fits
  • ✅ Real-world Docker use cases across industries

1.1 The Problem Docker Solves

Imagine you've built anihpj — a Django app with a jobpost module listing jobs filtered by Skills, Location, and Author. It works perfectly on your laptop. But when a teammate clones the repo, it crashes because they have Python 3.8 instead of 3.11. Or the staging server has Django 4.2 instead of 5.2. Or production has a different version of psycopg2.

This is "dependency hell" — the universal developer frustration. Docker solves this by packaging your app AND all its dependencies into a single, standardized unit called a container that runs identically everywhere.

The "Works on My Machine" Problem
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  🖥️  THE DEPENDENCY NIGHTMARE                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │   Developer Laptop              Staging Server            Production      │
  │   ┌────────────────┐          ┌────────────────┐       ┌──────────────┐  │
  │   │ Python 3.11 ✅ │          │ Python 3.8  ❌  │       │ Python 3.9   │  │
  │   │ Django 5.2  ✅ │          │ Django 4.2  ❌  │       │ Django 4.2   │  │
  │   │ psycopg2  ✅  │          │ psycopg2  ✅   │       │ psycopg2 ❌  │  │
  │   │ Node.js  ✅   │          │ Node.js  ❌    │       │ Node.js  ✅  │  │
  │   │ ───────────── │          │ ─────────────  │       │ ───────────  │  │
  │   │ App WORKS! 😊 │          │ App BROKEN! 😡 │       │ App BROKEN!  │  │
  │   └────────────────┘          └────────────────┘       └──────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │   SOLUTION: 🐳 Docker packages Python 3.11 + Django 5.2 + ALL deps      │
  │   into ONE portable container that runs IDENTICALLY everywhere!          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
😰
New Developer Onboarding

Without Docker: Install Python, Django, PostgreSQL, Redis, configure virtualenv, set env vars... (2+ hours)

With Docker: docker compose up (30 seconds)

🔥
Production Emergency at 3 AM

Without Docker: SSH into server, find right config, restart process manually, pray dependencies match...

With Docker: docker pull anihpj:v2 && docker compose up -d

📦
"It worked yesterday!"

Without Docker: System update changed Python version, pip packages drifting. Impossible to reproduce exact environment.

With Docker: Image is immutable snapshot. Yesterday's image = today's.

1.2 What is Docker? (The Simple Answer)

Docker is a platform for building, shipping, and running containers. A container is a lightweight, standalone, executable package that includes everything needed to run a piece of software: code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings.

The best analogy is shipping containers in the physical world. Before standardized shipping containers, every item (cars, furniture, food) had to be loaded differently onto ships, trucks, and trains. After standardization, any container fits on any ship, truck, or train — regardless of what's inside. Docker does the same for software.

The Shipping Container Analogy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             🚢 PHYSICAL SHIPPING  =  🐳 SOFTWARE CONTAINERS                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────┐               │
  │  │  📦 Standard Container│          │  🐳 Docker Image     │               │
  │  │  Same size, shape,   │          │  Same format, runs   │               │
  │  │  fits on any ship,   │          │  on any OS, any      │               │
  │  │  truck, or train     │          │  cloud, any server   │               │
  │  └─────────┬───────────┘          └─────────┬───────────┘               │
  │            │                                │                            │
  │            ▼                                ▼                            │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐                │
  │  │  🏗️ Standardized, Stackable, Portable, Isolated      │                │
  │  │  What's INSIDE doesn't matter to the transport!      │                │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Important Distinction

Docker Inc. is the company. Docker is the technology/platform. docker (lowercase) is the CLI tool you type commands into. All three are commonly referred to as "Docker."

1.3 Containers vs Virtual Machines — The Critical Difference

Understanding the difference between containers and VMs is fundamental. They solve similar problems but in completely different ways.

Virtual Machines virtualize the hardware — each VM runs a full guest OS with its own kernel. This gives strong isolation but is heavy (GBs of RAM, minutes to boot).

Containers virtualize the operating system — all containers share the host's kernel. This makes them lightweight (MBs, seconds to start) but with slightly weaker isolation.

VM vs Container Architecture
  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │        VIRTUAL MACHINES           │  │           CONTAINERS               │
  │                                   │  │                                   │
  │  ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ │  │  ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ │
  │  │App A│ │App B│ │App C│ │App D│ │  │  │App A│ │App B│ │App C│ │App D│ │
  │  └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ │  │  └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ │
  │  ┌──┴───────┴───────┴───────┴──┐ │  │  ┌──┴─────────────────────────┴──┐ │
  │  │  Guest OS (Full Kernel)     │ │  │  │     Docker Engine           │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘ │  │  └─────────────────────────────┘ │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐ │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │      Hypervisor            │ │  │  │ Host OS (Shared Kernel)     │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘ │  │  └─────────────────────────────┘ │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐ │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │    Host OS                 │ │  │  │     Hardware / Cloud         │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘ │  │  └─────────────────────────────┘ │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────┐ │  │                                   │
  │  │    Hardware / Cloud        │ │  │  ❌ NO hypervisor, NO guest OS!   │
  │  └────────────────────────────┘ │  │  ✅ Shared kernel = lightweight   │
  └───────────────────────────────────┘  └───────────────────────────────────┘
MetricVirtual MachineDocker ContainerWinner
Startup Time30-90 seconds1-3 seconds🐳 x30 faster
Memory Usage1-2 GB per VM~50 MB per container🐳 x20-40 less
Disk Space10-40 GB per VM~100 MB per image🐳 x100+ less
CPU OverheadSignificant (hypervisor)Near-native🐳
Density per Host~10 VMs100s of containers🐳 x10+
Isolation StrengthFull OS isolationProcess-level (weaker)VM
PortabilityHypervisor-dependentRuns anywhere Docker runs🐳

1.4 Docker Architecture — How It All Fits Together

Docker uses a client-server architecture. The Docker client (docker CLI) talks to the Docker daemon (dockerd), which does the heavy lifting: building images, running containers, managing networks and volumes.

Docker Architecture — Client-Daemon-Registry
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                      🐳 DOCKER ARCHITECTURE                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │    Docker CLI        │  REST    │        DOCKER HOST                │ │
  │  │    (Client)          │  API     │                                  │ │
  │  │  $ docker run       │─────────▶│  ┌────────────────────────────┐  │ │
  │  │  $ docker build     │  over    │  │      dockerd (Daemon)      │  │ │
  │  │  $ docker push      │  Unix    │  │  ┌──────────────────────┐  │  │ │
  │  │                     │  Socket  │  │  │    containerd         │  │  │ │
  │  └──────────────────────┘          │  │  │  (container runtime)  │  │  │ │
  │                                   │  │  └──────────┬───────────┘  │  │ │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐          │  │      ┌──────┴──────┐       │  │ │
  │  │   🗄️ Registry        │          │  │      │    runc     │       │  │ │
  │  │   Docker Hub         │◀─────────│──│      │(OCI runtime) │       │  │ │
  │  │   ECR / GCR / ACR   │ pull/push│  │      └──────┬──────┘       │  │ │
  │  │   ghcr.io / Harbor   │          │  │      ┌──────┴──────┐       │  │ │
  │  └──────────────────────┘          │  │      │  Containers │       │  │ │
  │                                   │  │      │  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ │       │  │ │
  │                                   │  │      │  │C1│ │C2│ │       │  │ │
  │                                   │  │      └────────────┘       │  │ │
  │                                   │  └────────────────────────────┘  │ │
  │                                   └──────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🐳 Docker Client

The CLI tool you interact with. Sends commands to the daemon via REST API over a Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock) or TCP.

⚙️ Docker Daemon (dockerd)

The background service that does the actual work: building images, running containers, managing networks and volumes. Uses containerd as the container runtime.

🗄️ Docker Registry

Stores and distributes Docker images. Docker Hub is the default public registry. Private options include Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure ACR, and GitHub Container Registry.

🔧 Under the Hood — How the Daemon Actually Runs Containers: containerd → runc → OCI Runtime
🗺️ The Container Runtime Chain

When you run docker run, here's the actual chain of components:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🔧 DOCKER DAEMON INTERNALS                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  dockerd ───▶ containerd ───▶ containerd-shim ───▶ runc ───▶ Container  │
  │  (API,       (Image mgmt,     (Handles stdio,     (OCI      (Your app)   │
  │   Build,      Pull/Push,      exit signals,       runtime,              │
  │   Network)    Lifecycle)      keeps container     creates               │
  │                               alive after         namespaces)            │
  │                               dockerd restart)                           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Key: dockerd manages HIGH-LEVEL stuff (API, build, networking)          │
  │        containerd manages MID-LEVEL (image pull/push, lifecycle)         │
  │        runc does the LOW-LEVEL (creates namespaces, cgroups, starts proc)│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

dockerd — The Docker daemon. Handles the Docker API, builds images, manages networks. Does NOT directly run containers.

containerd — The container runtime. Manages the complete container lifecycle: image transfer, container execution, storage, and networking. Originally spun out from Docker, now a CNCF graduated project used by Kubernetes too.

containerd-shim — A small process that stays between containerd and the container. Allows containerd to be restarted without killing running containers, and handles STDIO.

runc — The OCI runtime. Creates and starts containers by setting up Linux namespaces (PID, NET, MNT, IPC, UTS, USER, CGROUP) and cgroups. This is where the actual Linux magic happens.

📖 Why This Matters for DCA

The DCA exam expects you to understand this architecture chain, especially for the Installation & Configuration domain (15%). Questions may ask about containerd's role, how to configure the daemon (daemon.json), or what happens when you restart dockerd (shim keeps containers alive).

1.5 The Docker Ecosystem

Docker isn't just one tool — it's a whole platform with an ecosystem of tools around the core engine.

The Docker Ecosystem
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🌍 THE DOCKER ECOSYSTEM                               │
  │                                                                          │
  │                         ┌──────────────┐                                 │

  │  │ Multi-    │  │      🐳 DOCKER ENGINE       │  │ Native   │           │
  │  │ Container │  │      (dockerd+containerd)   │  │ Cluster  │           │
  │  └──────────┘  └────────────┬───────────────┬─┘  └──────────┘           │
  │                    ┌────────┴──────┐  ┌─────┴────────┐                  │

  │  │ 🏗️Buildx│  │ 🗄️Hub    │  │ 🔍Scout  │  │ ☁️Build Cloud│            │
  │  │ Advanced │  │ Registry │  │ Vuln.    │  │ Remote       │            │
  │  │ Builder  │  │ + Teams  │  │ Scanner  │  │ Builds       │            │
  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────────┘            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🐳 Docker Engine

The core. Includes the daemon (dockerd), the CLI (docker), and the container runtime (containerd). This is what actually builds and runs containers.

🎼 Docker Compose

Tool for defining and running multi-container apps. One YAML file (compose.yaml) defines your entire stack. One command (docker compose up) starts everything.

🐝 Docker Swarm

Docker's native clustering and orchestration tool. Turns a pool of Docker hosts into a single virtual host. Simpler than Kubernetes but less feature-rich.

🖥️ Docker Desktop

All-in-one package for Mac/Windows/Linux: Docker Engine, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, Docker Scout, and a GUI dashboard. The recommended way to run Docker on development machines.

1.7 Real-World Docker Use Cases

🏗️
Microservices

Each service in its own container — independent deploy, independent scale. Django anihpj app, Auth service, Payment service, Celery worker — each gets its own container with its own dependencies.

🚀
CI/CD Pipeline

Build → Test → Push → Deploy — every step runs in an identical Docker container. No more "it works in CI but not in prod." The exact same image that passed tests is what gets deployed.

💻
Development Environment

docker compose up starts PostgreSQL, Redis, Django, and Nginx in 30 seconds. No installing databases, no configuring caches. Team members get identical environments instantly.

🏚️
Legacy Modernization

Old PHP 5.6 app? Containerize it with a PHP 5.6 Apache image. NO rewriting needed. It runs the SAME on modern infrastructure. This is how enterprises migrate to the cloud without rewrites.

These are the commands you will type most on the DCA exam

docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name app IMAGE`ndocker ps -a`ndocker logs -f CONTAINER`ndocker exec -it CONTAINER sh`ndocker inspect CONTAINER`ndocker build -t name:tag .`ndocker push REGISTRY/name:tag

⚠️ Chapter 1 Exam Gotchas

  • "Containers are lightweight VMs" → Containers share the host kernel; VMs have their own. Completely different architectures.
  • docker stop = docker kill → stop sends SIGTERM (graceful); kill sends SIGKILL (immediate).
  • EXPOSE publishes ports → EXPOSE is documentation only. Use -p or ports: to actually publish.
  • Data survives container deletion → All container data is lost on deletion unless stored in volumes.

📝 Chapter 1 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What is the primary problem that Docker solves in software development?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker solves the "works on my machine" problem by packaging applications and ALL their dependencies into standardized containers that run identically across any environment — development, staging, and production.

EXPLANATION

Before Docker, each environment (dev, staging, prod) could have different OS versions, library versions, and configurations. A container bundles the application code WITH its exact runtime environment, ensuring consistency everywhere.

# Before Docker — "Works on my machine"
# Dev: Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04
# Prod: Python 3.10, CentOS 7

# With Docker — identical everywhere:
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY . /app
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q2
What is the key architectural difference between containers and virtual machines?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Virtual Machines virtualize the HARDWARE and each runs a full guest OS with its own kernel. Containers virtualize the OPERATING SYSTEM and share the host's kernel.

EXPLANATION

This is why containers are so much lighter: they don't need to boot a full OS, don't need a hypervisor, and can share memory and disk resources. A VM needs GBs of RAM for the guest OS alone; a container adds only MBs on top of the host.

  VIRTUAL MACHINES:                    CONTAINERS:
  ┌──────────────────────┐             ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ App A │ App B        │             │ App A │ App B        │
  │ Bins/  │ Bins/        │             │ Bins/  │ Bins/        │
  │ Libs   │ Libs         │             │ Libs   │ Libs         │
  │┌──────┐│┌──────┐     │             │        │             │
  ││Guest │││Guest │     │             │  Docker Engine       │
  ││OS    │││OS    │     │             │  (containerd+runc)   │
  │└──────┘│└──────┘     │             │        │             │
  │   Hypervisor         │             │   Host OS (kernel)   │
  │──────────────────────│             │──────────────────────│
  │   Host OS (kernel)   │             │   Hardware            │
  │──────────────────────│             └──────────────────────┘
  │   Hardware            │              Each VM = GBs RAM
  └──────────────────────┘              Each container = MBs RAM
   Each VM = full guest OS               All share ONE kernel
Q3
Name the three main components of Docker's architecture and their roles.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. Docker Client — CLI that sends commands to the daemon via REST API.
2. Docker Daemon (dockerd) — Background service that builds images, runs containers, manages networks/volumes.
3. Docker Registry — Stores and distributes images (Docker Hub, ECR, etc.)

EXPLANATION

The client and daemon can run on the same machine or different machines. Communication happens over a Unix socket (default: /var/run/docker.sock) or TCP. The registry is where images are pushed to and pulled from — Docker Hub being the default public registry.

# Docker Client ↔ Daemon communication
# Local (Unix socket — default):
docker run nginx          # → /var/run/docker.sock → dockerd

# Remote (TCP — requires TLS):
docker -H tcp://192.168.1.10:2376 run nginx

# Registry interaction:
docker pull nginx         # ← Docker Hub (default)
docker pull myreg.com:5000/app:v1  # ← Private registry
docker push myreg.com:5000/app:v1  # → Private registry
Q4
A developer says "Docker containers are just like lightweight VMs." Is this accurate? Explain.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Not accurate. While both provide isolation, containers share the host OS kernel and do NOT include a full operating system. VMs each have their own kernel, making them fundamentally different architecturally.

EXPLANATION

This misunderstanding is common. Containers feel like VMs because they provide process isolation, but under the hood they use Linux namespaces and cgroups — NOT hardware virtualization. This is why you can't run a Windows container on a Linux host (kernel must match).

# Linux namespaces — the isolation building blocks:
# PID namespace:    container sees only its own processes
# NET namespace:    container has its own network stack
# MNT namespace:    container has its own filesystem mount
# UTS namespace:    container has its own hostname
# IPC namespace:    container has isolated shared memory
# USER namespace:   container UIDs mapped to host UIDs

# Verify isolation:
docker run --rm alpine ps aux
# Shows only container processes — NOT the host''s 200+ processes

# cgroups limit resources:
docker run --memory=256m --cpus=1 nginx
# Kernel enforces: container cannot exceed 256MB RAM
Q5
Which container runtime does modern Docker use, and what is its role?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Modern Docker uses containerd as the container runtime. containerd manages the complete container lifecycle: image transfer, container execution, storage, and networking. It uses runc (an OCI-compliant runtime) to actually create and start containers.

EXPLANATION

Docker's architecture evolved: originally dockerd did everything. Now dockerd delegates to containerd, which delegates to runc. This modular design means you can swap components (e.g., use CRI-O instead of containerd in Kubernetes).

  DOCKER RUNTIME CHAIN (from high-level to low-level):
  
  docker CLI ──REST API──▶ dockerd ──gRPC──▶ containerd ──shim──▶ runc ──▶ CONTAINER
  (user types)            (daemon)          (runtime)   (per-ctr) (OCI)
  
  KEY INSIGHT: The shim keeps containers alive
  even when dockerd restarts!
  
  # Check runtime:
  docker info | grep Runtime
  # Runtime: runc
  
  # Containers survive daemon restart (with shim):
  sudo systemctl restart docker
  docker ps  # Containers still running!
Q6
What is Docker Hub? How does it differ from a private registry like Amazon ECR?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Hub is Docker's public registry — anyone can pull public images and push their own (with an account). Private registries like Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, or Azure ACR are hosted within your cloud account, offering better security, lower latency, and integration with your cloud's IAM.

EXPLANATION

For production, you typically use a private registry close to your deployment environment. ECR ensures your images stay within your AWS VPC, reducing pull latency and eliminating public exposure. Docker Hub is great for development and sharing open-source images.

# ── Docker Hub (public) ──
docker login                                    # Interactive
docker push myuser/anihpj:v1
docker pull myuser/anihpj:v1

# ── AWS ECR (private) ──
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 |   docker login --username AWS --password-stdin   123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
docker tag anihpj:v1 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1
docker push 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1

# ── Self-hosted (Harbor/Artifactory) ──
docker login registry.company.com
docker push registry.company.com/anihpj:v1
Q7
You can run 100 containers on a single host. How many VMs could you typically run on the same hardware?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Typically only 5-15 VMs on the same hardware that can run 100+ containers. Containers share the host kernel and use MBs of RAM each, while each VM needs GBs for its own OS.

EXPLANATION

This is the "density advantage" of containers. A 16GB RAM server can run ~10 VMs (each needing ~1.5GB OS overhead) but can run 100+ containers (each adding only ~50MB). This is why cloud-native architectures favor containers.

  DENSITY COMPARISON — Same hardware (16GB RAM / 8 cores):

  ┌──────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │  VIRTUAL MACHINES         │  │  CONTAINERS               │
  │                           │  │                           │
  │  VM1: Ubuntu (1.5GB)     │  │  C1: nginx     (~20MB)   │
  │  VM2: RHEL   (1.5GB)     │  │  C2: anihpj    (~80MB)   │
  │  VM3: Debian (1.5GB)     │  │  C3: postgres  (~50MB)   │
  │  VM4: CentOS (1.5GB)     │  │  C4: redis     (~20MB)   │
  │  VM5: Ubuntu (1.5GB)     │  │  C5: celery    (~60MB)   │
  │  ────────────────────     │  │  ... 95 more containers   │
  │  MAX: ~10 VMs             │  │  ────────────────────     │
  │  OS overhead: ~15GB       │  │  MAX: 100+ containers     │
  │  App RAM left: ~1GB       │  │  OS overhead: ~0MB (share)│
  └──────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘
Q8
What are Docker Desktop, Docker Engine, and Docker Compose? How do they relate?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Engine = core (daemon + CLI + containerd). Docker Desktop = Engine + GUI + Kubernetes + Scout + Compose bundled for dev machines. Docker Compose = tool for defining multi-container apps with YAML — included in Desktop, installable separately on Linux.

EXPLANATION

Docker Desktop is the "batteries included" package for development. On production Linux servers, you typically install only Docker Engine. Compose is always useful (dev AND production-like environments), but on production you'd more likely use Kubernetes or Swarm for orchestration.

# ── Docker Engine (Linux server) ──
sudo apt install docker.io
sudo systemctl start docker
docker run -d nginx

# ── Docker Desktop (dev machine) ──
# GUI + Engine + Compose + K8s + Scout
# Installed via .dmg/.exe — managed through Settings UI

# ── Docker Compose (both) ──
# Included in Desktop; install separately on Linux:
sudo apt install docker-compose-v2
docker compose up -d      # Start multi-container app

# Check what''s installed:
docker version             # Client + Server
docker compose version     # Compose plugin
docker scout version       # Vulnerability scanner
Q9
A container is deleted. What happens to the data inside the container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

By default, ALL data inside a container is lost permanently when the container is deleted. Containers are ephemeral by design. To persist data, you must use Docker volumes or bind mounts — these exist independently of the container.

EXPLANATION

This is a critical concept for the DCA exam. A common mistake is storing database data inside the container without a volume. The mantra: "Containers are cattle, not pets." They should be disposable. Persistent data belongs in volumes.

# DATA LOST — No volume:
docker run -d --name mydb postgres:15
# ... use database, store 5GB of data ...
docker rm mydb              # ❌ ALL 5GB LOST!

# DATA SAFE — With volume:
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name mydb -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15
# ... use database, store 5GB of data ...
docker rm mydb              # Container gone
docker volume ls            # pgdata STILL EXISTS with 5GB ✅
docker run -d --name newdb -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15
# New container sees all 5GB!
Q10
Which Docker tool would you use to scan images for vulnerabilities before pushing to production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Scout — built into Docker Desktop and available as a CLI command: docker scout quickview <image>. It analyzes image layers, identifies known vulnerabilities (CVEs), and provides remediation recommendations.

EXPLANATION

Docker Scout replaced the older docker scan command. It integrates with Docker Hub and can be used in CI/CD pipelines. Alternative tools include Trivy (Aqua Security, open source) and Snyk. The DCA exam may test knowledge of image scanning as part of the Security domain (15%).

# docker scout quickview 
# docker scan

Chapter 2: Docker Core Concepts — Images, Containers & Registries

Now that you understand why Docker exists, let's dive into the what — the fundamental building blocks: Images, Containers, Registries, Layers, and Tags. These five concepts form the foundation of everything you'll do with Docker.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours📖 Core Concepts

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The difference between Images (blueprints) and Containers (running instances)
  • ✅ How image layers work and why they make builds fast
  • ✅ How registries store and distribute images
  • ✅ Container lifecycle — created, running, paused, stopped, deleted
  • ✅ Tagging strategies and multi-architecture images

2.1 Docker Images — The Blueprint

A Docker image is a read-only template containing your application code, runtime, libraries, environment variables, and configuration files. Think of an image as a class in programming — it's a blueprint. A container is an instance of that class — a running object.

Images are identified by repository:tag (e.g., anihpj:v1.0, python:3.11-slim). If no tag is specified, Docker defaults to :latest.

Image vs Container — Class vs Object Analogy
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            📦 IMAGE (Blueprint)  →  ▶️  CONTAINER (Running Instance)       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐        │
  │  │  Class in Python:       │         │  Object in Python:       │        │
  │  │  class Car:             │         │  my_car = Car()          │        │
  │  │      wheels = 4         │ create  │  my_car.wheels → 4       │        │
  │  │      color = "red"      │────────▶│  my_car.start()          │        │
  │  └─────────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────────┘        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐        │
  │  │  Docker Image:          │         │  Docker Container:       │        │
  │  │  anihpj:v1.0            │ docker  │  docker run anihpj:v1.0  │        │
  │  │  (read-only layers)     │  run    │  (read-write layer on    │        │
  │  │  stored on disk         │────────▶│   top, running process)  │        │
  │  └─────────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────────┘        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

2.2 Docker Containers — The Running Instance

A container is a runnable instance of an image. You can create, start, stop, move, or delete a container using the Docker CLI. Containers are ephemeral by design — treat them like cattle, not pets. If one dies, you spin up a new one from the same image.

Key characteristics: containers are isolated (process, network, filesystem), lightweight (share host kernel), and portable (run anywhere Docker runs).

Container Lifecycle State Machine
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🔄 CONTAINER LIFECYCLE                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │                            docker create                                 │
  │                        ┌───────────────────┐                            │
  │                        ▼                   │                            │
  │  ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐                      │
  │  │  📦      │   │ ▶️ CREATED  │     │ ▶️ RUNNING  │                      │
  │  │ Image   │──▶│             │────▶│             │                      │
  │  │         │   │ (on disk,   │     │ (process     │                      │
  │  │(blueprint)│  │  not started)│     │  active)    │                      │
  │  └─────────┘   └──────┬──────┘     └──┬──┬──┬───┘                      │
  │                       │               │  │  │                            │
  │                       │ docker start  │  │  │ docker stop (SIGTERM)      │
  │                       └───────────────┘  │  └──────────────┐             │
  │                                          │                 │             │
  │                                   docker │ pause    docker  │ kill        │
  │                                          │          │      │             │
  │                                          ▼          ▼      ▼             │
  │                                    ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌─────────┐   │
  │                                    │ ⏸️     │ │ ⏹️      │ │ 💀      │   │
  │                                    │PAUSED  │ │STOPPED │ │ DELETED │   │
  │                                    │(frozen)│ │(exited)│ │ (gone)  │   │
  │                                    └────────┘ └────────┘ └─────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

2.3 Docker Registries — The Storage

A registry is a storage and content delivery system for Docker images. You push images to a registry and pull them from it. Docker Hub is the default public registry, but enterprises typically use private registries.

RegistryTypePricingBest For
Docker HubPublicFree (1 private repo)Public images, OSS
Amazon ECRCloudPay per GB storedAWS workloads
Google Artifact RegistryCloudPay per GB storedGCP workloads
Azure ACRCloudPay per SKUAzure workloads
GitHub Container RegistryPublicFree (public)GitHub CI/CD integration
HarborSelf-HostedFree (OSS)Enterprise, air-gapped

2.4 Image Layers — The Secret to Docker's Speed

Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a layer. Layers are stacked to form the final image. Layers are cached — if a layer hasn't changed, Docker reuses it instead of rebuilding. This is why Docker builds are so fast after the first one.

Docker Image Layer Cake — anihpj Example
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Layer 6 (R/W): Container Writable Layer      │  ← Container-only (ephemeral!)
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 5: CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:app"] │  ← Startup command (~0 bytes)
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 4: COPY . /app/                        │  ← Your code! (~500 KB)
  │  (models.py, views.py, urls.py, settings.py)  │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 3: RUN pip install -r requirements.txt │  ← Dependencies (~80 MB)
  │  (Django 5.2, gunicorn, psycopg2, etc.)      │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 2: COPY requirements.txt .             │  ← Deps list (~200 bytes)
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Layer 1: FROM python:3.11-slim               │  ← Base image (~150 MB)
  │  (Debian 12 + Python 3.11)                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Layer Caching Strategy

Order your Dockerfile from LEAST to MOST frequently changing. Copy requirements.txt BEFORE copying your source code. This way, when you change your code (Layer 4), Layers 1-3 remain cached — saving minutes of rebuild time!

🔧 Under the Hood — Copy-on-Write (CoW) and Union Filesystems (Overlay2)
🗺️ How Docker Stores Images Efficiently

Docker uses two key Linux technologies to make images fast and space-efficient:

Copy-on-Write (CoW) — When a container modifies a file from the image, Docker doesn't copy the entire image. Instead, it copies ONLY the specific file being modified to the container's writable layer. This means 100 containers from the same image share 99.9% of the storage — only their changes take extra space.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   📋 COPY-ON-WRITE (CoW) IN ACTION                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Image Layers (READ-ONLY, shared)       Container Layer (READ-WRITE)      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ /app/models.py   ← SHARED │       │ (no copy needed!)           │   │
  │  │ /app/views.py    ← SHARED │       │                             │   │
  │  │ /usr/lib/python  ← SHARED │       │                             │   │
  │  │ /etc/os-release  ← SHARED │──COPY▶│ /etc/os-release (modified)  │   │
  │  │                  100 containers     │ ← ONLY this file copied!    │   │
  │  │                  share these!       │   (rest still shared)       │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Union Filesystem (Overlay2) — The default storage driver. It "stacks" the read-only image layers and the read-write container layer into a single unified view. The container sees one filesystem, but it's actually composed of multiple layers. Overlay2 uses:

  • LowerDir — The read-only image layers (your Dockerfile instructions)
  • UpperDir — The writable container layer (changes made at runtime)
  • Merged — The unified view the container sees (LowerDir + UpperDir combined)
  • WorkDir — Internal working directory for Overlay2 operations

2.5 Tags and Versioning

A tag is a human-readable label for a specific version of an image. The :latest tag is convenient but dangerous — it always points to the most recent build, which can cause unexpected changes in production.

StrategyExampleProsCons
Semantic Versioninganihpj:1.2.3Clear, predictableManual tagging
Git Commit SHAanihpj:abc1234Traceable to codeNot human-friendly
Date-basedanihpj:2026-06-12ChronologicalNo semantic meaning
Environmentanihpj:stagingClear intentMutable (changes over time)

2.6 Docker Manifest and Multi-Architecture Images

A manifest is a JSON file that describes an image — its layers, digests, architecture, and OS. Multi-architecture images use a manifest list to point to different platform-specific images. One tag (anihpj:v1) can serve linux/amd64, linux/arm64, and windows/amd64 — Docker automatically pulls the right one for your platform.

📖 Buildx for Multi-Arch

Use docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t anihpj:v1 . to build a single tag that works on both Intel/AMD and Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3) machines. This is essential for modern development teams with mixed hardware.

2.7 Docker Daemon Configuration — daemon.json Deep Dive

The Docker daemon is configured via /etc/docker/daemon.json on Linux. This single JSON file controls logging, storage, networking, security, and runtime behavior. Invalid JSON = daemon won''t start. The DCA Installation & Configuration domain (15%) tests this heavily.

daemon.json — Complete Configuration Map
  /etc/docker/daemon.json
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  {                                                         │
  │    // ── LOGGING ──                                        │
  │    "log-driver": "json-file",     // json-file|syslog|     │
  │    "log-opts": {                  //   journald|gelf|      │
  │      "max-size": "10m",           //   fluentd|awslogs|    │
  │      "max-file": "3",             //   splunk|gcplogs      │
  │      "labels": "env,service"                               │
  │    },                                                      │
  │    // ── STORAGE ──                                        │
  │    "storage-driver": "overlay2",  // overlay2|btrfs|zfs|   │
  │    "storage-opts": [               //   devicemapper|vfs   │
  │      "overlay2.override_kernel_check=true"                 │
  │    ],                                                      │
  │    "data-root": "/var/lib/docker",// Custom data directory │
  │    // ── NETWORKING ──                                     │
  │    "icc": false,                  // Inter-container comm  │
  │    "dns": ["8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1"],                         │
  │    "dns-search": ["example.com"],                          │
  │    "bip": "172.17.0.1/16",       // Default bridge IP      │
  │    "default-address-pools": [                              │
  │      {"base": "10.10.0.0/16", "size": 24}                 │
  │    ],                                                      │
  │    // ── SECURITY ──                                       │
  │    "userns-remap": "default",     // User namespace remap  │
  │    "live-restore": true,          // Keep containers alive │
  │    "tls": true,                   // Daemon TLS            │
  │    "tlscert": "/etc/docker/cert.pem",                      │
  │    "tlskey": "/etc/docker/key.pem",                        │
  │    "tlsverify": true,                                      │
  │    // ── REGISTRY ──                                       │
  │    "registry-mirrors": [                                   │
  │      "https://mirror.gcr.io"                               │
  │    ],                                                      │
  │    "insecure-registries": [                                │
  │      "my-registry:5000"                                    │
  │    ],                                                      │
  │    // ── RUNTIME ──                                        │
  │    "default-runtime": "runc",                              │
  │    "runtimes": {                                           │
  │      "nvidia": {"path": "nvidia-container-runtime"}       │
  │    },                                                      │
  │    "default-ulimits": {                                    │
  │      "nofile": {"Name": "nofile", "Hard": 64000}         │
  │    }                                                       │
  │  }                                                         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝
Logging Drivers

json-file (default): logs to host disk. syslog: central syslog server. journald: systemd journal. gelf: Graylog. fluentd: EFK stack. awslogs/splunk/gcplogs: cloud-native. Set rotation: {"max-size":"10m","max-file":"3"} to prevent disk exhaustion.

💾
Storage Drivers

overlay2: default, recommended for all modern kernels. devicemapper: RHEL7 legacy, needs direct-lvm for production. btrfs/zfs: advanced snapshots. vfs: no CoW, testing only. Check current: docker info | grep "Storage Driver". Changing loses all data.

🔒
Security Config

userns-remap: container root maps to high UID on host. icc: false: blocks inter-container communication on default bridge. live-restore: true: containers survive daemon restart. tlsverify: true: mutual TLS for Docker API. no-new-privileges: block privilege escalation.

⚠️ Critical: live-restore

Without "live-restore": true in daemon.json, restarting the Docker daemon (systemctl restart docker) KILLS all running containers. With live-restore, containers keep running during daemon updates or crashes. This is essential for production — set it in every production daemon.json. Docker Desktop enables it by default.

daemon.json KeyValuesDCA Exam Context
log-driverjson-file, syslog, journald, gelf, fluentd, awslogs, splunk, gcplogsConfigure logging for production; set rotation to prevent disk full
log-opts{"max-size":"10m","max-file":"3"}Prevent unbounded log growth; json-file default has no rotation
storage-driveroverlay2 (default), devicemapper, btrfs, zfs, vfsoverlay2 for all modern kernels; devicemapper needs direct-lvm
data-root/var/lib/docker (default) or custom pathMove Docker data to separate partition/disk
icctrue (default), falsefalse = containers on default bridge cannot communicate
userns-remap"default" or "username:userns"Container root → host high UID; strongest user isolation
live-restoretrue, false (default)Keep containers alive when daemon stops/restarts
registry-mirrors["https://mirror.example.com"]Cache Docker Hub images locally; reduces pull latency
insecure-registries["my-registry:5000"]Allow HTTP (non-HTTPS) registries; testing only
tlsverifytrue/falseEnable mutual TLS for Docker daemon API (port 2376)
default-address-pools[{"base":"10.10.0.0/16","size":24}]Control subnet allocation for custom networks
daemon.json DCA Checklist: 1. Know default location: /etc/docker/daemon.json. 2. Always validate JSON: python3 -m json.tool /etc/docker/daemon.json. 3. Restart to apply: sudo systemctl restart docker. 4. docker info shows active config. 5. Bad JSON = daemon won''t start (check journalctl -u docker). 6. Docker Desktop: Settings UI manages daemon.json internally — don''t edit manually.

⚠️ Chapter 2 Exam Gotchas

  • Forgetting to add user to docker group → Without it, every docker command needs sudo. Run usermod -aG docker $USER then log out/in.

📝 Chapter 2 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What is the relationship between a Docker image and a Docker container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

An image is a read-only template (like a class). A container is a runnable instance of an image (like an object). One image can spawn many containers, just as one class can create many objects.

EXPLANATION

Think of the image as a frozen snapshot — it contains the OS, libraries, application code, and configuration ALL bundled together. When you docker run, Docker adds a thin writable layer on top and starts the process. You can run 100 containers from the same image — each gets its own writable layer but shares the read-only image layers. This is why containers start in milliseconds.

# docker run
Q2
How do Docker image layers work, and why does layer order matter?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Each Dockerfile instruction creates a read-only layer. Layers are cached. If a layer changes, ALL layers after it are rebuilt. Therefore, put frequently-changing layers (source code) LAST and rarely-changing layers (base image, dependencies) FIRST.

EXPLANATION

Docker cache is sequential: Layer 1 → Layer 2 → Layer 3. If Layer 2 changes, Layers 3+ ALL rebuild. For anihpj: FROM python:3.11-slim (never changes) → COPY requirements.txt (changes weekly) → RUN pip install (depends on requirements) → COPY . . (changes constantly). Code changes only rebuild the last layer — pip install stays cached, saving 2-3 minutes per build.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q3
What is the difference between Docker Hub and a private registry like ECR?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Hub is a public registry with free tier. Private registries (ECR, GCR, ACR) are cloud-managed, provide lower latency, better security (IAM integration), and are typically used for production workloads.

EXPLANATION

Docker Hub is like GitHub for images — anyone can pull public images, rate-limited for anonymous users. Private registries run in your VPC: images never leave your network, IAM controls who can push/pull, and latency is sub-millisecond. The DCA exam expects you to know how to authenticate to both: docker login for Hub, aws ecr get-login-password | docker login ... for ECR.

# docker login
# aws ecr get-login-password | docker login ...
Q4
What are the valid states in a container's lifecycle?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Created → Running → Paused / Stopped → Deleted. A container starts as "created" (on disk but not started), transitions to "running," can be "paused" (frozen) or "stopped" (exited), and finally "deleted" (gone).

EXPLANATION

The container lifecycle is fundamental to the DCA exam. Created: filesystem prepared but process not started. Running: PID 1 is executing. Paused: all processes frozen (SIGSTOP) — useful for debugging without destroying state. Stopped: process exited but filesystem and metadata preserved. Deleted: everything gone. Check state with docker ps -a and inspect with docker inspect CONTAINER.

# docker ps -a
# docker inspect CONTAINER
Q5
Why is the :latest tag considered dangerous for production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

:latest is mutable — it points to whatever was most recently built/pushed. This means docker pull anihpj:latest can silently pull a completely different version than expected, causing production incidents. Always use explicit version tags.

EXPLANATION

:latest is a moving target. If you docker push anihpj:latest today and someone pulls tomorrow, they get whatever was pushed most recently — not necessarily your image. In production, this means your deployment could silently change versions. Always tag with semver (anihpj:v1.2.3) or Git SHA (anihpj:abc1234). For ultimate immutability, use digests: anihpj@sha256:def5678...

# docker pull anihpj:latest
# docker push anihpj:latest
# anihpj:v1.2.3
# anihpj:abc1234
# anihpj@sha256:def5678...
Q6
What is a multi-architecture image and how is it built?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A multi-architecture image uses a manifest list to serve different platform-specific images (amd64, arm64) under a SINGLE tag. Built with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t anihpj:v1 .

EXPLANATION

Multi-arch images solve the "works on my Mac (ARM) but not on the server (x86)" problem. A manifest list contains pointers to platform-specific images. When you docker pull anihpj:v1, Docker automatically selects the image matching your architecture. Build with docker buildx: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push -t anihpj:v1 .. This pushes a manifest list + both platform images.

# docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t anihpj:v1 .
# docker pull anihpj:v1
# docker buildx
# docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push -t anihpj:v1 .
Q7
What happens to data stored inside a container when the container is deleted?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

All data inside the container's writable layer is permanently lost. Only data stored in Docker volumes or bind mounts survives container deletion. This is by design — containers are meant to be ephemeral.

EXPLANATION

This is the #1 mistake beginners make: storing database files inside the container. When docker rm CONTAINER runs, the writable layer is destroyed — all data gone forever. The solution: use volumes or bind mounts. docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres stores the database in a named volume that survives container deletion. Containers are cattle, not pets — they should be disposable.

# docker rm CONTAINER
# docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
Q8
What command authenticates you to a private Docker registry?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker login <registry-url> — e.g., docker login (Docker Hub), docker login ghcr.io (GitHub), or aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <aws-account-id>.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com (ECR).

EXPLANATION

docker login stores credentials in ~/.docker/config.json. For security, Docker uses credential helpers (osxkeychain, wincred, pass) instead of storing plaintext passwords. After login, docker push and docker pull automatically include authentication. To use ECR: aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. Tokens expire after 12 hours.

# docker login 
# docker login
# docker login ghcr.io
# aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin .dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com
# docker login
Q9
How does Docker's layer caching decide whether to rebuild a layer?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker compares the instruction text AND the files being copied (checksums). If either changed, the layer is rebuilt — and ALL SUBSEQUENT layers are also rebuilt. This is why order matters: keep frequently-changing layers at the bottom.

EXPLANATION

Docker computes checksums for COPY/ADD instructions. For RUN instructions, it hashes the command string. If an earlier layer's hash matches the cache, Docker reuses it. If ANY layer changes, all subsequent layers are rebuilt from scratch. This is why COPY requirements.txt . should come before COPY . . — requirements changes are rare, code changes are frequent. The pip install layer stays cached even when your code changes daily.

# COPY requirements.txt .
Q10
What is an image digest and why is it more reliable than a tag?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

An image digest is a SHA256 hash of the image's content — it's immutable. Tags like :latest can be moved to point to different images, but a digest always identifies the EXACT same image. Use anihpj@sha256:abc123... for guaranteed reproducibility.

EXPLANATION

Tags are like symlinks — they can be moved. A malicious actor who gains push access could retag a compromised image as :latest and no one would notice. Digests are content-addressable: the hash is computed FROM the image content, so any change produces a different digest. For production deployments, always pin by digest: docker pull anihpj@sha256:abc123.... Docker Content Trust (DCT) also signs images to verify publisher identity.

# anihpj@sha256:abc123...
# docker pull anihpj@sha256:abc123...

Chapter 3: Installing Docker & Your First Container

Time to get hands-on! We'll install Docker, run the classic "Hello World" container, understand what actually happens behind the scenes, and run our first anihpj container interactively.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1.5 hours💻 Hands-On

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Install Docker Desktop on Windows/Mac or Docker Engine on Linux
  • ✅ Run your first container with docker run hello-world
  • ✅ Understand the 5-step process behind every docker run
  • ✅ Run Python interactively in a container
  • ✅ Master essential docker run flags
  • ✅ Understand the Docker CLI command structure

3.1 Installing Docker Desktop (Windows/Mac)

Docker Desktop is the recommended way to run Docker on development machines. It includes Docker Engine, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, Docker Scout, and a GUI dashboard — all in one package.

📖 Installation Steps

1. Download from docker.com
2. Run the installer (Windows: enable WSL2 if prompted — Docker Desktop uses WSL2 as its Linux backend for better performance)
3. Launch Docker Desktop — the whale icon appears in your system tray
4. Open a terminal and verify: docker --version and docker run hello-world

💡 Windows + WSL2

On Windows, Docker Desktop runs inside WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux 2). This gives you a real Linux kernel, near-native performance, and full compatibility with Linux containers. Make sure WSL2 is installed and set as the default: wsl --install and wsl --set-default-version 2.

3.2 Installing Docker Engine on Linux

For Linux servers, install Docker Engine directly (no Desktop GUI). The process varies by distribution:

📖 Ubuntu/Debian

sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
Then: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER (add yourself to docker group, log out and back in)
Start on boot: sudo systemctl enable docker

📖 CentOS/RHEL/Fedora

sudo yum install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
Then: sudo systemctl enable --now docker

💡 Verify Installation

After installation, verify with: docker --version (shows client + server version) and docker info (shows detailed system info including Storage Driver, Cgroup Driver, number of containers/images). Both must succeed before proceeding.

3.3 Your First Docker Command — Hello World

The docker run hello-world command is the "Hello World" of Docker. It pulls a tiny image (~13KB), runs it, and prints a message confirming Docker is working. Let's understand exactly what happens:

docker run hello-world — 5 Steps
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              ⚡ docker run hello-world — WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1. You type: $ docker run hello-world                                   │
  │  2. Docker Client sends command to Docker Daemon (dockerd)               │
  │  3. Daemon checks local images → "hello-world" NOT FOUND                 │
  │  4. Daemon PULLS hello-world image from Docker Hub (~13 KB)              │
  │  5. Daemon creates a container FROM the image → runs → prints message → EXITS│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 Key Insight

Notice that Docker automatically PULLS the image when it's not found locally. You don't need to run docker pull separately. Every docker run implicitly checks local images first, then pulls from the registry if needed.

3.4 Running anihpj in Docker — First Contact

Let's run Python interactively inside a container. We'll pull the official Python image, get a shell inside it, and explore:

TERMINAL
# Pull the Python base image (only needed once)
$ docker pull python:3.11-slim

# Run interactively with a bash shell
$ docker run -it python:3.11-slim bash

# Now you're INSIDE the container!
root@abc123:/# python --version
Python 3.11.9

root@abc123:/# ls
bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  media  mnt  opt  proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var

root@abc123:/# exit
$ # Back on your host machine

# See the container (now stopped)
$ docker ps -a
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE                COMMAND   CREATED         STATUS
abc123def456   python:3.11-slim     "bash"    2 minutes ago   Exited (0)
📖 Understanding -it Flags

-i = interactive (keep STDIN open). -t = TTY (allocate a pseudo-terminal for proper shell display). Together, -it gives you an interactive shell session inside the container.

🔧 Under the Hood — Linux Namespaces & cgroups: How Docker Actually Isolates Containers
🗺️ The Two Linux Kernel Features That Make Containers Possible

Docker containers aren't magic — they're built on two Linux kernel features that have existed since the mid-2000s. Understanding these helps you grasp why containers are lightweight (they use kernel features, not hardware virtualization).

1. Linux Namespaces — "What You Can See"

Namespaces limit what a process can see. Each container gets its own set of namespaces, making it think it's the only thing running on the system. There are 7 types:

NamespaceWhat It IsolatesContainer Effect
PIDProcess IDsContainer sees its own PID 1 (init), can't see host processes
NETNetwork interfacesContainer has its own eth0, routing table, iptables
MNTMount pointsContainer has its own root filesystem view
UTSHostname, domainContainer can have its own hostname
IPCInter-process communicationContainer's shared memory is isolated
USERUser/group IDsUID 0 (root) in container ≠ root on host (with userns)
CGROUPControl group viewContainer sees only its own cgroup limits
2. Control Groups (cgroups) — "What You Can Use"

cgroups limit what a process can use. They enforce resource limits so one container can't hog all the CPU or RAM. When you type docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5, Docker configures cgroups behind the scenes.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🔧 HOW DOCKER RUN ACTUALLY WORKS (Kernel Level)               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  $ docker run -d --name web --memory=512m nginx                          │
  │       │                                                                  │
  │       ▼                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  STEP 1: runc creates 7 NAMESPACES for isolation:                 │   │
  │  │    PID (own process tree)  │ NET (own network stack)              │   │
  │  │    MNT (own filesystem)    │ UTS (own hostname)                   │   │
  │  │    IPC (own shared memory) │ USER (own UID mapping)               │   │
  │  │    CGROUP (own limits)     │                                      │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │  STEP 2: runc configures CGROUPS for resource limits:             │   │
  │  │    memory.limit_in_bytes = 536870912 (512 MB)                     │   │
  │  │    cpu.shares = 1536 (1.5 CPUs)                                   │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │  STEP 3: Container process starts, BELIEVES it's the ONLY thing  │   │
  │  │  on a fresh Linux system (because namespaces hide everything else)│   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  This is why containers are NOT VMs: they don't emulate hardware.        │
  │  They use kernel features to create the ILLUSION of a separate OS.       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Why This Matters for DCA

The DCA exam tests your understanding of container isolation. Questions may ask about which namespace provides which isolation, how --memory limits are enforced (cgroups), or what happens when you run a container with --pid=host (it shares the host's PID namespace — can see all host processes). Understanding namespaces and cgroups is foundational for the Security domain (15%).

⚠️ Chapter 3 Exam Gotchas

  • docker build (forgot -t) → Without -t, image gets a random name. Always tag: docker build -t app:v1 .
  • docker run (forgot -d for daemon) → Without -d, the container runs in foreground and blocks your terminal.
  • docker attach for debugging → Use docker exec -it CONTAINER sh instead. attach connects to PID 1; exec starts a new process.
  • Forgetting --rm on temporary containers → Without --rm, stopped containers accumulate and waste disk space.

📝 Chapter 3 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What happens when you run docker run hello-world for the first time?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. Docker Client sends the command to the Daemon. 2. Daemon checks local images (not found). 3. Daemon pulls "hello-world" from Docker Hub. 4. Daemon creates a new container from the image. 5. Container runs, prints a message, and exits.

EXPLANATION

The hello-world container is the simplest possible Docker demonstration: it prints a message and exits with code 0 (success). Key insight: Docker does NOT keep containers running after their main process exits. If your CMD is echo "hello", the container will exit immediately after printing. For long-running services, your CMD must be a process that stays alive (web server, database, etc.).

# docker run hello-world
# echo "hello"
Q2
What do the -i and -t flags do in docker run -it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

-i = interactive (keep STDIN open so you can type input). -t = TTY (allocate a pseudo-terminal for proper shell display). Together they give you an interactive terminal session.

EXPLANATION

-i and -t are almost always used together because an interactive shell needs STDIN (to read your keystrokes) AND a TTY (to render the shell prompt, colors, and control characters). Without -t, you get raw output without a prompt. Without -i, you can't type anything. Memory aid: -it = "interactive terminal."

# docker run -it
Q3
How do you run a container in the background (detached mode)?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Use the -d flag: docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name anihpj anihpj:v1. The container runs in the background and prints the container ID.

EXPLANATION

-d (detach) is essential for production and most development work. Without it, docker run blocks your terminal — the container's stdout streams to your screen and Ctrl+C kills it. With -d, the container runs as a background daemon, printing only the container ID. You can then use docker logs, docker exec, and docker stop to manage it.

# docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name anihpj anihpj:v1
# docker run
# docker logs
# docker exec
# docker stop
Q4
What's the difference between docker ps and docker ps -a?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker ps shows only RUNNING containers. docker ps -a shows ALL containers — running, stopped, exited, created. This is crucial for debugging: a container that immediately exited won't show in docker ps but WILL show in docker ps -a.

EXPLANATION

This is a critical debugging distinction. A container that crashes immediately after starting (wrong CMD, missing file, port conflict) will show in docker ps -a with status "Exited (1)" but won't appear in docker ps. Always use -a when troubleshooting. Pro tip: docker ps -a --filter "status=exited" shows only exited containers, and docker ps -a --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}" gives a cleaner view.

# docker ps
# docker ps -a
# docker ps
# docker ps -a
# docker ps
Q5
How do you map port 8000 on your host to port 8000 in the container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run -p 8000:8000 anihpj:v1. The format is -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT. This makes the container's port 8000 accessible at http://localhost:8000 on your host.

EXPLANATION

The -p flag creates iptables DNAT rules that forward host port traffic to the container port. You can bind to specific interfaces: -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 (localhost only, more secure) or -p 8000:8000 (all interfaces). To publish all EXPOSEd ports: -P (capital). Verify mappings: docker port CONTAINER.

# docker run -p 8000:8000 anihpj:v1
# -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT
# http://localhost:8000
Q6
What is the Docker CLI command structure pattern?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker [GLOBAL_OPTIONS] COMMAND [SUBCOMMAND] [OPTIONS] [ARGUMENTS]. Example: docker container run -d -p 8000:8000 --name web nginx:alpine.

EXPLANATION

Docker's CLI follows a consistent pattern: GLOBAL options come first (before the command), then the command, then command-specific options, then arguments. Example breakdown: docker --log-level debug container run -d --name web nginx:alpine. --log-level debug is global, container run is command+subcommand, -d --name web are options, nginx:alpine is the argument. This structure applies to ALL docker commands.

# docker [GLOBAL_OPTIONS] COMMAND [SUBCOMMAND] [OPTIONS] [ARGUMENTS]
# docker container run -d -p 8000:8000 --name web nginx:alpine
# docker --log-level debug container run -d --name web nginx:alpine
# --log-level debug
# container run
Q7
Why is python:3.11-slim preferred over python:3.11 for web apps?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The -slim variant is based on Debian but strips out build tools, documentation, and unnecessary packages. It's ~150 MB vs ~900 MB for the full image — faster pulls, less attack surface, and sufficient for running web applications.

EXPLANATION

Docker image variants: python:3.11 (~900 MB, full Debian with build tools), python:3.11-slim (~150 MB, Debian without build tools), python:3.11-alpine (~50 MB, uses musl libc instead of glibc). Slim is the sweet spot for web apps — small enough for fast CI/CD, big enough that most Python packages work. Alpine is even smaller but some packages (Pillow, numpy) need compilation against musl which can cause issues.

# python:3.11-slim
# python:3.11
# python:3.11
# python:3.11-slim
# python:3.11-alpine
Q8
How do you see the logs of a detached container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker logs <container-name-or-id>. Add -f to follow (like tail -f): docker logs -f anihpj-dev. Add --tail 100 to see only the last 100 lines.

EXPLANATION

docker logs reads stdout/stderr from the container's PID 1. The output is stored in JSON files on the host (/var/lib/docker/containers/.../*.log). Key flags: -f (follow, like tail -f), --tail N (last N lines), --since 10m (last 10 minutes), --timestamps (show when each line was logged). Logs persist even after the container stops — they're only deleted when the container is removed.

# docker logs 
# docker logs -f anihpj-dev
# --tail 100
# docker logs
# /var/lib/docker/containers/.../*.log
Q9
What does docker run --rm do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The --rm flag automatically removes the container when it exits. This keeps your system clean — no accumulation of stopped containers. Great for one-off commands and CI/CD pipelines.

EXPLANATION

--rm is the CI/CD best practice flag. Without it, every docker run leaves behind a stopped container that consumes disk space. Over hundreds of pipeline runs, this can fill your CI agent's disk. --rm ensures cleanup is automatic. Combine with meaningful names: docker run --rm --name test-${BUILD_ID} anihpj:v1 pytest. The container exists only for the test duration, then self-destructs.

# docker run --rm
# docker run
# docker run --rm --name test-${BUILD_ID} anihpj:v1 pytest
Q10
After installing Docker Engine on Linux, a user runs docker ps and gets "permission denied." What's the fix?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Add the user to the docker group: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then log out and back in. The Docker daemon socket (/var/run/docker.sock) is owned by root:docker — only users in the docker group can access it without sudo.

EXPLANATION

The Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) is owned by root:docker with permissions 660. Only root and members of the docker group can access it. Adding a user to the docker group grants them effective root access on the host (via the daemon). For production, consider rootless Docker or Podman. After adding yourself: newgrp docker avoids logging out. Verify: docker ps should work without sudo.

# docker ps
# sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
# /var/run/docker.sock
# /var/run/docker.sock
# root:docker
