Chapter 4: The Dockerfile — Your App's Recipe

The Dockerfile is where you define your application's environment. It's a simple text file with instructions that tell Docker how to build your image. Master the Dockerfile, and you master Docker itself.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours📝 Code🎯 Core Skill

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Write production-ready Dockerfiles for Python/Django apps
  • ✅ Master all 18+ Dockerfile instructions
  • ✅ Understand CMD vs ENTRYPOINT (the #1 confusion point)
  • ✅ Build the complete anihpj Dockerfile step-by-step
  • ✅ Use multi-stage builds to create smaller, safer images
  • ✅ Apply Dockerfile best practices

4.1 What is a Dockerfile?

A Dockerfile is a text file containing a series of instructions that Docker reads to automatically build an image. Each instruction creates a layer. Think of it as a recipe: Dockerfile → docker build → Image → docker run → Container.

📝
Dockerfile

A text file named Dockerfile (no extension). Contains instructions like FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD. This is what YOU write.

📦
Image

The output of docker build. A read-only template containing your app + all dependencies. This is what gets STORED and SHARED.

▶️
Container

A running instance of an image. Created by docker run. Has its own writable layer, network, and process space.

4.2 Dockerfile Instruction Reference

Every Dockerfile instruction serves a specific purpose. Here are ALL the instructions you need to know for the DCA exam:

InstructionPurposeanihpj Example
FROMBase image (MANDATORY, always first)FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIRSet working directoryWORKDIR /app
COPYCopy files from host to imageCOPY requirements.txt .
ADDLike COPY, but also handles URLs and tar extractionADD https://example.com/file.tar.gz /app/
RUNExecute commands during buildRUN pip install -r requirements.txt
ENVSet environment variables (persist at runtime)ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings
ARGBuild-time variables (NOT in final image by default)ARG DJANGO_VERSION=5.2
EXPOSEDocument which port the app listens on (NOT publish!)EXPOSE 8000
CMDDefault command (overridable at runtime)CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application"]
ENTRYPOINTFixed executable (harder to override)ENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"]
USERSwitch to non-root user for securityUSER appuser
VOLUMECreate a mount point for external volumesVOLUME ["/app/static"]
HEALTHCHECKCommand to check container healthHEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/
LABELAdd metadata to imageLABEL version="1.0" maintainer="anihpj"
SHELLChange default shell for RUNSHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
STOPSIGNALSignal to stop containerSTOPSIGNAL SIGTERM

4.3 CMD vs ENTRYPOINT — The Most Confusing Part

This is the #1 source of confusion for Docker beginners — and a favorite DCA exam topic. The key difference:

CMD = Default command that can be easily overridden when you docker run.
ENTRYPOINT = Fixed command that always runs; arguments to docker run are appended to it.

CMD vs ENTRYPOINT Decision Matrix
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                🎯 CMD vs ENTRYPOINT — WHICH TO USE?                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │              │      CMD             │       ENTRYPOINT             │  │
  │  ├──────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤  │
  │  │ Purpose      │ Default command      │ Fixed executable             │  │
  │  │ Overridable? │ ✅ Easily            │ ❌ Needs --entrypoint flag   │  │
  │  │ Use When...  │ App has one main     │ App is a wrapper/tool that   │  │
  │  │              │ purpose but may vary │ should always run the same   │  │
  │  │ Analogy      │ Default radio station│ Car ENGINE (not optional!)   │  │
  │  └──────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  [6 COMBINATIONS — What Happens?]                                        │
  │  # | Dockerfile                    | docker run img | Result            │
  │  1 | CMD ["echo", "hello"]        | (none)          | echo hello        │
  │  2 | CMD ["echo", "hello"]        | world            | error (no cmd)   │
  │  3 | ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]           | (none)          | echo (no arg)    │
  │  4 | ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]           | hello           | echo hello        │
  │  5 | ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]+CMD["Hi"]| (none)          | echo Hi           │
  │  6 | ENTRYPOINT ["echo"]+CMD["Hi"]| world (OVERRIDES!)| echo world      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🏆 Best Practice for anihpj

ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"] (always run gunicorn) + CMD ["anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"] (default WSGI app + bind, but you can override with different worker count at runtime).

4.4 Building an anihpj Dockerfile — Step by Step

Let's build the complete Dockerfile for our anihpj Django application. We'll evolve from a naive first attempt to a production-ready multi-stage Dockerfile. Every line is explained:

🥚
Stage 1
Naive Dockerfile

FROM python:latest
COPY . .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver"]

❌ ~950 MB, runs as root
🐣
Stage 2
Slim Base + Layer Order

FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

⚠️ ~230 MB, better caching
🐔
Stage 3
Production Server

+ gunicorn instead of runserver
+ ENV variables
+ EXPOSE
+ non-root USER

✅ ~180 MB, production-ready
🦅
Stage 4
Multi-Stage Mastery

FROM python:3.11 AS build
... build stage ...
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=build ...

🏆 ~150 MB, minimal attack surface
DOCKERFILE
# Step 1: Choose the base image
# python:3.11-slim = Debian + Python 3.11, stripped down (~150 MB)
# Why slim not alpine? Alpine uses musl libc, can cause issues with some Python packages
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Step 2: Set working directory (all subsequent commands run here)
WORKDIR /app

# Step 3: Copy requirements FIRST (layer caching trick!)
# If requirements.txt hasn't changed, this layer is CACHED
COPY requirements.txt .

# Step 4: Install dependencies
# --no-cache-dir: don't cache pip packages (saves ~100 MB in image)
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Step 5: Copy application code (changes most often, so goes LAST)
COPY . .

# Step 6: Set environment variables
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \    # Don't generate .pyc files
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \            # Don't buffer stdout (better logging)
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings

# Step 7: Document the port (does NOT publish it — use -p flag with docker run)
EXPOSE 8000

# Step 8: Command to run when container starts
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]
📖 Why This Order?

The order is intentional: FROM (never changes) → requirements.txt (rarely changes) → pip install (rarely changes) → source code (changes constantly). This maximizes layer caching. When you edit views.py, only the last COPY layer rebuilds — everything else is cached!

Layer Visualization — Which Line Creates Which Layer
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🍰 HOW THE anihpj DOCKERFILE MAPS TO LAYERS                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  DOCKERFILE LINE                          →  IMAGE LAYER                 │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
  │  FROM python:3.11-slim                    →  Layer 1: Base (~150 MB)     │
  │  WORKDIR /app                             →  Layer 2: Directory (0 B)    │
  │  COPY requirements.txt .                  →  Layer 3: Deps list (~200 B) │
  │  RUN pip install --no-cache-dir \         →  Layer 4: Packages (~80 MB)  │
  │      -r requirements.txt                                               │
  │  COPY . .                                 →  Layer 5: Your code (~500KB) │
  │  ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 ...        →  Layer 6: Config (0 B)       │
  │  EXPOSE 8000                              →  Layer 7: Metadata (0 B)     │
  │  CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:app", ...] →  Layer 8: Startup (0 B)     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  LAYERS 1-3 + 5-8 = READ-ONLY (shared by all containers)                │
  │  CONTAINER gets an additional READ-WRITE layer on top                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  CACHING: Change models.py → only Layer 5 rebuilds (~0.5s)             │
  │           Change requirements.txt → Layers 3-4 rebuild (~45s)            │
  │           Change base image → ALL layers rebuild (~2 min)                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

4.5 Multi-Stage Dockerfiles — Smaller, Safer Images

A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM statements in a single Dockerfile. Each FROM starts a new stage. You can copy artifacts from earlier stages into later ones — keeping build tools OUT of your final image.

Multi-Stage Build Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   🏗️ MULTI-STAGE BUILD ARCHITECTURE                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STAGE 1: BUILDER (python:3.11)              STAGE 2: FINAL (slim)        │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────┐              ┌───────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11 AS build │              │ FROM python:3.11-slim     │ │
  │  │                           │              │                           │ │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .   │              │ COPY --from=build         │ │
  │  │ RUN pip install --user    │   COPY       │      /root/.local          │ │
  │  │   -r requirements.txt     │─────────────▶│      /root/.local          │ │
  │  │                           │  artifacts   │                           │ │
  │  │ RUN python manage.py      │              │ COPY --from=build         │ │
  │  │   collectstatic --noinput │─────────────▶│      /app/static           │ │
  │  │                           │  static      │                           │ │
  │  │ Includes: gcc, make,      │              │ NO gcc, NO build tools!   │ │
  │  │   git, headers, dev libs  │              │ Only runtime deps.        │ │
  │  │                           │              │                           │ │
  │  │ SIZE: ~850 MB             │              │ SIZE: ~180 MB (5x smaller!)│ │
  │  └───────────────────────────┘              └───────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
MetricSingle-StageMulti-StageImprovement
Image Size~850 MB~180 MB✅ 5x smaller
Build Time45s42s (similar)✅ Slightly faster
Attack SurfaceLarge (gcc, git, make)Small (only runtime deps)✅ 70% fewer CVEs
CVEs (vulnerabilities)120+30-40✅ 3-4x fewer
Pull Time (10 Mbps)~11 min~2.4 min✅ 4.5x faster
Disk Usage (10 deploys)8.5 GB1.8 GB✅ 4.7x less storage
🏆 The Multi-Stage Advantage

Multi-stage builds aren't just about size — they're about security. Build tools like GCC, make, and git are powerful attack vectors. By keeping them out of your production image, you eliminate entire classes of vulnerabilities. The DCA exam expects you to know when and why to use multi-stage builds.

DOCKERFILE: Multi-Stage for anihpj
# ═══════ STAGE 1: BUILD ═══════
FROM python:3.11 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
# Install to /root/.local so we can copy just the packages
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
# Collect static files (Django)
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# ═══════ STAGE 2: FINAL (PRODUCTION) ═══════
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
# Copy ONLY the installed packages from build stage
COPY --from=build /root/.local /root/.local
# Copy ONLY the collected static files
COPY --from=build /app/static /app/static
# Copy application code
COPY . .
# Ensure scripts in .local are findable
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
EXPOSE 8000
# Create non-root user for security
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app
USER app
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

4.6 Dockerfile Best Practices

Production Dockerfiles follow well-established conventions. These best practices are tested on the DCA exam and expected in real-world Docker environments:

✅ DO❌ DON'T
Use specific tags: python:3.11-slimUse :latest (unpredictable builds)
Chain RUN commands with && to reduce layersSeparate RUN for each package (more layers)
Clean up after package managers: rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*Leave package caches in the image (wasted space)
COPY requirements.txt BEFORE source codeCOPY everything at once (breaks caching)
Use .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary filesSend entire project directory as build context
Run as non-root user: USER appuserRun as root (critical security risk)
Use multi-stage builds for smaller, safer imagesInclude build tools (gcc, git) in production image
Use COPY instead of ADD for local filesUse ADD for local files (COPY is explicit)
Set WORKDIR explicitly (not cd in RUN)Use RUN cd /app && ... — fragile and unclear
Use HEALTHCHECK for production containersSkip health checks — orchestrator can't detect failures
Pin APT/PIP package versions for reproducibilityInstall latest versions (builds break unexpectedly)
Lint Dockerfiles with HadolintSkip linting — subtle errors reach production
Use --no-cache-dir with pip installLet pip cache bloat the image (~100 MB wasted)
Set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1Allow .pyc files in immutable image layers
Use tini or --init for proper signal handlingLet PID 1 be your app (zombie process risk)
🔢 The 15-Point Dockerfile Quality Checklist

✅ 1. Specific base tag   ✅ 2. WORKDIR set   ✅ 3. .dockerignore present   ✅ 4. COPY before RUN (cache)   ✅ 5. Chained RUNs   ✅ 6. Non-root USER   ✅ 7. HEALTHCHECK defined   ✅ 8. Multi-stage (if applicable)   ✅ 9. COPY not ADD   ✅ 10. Pinned versions   ✅ 11. Cleaned package caches   ✅ 12. No secrets in ENV   ✅ 13. Proper CMD/ENTRYPOINT   ✅ 14. --no-cache-dir   ✅ 15. Hadolint passed

📊 Chapter 4 — Recap

📝Dockerfile = Recipe for Image
16Instructions to Master
CMDDefault (Overridable)
ENTRYFixed (Not Overridable)
🪜Multi-Stage = Smaller + Safer

📋 Dockerfile Skeleton — Type From Memory

You must be able to write this from scratch on the DCA exam

FROM python:3.11-slim`nWORKDIR /app`nCOPY requirements.txt .`nRUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt`nCOPY . .`nRUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app`nUSER app`nEXPOSE 8000`nHEALTHCHECK --interval=30s CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/ || exit 1`nCMD [""gunicorn"",""app:application"",""--bind"",""0.0.0.0:8000""]

⚠️ Chapter 4 Exam Gotchas

  • COPY . /app (wrong order) → COPY source code LAST. COPY requirements.txt first, then RUN pip install, THEN COPY . .
  • Using ADD instead of COPY → Use COPY for local files. ADD only when you need tar auto-extraction.
  • RUN apt update && apt install (no cleanup) → Always chain with cleanup: RUN apt update && apt install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
  • CMD vs ENTRYPOINT confusion → ENTRYPOINT = fixed executable. CMD = default arguments. Combined: ENTRYPOINT ["python"] + CMD ["app.py"]

📝 Chapter 4 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Which Dockerfile instruction is mandatory and must always be the first instruction?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

FROM — it specifies the base image. Every Dockerfile must start with FROM (or ARG before FROM if you need a build arg in the FROM line).

EXPLANATION

FROM can appear multiple times in a multi-stage build. The only instruction allowed before the first FROM is ARG. Without FROM, Docker has no base to build upon.

# FROM
# FROM
# ARG
Q2
What's the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT? When would you use each?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

CMD provides defaults that can be overridden at runtime. ENTRYPOINT defines a fixed executable — arguments to docker run are appended to it. Use CMD when you want flexibility, ENTRYPOINT when the container should always run the same binary.

EXPLANATION

For anihpj: ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"] ensures gunicorn always runs. CMD ["anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"] provides default arguments that can be overridden: docker run anihpj --workers 5 overrides CMD but gunicorn still runs.

# ENTRYPOINT
# docker run
# ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"]
# CMD ["anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
# docker run anihpj --workers 5
Q3
Why should you COPY requirements.txt BEFORE copying your source code?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

For layer caching optimization. requirements.txt changes rarely; source code changes constantly. When you change source code, Docker reuses the cached layer for pip install — saving minutes of rebuild time.

EXPLANATION

Docker's cache invalidation is sequential: if layer N changes, layers N+1, N+2, etc. ALL rebuild. By putting requirements.txt (rarely changes) BEFORE source code (frequently changes), only the last COPY layer rebuilds on code changes. The pip install layer stays cached. This is the single most impactful Dockerfile optimization you can make.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q4
What is a multi-stage build and why use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM statements. The first stage builds the app with all tools (compilers, dev headers). Later stages copy only the built artifacts — resulting in a much smaller, more secure final image without build tools.

EXPLANATION

Without multi-stage, you'd need two Dockerfiles: one for building, one for running. Multi-stage combines them into one. The key is COPY --from=build — it copies artifacts from an earlier stage. Typical reduction: 850 MB (with build tools) → 180 MB (runtime only). The DCA exam expects you to know this pattern.

# COPY --from=build
Q5
What does EXPOSE 8000 actually do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

EXPOSE is documentation only. It does NOT publish the port or make it accessible from the host. It's a hint that the container listens on port 8000. To actually publish the port, use docker run -p 8000:8000.

EXPLANATION

This is a common exam trap. EXPOSE only adds metadata to the image. The -p flag in docker run actually maps ports. The two are independent — you can publish a port not listed in EXPOSE, and EXPOSEd ports won't be accessible without -p (or -P to publish all EXPOSEd ports).

# EXPOSE 8000
# docker run -p 8000:8000
# docker run
Q6
What's wrong with this Dockerfile? FROM python:latest
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Using :latest makes builds non-reproducible. Today's build might use Python 3.11, tomorrow's might use 3.13 — with breaking changes. Always pin to a specific version: FROM python:3.11-slim.

EXPLANATION

The :latest tag is mutable — it moves to point to whatever was most recently pushed. Two builds one day apart can produce completely different images. For production, always use specific tags or digests (python:3.11-slim@sha256:abc...).

# FROM python:latest
# FROM python:3.11-slim
# python:3.11-slim@sha256:abc...
Q7
What's the difference between COPY and ADD?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

COPY copies local files into the image. ADD does the same PLUS can fetch URLs and auto-extract tar archives. Docker recommends COPY for local files (more explicit, less surprising). Use ADD only when you need its extra features.

EXPLANATION

ADD has two extra behaviors: (1) If the source is a URL, it downloads it. (2) If the source is a tar archive, it automatically extracts it into the destination. These "magic" behaviors can be surprising — COPY is more predictable. Use ADD only for tar auto-extraction.

# COPY
# ADD
# COPY
Q8
How do you set an environment variable that's available at RUNTIME but NOT during build?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

You can't set it in the Dockerfile if you want it ONLY at runtime. Use docker run -e VAR=value or --env-file at runtime. ENV in Dockerfile sets it at both build AND runtime. ARG is build-time only.

EXPLANATION

The three options: ARG (build only, gone after), ENV (build + runtime, visible in history), docker run -e (runtime only, not in image). For secrets like API keys, never use ENV — it's visible in docker history. Use runtime injection or Docker secrets instead.

# docker run -e VAR=value
# --env-file
# docker run -e
# docker history
Q9
What does docker build -t anihpj:v1 . do with the dot at the end?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The dot (.) is the build context — the directory sent to the Docker daemon for the build. Docker sends ALL files in this directory (except those in .dockerignore) to the daemon. The Dockerfile is expected to be in this directory.

EXPLANATION

The build context is the FIRST thing Docker does. Before reading the Dockerfile, it tars up the context directory and sends it to the daemon. If your directory is 2 GB, the build starts with a 2 GB upload. That's why .dockerignore is so critical — it slims the context before the tar is created.

# docker build -t anihpj:v1 .
# .dockerignore
Q10
What instruction would you use to switch to a non-root user for security?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

USER appuser (after creating the user with RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app). Running as non-root is a critical security practice — if an attacker compromises your container, they won't have root privileges.

EXPLANATION

By default, Docker containers run as root. If an attacker exploits your app, they get root inside the container — and potentially on the host if they break out. Creating a non-root user and using USER is a fundamental security hardening step. The --system flag creates a system user (no login, no home directory).

# USER appuser
# RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app

Chapter 5: Building Images — docker build Deep Dive

Now that you can write Dockerfiles, let's master the build process itself. Understanding build context, layer caching, build arguments, and multi-platform builds is essential for the DCA exam and daily Docker work.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1.5 hours🏗️ Build

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Master docker build with all key flags
  • ✅ Understand build context and .dockerignore
  • ✅ Leverage layer caching for lightning-fast rebuilds
  • ✅ Use ARG and ENV correctly
  • ✅ Build multi-platform images with Buildx

5.1 docker build Fundamentals

docker build reads a Dockerfile and builds an image from it. The basic syntax is: docker build [OPTIONS] PATH. The PATH is the build context — the directory sent to the Docker daemon.

TERMINAL
# Basic build
$ docker build -t anihpj:v1 .

# Build with BuildKit (recommended — faster, better output)
$ DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build -t anihpj:v1 .

# Build with no cache (force full rebuild)
$ docker build --no-cache -t anihpj:v1 .

# Build from a specific Dockerfile
$ docker build -f Dockerfile.prod -t anihpj:prod .

# Build with build arguments
$ docker build --build-arg DJANGO_VERSION=5.2 -t anihpj:v1 .

# Build and tag with multiple tags
$ docker build -t anihpj:v1 -t anihpj:latest -t ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1 .
Build Output (Annotated)
$ docker build -t anihpj:v1 .
[+] Building 45.3s (11/11) FINISHED
 => [internal] load build definition from Dockerfile    0.1s  ← Reads Dockerfile
 => => transferring dockerfile: 502B                    0.0s
 => [internal] load .dockerignore                       0.1s  ← Reads .dockerignore
 => => transferring context: 185B                       0.0s
 => [internal] load metadata for docker.io/library/     2.1s  ← Checks for base image updates
    python:3.11-slim
 => [1/5] FROM docker.io/library/python:3.11-slim       3.2s  ← Pulls/uses base image (CACHED)
 => [internal] load build context                       0.3s  ← Sends files to daemon
 => => transferring context: 15.82MB                    0.2s
 => [2/5] WORKDIR /app                                  0.1s  ← Layer 2: Working directory
 => [3/5] COPY requirements.txt .                       0.1s  ← Layer 3: Dependencies list (CACHED)
 => [4/5] RUN pip install --no-cache-dir \             38.2s  ← Layer 4: Install packages
    -r requirements.txt
 => [5/5] COPY . .                                      0.3s  ← Layer 5: Your application code
 => exporting to image                                  1.0s  ← Creates final image
 => => exporting layers                                 0.8s
 => => writing image sha256:abc123...                   0.1s
 => => naming to docker.io/library/anihpj:v1            0.0s  ← Tags the image

# Notice: Layers marked "CACHED" took 0.1s each
# The pip install layer took 38.2s (only runs when requirements change)
# Total: 45s first build, ~3s on code-only changes!

5.2 Build Context & .dockerignore

The build context is ALL files in the specified directory that Docker sends to the daemon. A large context means slow builds. .dockerignore excludes unnecessary files — just like .gitignore for Git.

.dockerignore
# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.pyo
*.egg-info/
dist/
build/

# Django
*.sqlite3
media/
staticfiles/

# Virtual environment
env/
venv/
.venv/

# Git
.git/
.gitignore
.gitattributes

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/
*.swp

# OS
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# Documentation
README.md
docs/

# Docker
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
docker-compose*.yml

5.3 Layer Caching Deep Dive

Layer caching is Docker's superpower. When rebuilding, Docker checks if each instruction's result is already cached. If it is, Docker SKIPS that instruction and uses the cached layer. This is why smart Dockerfiles rebuild in seconds.

Cache Hit vs Cache Miss
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               🏎️ LAYER CACHING — WHY ORDER MATTERS                        │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BAD ORDER (cache useless after code change):                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐         │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim    │ ✅ CACHED (never changes)        │         │
  │  │ COPY . /app/             │ ❌ REBUILT (code changed!)       │         │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .  │ ❌ REBUILT (previous changed)    │         │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req.. │ ❌ REBUILT (rerun install!)     │         │
  │  └──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  GOOD ORDER (only changed layers rebuilt):                               │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐         │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim    │ ✅ CACHED (never changes)        │         │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .  │ ✅ CACHED (same requirements)    │         │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req.. │ ✅ CACHED (same install)         │         │
  │  │ COPY . /app/             │ ❌ REBUILT (only code changed!) │         │
  │  └──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  RESULT: Good = 3 layers cached (~3 sec) | Bad = 4 layers rebuilt (~45s)│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 --cache-from: External Cache for CI/CD

In CI/CD pipelines, each build starts with an empty cache (fresh runner). Use --cache-from to pull a previous build's layers from a registry as cache: docker build --cache-from=anihpj:latest -t anihpj:v2 .. For multi-stage builds, specify each stage: --cache-from=anihpj:build --cache-from=anihpj:final. This can cut CI build times from minutes to seconds.

⚠️ Cache Gotchas

1. COPY always checks checksums — even if the file hasn't changed, a different timestamp invalidates cache. Use COPY --chmod to control permissions. 2. RUN apt-get update is NOT cached if you use apt-get update && apt-get install — the update command always runs. 3. BuildKit (DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1) has smarter cache invalidation than the legacy builder — it only rebuilds what actually changed, not everything after a changed COPY.

5.4 Build Arguments (ARG) & Environment Variables (ENV)

The distinction is critical for the DCA exam:

AspectARGENV
Available during build?✅ Yes✅ Yes
Available at runtime?❌ No (gone after build)✅ Yes (persists)
Visible in docker history?❌ No (if not persisted to ENV)✅ Yes (caution with secrets!)
How to set--build-arg VAR=value-e VAR=value at runtime
Use caseBuild-time config (version, env name)Runtime config (settings, URLs)
DOCKERFILE: ARG vs ENV
# ARG — build-time only, NOT in final image
ARG DJANGO_VERSION=5.2
ARG ENVIRONMENT=production
RUN echo "Building for Django ${DJANGO_VERSION} in ${ENVIRONMENT}"
# Docker build: docker build --build-arg DJANGO_VERSION=5.2 -t anihpj .
# At container runtime: ${DJANGO_VERSION} is EMPTY (ARG doesn't persist!)

# ENV — persists into the final image AND at runtime
ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# At container runtime: these vars are available to your app

# TIP: To use ARG value at runtime, persist it to ENV:
ARG VERSION=unknown
ENV APP_VERSION=${VERSION}  # Now available at runtime!

5.5 Multi-Platform Builds with Buildx

Modern development teams use a mix of Intel (amd64) and Apple Silicon (arm64) machines. Buildx lets you build ONE image that works on BOTH — and on cloud servers too.

TERMINAL
# Create a new builder instance
$ docker buildx create --name multiarch --use

# Build for multiple platforms simultaneously
$ docker buildx build \
    --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
    -t ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1 \
    --push .

# Verify the image supports multiple architectures
$ docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1
Name:      ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1
MediaType: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json
Manifests:
  Name:      ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1@sha256:abc... (linux/amd64)
  Name:      ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1@sha256:def... (linux/arm64)
📖 How Buildx Works: QEMU Emulation

When you build for linux/arm64 on an amd64 machine (or vice versa), Buildx uses QEMU — a processor emulator — to run the foreign architecture's binaries. This is automatic when you create a Buildx builder: docker buildx create --name multiarch --use sets up QEMU binfmt_misc handlers. Native builds (matching host arch) are faster than emulated ones. For CI/CD, consider using native ARM64 runners (like AWS Graviton) for faster ARM64 builds.

🎯 DCA Exam Tip: Manifest Lists

A multi-platform build produces a manifest list (also called a "fat manifest") — not a single image. When a user runs docker pull, Docker automatically selects the correct platform-specific image from the list. This is transparent: your Intel Mac, your colleague's M2 Mac, and your production AMD64 server all use the same tag — Docker handles the architecture matching automatically.

5.6 docker buildx bake — Advanced Builds

When you need to build multiple related images simultaneously (e.g., your app + a worker + a migrations runner), docker buildx bake orchestrates them in parallel — much faster than sequential builds.

docker-bake.hcl
# Define build targets for anihpj variants
group "default" {
  targets = ["django", "celery-worker", "migrations"]
}

target "django" {
  context    = "."
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile"
  tags       = ["anihpj:latest", "anihpj:django"]
  platforms  = ["linux/amd64", "linux/arm64"]
}

target "celery-worker" {
  context    = "."
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile.worker"
  tags       = ["anihpj:worker"]
  args = {
    WORKER_CONCURRENCY = "4"
  }
}

target "migrations" {
  context    = "."
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile.migrations"
  tags       = ["anihpj:migrations"]
}

# Build all targets in parallel:
# $ docker buildx bake
📖 When to Use Bake

Use bake when you have a microservice architecture with 3+ Dockerfiles that need to be built together. It handles parallel builds, shared layers, and multi-platform output — all from a single command. For simple single-image projects, stick with docker build.

📋 Multi-Stage Skeleton — Exam Essential

Multi-stage builds are 20% of the DCA Image Management domain

FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder`nWORKDIR /app`nCOPY requirements.txt .`nRUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt`nCOPY . .`nRUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput`n`nFROM python:3.11-slim`nWORKDIR /app`nCOPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local`nCOPY --from=builder /app/static /app/static`nCOPY . .`nENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH`nUSER app`nCMD [""gunicorn"",""app:application""]

⚠️ Chapter 5 Exam Gotchas

  • Key difference: COPY --from copies FILES between stages; each FROM starts a FRESH stage.
  • Multi-stage builds don't automatically reduce size → Only the FINAL stage becomes the image. Previous stages are discarded.
  • Forgetting .dockerignore → Build context size affects build speed. Always exclude node_modules, .git, venv.
  • ARG before FROM has different scope → ARG before FROM is only available in FROM lines. ARG after FROM is available in that stage.

📝 Chapter 5 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What is the build context in docker build -t app:v1 .?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The current directory (.) — ALL files in it (except .dockerignore exclusions) are sent to the Docker daemon as the build context.

EXPLANATION

The build context is the FIRST thing sent to the daemon — Docker tars up the entire directory and uploads it before even reading the Dockerfile. This is why large directories without .dockerignore cause slow builds.

# docker build -t app:v1 .
Q2
How do you force a complete rebuild without using any cached layers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker build --no-cache -t app:v1 . — forces every instruction to re-execute, ignoring all cached layers.

EXPLANATION

Use --no-cache when you suspect cache corruption, when base images have been updated and you want fresh packages, or when debugging build issues. It ensures every RUN command executes fresh.

# docker build --no-cache -t app:v1 .
# --no-cache
Q3
What's the purpose of .dockerignore?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Excludes files from the build context, making builds faster and preventing sensitive files (secrets, local config) from being accidentally copied into the image.

EXPLANATION

Without .dockerignore, Docker sends EVERYTHING in the context directory — including .git (potentially huge), node_modules, .env files with secrets, and IDE configs. This bloats the context AND may leak sensitive data into the image if COPY . . is used.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q4
What's the difference between ARG and ENV?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ARG is build-time only (gone after build). ENV persists into the final image and is available at runtime. Use ARG for build configuration, ENV for runtime configuration. Never put secrets in ENV — they're visible in docker history.

EXPLANATION

To make an ARG value available at runtime, persist it to ENV: ARG VERSION=unknown; ENV APP_VERSION=$VERSION. The DCA exam frequently tests this distinction.

# docker history
# ARG VERSION=unknown; ENV APP_VERSION=$VERSION
Q5
What tool builds images for multiple platforms (amd64 + arm64) simultaneously?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Buildx — docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t app:v1 .

EXPLANATION

Buildx uses QEMU emulation (or native builders) to compile for different architectures. The result is a manifest list — a single tag that automatically serves the correct platform-specific image. This is critical for teams with mixed Intel Mac and Apple Silicon machines.

# docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t app:v1 .
Q6
What happens to the cache when a layer changes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

That layer AND ALL subsequent layers are rebuilt. Docker cannot know if later layers depend on the changed one, so it rebuilds everything after the changed layer.

EXPLANATION

This is the "cache avalanche" effect. If Layer 1 changes, all N layers rebuild. If Layer N changes, only layer N rebuilds. That's why you put the most stable layers FIRST (base image, dependencies) and the most volatile LAST (application code).

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q7
How do you pass a value to an ARG during build?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker build --build-arg VERSION=1.0 -t app:v1 . — sets ARG VERSION to "1.0" during the build.

EXPLANATION

Multiple ARGs can be passed: --build-arg VAR1=val1 --build-arg VAR2=val2. If an ARG has a default in the Dockerfile (ARG VERSION=latest), the --build-arg flag overrides it.

# docker build --build-arg VERSION=1.0 -t app:v1 .
# ARG VERSION
# --build-arg VAR1=val1 --build-arg VAR2=val2
# ARG VERSION=latest
# --build-arg
Q8
What does DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 enable?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

BuildKit — Docker's next-generation build engine. Provides faster builds, better caching, parallel stage execution, secrets mounting, and improved output formatting. It's the default in recent Docker versions.

EXPLANATION

BuildKit is backward-compatible but dramatically better. Key features: parallel multi-stage builds, build secrets (--secret), remote cache (--cache-from), and SSH forwarding (--ssh). If you see # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 at the top of a Dockerfile, it's using BuildKit features.

# --cache-from
# # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
Q9
How do you build from a Dockerfile with a different name?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker build -f Dockerfile.prod -t app:prod . — the -f flag specifies a custom Dockerfile path/name.

EXPLANATION

The -f flag is useful for projects with multiple Dockerfiles (e.g., Dockerfile, Dockerfile.prod, Dockerfile.dev). Without -f, Docker looks for a file named Dockerfile in the build context root.

# docker build -f Dockerfile.prod -t app:prod .
# Dockerfile
Q10
Your build is slow because the build context is 2 GB. How do you fix this?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Create a .dockerignore file to exclude large/unnecessary files (node_modules, .git, databases, logs, virtual environments). This reduces the build context sent to the daemon, dramatically speeding up builds.

EXPLANATION

Also consider: using a .dockerignore with patterns like **/node_modules, **/.git, *.log. You can check context size with docker build --no-cache 2>&1 | grep "transferring context". A good target is < 50 MB for the build context.

# .dockerignore
# .dockerignore
# **/node_modules
# docker build --no-cache 2>&1 | grep "transferring context"

Chapter 6: Running Containers — docker run & Container Management

Building images is half the battle. Running and managing containers is where the real work happens. This chapter covers everything from basic docker run to advanced container lifecycle management.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~1.5 hours🏃 Runtime

6.1 docker run — The Complete Reference

docker run is your most-used command. It creates AND starts a container in one step. Understanding every option is critical for both the DCA exam and daily work.

Run Modes

ModeFlagsUse Case
Foreground (interactive)-itDebugging, exploring inside container
Detached (background)-dProduction, long-running services
Ephemeral (auto-cleanup)--rmOne-off commands, CI/CD, testing

Port Mapping

-p HOST:CONTAINER — Maps a port on your host to a port in the container. Example: -p 8000:8000 makes the container's port 8000 accessible at http://localhost:8000. Use -P to publish all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports.

Environment Variables

-e VAR=value sets a single variable. --env-file .env loads variables from a file. Environment variables are the primary way to configure containers at runtime — they keep configuration out of your image.

Naming & Restart Policies

PolicyBehavior
noNever restart (default)
on-failure[:max-retries]Restart only on non-zero exit code
alwaysAlways restart (even if stopped manually)
unless-stoppedAlways restart unless manually stopped

6.2 Container Lifecycle Management

Containers have a well-defined lifecycle. Understanding the states and transitions helps you debug and manage containers effectively.

Container Lifecycle State Diagram
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🔄 CONTAINER LIFECYCLE STATES                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │                            docker create                                 │
  │                        ┌───────────────────┐                            │
  │                        ▼                   │                            │
  │  ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐                      │
  │  │  Image   │   │ ▶️ CREATED  │     │ ▶️ RUNNING  │                      │
  │  │         │──▶│             │────▶│             │                      │
  │  │(blueprint)│  │ (exists on  │     │ (process     │                      │
  │  └─────────┘   │  disk, not   │     │  active,     │                      │
  │                │  started)    │     │  CPU running)│                      │
  │                └──────┬──────┘     └──┬──┬──┬───┘                      │
  │                       │               │  │  │                            │
  │                       │ docker start  │  │  │ docker stop (SIGTERM,     │
  │                       └───────────────┘  │  │  then SIGKILL after       │
  │                                          │  │  10s grace period)         │
  │                                   docker │   │                           │
  │                                   pause  │   │ docker kill (SIGKILL)     │
  │                                          ▼   ▼                           │
  │                                    ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌─────────┐   │
  │                                    │ ⏸️     │ │ ⏹️      │ │ 💀      │   │
  │                                    │PAUSED  │ │STOPPED │ │ DELETED │   │
  │                                    │(frozen │ │(exited │ │ (gone)  │   │
  │                                    │ processes)│ │process)│ │         │   │
  │                                    └───┬────┘ └───┬────┘ └─────────┘   │
  │                                        │         │                       │
  │                             docker unpause  docker start                │
  │                                        │         │                       │
  │                                        ▼         ▼                       │
  │                                   ┌────────────────┐                    │
  │                                   │  ▶️ RUNNING     │                    │
  │                                   └────────────────┘                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Containers Are "Cattle, Not Pets"

In traditional server management, servers are treated like pets — you name them, nurse them back to health, and panic when they go down. Containers are cattle — you number them, expect them to die, and automatically replace them from the same image. This mindset shift is fundamental to Docker: never manually fix a broken container; just docker rm it and docker run a fresh one from the same image.

TERMINAL
# Create a container (but don't start it)
$ docker create --name anihpj-dev anihpj:v1

# Start a stopped container
$ docker start anihpj-dev

# Stop a running container (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after grace period)
$ docker stop anihpj-dev

# Force kill immediately (SIGKILL)
$ docker kill anihpj-dev

# Pause / Unpause (freeze all processes)
$ docker pause anihpj-dev
$ docker unpause anihpj-dev

# Restart a container
$ docker restart anihpj-dev

# Remove a container (must be stopped first, or use -f)
$ docker rm anihpj-dev
$ docker rm -f anihpj-dev  # Force remove (even if running)

6.3 Viewing & Inspecting Containers

TERMINAL
# List running containers
$ docker ps
$ docker container ls  # same command, newer syntax

# List ALL containers (including stopped)
$ docker ps -a

# View logs
$ docker logs anihpj-dev           # Show all logs
$ docker logs -f anihpj-dev        # Follow (like tail -f)
$ docker logs --tail 50 anihpj-dev # Last 50 lines
$ docker logs --since 10m anihpj-dev # Last 10 minutes

# Live resource usage (CPU, RAM, Network, Disk)
$ docker stats anihpj-dev

# Show processes running inside container
$ docker top anihpj-dev

# Detailed JSON metadata about container
$ docker inspect anihpj-dev
$ docker inspect -f '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}' anihpj-dev  # Just the IP

6.4 Executing Commands Inside Containers

docker exec runs commands inside an already-running container. This is how you debug, run migrations, or check application state.

TERMINAL
# Get an interactive shell inside the container
$ docker exec -it anihpj-dev bash

# Run a single command
$ docker exec anihpj-dev python manage.py check --deploy

# Run Django migrations
$ docker exec anihpj-dev python manage.py migrate

# Check the Django settings
$ docker exec anihpj-dev python -c "from django.conf import settings; print(settings.DEBUG)"

# Run as a specific user
$ docker exec -u appuser anihpj-dev whoami
#Scenariodocker exec CommandWhy This Works
1Get a shelldocker exec -it anihpj-dev bash-i (stdin open) + -t (TTY) = interactive shell
2Run Django migrationsdocker exec anihpj-dev python manage.py migrateExecutes the command, prints output, exits — no TTY needed
3Check Django deploymentdocker exec anihpj-dev python manage.py check --deployValidates settings for production readiness
4Create Django superuserdocker exec -it anihpj-dev python manage.py createsuperuserNeeds -it because createsuperuser prompts for password
5View environment variablesdocker exec anihpj-dev env | sortShows all env vars the container sees (including Dockerfile ENV)
6Check installed packagesdocker exec anihpj-dev pip freezeLists all Python packages and versions inside the container
7Test database connectivitydocker exec anihpj-dev python -c "import psycopg2; print('OK')"Quick connectivity check without running the full app
8Clear Django cachedocker exec anihpj-dev python manage.py clear_cacheClears app cache without restarting the container
9View running processesdocker exec anihpj-dev ps auxShows all processes inside the container (alternative to docker top)
10Run as specific userdocker exec -u root anihpj-dev apt updateTemporarily runs as root (use sparingly — breaks security model)
⚠️ Golden Rule: Don't Modify Running Containers

Use docker exec for read-only inspection and debugging — not for making permanent changes. If you install packages or modify configs with docker exec, those changes disappear when the container restarts. Instead, update your Dockerfile and rebuild. Containers are immutable — treat them that way.

6.5 Copying Files To/From Containers

docker cp copies files between your host and a container — useful for extracting logs, backups, or injecting config files.

TERMINAL
# ─── SCENARIO 1: Extract database backup ───
$ docker cp anihpj-dev:/app/db.sqlite3 ./backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).sqlite3

# ─── SCENARIO 2: Inject updated settings ───
$ docker cp ./new-settings.py anihpj-dev:/app/anihpj/settings.py
$ docker restart anihpj-dev  # Restart to pick up new settings

# ─── SCENARIO 3: Backup entire static files directory ───
$ docker cp anihpj-dev:/app/static ./static-backup/

# ─── SCENARIO 4: Extract logs from a crashed container ───
$ docker cp crashed-container:/var/log/app/error.log ./debug-error.log

# ─── SCENARIO 5: Seed database from host ───
$ docker cp ./fixtures.json anihpj-dev:/tmp/
$ docker exec anihpj-dev python manage.py loaddata /tmp/fixtures.json
📖 docker cp vs Volumes

docker cp is a one-time, manual file transfer. For ongoing file sharing (development, config files, persistent data), use bind mounts (-v /host/path:/container/path) or named volumes (-v myvolume:/container/path). These sync automatically — no need to manually cp each time you change a file. docker cp is best for one-off operations: backups, debugging, injecting configs.

6.6 Container Resource Limits

Without limits, one container can consume all available CPU and RAM — the "noisy neighbor" problem. Resource limits are essential for production deployments.

FlagPurposeExample
--memory or -mRAM limit--memory=512m (512 MB)
--memory-swapTotal memory + swap limit--memory=512m --memory-swap=1g
--cpusCPU limit (fractional OK)--cpus=1.5 (1.5 cores)
--cpu-sharesCPU relative weight (default 1024)--cpu-shares=512 (half priority)
--pids-limitMax number of processes--pids-limit=100
--blkio-weightBlock I/O relative weight--blkio-weight=500

⚡ Chapter 6 Exam Speed Commands

TaskCommand
Create a volumedocker volume create pgdata
List volumesdocker volume ls
Run with volumedocker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
Bind mount for devdocker run -v $(pwd):/app app:dev
tmpfs mountdocker run --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec alpine
Backup volumedocker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pg.tar.gz -C /data .

📋docker ps / logs / inspect

⚠️ Chapter 6 Exam Gotchas

  • Mounting a host path that doesn't exist → Bind mounts require the host path to exist first. Named volumes auto-create.
  • docker compose down -v deletes named volumes → The -v flag removes ALL volumes. Omit it to preserve data.
  • Anonymous volumes get left behind → docker run -v /data (no name) creates anonymous volumes. Use named volumes or docker volume prune.

📝 Chapter 6 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What's the difference between docker run and docker start?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run creates a NEW container from an image and starts it. docker start starts an EXISTING stopped container. Run = create + start. Start = start only.

EXPLANATION

docker run is actually docker create + docker start combined. Each docker run creates a UNIQUE container — even from the same image. Running docker run nginx twice creates two separate containers. docker start reuses an existing one.

# docker run
# docker start
# docker run
# docker start
# docker run
Q2
How do you run a container in the background and automatically remove it when it exits?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run -d --rm --name temp anihpj:v1. -d detaches, --rm auto-removes on exit. Perfect for one-off tasks and CI pipelines.

EXPLANATION

Without --rm, stopped containers accumulate and consume disk space. In CI/CD, this can fill up build agents quickly. --rm ensures cleanup is automatic.

# docker run -d --rm --name temp anihpj:v1
Q3
What's the difference between docker stop and docker kill?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker stop sends SIGTERM (graceful shutdown, 10s default grace period), then SIGKILL if still running. docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately — no cleanup, no grace period.

EXPLANATION

SIGTERM allows the app to gracefully shut down (close database connections, finish in-flight requests, clean up temp files). SIGKILL terminates immediately — the OS kills the process without warning. Always use stop for production; use kill only when the container is frozen.

# docker stop
# docker kill
# docker stop
# docker kill
Q4
How do you see the logs of a container that's running in detached mode?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker logs anihpj-dev. Add -f to follow (stream), --tail 100 for last 100 lines, --since 10m for last 10 minutes.

EXPLANATION

Logs are stdout/stderr from the container's PID 1. They persist even after the container stops. Use docker logs --timestamps to see when each line was logged.

# docker logs anihpj-dev
# --tail 100
# --since 10m
# docker logs --timestamps
Q5
How do you get an interactive bash shell inside a running container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker exec -it anihpj-dev bash. -i keeps STDIN open, -t allocates a TTY. Without both, you won't get a proper shell.

EXPLANATION

-i (interactive) = you can type. -t (TTY) = proper terminal formatting (colors, cursor positioning, tab completion). Using just -i gives a partially broken experience; using neither gives no interaction at all.

# docker exec -it anihpj-dev bash
Q6
What restart policy would you use for a production web server that should ALWAYS be running?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--restart unless-stopped. It restarts the container if it crashes, and survives Docker daemon restarts. It only stays stopped if YOU manually stop it.

EXPLANATION

The four policies: no (default, never restart), on-failure (only on non-zero exit), always (always, even after manual stop — annoying for maintenance), unless-stopped (always unless you manually stop — best for production).

# --restart unless-stopped
# on-failure
# unless-stopped
Q7
How do you limit a container to 512 MB of RAM and 1.5 CPU cores?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 anihpj:v1. Without limits, the container can use ALL host resources.

EXPLANATION

Resource limits are enforced via Linux cgroups. If a container exceeds --memory, it gets OOM-killed. --cpus throttles CPU time. For production, always set limits to prevent the "noisy neighbor" problem where one container starves others.

# docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 anihpj:v1
Q8
How do you copy a file from a container to your host?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker cp anihpj-dev:/app/db.sqlite3 ./backup.sqlite3. The syntax is docker cp CONTAINER:SRC_PATH DEST_PATH (or vice versa).

EXPLANATION

docker cp works whether the container is running or stopped. It's a one-time copy, not a sync. For ongoing file sharing, use volumes or bind mounts instead.

# docker cp anihpj-dev:/app/db.sqlite3 ./backup.sqlite3
# docker cp CONTAINER:SRC_PATH DEST_PATH
# docker cp
Q9
What command shows real-time CPU, memory, and network usage for all running containers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker stats. Shows live CPU %, memory usage/limit, network I/O, block I/O, and PIDs for each container. Like top but for containers.

EXPLANATION

docker stats --no-stream gives a one-shot snapshot (useful for scripting). docker stats --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}" customizes the output.

# docker stats
# docker stats --no-stream
# docker stats --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}"
Q10
A container exited immediately. How do you debug what happened?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. docker ps -a — find the exited container. 2. docker logs <container-id> — see what it printed before crashing. 3. docker inspect <container-id> — check exit code, mounts, env vars.

EXPLANATION

Exit code 0 = normal exit, 1 = application error, 137 = SIGKILL (OOM or manual kill), 139 = SIGSEGV (segfault). Also check: docker inspect -f '{{.State.Error}}' <id> for daemon-level errors.

# docker ps -a
# docker logs 
# docker inspect 
# docker inspect -f '{{.State.Error}}'

Part 2 covers the hands-on core of Docker — writing Dockerfiles, building images, and running containers. Here's what you should take away:

  • Dockerfile (Ch 4): The blueprint for your image. Master ALL instructions — especially CMD vs ENTRYPOINT (exam favorite). Order layers from least to most frequently changing for optimal caching. Multi-stage builds give you 5x smaller, 3x safer images.
  • docker build (Ch 5): The .dockerignore is your first line of defense against bloated builds. BuildKit enables parallel builds, secrets, and remote caching. Buildx handles multi-platform images so one tag works everywhere.
  • docker run (Ch 6): Containers are cattle, not pets — never fix, just replace. Master the lifecycle: create → start → pause → stop → rm. Use resource limits in production. docker exec for debugging, NOT for modifying.
🔄 Implementation: From Local to Production

Write Dockerfile → docker build -t anihpj:v1 . → docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name anihpj-prod --restart unless-stopped --memory=512m --cpus=1 anihpj:v1 → docker logs -f anihpj-prod to verify. That's the complete workflow — from code to running production container in 4 commands.

Chapter 7: Image Management — docker image Commands

Now that you can build and run containers, let's master the complete image lifecycle: listing, tagging, pushing, pulling, saving, loading, and cleaning up. These are your day-to-day Docker operations.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours📦 Images🎯 DCA 20%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ List, filter, and format Docker images
  • ✅ Tag images properly for registries
  • ✅ Push to and pull from Docker Hub and private registries

7.1 Listing & Filtering Images

docker images (or docker image ls) shows all images on your system. With filters and formatting, you can find exactly what you need.

TERMINAL
# List all images
$ docker images
REPOSITORY    TAG          IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
anihpj        v1.0         abc123def456   2 hours ago    180MB
anihpj        latest       abc123def456   2 hours ago    180MB
python        3.11-slim    xyz789ghi012   3 days ago     150MB
nginx         alpine       def456jkl345   5 days ago     42MB

# List with newer syntax (same output)
$ docker image ls

# Filter: show only dangling images (untagged, :)
$ docker images --filter "dangling=true"

# Filter: show images matching a pattern
$ docker images --filter "reference=anihpj*"
$ docker images --filter "reference=python:*"

# Filter: show images created before/after a date
$ docker images --filter "before=anihpj:v1.0"

# Format output (Go templates)
$ docker images --format "table {{.Repository}}\t{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}"
$ docker images --format "{{.ID}}: {{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} ({{.Size}})"

# Show only image IDs (useful for scripting)
$ docker images -q
abc123def456
xyz789ghi012

7.2 Tagging Images Properly

A tag is a human-readable label pointing to a specific image. One image can have multiple tags. Understanding this is key for registry pushes and version management.

TERMINAL
# Tag an existing image
$ docker tag anihpj:v1.0 anihpj:latest
# Both tags now point to the SAME Image ID!

# Tag for a specific registry
$ docker tag anihpj:v1.0 ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0
$ docker tag anihpj:v1.0 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.0

# Tag with multiple labels
$ docker tag anihpj:v1.0 anihpj:stable
$ docker tag anihpj:v1.0 anihpj:2026-06-12
$ docker tag anihpj:v1.0 anihpj:abc1234  # git commit SHA

# See all tags for an image
$ docker images anihpj
REPOSITORY  TAG           IMAGE ID       CREATED
anihpj      v1.0          abc123def456   2 hours ago
anihpj      latest        abc123def456   2 hours ago
anihpj      stable        abc123def456   2 hours ago
# All same IMAGE ID — they're the SAME image!
One Image ID → Multiple Tags
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   🏷️ TAGS POINT TO IMAGE IDs                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │                        ┌─────────────────┐                              │
  │      anihpj:v1.0 ─────▶│                 │                              │
  │      anihpj:latest ───▶│  IMAGE ID:      │                              │
  │      anihpj:stable ───▶│  abc123def456   │                              │
  │      anihpj:20260612──▶│                 │                              │
  │                        └─────────────────┘                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  docker rmi anihpj:v1.0  → removes the TAG only (image stays!)          │
  │  docker rmi abc123def456  → removes the IMAGE (all tags gone!)          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

7.3 Pushing & Pulling Images

Images flow between your local machine and registries via push and pull. This is how you share images with your team and deploy to servers.

TERMINAL
# Login to a registry first
$ docker login                              # Docker Hub (default)
$ docker login ghcr.io                      # GitHub Container Registry
$ docker login registry.example.com         # Self-hosted registry
# (AWS ECR uses a different auth method — see below)

# Push an image
$ docker push anihpj:v1.0                  # Push to Docker Hub
$ docker push ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0 # Push to GitHub

# Push all tags for an image
$ docker push -a anihpj                     # Pushes ALL tags of "anihpj"

# Pull an image
$ docker pull python:3.11-slim
$ docker pull ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0

# AWS ECR login (special — uses AWS CLI)
$ aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | \
  docker login --username AWS --password-stdin \
  123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
Push/Pull Flow Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                        📤 PUSH / 📥 PULL FLOW                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │    YOUR MACHINE                          REGISTRY                        │
  │  ┌──────────────┐                    ┌──────────────────┐               │
  │  │              │    docker push     │                  │               │
  │  │  anihpj:v1.0 │──────────────────▶│  anihpj:v1.0     │               │
  │  │  (local)     │                    │  (remote copy)   │               │
  │  │              │◀──────────────────│                  │               │
  │  │              │    docker pull     │                  │               │
  │  └──────────────┘                    └──────────────────┘               │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Registry Types:                                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ Docker Hub       │ GHCR (GitHub)     │ AWS ECR                      │  │
  │  │ docker.io/…      │ ghcr.io/…         │ aws_account_id.dkr.ecr.…    │  │
  │  │ Public + Private  │ GitHub integrated  │ IAM auth (temporary token)  │  │
  │  │ docker login      │ docker login ghcr  │ aws ecr get-login-password  │  │
  │  └─────────────────┴──────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  docker tag anihpj:v1.0 ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0  ← registry prefix │
  │  docker push ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0                               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

7.4 Saving & Loading Images (Offline Transfer)

When you can't use a registry (air-gapped environments, USB transfer), docker save and docker load let you move images as tar files.

CommandWhat It DoesUse Case
docker save -o file.tar image:tagExports image + layers + tags as a tar archiveTransfer to another machine
docker load -i file.tarImports an image from a tar archiveReceive from another machine
docker export -o file.tar containerExports container FILESYSTEM (flat, no layers/history)Create a "snapshot" of container state
docker import file.tar image:tagCreates an image from a flat filesystemImport from export (no layers!)
⚠️ Critical: save vs export

docker save preserves layers, tags, and history. docker export creates a FLAT filesystem — all layers are merged, tags and history are lost. Always use save/load for image transfer.

7.5 Removing Images & Cleanup

Docker images accumulate quickly. Regular cleanup prevents running out of disk space — especially important on CI/CD build agents.

TERMINAL
# Remove a specific image (by tag or ID)
$ docker rmi anihpj:v1.0
$ docker rmi abc123def456          # Remove by IMAGE ID
$ docker rmi -f abc123def456       # Force remove (even if in use)

# Remove dangling images (:)
$ docker image prune
# WARNING! This will remove all dangling images.
# Are you sure? [y/N] y
# Deleted: sha256:abc...
# Total reclaimed space: 1.2 GB

# Remove ALL unused images (not referenced by any container)
$ docker image prune -a

# Check disk usage
$ docker system df
TYPE            TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images          15        8         3.2 GB    1.8 GB (56%)
Containers      6         2         150 MB    120 MB (80%)
Local Volumes   4         2         500 MB    200 MB (40%)

# Nuclear option: remove EVERYTHING unused
$ docker system prune -a --volumes
# Removes: all stopped containers, unused networks,
#          dangling images, unused build cache, ALL unused volumes

7.6 Image History & Inspection

Understanding what's INSIDE your images is critical for debugging and optimization.

TERMINAL
# Show image layers (each with size and command)
$ docker image history anihpj:v1.0
IMAGE          CREATED        CREATED BY                           SIZE
abc123def456   2 hours ago    CMD ["gunicorn" "anihpj.wsgi:app"]   0B
def456ghi789   2 hours ago    COPY . /app/                         500kB
ghi789jkl012   2 hours ago    RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  80MB
jkl012mno345   2 hours ago    COPY requirements.txt .              200B
mno345pqr678   3 days ago     /bin/sh -c #(nop) WORKDIR /app       0B
pqr678stu901   3 days ago     /bin/sh -c #(nop) CMD ["python3"]    0B
      3 days ago     /bin/sh -c set -ex; ...              150MB

# Detailed JSON metadata
$ docker image inspect anihpj:v1.0
# Returns: ID, Created, Architecture, OS, Layers, Env, CMD, Entrypoint,
#          Volumes, WorkingDir, Labels, and more...

# Extract specific fields with --format (Go template)
$ docker image inspect -f '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}' anihpj:v1.0
linux/amd64

$ docker image inspect -f '{{range .RootFS.Layers}}{{println .}}{{end}}' anihpj:v1.0
sha256:abc...
sha256:def...
🔑 Image ID vs Digest — Critical Distinction

Image ID is a local short SHA (e.g., abc123def456) — unique on YOUR machine but different across machines. Digest is a content-addressable SHA256 (e.g., sha256:abc123...) — IDENTICAL everywhere. Always reference images by digest for guaranteed reproducibility: python:3.11-slim@sha256:abc.... Tags are mutable, digests are immutable.

🔐 Docker Content Trust (DCT) — Image Signing

Docker Content Trust uses Notary to sign images, ensuring the image you pull is exactly what the publisher intended — not tampered with in transit. Enable with export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1. When enabled: docker pull only succeeds if the image is signed by a trusted publisher. docker push automatically signs images. This is critical for supply chain security — the DCA exam tests awareness of DCT as part of the Security domain.

⚠️ Chapter 7 Exam Gotchas

  • Default bridge = no DNS → Use user-defined bridge networks for automatic DNS resolution between containers.
  • Ports not published on correct interface → -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 binds to localhost only. -p 8080:80 binds to all interfaces.
  • EXPOSE in Dockerfile publishes ports → EXPOSE is metadata only. -p or ports: are required to actually publish.

📝 Chapter 7 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What command lists all Docker images on your system with their sizes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker images or docker image ls. Shows REPOSITORY, TAG, IMAGE ID, CREATED, and SIZE for each image.

EXPLANATION

docker images is the older syntax, docker image ls is the newer Docker CLI structured syntax. Both produce identical output. The docker image subcommand group includes ls, pull, push, rm, prune, history, inspect — all image management operations under one namespace.

# docker images
# docker image ls
# docker images
# docker image ls
# docker image
Q2
How do you tag an existing image for pushing to GitHub Container Registry?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker tag anihpj:v1.0 ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0

EXPLANATION

The tag format for registries is registry/namespace/repository:tag. For Docker Hub, the registry prefix (docker.io) is implicit and can be omitted. For all other registries, you must include the full registry URL.

# docker tag anihpj:v1.0 ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0
# registry/namespace/repository:tag
# docker.io
Q3
What's the critical difference between docker save and docker export?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker save preserves ALL image layers, tags, and metadata. docker export creates a flat filesystem snapshot of a container's files — layers and history are LOST. Always use save/load for image transfer, never export/import.

EXPLANATION

Think of save as "serialize the complete image with its layer cake intact" and export as "flatten the container's filesystem into a single blob." The difference becomes critical in air-gapped environments: save preserves all metadata for proper image restoration; export gives you a filesystem with no Docker metadata — you'd have to rebuild FROM scratch-like images.

# docker save
# docker export
# docker save
# docker export
Q4
What command removes all unused Docker images?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker image prune -a — removes all images not referenced by at least one container. Without -a, only dangling images (<none>:<none>) are removed.

EXPLANATION

Dangling images occur when you rebuild with the same tag — the old image loses its tag and becomes <none>:<none>. prune (no flags) removes only these. prune -a removes ALL images not currently used by any container. For complete cleanup: docker system prune -a --volumes adds containers, networks, build cache, and unused volumes.

# docker image prune -a
# docker system prune -a --volumes
Q5
How do you filter images to show only those matching "anihpj*"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker images --filter "reference=anihpj*"

EXPLANATION

The --filter flag supports multiple filter types: reference (name:tag pattern), dangling (true/false), before/since (filter by image), and label (metadata). You can chain filters: docker images --filter "dangling=false" --filter "reference=*anihpj*".

# docker images --filter "reference=anihpj*"
# reference
# docker images --filter "dangling=false" --filter "reference=*anihpj*"
Q6
What happens when you docker rmi anihpj:v1.0 and the image also has the tag anihpj:latest?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Only the :v1.0 TAG is removed — the image itself stays because it's still referenced by :latest. The image is only deleted when ALL tags pointing to it are removed.

EXPLANATION

Docker uses reference counting for images. Each tag increments the reference count. docker rmi <tag> decrements it. When the count reaches zero AND no container references the image, the layers are actually deleted. This is why you can have 5 tags on one image and safely remove 4 of them.

# docker rmi anihpj:v1.0
# anihpj:latest
# docker rmi
Q7
How do you check total Docker disk usage and reclaimable space?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker system df — shows disk usage by Images, Containers, Local Volumes, and Build Cache, with RECLAIMABLE percentages.

EXPLANATION

docker system df -v gives verbose output showing each image/container/volume individually with its size. Use this before docker system prune to see exactly what you'll reclaim. The RECLAIMABLE column shows space that can be freed by pruning unused objects.

# docker system df
# docker system df -v
# docker system prune
Q8
What authentication method does AWS ECR use that's different from other registries?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ECR uses aws ecr get-login-password piped to docker login --password-stdin — it generates a temporary token via AWS IAM, not a permanent username/password. The token expires after 12 hours.

EXPLANATION

This is more secure than a static password: the token is short-lived and tied to your AWS IAM credentials. In CI/CD, you typically run this command in every pipeline job (or use an ECR credential helper). Other registries (Docker Hub, GHCR) use personal access tokens that don't auto-expire.

# aws ecr get-login-password
# docker login --password-stdin
Q9
How do you see the size contribution of each layer in an image?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker image history anihpj:v1.0 — shows each layer with its SIZE column. This is how you identify which layers are bloating your image (e.g., a RUN apt-get install that added 500 MB).

EXPLANATION

Each layer's SIZE is the delta from the previous layer. A COPY . . that adds 500KB of code shows as 500KB. A RUN apt-get install that adds 500MB shows as 500MB. Use docker image history --no-trunc to see full command strings. For even deeper analysis: dive <image> (third-party tool) shows per-file changes in each layer.

# docker image history anihpj:v1.0
# RUN apt-get install
# RUN apt-get install
# docker image history --no-trunc
# dive
Q10
How do you transfer a Docker image to an air-gapped server with no internet access?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker save -o anihpj.tar anihpj:v1.0 on the connected machine, transfer the tar via USB, then docker load -i anihpj.tar on the air-gapped server. This preserves all layers, tags, and metadata.

EXPLANATION

You can also pipe save/load over SSH to skip the intermediate tar file: docker save anihpj:v1.0 | ssh user@airgap 'docker load'. For multiple images: docker save img1 img2 img3 -o bundle.tar. The tar contains layer blobs + a manifest.json describing how to reassemble them.

# docker save -o anihpj.tar anihpj:v1.0
# docker load -i anihpj.tar
# docker save anihpj:v1.0 | ssh user@airgap 'docker load'
# docker save img1 img2 img3 -o bundle.tar
