Chapter 8: Optimizing Docker Images — Smaller, Faster, Safer

Image size directly impacts build speed, deployment time, attack surface, and disk costs. A lean image can be 10x smaller than a bloated one — and dramatically more secure.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours⚡ Optimization🎯 DCA 20%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Choose the optimal base image for your workload
  • ✅ Apply layer optimization techniques
  • ✅ Use Python/Django-specific optimizations
  • ✅ Scan images for vulnerabilities with Docker Scout
  • ✅ Understand distroless images for maximum security

8.1 Why Image Size Matters

Every megabyte in your image costs you: slower builds (more to process), slower deployments (more to pull), larger attack surface (more packages = more CVEs), and more disk usage on every node and registry. Target: keep production images under 200 MB.

Image Size Impact
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    📊 IMAGE SIZE — WHY EVERY MB COUNTS                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Metric                │  850 MB (Bloated)  │  180 MB (Optimized)        │
  │  ──────────────────────┼────────────────────┼─────────────────────────   │
  │  Build Time            │  ~2 min             │  ~45 sec                   │
  │  Push to Registry      │  ~8 min (10 Mbps)   │  ~1.5 min                  │
  │  Pull on New Node      │  ~8 min             │  ~1.5 min ⚡ (6x faster)  │
  │  Disk per 10 Deploys   │  8.5 GB             │  1.8 GB                    │
  │  CVEs (Vulnerabilities)│  120+               │  30-40 ✅ (3x safer)       │
  │  Attack Surface        │  Large (gcc, git..) │  Minimal                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

8.2 Choosing the Right Base Image

The base image is the foundation. Choose wisely — it determines your image's size, compatibility, and security posture.

ImageSizeBased OnBest ForWatch Out
Alpine~5 MBAlpine Linux (musl libc)Go apps, simple servicesmusl libc ≠ glibc — some Python packages break!
Slim~40-80 MBDebian (glibc, stripped)Python/Django, Node.jsBest balance for web apps ✅
Full Debian/Ubuntu~100-200 MBDebian/Ubuntu (full)Legacy apps, complex depsLarge, many CVEs
Distroless~20 MBDebian (no shell!)Maximum securityNo shell = harder to debug
Scratch0 MBEmptyStatic binaries (Go, Rust)No shell, no libs, no TLS certs
🏆 For anihpj (Django): Use python:3.11-slim

Alpine is tempting (5 MB!) but its musl libc causes issues with many Python C-extensions (psycopg2, Pillow, numpy). Slim gives you Debian compatibility at a reasonable size (~150 MB base + ~30 MB deps = ~180 MB total).

8.3 Layer Optimization Techniques

Technique❌ Bad✅ Good
Chain RUN commandsRUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install pkg		RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
Clean up in same layerLeave apt cache, pip cache&& rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* && pip cache purge
Use .dockerignoreNo .dockerignoreExclude __pycache__, .git, env/, *.pyc
COPY specific filesCOPY . . (copies everything)COPY requirements.txt . then COPY ./anihpj ./anihpj
Multi-stage buildsSingle stage with build toolsBuild stage + slim runtime stage
Before vs After: Optimized Layer Structure
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               🔧 BEFORE OPTIMIZATION (850 MB, 120 CVEs)                     │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11            # 900 MB base, includes gcc, git       │  │
  │  │ COPY . /app/                # Copies EVERYTHING (db.sqlite3, .git) │  │
  │  │ RUN apt-get update           # Creates layer with stale apt cache  │  │
  │  │ RUN apt-get install -y gcc  # Another layer, no cleanup            │  │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r req.txt  # pip cache bloats this layer          │  │
  │  │ CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver"]  # Dev server in prod!   │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │               ✅ AFTER OPTIMIZATION (180 MB, 30 CVEs)                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder  # 150 MB, no build tools         │  │
  │  │ WORKDIR /app                                                        │  │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .         # Only deps list (cached!)         │  │
  │  │ RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt          │  │
  │  │                                                                    │  │
  │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim           # Second stage: clean              │  │
  │  │ COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local  # Only packages!    │  │
  │  │ COPY . .                        # .dockerignore filters junk      │  │
  │  │ USER app                        # Non-root security                │  │
  │  │ HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f localhost:8000/health/                     │  │
  │  │ CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]│
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

8.4 Python/Django Specific Optimizations

Optimized Dockerfile for Django
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
# Copy only installed packages (not build tools!)
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
# Copy application code
COPY . .
# Security: run as non-root
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app
USER app
# No build tools, no caches, minimal attack surface!
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
💡 Django Optimization Checklist

✅ Use --no-cache-dir with pip. ✅ Set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1. ✅ Multi-stage: collect static in builder, serve from final. ✅ Remove dev dependencies for production (pip install --no-dev). ✅ Use .dockerignore for __pycache__, .git, env/.

8.5 Image Scanning — Docker Scout

Docker Scout analyzes your images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs). It examines every layer, every package, and gives you actionable remediation advice.

TERMINAL
# Quick vulnerability summary
$ docker scout quickview anihpj:v1
  ✓ SBOM of image already cached, 123 packages indexed
  ## Overview
  │               Analyzed Image
  ├───────────────────────────────
  │ Target   │  anihpj:v1
  │     digest   │  abc12345
  │     platform │  linux/amd64
  │     vulnerabilities         │    0C     3H     12M     45L
  │     size     │  180 MB
  │     packages │  123

# Detailed CVE report
$ docker scout cves anihpj:v1

# Get fix recommendations
$ docker scout recommendations anihpj:v1
  Recommendation: Update base image
  Current: python:3.11-slim (Debian 12)
  Suggestion: Rebuild to get latest security patches
  Impact: Fixes 15 CVEs
🔴
Critical

Remote code execution, privilege escalation. Fix IMMEDIATELY — these can compromise your entire system. Example: CVE-2024-xxxx in libssl.

🟠
High

Can lead to data breach or denial of service. Fix within days. Example: buffer overflow in image processing library.

🟡
Medium/Low

Limited impact or requires unlikely conditions. Fix in regular update cycle. These still count as CVEs in your scan report.

📖 SBOM: Software Bill of Materials

Docker Scout generates an SBOM — a complete inventory of every package in your image, including transitive dependencies. Think of it as a nutrition label for your container. SBOMs are increasingly required for compliance (US Executive Order 14028). You can export yours: docker scout sbom anihpj:v1 --format spdx.

8.6 Distroless Images — The Ultimate Security

Distroless images, created by Google, contain ONLY your application and its runtime dependencies. No shell, no package manager, no curl, no utilities — nothing an attacker can use. They are the gold standard for container security.

🛡️
Why Distroless?

Every tool in your container is a weapon for an attacker. Shell = interactive access. Curl/wget = exfiltrate data. Package manager = install malware. Distroless removes ALL of these. If there's no shell, docker exec simply cannot work — blocking the most common post-exploitation vector.

🐛
How to Debug

No shell means no docker exec -it bash. Instead: (1) Use structured logging (JSON to stdout), (2) Use kubectl debug with ephemeral containers in Kubernetes, (3) Use sidecar debugging containers sharing the PID namespace, (4) Embed a health-check HTTP endpoint in your app.

DISTROLESS DOCKERFILE for anihpj
# Stage 1: Build (has all tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Stage 2: Distroless final (NO shell, NO package manager!)
FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12
WORKDIR /app
# Copy Python packages from builder
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
# Copy application code
COPY --from=builder /app /app
# Copy static files
COPY --from=builder /app/static /app/static
# Set Python path
ENV PYTHONPATH=/app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Run as non-root (distroless default user)
USER nonroot:nonroot
EXPOSE 8000
# No bash, no sh — just the Python binary
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/python3"]
CMD ["-m", "gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
FeatureStandard ImageDistroless Image
Shell (bash/sh)✅ Available❌ None — attacker can't exec
Package manager (apt/pip)✅ Available❌ None — can't install malware
Core utilities (curl, wget, netcat)✅ Available❌ None — can't exfiltrate data
Size (Python app)~180 MB (slim) / ~900 MB (full)~150 MB
CVEs30-120+~10-20 (only runtime libs)
Debuggingdocker exec -it bashkubectl debug / ephemeral containers
Best forDevelopment, debuggingProduction, regulated environments
⚠️ Distroless Requires Multi-Stage

You CANNOT use distroless as a single-stage build — there's no shell to run pip install. You MUST use a multi-stage build: the first stage (with shell) installs everything, the second stage (distroless) copies only the artifacts. The DCA exam may test this constraint.

📝 Chapter 8 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Why is Alpine Linux NOT always the best choice for Python applications?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Alpine uses musl libc instead of glibc. Many Python C-extensions (psycopg2, Pillow, numpy) are compiled against glibc and may fail or behave unexpectedly on musl. Slim images (Debian-based) avoid these issues.

EXPLANATION

Alpine is ~5 MB — incredibly small — but the musl tradeoff means you'll spend hours debugging cryptic C-extension errors. For Django apps, python:3.11-slim is the pragmatic choice: Debian compatibility at a reasonable size.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q2
What's the proper way to chain RUN commands to minimize layers and clean up?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg1 pkg2 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*. All in one RUN — one layer, no cached package lists bloating the image.

EXPLANATION

Separate RUN commands create separate layers. Even if you rm -rf in layer 3, the files still exist in layer 2 (just "deleted" from view). Chaining ensures the cleanup happens in the SAME layer, so the files truly never enter the image.

# RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg1 pkg2 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
Q3
What is a distroless image and when would you use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A distroless image contains ONLY your application and its runtime dependencies — no shell, no package manager, no utilities. It is used for maximum security: no shell means an attacker who compromises your container cannot exec into it.

EXPLANATION

Distroless images are built by Google — only your app, its runtime, and essential libraries. No shell means docker exec cannot work. Debug via logs or kubectl debug with ephemeral containers in Kubernetes.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q4
What command scans a Docker image for known vulnerabilities?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker scout quickview <image> for a summary, docker scout cves <image> for detailed CVEs.

EXPLANATION

Docker Scout replaced docker scan, generating an SBOM and checking every package against vulnerability databases.

# docker scout quickview 
# docker scout cves
Q5
How does a multi-stage build reduce image size?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The first stage includes build tools; the final stage copies only built artifacts. Build tools stay in the discarded first stage, slashing image size by 70-80%.

EXPLANATION

Without multi-stage: either include build tools (850 MB+) or build outside Docker (not reproducible). Multi-stage gives both.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q6
Why should you use --no-cache-dir with pip install in Dockerfiles?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Pip cache stores downloaded packages. In Docker, this cache is never reused (each build is fresh). --no-cache-dir prevents ~100 MB waste.

EXPLANATION

Pip caches wheels in ~/.cache/pip. In Docker builds, cache from previous builds does not carry over — it only wastes layer space.

# --no-cache-dir
# --no-cache-dir
Q7
What's the size difference between python:3.11 and python:3.11-slim?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

python:3.11 is ~900 MB (full Debian with build tools). python:3.11-slim is ~150 MB — 6x smaller, sufficient for running Python web apps.

EXPLANATION

The full image includes GCC, make, git, docs — none needed at runtime. Slim keeps glibc compatibility while removing development cruft.

# python:3.11
# python:3.11-slim
Q8
What Python environment variables help reduce image size?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 prevents .pyc generation. PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 ensures stdout is not buffered for better Docker logging.

EXPLANATION

Python compiles .py to .pyc on first import — wasting space in immutable container filesystems. The first variable skips this.

# PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
# PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
Q9
What is the Scratch base image and when is it appropriate?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Scratch is completely empty (0 bytes). Only for statically-compiled binaries (Go, Rust). No shell, no libc — binary must be fully self-contained.

EXPLANATION

Go example: FROM scratch; COPY --from=builder /app/server /server; CMD ["/server"]. Python/Node/Ruby cannot use Scratch.

# FROM scratch; COPY --from=builder /app/server /server; CMD ["/server"]
Q10
Your production image has 120 CVEs. What's the fastest way to fix most of them?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Rebuild with an updated base image. Most CVEs come from outdated system packages in the base image. Run docker pull python:3.11-slim (get the latest) and rebuild. Then run docker scout quickview to verify the fix.

EXPLANATION

System-level CVEs (in libc, OpenSSL, etc.) come from the base image. Rebuilding with the latest base image picks up all security patches. Application-level CVEs (in pip packages) require updating requirements.txt. Docker Scout recommendations tell you which category each CVE falls into.

# docker pull python:3.11-slim
# docker scout quickview

9.1 Project Structure Review

The anihpj project is a Django 5.2 application with a jobpost app containing 5 models: Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, and User (via Django's auth system).

anihpj Project Structure
  anihpj/
  ├── manage.py                    # Django CLI entry point
  ├── db.sqlite3                   # SQLite database (dev only)
  ├── requirements.txt             # Python dependencies
  ├── anihpj/                      # Django project package
  │   ├── __init__.py
  │   ├── settings.py              # Django settings
  │   ├── urls.py                  # URL routing
  │   ├── wsgi.py                  # WSGI entry point
  │   └── asgi.py                  # ASGI entry point
  └── jobpost/                     # Django app (your application)
      ├── __init__.py
      ├── models.py                # Skills, Author, Location, JobPost

9.2 Writing the Dockerfile

Dockerfile
# === anihpj Production Dockerfile ===
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Set environment variables
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings

WORKDIR /app

# Install system dependencies (if needed)
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc libpq-dev && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Install Python dependencies
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt && \
    apt-get purge -y gcc && \
    apt-get autoremove -y

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Create non-root user
RUN addgroup --system app && \
    adduser --system --group app && \
    chown -R app:app /app
USER app

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]
LineInstructionWhy This Choice
1FROM python:3.11-slimSlim = Debian-based, glibc compatibility. Alpine would break psycopg2 and Pillow C-extensions. Pinned to 3.11, not :latest.
3-5ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1Stops .pyc generation in immutable image layers — saves MBs and prevents unnecessary layer deltas.
7WORKDIR /appCreates /app if missing; all subsequent commands run here. Better than RUN mkdir /app && cd /app.
10-12RUN apt-get install gcc libpq-devlibpq-dev is needed to compile psycopg2 (PostgreSQL driver). gcc is removed after pip install to keep image lean.
15COPY requirements.txt .Copied BEFORE source code — maximizes layer caching. requirements.txt rarely changes.
16-18RUN pip install --no-cache-dir--no-cache-dir prevents ~100 MB wasted pip cache. Purge gcc after install to remove build tool from final image.
21COPY . .Copies application code LAST (changes most frequently). .dockerignore filters out db.sqlite3, __pycache__, .git.
24-26RUN addgroup/adduser + USER appCreates system user (no login, no home dir). Switches from root — defense-in-depth security. Must chown app files.
28EXPOSE 8000Documentation — tells readers the app listens on 8000. Does NOT publish the port; use -p 8000:8000 at runtime.
30-31CMD ["gunicorn", ...]Gunicorn = production WSGI server. NOT runserver. --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 accepts external connections. --workers 3 = 3 worker processes.
💡 Why Not Alpine for Django?

Alpine is 5 MB — incredibly tempting! But it uses musl libc instead of glibc. Many Python C-extensions (psycopg2, Pillow, numpy, lxml) are pre-compiled for glibc. On Alpine, they either fail to install or crash at runtime with cryptic errors. Slim images keep glibc compatibility while stripping development cruft — the pragmatic sweet spot for Python web apps.

9.3 Writing .dockerignore

.dockerignore
# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.egg-info/

# Django
*.sqlite3
media/
staticfiles/

# Virtual Environment
env/
venv/

# Git
.git/
.gitignore

# IDE
.vscode/
.idea/

# OS
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# Docker
Dockerfile
.dockerignore
docker-compose*.yml
EntryWhat It ExcludesWhy Exclude It
__pycache__/, *.py[cod]Python bytecode cacheGenerated at runtime — baking stale .pyc from your machine wastes space and may cause version mismatch errors.
*.sqlite3SQLite database files🛑 CRITICAL: Contains local dev data. If baked into image, it's in your registry forever — a data leak. Production uses PostgreSQL.
media/, staticfiles/Uploaded files, collected staticGenerated content — media can be GBs of uploads. Static should be collected during build, not copied from dev machine.
env/, venv/Python virtual environmentsLocal venv has machine-specific binaries. The image creates its own Python environment during pip install.
.git/Git repository metadata.git can be hundreds of MBs of commit history — no place in production, and could leak source history.
.vscode/, .idea/IDE configurationEditor settings irrelevant to the container. Adds noise and potential local path references.
Dockerfile, .dockerignoreDocker build filesBuild instructions, not application code. Including them leaks your build configuration unnecessarily.
.DS_Store, Thumbs.dbOS metadata filesmacOS/Windows auto-generated binary junk — zero value inside a Linux container.
🛑 The .dockerignore Security Rule

If you have a .env file with secrets, ALWAYS add it to .dockerignore. A single COPY . . without protection bakes secrets into the image — visible via docker history or registry pull. Secrets belong in runtime injection (docker run -e, Docker secrets, Kubernetes Secrets), NEVER in images.

9.6 Debugging When Things Go Wrong

Every Docker + Django developer encounters these issues. Here's your troubleshooting reference — 10 common problems with their causes and exact debug commands:

#SymptomLikely CauseDebug Command
1Container exits immediatelyWrong CMD, missing file, syntax errordocker logs <id>
2Port already in useAnother process using port 8000docker run -p 8001:8000 ... or lsof -i :8000
3Module not found: 'anihpj'Wrong WORKDIR or COPY pathdocker exec <id> ls /app && docker exec <id> pwd
4Django settings errorMissing DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE envdocker exec <id> env | grep DJANGO
5Database connection refusedDB_HOST pointing to localhostUse service name in compose, not localhost
6Permission deniedRunning as non-root without chownRUN chown -R app:app /app before USER app
7Static files 404 (white page)collectstatic not run or wrong STATIC_ROOTdocker exec <id> python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
8Gunicorn workers timing outRequest taking too long, worker count too lowIncrease --timeout 120 and --workers 4
9Image build fails on pip installMissing system deps (gcc, libpq-dev)Add RUN apt-get install -y gcc libpq-dev before pip
10Container runs but health check failsWrong HEALTHCHECK endpoint or portdocker inspect <id> | grep -A10 Health
🔧 Debugging Workflow: The 3-Step Method

Step 1: docker ps -a — find the container. Step 2: docker logs <id> — read what happened. Step 3: docker inspect <id> | grep -A20 State — check exit code, OOM status, error. 90% of issues are solved with these three commands. For the other 10%: docker exec -it <id> bash and explore interactively.

9.7 The Complete anihpj Dockerfile (Final Version)

After applying all optimizations from Chapters 7-8, here's the final production Dockerfile:

Dockerfile (Final Optimized)
# Stage 1: Build
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Run (slim, no build tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
COPY . .
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/')"
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]

⚠️ Chapter 9 Exam Gotchas

  • Django DEBUG=True in production → Always set DEBUG=False via environment variable. DEBUG=True exposes sensitive info.
  • Binding to 127.0.0.1 inside container → Gunicorn must bind to 0.0.0.0:8000, not 127.0.0.1, or the port won't be reachable.
  • Forgetting collectstatic → Django won't serve static files without running collectstatic during the build.

📝 Chapter 9 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What is the purpose of PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 in a Dockerfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Prevents Python from writing .pyc bytecode files to disk. In a Docker container, these cached files are unnecessary (the container is ephemeral) and waste space. Saves several MBs in the final image.

EXPLANATION

Python normally compiles .py to .pyc on first import and stores them in __pycache__/. In a Docker image, these files: (1) add MBs of bloat, (2) are never reused across container instances, and (3) create unnecessary layer deltas. Setting this env var tells Python to skip bytecode generation entirely.

# PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
# __pycache__/
Q2
Why create a non-root user in your Dockerfile instead of running as root?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Running as root is a security risk — if an attacker exploits your app, they get root access inside the container. A non-root user limits the damage. Create with RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app then USER app.

EXPLANATION

Docker containers share the host kernel. A root user inside a container has UID 0 — the same as host root. While namespaces provide some isolation, kernel vulnerabilities could allow container escape. Running as non-root is defense-in-depth: even if your app is compromised, the attacker starts with minimal privileges.

# RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app
Q3
What does the HEALTHCHECK instruction do in a Dockerfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It defines a command that Docker runs periodically to check if the container is healthy. The exit code determines health: 0 = healthy, 1 = unhealthy. Docker reports the status in docker ps and can auto-restart unhealthy containers.

EXPLANATION

Without HEALTHCHECK, Docker only knows if the process is running — not if it's actually working. A Django app might have gunicorn running but be stuck in a deadlock. HEALTHCHECK catches this: HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/ || exit 1. Docker shows status as (healthy), (unhealthy), or (starting).

# HEALTHCHECK
# docker ps
# HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/ || exit 1
# (healthy)
# (unhealthy)
Q4
Why should *.sqlite3 be in .dockerignore for a Django project?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

SQLite database files contain local development data, can be large (100+ MB), and should never be baked into a production image. Production uses PostgreSQL, not SQLite. Including it bloats the image and may leak data.

EXPLANATION

This is a real-world security incident waiting to happen. Developers often run python manage.py migrate locally, creating a db.sqlite3 with real-looking test data. If this gets baked into the image via COPY . ., it's now in your registry — accessible to anyone with pull access. Always exclude database files, media uploads, and any stateful data from Docker images.

# *.sqlite3
# python manage.py migrate
Q5
How do you run Django database migrations inside a running container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker exec anihpj-container python manage.py migrate. This runs the migration inside the already-running container where Django and all dependencies are available.

EXPLANATION

Migrations must run inside the container because: (1) the container has the exact Python version and dependencies, (2) the container has access to the database network, and (3) you avoid "works on my machine" issues. In production, migrations are often run as an init container or a one-shot Job in Kubernetes — never baked into the CMD.

# docker exec anihpj-container python manage.py migrate
Q6
Your container runs but you get "Connection refused" when accessing localhost:8000. Why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The app inside the container might be listening on 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0. 127.0.0.1 only accepts connections from within the container — not from the host. Always bind to 0.0.0.0 in containerized apps.

EXPLANATION

This is the #1 Docker networking gotcha. 127.0.0.1 means "only accept connections from localhost within this network namespace." Since the container has its own network namespace, the host is external. 0.0.0.0 means "accept connections on all interfaces." Gunicorn's default is 127.0.0.1:8000 — always override with --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 in Docker.

# 127.0.0.1
# 127.0.0.1
# 127.0.0.1
# 127.0.0.1:8000
# --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
Q7
Why use gunicorn instead of Django's manage.py runserver in production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

runserver is single-threaded, not designed for production, and explicitly warns "DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION." Gunicorn is a production WSGI server: multi-worker, handles concurrent requests, battle-tested.

EXPLANATION

runserver is a development convenience — it auto-reloads, serves static files, and shows debug pages. But it: (1) handles ONE request at a time, (2) has no timeout/keepalive settings, (3) leaks memory, and (4) has known security issues with --insecure static file serving. Gunicorn uses pre-fork worker model: one master + N worker processes for true concurrency.

# manage.py runserver
# runserver
# runserver
# --insecure
Q8
What command shows what's happening inside a container that's failing to start?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker logs <container-id> shows stdout/stderr from the container. Even if the container has exited, logs persist. This is the first debugging step for any container issue.

EXPLANATION

For containers that exit instantly, use docker ps -a to find the exited container ID, then docker logs <id>. Common issues visible in logs: syntax errors, missing modules (ModuleNotFoundError), wrong WORKDIR (can't find manage.py), or port binding failures. Also check docker inspect <id> | grep -A5 State for exit codes.

# docker logs 
# docker ps -a
# docker logs 
# ModuleNotFoundError
# can't find manage.py
Q9
What does --no-install-recommends do in apt-get?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It tells apt-get to install only the explicitly requested packages, NOT their "recommended" packages. This can save 50-200 MB in the final image. Recommended packages are often documentation, optional utilities, and non-essential libraries.

EXPLANATION

Debian packaging distinguishes between Depends (must install) and Recommends (should install). Without --no-install-recommends, a simple apt-get install python3 pulls in ~200 MB of documentation, man pages, and optional libs. With the flag, only the strictly required packages are installed. Always combine with rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* to clean the package index.

# --no-install-recommends
# --no-install-recommends
# apt-get install python3
# rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
Q10
What's the difference between development and production Dockerfiles for Django?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Dev: uses runserver, bind mounts for hot reload, DEBUG=True, includes dev tools. Prod: uses gunicorn, copies all code into image, DEBUG=False, non-root user, HEALTHCHECK, optimized layers. Dev = fast iteration; Prod = security + performance.

EXPLANATION

A common pattern is a single Dockerfile with a dev target: docker build --target dev -t anihpj:dev . using multi-stage. The dev stage mounts code via volume, reinstalls dependencies on change, and uses runserver. The prod stage is fully self-contained. This avoids maintaining two separate Dockerfiles.

# runserver
# docker build --target dev -t anihpj:dev .

Chapter 10: Docker Compose Fundamentals

Docker Compose is how you run MULTIPLE containers as a single application. Instead of remembering 4+ docker run commands, you declare everything in one YAML file and start it with one command. This is the foundation of modern containerized development.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🎼 Compose🎯 DCA 20%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand what Docker Compose is and when to use it
  • ✅ Compare Compose vs raw docker run commands
  • ✅ Install and verify Docker Compose v2
  • ✅ Master every section of a compose.yaml file
  • ✅ Understand the DNS-powered automatic networking
COMPOSE vs DOCKER RUN — Multi-Container Simplification
WITHOUT COMPOSE — 4 separate commands:
docker network create anihpj-net
docker run -d --name postgres --network anihpj-net -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pass postgres:15
docker run -d --name redis --network anihpj-net redis:7
docker run -d --name django --network anihpj-net -p 8000:8000 anihpj:v1

WITH COMPOSE — 1 file, 1 command:
docker compose up -d
# All services, networks, volumes defined in compose.yaml

10.1 What is Docker Compose?

Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications. You write a compose.yaml (or docker-compose.yml) file that describes all your services, networks, and volumes — then start everything with docker compose up.

Real-world use case: anihpj needs 4 services to run — Django (app), PostgreSQL (database), Redis (cache), and Nginx (reverse proxy). Without Compose, you'd run 4 separate docker run commands, manually create a network, and manage startup order. With Compose: one file, one command.

Docker Compose — One Command, Four Containers
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  🎼 docker compose up — THE MAGIC                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐                                         │
  │  │  compose.yaml               │     ONE COMMAND:                        │
  │  │                             │     $ docker compose up -d              │
  │  │  services:                  │                                         │
  │  │    django:   build: .       │         │                               │
  │  │    postgres: image: pg:15   │         │                               │
  │  │    redis:    image: redis:7 │         ▼                               │
  │  │    nginx:    image: nginx   │                                         │
  │  └─────────────┬───────────────┘                                         │
  │                │                                                         │
  │                ▼                                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                    🐳 DOCKER HOST                                │    │
  │  │                                                                  │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐        │    │
  │  │  │ 🐍 Django │  │ 🐘 Postgres│ │ 🔴 Redis  │  │ 🟢 Nginx  │        │    │
  │  │  │  :8000   │  │  :5432   │  │  :6379   │  │  :80     │        │    │
  │  │  │          │  │          │  │          │  │          │        │    │
  │  │  │ anihpj   │  │ anihpj_db│  │ cache    │  │ reverse  │        │    │
  │  │  │ app      │  │ data 📂  │  │ backend  │  │ proxy    │        │    │
  │  │  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘        │    │
  │  │       └─────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────┘              │    │
  │  │                        │                                        │    │
  │  │           anihpj_default (auto-created network)                 │    │
  │  │           DNS: "django", "postgres", "redis", "nginx"           │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  🌐 Browser → http://localhost:80 → nginx → django:8000 → postgres:5432 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝
Declarative Configuration

Compose files are declarative — you describe the DESIRED state (4 containers, specific images, ports, volumes), and Docker figures out HOW to achieve it. This is the same philosophy as Kubernetes and Terraform.

🔄
Infrastructure as Code

Your compose.yaml lives in Git alongside your source code. Anyone on your team can clone the repo and run docker compose up — they get the EXACT same environment. No more "works on my machine" issues.

🏃
Level 1
docker run

One container per command. Manual networking. Shell scripts for startup order.

⚠️ Works but fragile
🎼
Level 2
docker compose

Multiple containers from one YAML file. Auto DNS networking. One command: up.

✅ Dev & single-server prod
☸️
Level 3
Kubernetes

Multi-node orchestration. Auto-scaling, rolling updates, self-healing. Cloud-native.

🏆 Production at scale

10.2 Docker Compose vs docker run

Why use Compose when you can just run docker run four times? Because Compose handles networking, startup order, configuration, and teardown automatically:

Aspectdocker rundocker compose
Containers per command1 container per commandMultiple in one file ✅
NetworkingManual (docker network create)Auto-created DNS network ✅
Startup OrderManual (wait + run sequence)depends_on + health checks ✅
ConfigurationCLI flags onlyDeclarative YAML file ✅
ReproducibilityShell script dependentcompose.yaml = single source ✅
Tear Downdocker rm for each containerdocker compose down (all at once) ✅
Environment Vars-e flag per container.env file + env_file key ✅
Volumes-v flag per mountvolumes: section (declarative) ✅
Team SharingShare shell scriptsShare compose.yaml (Git) ✅
Production Ready❌ No⚠️ Dev only (use K8s/Swarm for prod)

10.3 Installing Docker Compose

Docker Compose v2 is now built into Docker Desktop and available as docker compose (note: no hyphen!). On Linux, it's a plugin installed separately:

TERMINAL
# Docker Desktop (Windows/macOS): Already included — just use:
$ docker compose version
Docker Compose version v2.27.0

# Linux: Install as plugin
$ sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install docker-compose-plugin
# OR download binary:
$ sudo curl -SL "https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/latest/download/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
$ sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose

# Verify installation
$ docker compose version
$ docker-compose --version  # legacy (v1) syntax — still works
📖 Compose v1 vs v2

Compose v1 (docker-compose with hyphen) was a standalone Python script. Compose v2 (docker compose without hyphen) is a Docker CLI plugin written in Go — faster, better integrated, and actively maintained. Always use v2 for new projects. The v1 syntax (docker-compose up) still works for backward compatibility.

10.4 The compose.yaml File Structure

A compose.yaml file has 6 top-level sections. Here's the complete anatomy — every key you'll encounter on the DCA exam:

compose.yaml Anatomy — Every Key Explained
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    📋 compose.yaml ANATOMY                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ services:              ← CONTAINERS: your app stack               │   │
  │  │   django:              ← Service name (becomes DNS hostname!)     │   │
  │  │     build: .           ← Build from Dockerfile in current dir     │   │
  │  │     image: anihpj:v1   ← OR use pre-built image                   │   │
  │  │     ports:             ← Port mapping (HOST:CONTAINER)            │   │
  │  │       - "8000:8000"    ← Host 8000 → Container 8000               │   │
  │  │     environment:       ← Environment variables                    │   │
  │  │       - DEBUG=False    ← (use .env file for secrets!)             │   │
  │  │     volumes:           ← Mount storage                            │   │
  │  │       - ./src:/app     ← Bind mount (dev)                         │   │
  │  │       - static:/static ← Named volume (prod)                      │   │
  │  │     depends_on:        ← Startup order (NOT readiness!)           │   │
  │  │       postgres:        ← Wait for postgres container to START     │   │
  │  │         condition:     ← v2.1+: can wait for health check         │   │
  │  │           service_healthy                                        │   │
  │  │     healthcheck:       ← Container health monitoring              │   │
  │  │       test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/"]        │   │
  │  │       interval: 30s    ← Check every 30 seconds                   │   │
  │  │       retries: 3       ← 3 failures = unhealthy                   │   │
  │  │     restart: always    ← Restart policy                           │   │
  │  │     networks:          ← Which networks to join                   │   │
  │  │       - backend        ← Django on backend network                │   │
  │  │       - frontend       ← Django also on frontend (for nginx)      │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │ networks:              ← CUSTOM NETWORKS                           │   │
  │  │   backend:             ← Internal network (DB, Redis, Django)      │   │
  │  │     driver: bridge     ← Network driver                            │   │
  │  │   frontend:            ← External network (Nginx, Django)          │   │
  │  │     driver: bridge     ← Standard bridge network                   │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │ volumes:               ← NAMED VOLUMES                             │   │
  │  │   postgres_data:       ← Persists DB data across restarts          │   │
  │  │   static:              ← Persists collected static files           │   │
  │  │   media:               ← Persists user uploads                     │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │ secrets:               ← SWARM SECRETS (encrypted at rest)         │   │
  │  │   db_password:         ← Sensitive data — never in plain text!     │   │
  │  │     external: true     ← Pre-created: docker secret create        │   │
  │  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
  │  │ configs:               ← CONFIGURATION FILES (Swarm)               │   │
  │  │   nginx_conf:          ← Nginx configuration as config object      │   │
  │  │     file: ./nginx.conf ← Source file on host                       │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🐳
services

The containers that make up your app. Each service runs one image. Service names become DNS hostnames on the Compose network — Django can reach PostgreSQL at postgres:5432.

🌐
networks

Custom networks for isolation. The backend network connects Django + DB + Redis (internal). The frontend network connects Nginx + Django (external-facing).

💾
volumes

Named volumes persist data. Without volumes, PostgreSQL data disappears on docker compose down. Named volumes survive container restarts, recreations, and teardowns.

🔐
configs & secrets

Swarm-only features for secure configuration management. Secrets are encrypted at rest and only mounted into authorized services. For non-Swarm: use .env files + env_file.

⚠️ Chapter 10 Exam Gotchas

  • depends_on without healthcheck condition → depends_on only waits for container START, not READY. Use condition: service_healthy.
  • Hardcoding credentials in compose.yaml → Use .env file or Docker secrets for credentials. compose.yaml should reference vars.
  • Forgetting networks in compose → Services on different custom networks can't communicate. Use a shared network.

📝 Chapter 10 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What is Docker Compose and what problem does it solve?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a YAML file. It solves the problem of managing multiple containers that need to work together — networking, startup order, configuration, and teardown — all from one file and one command.

EXPLANATION

Without Compose, running a Django+PostgreSQL+Redis+Nginx stack requires 4+ docker run commands, manual docker network create, and shell scripts for startup order. Compose consolidates all of this into a single compose.yaml file that lives in Git — any developer can clone and run docker compose up.

# docker run
# docker network create
# compose.yaml
# docker compose up
Q2
What's the difference between docker compose (v2) and docker-compose (v1)?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

v2 (docker compose, no hyphen) is a Docker CLI plugin written in Go — faster, built into Docker Desktop. v1 (docker-compose, with hyphen) was a standalone Python script, now deprecated. Always use v2 for new projects.

EXPLANATION

The key difference is integration: v2 runs as part of the Docker CLI, sharing authentication and contexts. v1 was a separate binary that needed its own configuration. The DCA exam focuses on v2 syntax. All commands work the same (up, down, ps, logs), just the invocation differs.

# docker compose
# docker-compose
# docker compose
# docker-compose
Q3
How do service names work as DNS hostnames in Compose?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Compose automatically creates a Docker network and registers each service name as a DNS entry. Django can reach PostgreSQL at postgres:5432, Redis at redis:6379, and Nginx at nginx:80 — using the service name as the hostname. No IP addresses needed.

EXPLANATION

This is Docker's embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11. When a container resolves postgres, Docker's DNS returns the container IP of the postgres service. This is why you set DATABASE_HOST=postgres in Django settings — not localhost or an IP. The DNS name is the Compose service name.

# postgres:5432
# redis:6379
# 127.0.0.11
# DATABASE_HOST=postgres
# localhost
Q4
What are the 6 top-level sections of a compose.yaml file?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

services (containers), networks (custom networks), volumes (persistent storage), configs (config files, Swarm), secrets (sensitive data, Swarm), and name (project name override). Only services is required — all others are optional.

EXPLANATION

For the DCA exam, focus on services, networks, and volumes — these are the three you'll use daily. Configs and secrets are Swarm-mode features (not available in plain Compose). The name key was added in Compose v2.3+ to override the default project name (which is the directory name).

# services
# name
Q5
What does docker compose up -d do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Starts all services defined in compose.yaml in detached mode (background). It creates any needed networks and volumes, builds images if build: is specified, then starts all containers. The -d flag runs everything in the background so you get your terminal back.

EXPLANATION

Without -d, Compose runs in the foreground and streams all logs to your terminal — useful for debugging. With -d, containers run in the background like daemons. To see logs later: docker compose logs -f. To stop everything: docker compose down.

# docker compose up -d
# docker compose logs -f
# docker compose down
Q6
What's the difference between docker compose down and docker compose stop?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

stop stops containers but KEEPS networks, volumes, and container definitions. down stops containers AND removes networks and containers (but NOT volumes by default). To remove volumes too: docker compose down -v.

EXPLANATION

stop = pause (can start later). down = destroy (need to up again). Always use down for cleanup. The -v flag is dangerous — it deletes named volumes including database data. Only use it when you want to reset completely.

# docker compose down
# docker compose stop
# docker compose down -v
Q7
Where does Compose look for the compose file by default?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Compose looks for compose.yaml or docker-compose.yml in the current directory. It also automatically merges compose.override.yaml if present. Use -f to specify a different file.

EXPLANATION

The search order is: compose.yaml → compose.yml → docker-compose.yaml → docker-compose.yml. The override file (compose.override.yaml) is merged automatically — this is how you layer dev overrides on top of a base configuration without modifying the base file.

# compose.yaml
# docker-compose.yml
# compose.override.yaml
# compose.yaml
# compose.yml
Q8
How do you pass environment variables to Compose services?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Three ways: (1) environment: key directly in compose.yaml, (2) env_file: pointing to a .env file, (3) variables already set in your shell are automatically available. For secrets like database passwords, use env_file with .env (and add .env to .gitignore).

EXPLANATION

environment: is for non-sensitive config (DEBUG, LOG_LEVEL). env_file: loads from an external file — better for secrets because the file can be gitignored. Shell variables work because Compose does variable substitution: POSTGRES_PASSWORD=${DB_PASS} pulls from your shell or .env file.

# environment:
# env_file:
# .gitignore
# environment:
# env_file:
Q9
What command shows the status of all services in a Compose project?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose ps — shows container ID, name, image, command, service, status (running/exited), and ports for every service in the project.

EXPLANATION

Unlike docker ps (which shows ALL containers), docker compose ps only shows containers belonging to the current project. The project name defaults to the directory name. Use docker compose ps -a to also see stopped containers. Use docker compose ps --format json for scripting.

# docker compose ps
# docker ps
# docker compose ps
# docker compose ps -a
# docker compose ps --format json
Q10
What happens to named volumes when you run docker compose down?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Named volumes are preserved — they survive down. This is intentional: your database data persists across restarts. To remove volumes: docker compose down -v (destructive — deletes all data). Anonymous volumes (no name) ARE removed with down.

EXPLANATION

Named volumes (declared in the top-level volumes: section) persist indefinitely until explicitly deleted with docker volume rm or docker compose down -v. Anonymous volumes (inline in a service's volumes: without a top-level declaration) are removed by down. For production data, always use named volumes.

# docker compose down
# docker compose down -v
# docker volume rm
# docker compose down -v

Chapter 11: Compose for anihpj — The Complete Full Stack

Let's put Compose to work. We'll build the complete anihpj stack — Django + PostgreSQL + Redis + Nginx — all defined in one compose.yaml, all starting with one command. This is your real-world reference for any Django application.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🐍 Django🏗️ Hands-On

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Design a 4-service architecture for a Django application
  • ✅ Write a complete compose.yaml with all services
  • ✅ Configure Nginx as a reverse proxy for Django
  • ✅ Manage environment variables and secrets securely
  • ✅ Run the full stack and debug common Compose issues

11.1 Planning the anihpj Stack

The anihpj project needs 4 services to run in production-like mode: Django (application), PostgreSQL (relational database), Redis (cache/sessions), and Nginx (reverse proxy + static files). Here's how they connect:

anihpj Compose Stack — 4 Services Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               🏗️ anihpj DOCKER COMPOSE STACK                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │                    🌐 EXTERNAL TRAFFIC                             │   │
  │  │                    http://localhost:80                             │   │
  │  └────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                   │                                      │
  │                                   ▼                                      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │  🟢 NGINX (port 80 → django:8000)                               │    │
  │  │  Serves: /static/* (from static volume)                         │    │
  │  │  Proxies: /* → django:8000 (all requests to Django)             │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘    │
  │                                     │                                    │
  │                  ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐                │
  │                  ▼                                      ▼                │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  🐍 DJANGO (port 8000)        │  │  🔴 REDIS (port 6379)         │  │
  │  │  • anihpj project             │  │  • Django cache backend       │  │
  │  │  • jobpost app (5 models)     │  │  • Celery message broker      │  │
  │  │  • Gunicorn WSGI server       │  │  • Session storage            │  │
  │  └──────────────┬────────────────┘  └───────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                 │                                                       │
  │                 ▼                                                       │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐                                      │
  │  │  🐘 POSTGRESQL (port 5432)    │                                      │
  │  │  • Database: anihpj_db        │  💾 Volume: postgres_data            │
  │  │  • All Django model data      │     /var/lib/postgresql/data         │
  │  │  • User accounts & auth       │     PERSISTENT across restarts!      │
  │  │  • Job posts, skills, etc.    │                                      │
  │  └───────────────────────────────┘                                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  NETWORKS: frontend (nginx+django) + backend (django+postgres+redis)    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

11.2 compose.yaml — Django + PostgreSQL Service

Start with the two core services. Django needs PostgreSQL to be running first — depends_on handles this:

compose.yaml (Django + Postgres)
services:
  # ─── PostgreSQL Database ───
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    container_name: anihpj_db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: anihpj
      POSTGRES_USER: anihpj_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"           # Expose for external tools (DBeaver, pgAdmin)
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U anihpj_user -d anihpj"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      - backend

  # ─── Django Application ───
  django:
    build: .                   # Builds from Dockerfile in current dir
    container_name: anihpj_app
    command: gunicorn anihpj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 3
    environment:
      - DEBUG=False
      - DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://anihpj_user:${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}@postgres:5432/anihpj
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/app/static
      - media_volume:/app/media
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy  # Wait for health check, not just "started"!
    networks:
      - backend
      - frontend

volumes:
  postgres_data:
  static_volume:
  media_volume:

networks:
  backend:
    driver: bridge
  frontend:
    driver: bridge
⚠️ depends_on ≠ Ready

depends_on without condition: service_healthy only waits for the container to START — not for PostgreSQL to be ready to accept connections. Always add a healthcheck to PostgreSQL and use condition: service_healthy in depends_on. Otherwise Django may try to connect before PostgreSQL is initialized, causing a crash loop.

11.3 Adding Redis & Nginx Services

Redis provides caching and session storage. Nginx serves as the reverse proxy — handling static files directly and proxying all other requests to Django:

compose.yaml (Full 4-Service Stack)
  # ─── Redis Cache ───
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    container_name: anihpj_redis
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    networks:
      - backend
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      retries: 5

  # ─── Nginx Reverse Proxy ───
  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    container_name: anihpj_nginx
    ports:
      - "80:80"                # Expose to host — access at http://localhost
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro  # Custom config
      - static_volume:/static:ro                         # Serve static files
      - media_volume:/media:ro                           # Serve media files
    depends_on:
      - django
    networks:
      - frontend
nginx.conf
upstream django_app {
    server django:8000;           # Compose DNS resolves "django" to container IP
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name localhost;

    # Static files — Nginx serves directly (FAST)
    location /static/ {
        alias /static/;
        expires 30d;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
    }

    # Media files — uploaded by users
    location /media/ {
        alias /media/;
    }

    # Everything else → Django
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://django_app;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}
🏆 The Power of Compose DNS

Notice server django:8000; in nginx.conf — this works because Compose creates a DNS network where django resolves to the Django container's IP. No hardcoded IPs. No port mapping needed between services — they communicate directly on the internal network. This is the magic that makes Compose files portable across machines.

11.4 Environment Variables & Secrets in Compose

Never put secrets in compose.yaml. Use a .env file (gitignored) and reference variables with ${VAR} syntax:

.env
# anihpj environment variables — NEVER commit this file!
DB_PASSWORD=super_secret_db_password_123
SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-abc123xyz789
DEBUG=False
ALLOWED_HOSTS=localhost,127.0.0.1
REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0
🛑 The .env Security Rule

ALWAYS add .env to .gitignore. A committed .env file with database passwords is one of the most common security incidents in Docker projects. Provide a .env.example file instead — with placeholder values — so new developers know what variables to set.

11.6 Development Workflow with Docker Compose

Compose isn't just for running stacks — it's your daily development driver. Here's the workflow that replaces python manage.py runserver with a full production-like environment:

Development Workflow with Compose
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🔄 COMPOSE DEVELOPMENT WORKFLOW                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐          │
  │  │  ✏️ Edit  │───▶│  👀 Watch │───▶│  🔄 Sync │───▶│  🧪 Test  │          │
  │  │  Code    │    │  Changes │    │  to      │    │  Results  │          │
  │  │          │    │          │    │  Container│    │          │          │
  │  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  1. Edit views.py          3. Changes sync instantly to container       │
  │  2. Compose watch detects   4. Browser refresh → see changes!            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  OR with bind mounts (traditional approach):                             │
  │  volumes: - .:/app  →  changes reflect immediately (no rebuild needed)  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Running tests:                                                          │
  │  $ docker compose run django python manage.py test jobpost               │
  │  $ docker compose run django pytest                                      │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Debugging:                                                              │
  │  $ docker compose exec django bash              # Interactive shell      │
  │  $ docker compose exec django python manage.py shell  # Django shell    │
  │  $ docker compose exec postgres psql -U anihpj_user anihpj  # DB shell  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🏆 The Compose Development Advantage

Instead of installing PostgreSQL, Redis, and configuring them locally, you get a production-like environment with ONE command. Your entire team runs the same stack. No more "it works on my machine but not in staging" — your dev environment IS your staging environment, just with debug mode and volume mounts. This is the modern development workflow that the DCA exam expects you to understand.

📝 Chapter 11 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Why does the anihpj stack need 4 separate services instead of one?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Separation of concerns: each service has one job. Django handles HTTP requests, PostgreSQL stores data, Redis caches, Nginx serves static files and proxies. You can scale, update, or replace each independently. This follows the microservices principle even for a monolithic Django app.

EXPLANATION

The alternative — putting everything in one container — is an anti-pattern. One container = one process. A single container with Django+Postgres+Redis+Nginx would be impossible to manage, scale, or debug. Compose makes it trivial to run them as separate containers that communicate over a shared network.

# compose.yaml:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
Q2
Why use condition: service_healthy instead of plain depends_on?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Plain depends_on only waits for the container to START — not for the service inside to be ready. PostgreSQL starts its container instantly but takes 2-5 seconds to initialize the database and accept connections. condition: service_healthy waits until the healthcheck passes — meaning PostgreSQL is actually accepting queries.

EXPLANATION

Without service_healthy, Django tries to connect to PostgreSQL immediately after the container starts. PostgreSQL isn't ready yet → Django crashes → Docker restarts Django → it crashes again. This "crash loop" is one of the most common Compose issues. A healthcheck solves it: pg_isready returns success only when PostgreSQL is accepting connections.

# condition: service_healthy
# depends_on
# depends_on
# condition: service_healthy
# service_healthy
Q3
Why does Nginx reference server django:8000 instead of an IP address?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Compose's embedded DNS resolves service names to container IPs. django is the service name in compose.yaml, so it becomes a DNS hostname. This works across container restarts and IP changes — the DNS is always updated. No hardcoded IPs needed.

EXPLANATION

Docker's embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 handles name resolution. When Nginx resolves django, Docker returns the current IP of the django container. If the container restarts with a new IP, DNS updates automatically. This is why Compose configuration is portable — it works on any machine regardless of IP assignments.

# server django:8000
# 127.0.0.11
Q4
Why should .env never be committed to Git?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

.env contains secrets: database passwords, Django SECRET_KEY, API keys. Once committed to Git, these secrets are in the repository forever — accessible to anyone with repo access. Even if you delete the file later, it's still in git history. Always add .env to .gitignore.

EXPLANATION

Provide a .env.example file with placeholder values instead: DB_PASSWORD=changeme, SECRET_KEY=your-secret-key-here. This tells developers what variables are needed without exposing real secrets. Tools like git-secrets can scan commits to prevent accidental .env commits.

# .gitignore
# .env.example
# DB_PASSWORD=changeme
# SECRET_KEY=your-secret-key-here
# git-secrets
Q5
How do you run Django management commands inside a Compose service?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose exec django python manage.py migrate. exec runs a command inside an already-running service container. For one-off commands that need a fresh container: docker compose run django python manage.py createsuperuser.

EXPLANATION

The difference: exec runs in the existing container (fast, shared state). run creates a NEW container from the same image and configuration (isolated, disposable). Use run for interactive commands (createsuperuser, shell) and exec for operational commands (migrate, collectstatic).

# docker compose exec django python manage.py migrate
# docker compose run django python manage.py createsuperuser
# createsuperuser
# collectstatic
Q6
What does Nginx's location /static/ block do and why is it important?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Nginx serves static files (CSS, JS, images) directly from disk — bypassing Django entirely. This is MUCH faster: Nginx can serve thousands of static files per second with almost zero CPU, while Django would use a Python worker process for each request. It also reduces load on Django workers.

EXPLANATION

In production, Django should NEVER serve static files. Nginx is purpose-built for this — it uses sendfile() syscalls for zero-copy I/O. The static files are collected during build (python manage.py collectstatic) and mounted into Nginx via the static_volume named volume, shared between the django and nginx services.

# location /static/
# python manage.py collectstatic
# static_volume
Q7
What command shows logs for only the Django service?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose logs django — shows stdout/stderr from the django service only. Add -f to follow (stream), --tail 50 for last 50 lines, or --since 10m for last 10 minutes. For multiple services: docker compose logs django postgres.

EXPLANATION

Compose aggregates logs from all services. docker compose logs (no service name) shows everything — useful for debugging cross-service issues. docker compose logs -f streams all logs with color-coded service names. The logs come from each container's stdout/stderr — make sure your Django app logs to stdout for this to work.

# docker compose logs django
# --tail 50
# --since 10m
# docker compose logs django postgres
# docker compose logs
Q8
What's the difference between docker compose down and docker compose down -v?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

down stops containers and removes networks — but PRESERVES named volumes (your database data survives). down -v also DELETES all named volumes — wiping your database. Use down for normal shutdown; use down -v only when you want a complete reset.

EXPLANATION

Named volumes (postgres_data) persist across down/up cycles. down -v deletes them. This is a common "where did my data go?" moment for beginners. Tip: use docker volume ls to see all volumes, and docker compose down --volumes (same as -v) only when you're sure.

# docker compose down
# docker compose down -v
# postgres_data
# docker volume ls
# docker compose down --volumes
Q9
How would you add a healthcheck to the Django service?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Add to the django service: healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/health/"]; interval: 30s; timeout: 5s; retries: 3. This requires a /health/ endpoint in Django that returns 200 OK. Without that endpoint, use CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/')".

EXPLANATION

A Django healthcheck endpoint should be lightweight — don't query the database or make external calls. Just return HTTP 200: return HttpResponse("OK"). If it hits the DB, a slow query could cause the healthcheck to fail, making Docker think the container is unhealthy and restarting it unnecessarily.

# healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/health/"]; interval: 30s; timeout: 5s; retries: 3
# CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/')"
# return HttpResponse("OK")
Q10
How do you rebuild a Compose service after changing its Dockerfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose build django rebuilds the django service's image. Then docker compose up -d recreates the container with the new image. Or in one command: docker compose up -d --build rebuilds images for services with build: and restarts them.

EXPLANATION

docker compose up only rebuilds if the image doesn't exist locally. --build forces a rebuild. You can also use docker compose build --no-cache to force a full rebuild ignoring all cache layers. For hot-reload during development, use volume mounts (.:/app) instead of rebuilding — code changes reflect instantly.

# docker compose build django
# docker compose up -d
# docker compose up -d --build
# docker compose up
# docker compose build --no-cache
