Chapter 12: Docker Compose Advanced Features

Now that you can build a full stack, let's master Compose's advanced capabilities: profiles for environment-specific services, multiple Compose files for overrides, deep networking control, proper health-check-based startup ordering, hot reload with watch mode, and scaling.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours⚙️ Advanced🎯 DCA 10%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Use profiles to conditionally include services
  • ✅ Override config with multiple Compose files
  • ✅ Master Compose networking — custom networks, DNS, isolation
  • ✅ Write proper health checks and depends_on conditions
  • ✅ Use docker compose watch for hot reload development
  • ✅ Scale services to multiple replicas

12.1 Compose Profiles — Environment-Specific Services

Not all services need to run in every environment. Profiles let you tag services and include them only when a specific profile is active:

compose.yaml (with profiles)
services:
  django:
    build: .
    # No profile = always runs (default profile)

  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    # No profile = always runs

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    # No profile = always runs

  # Dev-only tools
  pgadmin:
    image: dpage/pgadmin4
    profiles: ["dev", "debug"]    # Only in dev/debug profiles
    ports: ["5050:80"]

  # Debugging tools
  mailhog:
    image: mailhog/mailhog
    profiles: ["debug"]           # Only in debug profile
    ports: ["8025:8025"]

  # Production monitoring
  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus
    profiles: ["prod"]            # Only in prod profile
    ports: ["9090:9090"]

# Start normally (only services without profiles):
$ docker compose up -d

# Start with dev tools:
$ docker compose --profile dev up -d

# Start with everything:
$ docker compose --profile dev --profile debug --profile prod up -d
💡 When to Use Profiles

Use profiles for: debugging tools (MailHog, pgAdmin), optional monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana), test runners (Selenium, Cypress), and expensive services (Elasticsearch) that not every developer needs. Don't use profiles for core application services — those should always run.

12.2 Compose Overrides — Multiple Compose Files

Compose automatically merges compose.override.yaml with compose.yaml. This lets you define a base configuration and layer environment-specific overrides:

compose.yaml (Base)
services:
  django:
    build: .
    environment:
      - DEBUG=False
      - DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  postgres_data:
compose.override.yaml (Dev Overrides — AUTO-MERGED)
services:
  django:
    environment:
      - DEBUG=True             # Override: enable debug in dev
    volumes:
      - .:/app                 # Add: bind mount for hot reload
    command: python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000  # Override CMD
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"            # Add: expose port for direct access
  postgres:
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"            # Add: expose DB for local tools
📖 Merge Rules

Compose merges multiple files left-to-right. Later files override earlier ones. For single-value keys (image, command), the last value wins. For list keys (ports, volumes, environment), lists are APPENDED — not replaced. For mapping keys (labels, deploy), keys are merged and later values override. Use docker compose config to see the merged result without starting anything.

12.3 Compose Networking Deep Dive

Understanding Compose networking is critical for the DCA exam. Each Compose project gets its own isolated network with built-in DNS:

Compose Networking — 4 Services Connected
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 🌐 DOCKER COMPOSE NETWORKING                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Network: anihpj_default (auto-created by compose)                       │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │                                                                     │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐       │  │
  │  │  │   nginx      │────▶│   django     │────▶│  postgres    │       │  │
  │  │  │  (port 80)   │     │  (port 8000) │     │  (port 5432) │       │  │
  │  │  │              │     │              │     │              │       │  │
  │  │  │  DNS: nginx  │     │  DNS: django │     │ DNS: postgres│       │  │
  │  │  │  PortMap:    │     │  PortMap:    │     │  PortMap:    │       │  │
  │  │  │  80:80       │     │  (internal)  │     │  (internal)  │       │  │
  │  │  └──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘       │  │
  │  │         │                   │                     │                │  │
  │  │         │    ┌──────────────┘                     │                │  │
  │  │         │    │                                    │                │  │
  │  │         │    │  docker exec django ping postgres   │                │  │
  │  │         │    │  → resolves! ✅                     │                │  │
  │  │         │    │                                    │                │  │
  │  │         ▼    ▼                                    │                │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐                                 │                │  │
  │  │  │    redis     │◀────────────────────────────────┘                │  │
  │  │  │  (port 6379) │   docker exec django redis-cli -h redis ping    │  │
  │  │  │              │   → PONG ✅                                      │  │
  │  │  │  DNS: redis  │                                                  │  │
  │  │  └──────────────┘                                                  │  │
  │  │                                                                     │  │
  │  │  EXTERNAL: curl http://localhost:80 → nginx → django                │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💡 Each service can reach any other service by its SERVICE NAME!        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Network Isolation

Each Compose project gets its own default network (named {project}_default). Services in different projects CANNOT communicate by default — they're on separate networks. To connect services across projects, use external: true networks: create a network with docker network create shared, then reference it in both compose files as networks: shared: external: true.

12.4 depends_on with Health Checks

The #1 Compose gotcha: depends_on without health checks. Let's fix it properly:

compose.yaml (Health Checks Done Right)
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U anihpj_user -d anihpj"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s   # Grace period before checking starts

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

  django:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy    # Wait for postgres to be READY
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy    # Wait for redis to be READY
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/health/"]
      interval: 30s
      retries: 3

12.5 docker compose watch — Hot Reload

Compose v2.22+ introduced watch — automatic file sync and rebuild during development. No more manual rebuilds:

compose.yaml (watch config)
services:
  django:
    build: .
    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync          # Copy changed files into container
          path: ./anihpj
          target: /app/anihpj
        - action: sync
          path: ./jobpost
          target: /app/jobpost
        - action: rebuild       # Rebuild image when deps change
          path: requirements.txt
        - action: restart       # Restart container when config changes
          path: compose.yaml
💡 Watch Actions

sync: copies changed files into the running container (fast, no rebuild). rebuild: rebuilds the image when Dockerfile or dependencies change. restart: restarts the container (good for config changes). sync+restart: copies files AND restarts the container (for compiled languages). Run with docker compose watch instead of docker compose up.

12.6 Scaling Services with Compose

Need more Django workers? Compose can scale services to multiple replicas — all on one host:

TERMINAL
# Scale django to 3 replicas
$ docker compose up -d --scale django=3
[+] Running 5/5
 ✔ Container anihpj-postgres-1  Running
 ✔ Container anihpj-redis-1     Running
 ✔ Container anihpj-django-1    Started
 ✔ Container anihpj-django-2    Started   # New replica!
 ✔ Container anihpj-django-3    Started   # New replica!
 ✔ Container anihpj-nginx-1     Running

# Nginx automatically load-balances across all 3 django replicas
# because upstream django_app { server django:8000; } resolves to all 3 IPs!
3 Django Replicas Behind Nginx
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    📊 SCALING WITH COMPOSE                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │                        🌐 http://localhost:80                             │
  │                               │                                          │
  │                               ▼                                          │
  │                    ┌──────────────────────┐                             │
  │                    │    🟢 NGINX (:80)    │                             │
  │                    │   upstream django {  │                             │
  │                    │     server django:8000 ← resolves to ALL 3 IPs!    │
  │                    │   }                  │                             │
  │                    └──┬────────┬──────────┘                             │
  │                       │        │        │                                │
  │              ┌────────▼──┐ ┌───▼─────┐ ┌─▼──────────┐                  │
  │              │ 🐍 Django  │ │ 🐍 Django│ │ 🐍 Django   │                  │
  │              │ Replica 1  │ │ Replica 2│ │ Replica 3   │                  │
  │              └────────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────────┘                  │
  │                       │        │        │                                │
  │                       └────────┼────────┘                                │
  │                                ▼                                         │
  │                    ┌──────────────────────┐                             │
  │                    │  🐘 PostgreSQL       │                             │
  │                    └──────────────────────┘                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ⚠️ All on ONE host — for multi-host scaling, use Kubernetes/Swarm      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Compose Scaling Limitations

Compose scaling runs all replicas on ONE host. For true horizontal scaling across multiple servers, you need Kubernetes or Docker Swarm. Compose is perfect for development, CI/CD, and single-server production — but not for multi-node clusters. Also: if you scale a service with port mappings (like "8000:8000"), only ONE replica can bind to the host port — remove the port mapping and let Nginx handle routing.

📝 Chapter 12 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What are Compose profiles and when would you use them?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Profiles are tags on services that control whether they start. Services without a profile always start. Services with a profile only start when that profile is activated with --profile. Use for optional tools: pgAdmin (dev), MailHog (debug), Prometheus (prod monitoring).

EXPLANATION

Profiles solve the "not everyone needs every service" problem. A frontend developer doesn't need Prometheus. A DBA doesn't need MailHog. Profiles let you keep all service definitions in one file while letting each developer activate only what they need: docker compose --profile dev up.

# --profile
# docker compose --profile dev up
Q2
How do you override service configuration for different environments?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Use multiple Compose files: a base compose.yaml with shared config, and compose.override.yaml (auto-merged) or compose.prod.yaml (explicitly merged with -f). Compose merges them left-to-right, with later files overriding earlier ones. Use docker compose config to preview the merged result.

EXPLANATION

The common pattern: compose.yaml (base: all services, production defaults), compose.override.yaml (dev: DEBUG=True, bind mounts, exposed ports), compose.prod.yaml (prod: resource limits, restart policies). Run dev with docker compose up (auto-merges override), run prod with docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up.

# compose.yaml
# compose.override.yaml
# compose.prod.yaml
# docker compose config
# compose.yaml
Q3
How do Compose services discover each other on the network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Compose creates a Docker network and runs an embedded DNS server. Each service name becomes a DNS hostname. Django reaches PostgreSQL at postgres:5432 — using the Compose service name, not an IP. Docker's DNS at 127.0.0.11 resolves service names to container IPs automatically.

EXPLANATION

This DNS-based discovery is what makes Compose portable. You never hardcode IPs. If a container restarts with a new IP, DNS updates. For scaled services (--scale django=3), DNS returns all 3 IPs in round-robin — Nginx's upstream directive automatically distributes requests across all replicas.

# postgres:5432
# 127.0.0.11
# --scale django=3
Q4
What's wrong with plain depends_on: [postgres] without a health check condition?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It only waits for the container to START, not for PostgreSQL to be ready to accept connections. PostgreSQL starts its container instantly but takes 2-5 seconds to initialize. Django will try to connect before PostgreSQL is ready → connection refused → crash → restart loop. Use condition: service_healthy.

EXPLANATION

The fix: add a healthcheck to PostgreSQL (pg_isready) and use depends_on: postgres: condition: service_healthy. Compose will wait until the healthcheck passes before starting Django. This eliminates the startup race condition that's been frustrating Docker developers for years.

# depends_on: [postgres]
# condition: service_healthy
# pg_isready
# depends_on: postgres: condition: service_healthy
Q5
What does docker compose watch do and how is it different from up?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

watch monitors source files and automatically takes action when they change: sync copies files into the container (fast), rebuild rebuilds the image (when Dockerfile/deps change), restart restarts the container (config changes). up starts containers once and doesn't watch for changes.

EXPLANATION

watch replaces the old workflow of: edit code → stop → rebuild → start. With watch, you edit code and changes appear in the container instantly (sync) or trigger an automatic rebuild. It's like nodemon for Node.js or Django's runserver auto-reload — but at the Compose level, working across all services.

# docker compose watch
# runserver
Q6
How do you scale a Compose service to 3 replicas?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose up -d --scale django=3. Creates 3 instances of the django service. Compose names them project-django-1, project-django-2, project-django-3. DNS returns all 3 IPs for the django hostname — Nginx load-balances across them.

EXPLANATION

Limitations: (1) all replicas run on the SAME host — no multi-node scaling; (2) you can't scale services with fixed port mappings ("8000:8000") — only one can bind to the host port; (3) for production multi-host scaling, use Kubernetes or Docker Swarm. Compose scaling is great for local load-testing and development.

# docker compose up -d --scale django=3
# project-django-1
# project-django-2
# project-django-3
# "8000:8000"
Q7
What command shows the effective (merged) Compose configuration?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose config — displays the fully merged and resolved Compose file. It shows the result after merging all files (base + override), resolving variables, and applying defaults. Use this to debug configuration issues before running up.

EXPLANATION

This is the "dry run" for Compose. It's invaluable when using multiple Compose files — you can see exactly what Compose WILL run. Use docker compose config --services to list only service names, docker compose config --volumes for volumes, or docker compose config --hash="*" for checksums useful for change detection.

# docker compose config
# docker compose config --services
# docker compose config --volumes
# docker compose config --hash="*"
Q8
How does Nginx load-balance across scaled Django replicas in Compose?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Nginx's upstream directive with server django:8000; works because Compose DNS returns ALL replica IPs when resolving django. Nginx uses these IPs for round-robin load balancing. No extra configuration needed — it's automatic when you scale the service.

EXPLANATION

Nginx resolves django at startup (or periodically with resolve parameter). Docker's embedded DNS returns all container IPs for the service. Nginx distributes requests using its default round-robin algorithm. For sticky sessions: use ip_hash; in the upstream block. For least connections: least_conn;.

# server django:8000;
# least_conn;
Q9
What's the difference between docker compose run and docker compose exec?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

exec runs a command inside an ALREADY-RUNNING service container. run creates a NEW container from the service definition — useful for one-off commands (createsuperuser, migrate). run is isolated; exec shares state with the running container.

EXPLANATION

Use run for: database migrations before the app starts, creating superusers, running tests (docker compose run django pytest). Use exec for: live debugging (docker compose exec django bash), checking running state (docker compose exec postgres psql), operational commands on a running stack. run respects depends_on; exec doesn't need to.

# docker compose run
# docker compose exec
# createsuperuser
# docker compose run django pytest
# docker compose exec django bash
Q10
Can you use Docker Compose in production? What are the limitations?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Compose is designed for development and testing. It CAN be used on a single production server, but has key limitations: no multi-node scaling, no rolling updates, no secret rotation, no built-in monitoring. For production at scale, use Kubernetes or Docker Swarm which provide orchestration, auto-healing, and multi-host deployment.

EXPLANATION

Compose is excellent for: local development, CI/CD pipelines, staging environments, single-server deployments (small projects). It is NOT suitable for: auto-scaling, zero-downtime deployments, multi-region failover, or managing hundreds of containers. The DCA exam draws a clear line: Compose = dev/CI; Swarm/K8s = production orchestration.

# compose.yaml:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

Part 4 covers everything you need to define, run, and manage multi-container applications with Docker Compose — the bridge between single-container development and orchestrated production:

  • Compose Fundamentals (Ch 10): Compose turns multiple docker run commands into one declarative YAML file. One command starts everything. Service names become DNS hostnames. Six top-level sections — master services, networks, and volumes.
  • anihpj Full Stack (Ch 11): Complete 4-service architecture: Django + PostgreSQL + Redis + Nginx. Health checks prevent race conditions. Environment variables via .env (gitignored). Nginx serves static files and proxies to Django — all on auto-created networks.
  • Advanced Features (Ch 12): Profiles for conditional services. Multiple Compose files for environment overrides. watch mode for hot reload. Scale services to multiple replicas behind Nginx load balancing. Know when to use Compose (dev/CI) vs Kubernetes/Swarm (production).
🔄 Implementation: The Complete Compose Workflow

Write compose.yaml → docker compose config (verify) → docker compose up -d (start) → docker compose ps (check status) → docker compose logs -f (monitor) → docker compose exec django python manage.py migrate (setup) → Open browser → docker compose down (cleanup). Seven commands from code to running full stack.

Networking is how containers communicate — with each other, with the host, and with the outside world. Docker provides a complete networking stack with multiple drivers, built-in DNS, and automatic service discovery. Master networking and you master multi-container Docker.

13.1 How Docker Networking Works

Docker networking is built on the Container Network Model (CNM) — a specification that defines how containers connect to networks. The CNM has three components:

🏖️
Sandbox

An isolated network stack: its own interfaces, routing table, and DNS config. Each container gets its own sandbox via Linux network namespaces.

🔌
Endpoint

A virtual network interface (veth pair) connecting a sandbox to a network. Think of it as a network cable plugged into the container.

🌐
Network

A collection of endpoints that can communicate. Implemented as a Linux bridge, overlay, or other driver. The docker0 bridge is the default network.

CNM Architecture — How Containers Connect
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🏗️ CONTAINER NETWORK MODEL (CNM)                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │                         DOCKER HOST                                │   │
  │  │                                                                   │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐       │   │
  │  │  │ Container C1 │    │ Container C2 │    │ Container C3 │       │   │
  │  │  │ ┌──────────┐ │    │ ┌──────────┐ │    │ ┌──────────┐ │       │   │
  │  │  │ │ SANDBOX  │ │    │ │ SANDBOX  │ │    │ │ SANDBOX  │ │       │   │
  │  │  │ │ eth0     │ │    │ │ eth0     │ │    │ │ eth0     │ │       │   │
  │  │  │ │ 172.17.0.2│    │ │172.17.0.3│    │ │172.17.0.4│ │       │   │
  │  │  │ └────┬─────┘ │    │ └────┬─────┘ │    │ └────┬─────┘ │       │   │
  │  │  └──────┼───────┘    └──────┼───────┘    └──────┼───────┘       │   │
  │  │         │                   │                    │                │   │
  │  │         │    ENDPOINT       │    ENDPOINT        │    ENDPOINT    │   │
  │  │         │  (veth pair)      │  (veth pair)       │  (veth pair)   │   │
  │  │         │                   │                    │                │   │
  │  │         ▼                   ▼                    ▼                │   │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │   │
  │  │  │              NETWORK: docker0 BRIDGE (172.17.0.0/16)       │  │   │
  │  │  │              + Embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11                  │  │   │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘  │   │
  │  │                             │ NAT (iptables)                       │   │
  │  │                             ▼                                      │   │
  │  │                     ┌──────────────┐                              │   │
  │  │                     │ eth0 (host)  │──▶ Internet / LAN             │   │
  │  │                     │ 192.168.1.100│                              │   │
  │  │                     └──────────────┘                              │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

13.2 Network Drivers Overview

Docker provides 5 network drivers, each with different isolation and connectivity characteristics. Choosing the right driver is a key DCA exam topic:

13.3 Bridge Networks — The Default

When you install Docker, it creates a default bridge network called bridge (using the docker0 Linux bridge). All containers join this network unless you specify otherwise. Bridge networks provide NAT-based connectivity with port mapping for external access:

Bridge Network Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🌉 BRIDGE NETWORK ARCHITECTURE                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  EXTERNAL WORLD (Internet / LAN)                                         │
  │       │                                                                  │
  │       │  curl http://host:8080                                           │
  │       ▼                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │                         HOST (192.168.1.100)                       │   │
  │  │                                                                   │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────────┐   │   │
  │  │  │  eth0 (physical) │         │       docker0 bridge          │   │   │
  │  │  │  192.168.1.100   │  NAT    │       172.17.0.1              │   │   │
  │  │  └────────┬─────────┘◀────────│                               │   │   │
  │  │           │                   │  -p 8080:80 → routes to C2:80│   │   │
  │  │           │     ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐                │   │   │
  │  │           │     ▼             ▼             ▼                │   │   │
  │  │           │  ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐               │   │   │
  │  │           │  │  C1  │    │  C2  │    │  C3  │               │   │   │
  │  │           │  │.0.2  │    │.0.3  │    │.0.4  │               │   │   │
  │  │           │  │anihpj│   │nginx │    │redis │               │   │   │
  │  │           │  │:8000 │    │:80   │    │:6379 │               │   │   │
  │  │           │  └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘               │   │   │
  │  │           │                                                  │   │   │
  │  │           │  DNS: C1 can ping "nginx" → resolves to .0.3    │   │   │
  │  │           │  DNS: C1 can ping "redis" → resolves to .0.4    │   │   │
  │  │           └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Custom Bridge vs Default Bridge

The default bridge network does NOT provide automatic DNS resolution between containers — you need --link (legacy, deprecated). Custom bridge networks (created with docker network create) DO provide automatic DNS. Always create custom bridge networks for your applications — never rely on the default bridge for multi-container communication.

13.4 docker network Commands

These are your daily networking commands. Every DCA candidate must know them:

TERMINAL
# List all networks
$ docker network ls
NETWORK ID     NAME              DRIVER    SCOPE
abc123def456   bridge            bridge    local
def456ghi789   host              host      local
ghi789jkl012   none              null      local
jkl012mno345   anihpj_backend    bridge    local

# Create a custom bridge network
$ docker network create --driver bridge anihpj-net

# Inspect network details (subnets, connected containers, IPs)
$ docker network inspect anihpj-net

# Connect a running container to a network
$ docker network connect anihpj-net anihpj-container

# Disconnect a container from a network
$ docker network disconnect anihpj-net anihpj-container

# Remove a network (must have no connected containers)
$ docker network rm anihpj-net

# Remove all unused networks
$ docker network prune

13.5 Container DNS & Service Discovery

Docker runs an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside each container. This DNS resolves container names to IP addresses — enabling automatic service discovery without hardcoded IPs:

DNS Resolution Flow
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🔍 DOCKER DNS RESOLUTION                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Container django wants to connect to postgres:                          │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────┐    ① DNS query         ┌──────────────────────┐       │
  │  │   django    │──────────────────────▶ │  Docker DNS Server    │       │
  │  │ 172.17.0.2  │    "Where is postgres?"│  127.0.0.11:53        │       │
  │  │             │◀────────────────────── │                       │       │
  │  └─────────────┘    ② DNS response       │  Container Registry:  │       │
  │                      "postgres = .0.3"   │  ├ nginx   → 172.17.0.4      │
  │                                          │  ├ postgres→ 172.17.0.3      │
  │  ┌─────────────┐    ③ Connect             │  └ redis   → 172.17.0.5      │
  │  │  postgres   │◀──────────────────────  └──────────────────────┘       │
  │  │ 172.17.0.3  │    TCP 172.17.0.3:5432                                  │
  │  └─────────────┘                                                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  --network-alias adds extra names:                                       │
  │  docker run --network-alias db --network-alias database postgres         │
  │  Now BOTH "db" and "database" resolve to the postgres container!         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Avoid --link (Legacy)

The --link flag was Docker's original service discovery mechanism — it injected environment variables and /etc/hosts entries. It's deprecated and should never be used in new projects. Use custom networks with automatic DNS instead: containers on the same custom network can resolve each other by name with zero configuration.

📝 Chapter 13 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What are the three components of the Container Network Model (CNM)?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Sandbox (isolated network stack per container), Endpoint (virtual interface connecting sandbox to network), and Network (collection of endpoints that can communicate). Each container gets its own sandbox via Linux network namespaces.

EXPLANATION

The CNM is a specification, not an implementation. Docker's libnetwork implements it. Understanding CNM helps you reason about container networking: each container has an isolated network namespace (sandbox), connects via veth pairs (endpoints), and joins a bridge or overlay (network). This is the foundation all Docker networking is built on.

# Network diagnostics:
docker network ls
docker network inspect bridge
docker run --rm --net host alpine ip addr
docker run --rm --net none alpine ping 8.8.8.8  # Fails!
Q2
What's the difference between the default bridge network and a custom bridge network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The default bridge (docker0) does NOT provide automatic DNS resolution — containers can only communicate by IP. Custom bridge networks (created with docker network create) DO provide automatic DNS — containers can resolve each other by name. Always use custom bridges for applications.

EXPLANATION

This is one of the most important distinctions on the DCA exam. The default bridge is a legacy network with limited features. Custom bridges add: automatic DNS resolution, container isolation from the default bridge, and the ability to connect/disconnect containers at runtime. The default bridge is only useful for quick testing of a single container.

# docker network create
Q3
Which network driver should you use for maximum container isolation?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

none — the container has no network interface except loopback (127.0.0.1). It cannot communicate with anything outside itself. Use for security-sensitive workloads that don't need network access (batch processors, data transformers).

EXPLANATION

The none driver creates a container with only a loopback interface. Even if another container on the same host is compromised, it cannot reach the isolated container. This is the networking equivalent of running in a Faraday cage — maximum security at the cost of zero connectivity.

# none
Q4
What command creates a custom bridge network named "anihpj-net"?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker network create anihpj-net (bridge is the default driver) or explicitly: docker network create --driver bridge anihpj-net. You can also specify subnet: docker network create --subnet 10.0.0.0/24 anihpj-net.

EXPLANATION

Custom networks can be configured with: --subnet (IP range), --gateway (default gateway IP), --ip-range (allocatable IPs within subnet), and --label (metadata). Use docker network inspect anihpj-net to verify the configuration after creation.

# docker network create anihpj-net
# docker network create --driver bridge anihpj-net
# docker network create --subnet 10.0.0.0/24 anihpj-net
# --gateway
# --ip-range
Q5
How does Docker DNS resolve container names to IPs?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker runs an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside each container. When a container performs a DNS lookup for another container's name (or --network-alias), the Docker DNS server returns the target container's IP. This works automatically on custom networks — no configuration needed.

EXPLANATION

The DNS server maintains a registry of container-name-to-IP mappings. It updates in real-time as containers start, stop, or change IPs. For external DNS (google.com), Docker forwards to the host's DNS servers. The embedded DNS only resolves .container-name style queries — everything else is forwarded upstream.

# 127.0.0.11
# --network-alias
# .container-name
Q6
Which network driver enables multi-host container communication in Swarm?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

overlay — it uses VXLAN tunneling to encapsulate container traffic across physical hosts. Containers on different Swarm nodes can communicate as if they're on the same local network. Enable encryption with --opt encrypted for secure cross-host traffic.

EXPLANATION

Overlay networks are the backbone of Docker Swarm. They create a virtual Layer 2 network spanning multiple hosts using VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN). Each packet is encapsulated in a UDP packet and sent to the destination host, where it's decapsulated and delivered to the target container. This enables transparent multi-host networking.

# --opt encrypted
Q7
What happens when you run a container with --network host?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The container shares the host's network namespace directly — no virtual bridge, no NAT, no port mapping. The container sees and can use the host's network interfaces directly. Port -p flags are ignored because there's no isolation. Maximum performance, zero network isolation.

EXPLANATION

Host networking is the fastest option because there's no network translation overhead. But it comes with serious caveats: (1) port conflicts — if the host uses port 80, your container can't; (2) no isolation — the container can see all host network traffic; (3) the container can bind to privileged ports (<1024). Use only when you absolutely need bare-metal network performance.

# --network host
Q8
Why is --link deprecated and what should you use instead?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--link was Docker's original container-to-container communication mechanism — it injected environment variables and /etc/hosts entries. It's deprecated because: single-direction, fragile (breaks on container restart), and doesn't work across hosts. Use custom networks instead — they provide automatic bidirectional DNS on the same network.

EXPLANATION

Custom networks solve all of --link's problems: (1) bidirectional communication, (2) survives container restarts (DNS updates), (3) works across multiple containers, (4) can be created/destroyed independently, (5) supports overlay for multi-host. The DCA exam expects you to know that --link is deprecated and custom networks are the replacement.

# --link
# --link
Q9
How do you connect a running container to a new network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker network connect anihpj-net my-container. This adds a new network interface to the running container without restarting it. Verify with docker inspect my-container — you'll see two networks now. Disconnect with docker network disconnect anihpj-net my-container.

EXPLANATION

This is powerful for dynamic network topologies. You can start a container on one network, then connect it to additional networks at runtime. The container gets a new IP on each network. Use --ip to assign a specific IP: docker network connect --ip 172.20.0.100 anihpj-net my-container. Use --alias to add DNS names on the new network.

# docker network connect anihpj-net my-container
# docker inspect my-container
# docker network disconnect anihpj-net my-container
# docker network connect --ip 172.20.0.100 anihpj-net my-container
Q10
How can containers on different Docker hosts communicate?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Three options: (1) Overlay network (Swarm) — VXLAN tunnel across hosts, (2) Port publishing — expose container ports on the host and connect via host IP, (3) External service discovery — use Consul/etcd for DNS-based discovery across hosts. Overlay is the Docker-native solution for multi-host networking.

EXPLANATION

Overlay networks require Docker Swarm mode. They create an encrypted (optional) VXLAN tunnel between all Swarm nodes. Containers on the same overlay can communicate by name regardless of which host they're on. For non-Swarm setups, you'd need external tools like Weave, Calico, or Flannel — or simply use Kubernetes which has its own networking model (CNI).

# Network diagnostics:
docker network ls
docker network inspect bridge
docker run --rm --net host alpine ip addr
docker run --rm --net none alpine ping 8.8.8.8  # Fails!

Chapter 14: Networking anihpj Containers

Let's apply networking concepts to the anihpj stack. We'll design a two-network architecture — backend for internal services and frontend for external access — then implement it with Docker networks and Compose.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🌐 Network🏗️ Hands-On

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Design secure multi-network architectures
  • ✅ Create and manage custom Docker networks
  • ✅ Connect containers to specific networks
  • ✅ Master port publishing and exposure
  • ✅ Understand service discovery in Compose

14.1 Network Design for anihpj Stack

Security best practice: separate your services into network zones. The database and cache should be on an internal network — not directly accessible from outside. Only Nginx and Django need to be on the frontend network:

anihpj Two-Network Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               🔒 anihpj TWO-NETWORK DESIGN                                 │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────┐    ┌───────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │    frontend NETWORK           │    │    backend NETWORK             │  │
  │  │    (external-facing)          │    │    (internal-only)             │  │
  │  │                               │    │                               │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │    │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │  │
  │  │  │  Nginx   │ │  Django  │   │    │  │  Django  │ │ Postgres │   │  │
  │  │  │  :80     │─│  :8000   │───┼────┼──│  :8000   │─│  :5432   │   │  │
  │  │  │          │ │          │   │    │  │          │ │          │   │  │
  │  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘   │    │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘   │  │
  │  │                     │         │    │       │            │          │  │
  │  └─────────────────────┼─────────┘    │       │            │          │  │
  │                        │              │       │  ┌──────────┐        │  │
  │                        │              │       └──│  Redis   │        │  │
  │                        │              │          │  :6379   │        │  │
  │                        │              │          └──────────┘        │  │
  │                        │              │                               │  │
  │  🌐 External traffic    │              │  🔒 Internal — NOT exposed    │  │
  │     http://localhost:80 │              │     to host or internet      │  │
  └────────────────────────┼──────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘  │
                           │                                                  │
                    Django spans BOTH networks — frontend (for Nginx)         │
                    and backend (for Postgres + Redis)                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.2 Creating Custom Networks for anihpj

TERMINAL
# Create backend network (internal — DB and cache)
$ docker network create --driver bridge anihpj-backend
abc123def456

# Create frontend network (external-facing)
$ docker network create --driver bridge anihpj-frontend
def456ghi789

# Verify networks
$ docker network ls | grep anihpj
abc123def456   anihpj-backend    bridge    local
def456ghi789   anihpj-frontend   bridge    local

# Inspect backend network
$ docker network inspect anihpj-backend
[
    {
        "Name": "anihpj-backend",
        "Driver": "bridge",
        "Subnet": "172.20.0.0/16",
        "Gateway": "172.20.0.1",
        "Containers": {}       # No containers connected yet
    }
]

14.3 Connecting Containers to Networks

TERMINAL
# Start PostgreSQL on backend only
$ docker run -d --name anihpj-db \
    --network anihpj-backend \
    -e POSTGRES_DB=anihpj \
    postgres:15-alpine

# Start Redis on backend only
$ docker run -d --name anihpj-redis \
    --network anihpj-backend \
    redis:7-alpine

# Start Django on backend first, then connect to frontend
$ docker run -d --name anihpj-app \
    --network anihpj-backend \
    anihpj:v1.0
$ docker network connect anihpj-frontend anihpj-app

# Start Nginx on frontend only
$ docker run -d --name anihpj-nginx \
    --network anihpj-frontend \
    -p 80:80 \
    nginx:alpine

# Verify connectivity
$ docker exec anihpj-app ping anihpj-db      # Works! (same backend network)
$ docker exec anihpj-app ping anihpj-redis   # Works! (same backend network)
$ docker exec anihpj-app ping anihpj-nginx   # Works! (same frontend network)
$ docker exec anihpj-db ping anihpj-app      # Works! (same backend network)
$ docker exec anihpj-db ping anihpj-nginx    # FAILS! (different networks)

14.4 Port Publishing & Exposure

The distinction between EXPOSE and publish (-p) is one of the most tested DCA topics:

MechanismSyntaxWhat It DoesRequired for External Access?
EXPOSE (Dockerfile)EXPOSE 8000Documentation only — metadata saying "this container listens on 8000"❌ No — does NOT publish ports
-p (short publish)-p 8000:8000Maps host port 8000 to container port 8000✅ Yes
-P (publish all)-PPublishes ALL EXPOSEd ports to random host ports✅ Yes
--publish (long syntax)--publish mode=host,target=80,published=8080Full control: mode (host/ingress), protocol (tcp/udp)✅ Yes
⚠️ EXPOSE Does NOT Publish Ports!

This is the most common Docker networking misconception. EXPOSE 8000 in a Dockerfile is purely documentation — like a comment. It does NOT make the port accessible from the host. Only -p or -P in docker run actually publishes ports. The DCA exam will test this distinction.

14.5 Service Discovery in Compose

Compose's networking is where its real power shines. Unlike raw docker run, Compose automatically creates a custom bridge network and registers every service name as a DNS entry — zero configuration needed:

compose.yaml (network config)
services:
  django:
    build: .
    networks:
      - backend
      - frontend
    environment:
      # Service name "postgres" → resolves via Compose DNS!
      - DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@postgres:5432/anihpj
      - REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0

  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    networks:
      - backend       # Only on internal network

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    networks:
      - backend       # Only on internal network

  nginx:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports: ["80:80"]
    networks:
      - frontend      # Only on external-facing network
    # nginx.conf: upstream django { server django:8000; }
    # Compose DNS resolves "django" to the container IP!

networks:
  frontend:
    driver: bridge
  backend:
    driver: bridge
    internal: true    # No internet access for backend services
🏆 Compose DNS vs Manual Networking

With manual docker run: create networks → specify --network on every container → manually verify connectivity. With Compose: write service names → they become DNS hostnames → docker compose up → everything just works. This is why Compose is the default development tool — it eliminates networking boilerplate entirely.

📝 Chapter 14 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Why use two separate networks (frontend + backend) instead of one?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Security isolation. PostgreSQL and Redis on the backend network are NOT accessible from outside — only Django can reach them. If Nginx is compromised, the attacker still can't reach the database because Nginx is only on the frontend network. This is defense-in-depth at the network level.

EXPLANATION

This is the same principle as AWS security groups or Kubernetes NetworkPolicies. By limiting which services are on which networks, you limit the blast radius of any compromise. A single flat network means any compromised container can reach all others — a two-network design cuts off the database and cache from external-facing services.

# Network diagnostics:
docker network ls
docker network inspect bridge
docker run --rm --net host alpine ip addr
docker run --rm --net none alpine ping 8.8.8.8  # Fails!
Q2
How do you connect a running container to an additional network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker network connect anihpj-frontend anihpj-app. This adds a second network interface to the running container. It now has IPs on both networks and can communicate with containers on both.

EXPLANATION

Containers can be connected to multiple networks simultaneously — each gets its own IP on each network. The anihpj Django container is on both backend (to reach DB/Redis) and frontend (to be reached by Nginx). Use docker inspect anihpj-app to see all its network connections and IPs.

# docker network connect anihpj-frontend anihpj-app
# docker inspect anihpj-app
Q3
What's the difference between EXPOSE and -p?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

EXPOSE (in Dockerfile) is documentation only — metadata that says "this container listens on port X." It does NOT make the port accessible. -p (in docker run) actually maps a host port to a container port, making it accessible from outside. EXPOSE is optional; -p is what makes things work.

EXPLANATION

You can publish a port that's NOT EXPOSEd — it works fine. You can EXPOSE a port without publishing it — it won't be accessible from the host. -P (capital P) publishes all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports. The DCA exam frequently tests this distinction — don't confuse EXPOSE (documentation) with publish (actual port mapping).

# -P
Q4
Why can't anihpj-db ping anihpj-nginx in the two-network design?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

They're on different networks — anihpj-db is only on anihpj-backend, and anihpj-nginx is only on anihpj-frontend. Docker networks provide full isolation — containers on different networks cannot communicate unless a container is connected to both (like Django, which bridges them).

EXPLANATION

This is the security benefit of network segmentation. The database literally cannot see the internet-facing Nginx container. Even if Nginx is fully compromised, the attacker can't reach the database because there's no network path. This is why Django needs to be on both networks — it acts as the controlled bridge between external and internal zones.

# anihpj-backend
# anihpj-frontend
Q5
How many networks is the anihpj Django container connected to, and why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Two: anihpj-backend (to reach PostgreSQL and Redis) and anihpj-frontend (to be reached by Nginx). Django is the bridge — it accepts requests from the frontend and queries the backend. This is the application-layer gateway pattern.

EXPLANATION

Django needs backend access for database queries and cache operations. It needs frontend access to receive proxied requests from Nginx. But PostgreSQL should NOT be on the frontend (no direct external access to the database). Redis should NOT be on the frontend (no external cache queries). Django is the controlled chokepoint.

# anihpj-backend
# anihpj-frontend
Q6
What command shows which containers are connected to a specific network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker network inspect anihpj-backend — the JSON output includes a "Containers" section listing every container on that network with its name, IP, and MAC address. For a quick list: docker network inspect -f '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{end}}' anihpj-backend.

EXPLANATION

docker network inspect is the Swiss Army knife of network debugging. It shows: subnet, gateway, connected containers (with IPs), driver, scope, and options. Use it whenever containers can't communicate — first verify they're actually on the same network.

# docker network inspect anihpj-backend
# docker network inspect -f '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{end}}' anihpj-backend
# docker network inspect
Q7
What happens if you don't specify --network when running a container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The container joins the default bridge network (docker0). This network does NOT provide automatic DNS resolution — containers can only communicate by IP address, not by name. It's fine for single-container testing but unsuitable for multi-container applications.

EXPLANATION

The default bridge is a legacy network that predates custom bridge networks. On custom bridges (created with docker network create), you get automatic DNS. On the default bridge, you don't. This is why every Docker tutorial tells you to create a network first: docker network create myapp then docker run --network myapp ....

# --network
# docker network create
# docker network create myapp
# docker run --network myapp ...
Q8
How does Compose handle networking differently from manual docker run?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Compose automatically creates a custom bridge network for each project. All services join that network and get automatic DNS resolution by service name. You don't need to manually create networks or connect containers — Compose handles everything declaratively from compose.yaml.

EXPLANATION

This is one of Compose's biggest advantages over raw docker run. With docker run, you must: create network, specify --network on every run command, and manually manage connections. With Compose, just list the networks and services — Docker figures out the rest. The network is named {project}_default.

# {project}_default
Q9
What is the long syntax for publishing a port in docker run?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--publish published=8080,target=80,protocol=tcp,mode=host. This gives full control: which host port (published), which container port (target), protocol (tcp/udp/sctp), and mode (host for local-only, ingress for Swarm routing mesh).

EXPLANATION

The short syntax -p 8080:80 is equivalent to --publish published=8080,target=80,protocol=tcp. The long syntax is useful when you need UDP (protocol=udp) or Swarm-specific modes. For 99% of cases, the short syntax is all you need.

# --publish published=8080,target=80,protocol=tcp,mode=host
# -p 8080:80
# --publish published=8080,target=80,protocol=tcp
# protocol=udp
Q10
Why should PostgreSQL NOT be on the frontend network in the anihpj design?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Security. If PostgreSQL is on the frontend network and you publish port 5432, anyone who can reach the host can try to connect to your database. Keeping it on the backend network means only Django (which is authenticated and controlled) can reach it. This follows the principle of least privilege.

EXPLANATION

Database breaches are one of the most common security incidents. Exposing PostgreSQL directly (even with a password) dramatically increases your attack surface. On the backend network, an attacker would need to first compromise Django (which is on both networks) before even seeing PostgreSQL. This is defense-in-depth.

docker run --rm --net none alpine ping 8.8.8.8  # Fails!

Chapter 15: Advanced Docker Networking

Beyond basic bridge networking, Docker supports host-mode for maximum performance, macvlan/ipvlan for physical network integration, overlay for multi-host Swarm, and powerful troubleshooting tools. These are the advanced topics the DCA exam expects.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours🌐 Network🎯 DCA 10%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Use host networking for maximum performance
  • ✅ Understand macvlan/ipvlan for physical network integration
  • ✅ Configure overlay networks for Swarm
  • ✅ Troubleshoot network issues with diagnostic tools
  • ✅ Apply network security best practices

15.1 Host Networking

Host networking removes Docker's network virtualization entirely — the container uses the host's network stack directly. No bridge, no NAT, no port mapping needed:

AspectBridge NetworkHost Network
Network isolation✅ Full isolation❌ No isolation — shares host stack
Port mapping-p 8080:80 requiredNot needed — container uses host ports directly
Performance🟡 Slight NAT overhead🟢 Bare-metal speed (no translation)
Port conflicts✅ Can't conflict (different namespace)❌ WILL conflict if host uses same port
Use caseStandard applicationsHigh-throughput network apps, monitoring agents
⚠️ Host Networking Caveats

Only works on Linux. On Docker Desktop (Windows/macOS), host networking uses the VM's network, not your laptop's. The container can bind to privileged ports (<1024). Multiple containers using host networking CANNOT use the same port — they'll conflict. Use only when you absolutely need bare-metal network performance and can accept zero isolation.

15.2 Macvlan / IPvlan Networking

Macvlan gives each container its own MAC address and IP on the physical network — the container appears as a separate physical device. IPvlan shares the host's MAC but gives containers unique IPs:

Macvlan vs IPvlan
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🔌 MACVLAN vs IPVLAN                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  MACVLAN: Each container has OWN MAC address                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ Physical Switch: 192.168.1.0/24                                    │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                     │   │
  │  │  │  Host    │   │ Container│   │ Container│                     │   │
  │  │  │MAC: aa:bb│   │MAC: cc:dd│   │MAC: ee:ff│                     │   │
  │  │  │IP: .100  │   │IP: .101  │   │IP: .102  │                     │   │
  │  │  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘                     │   │
  │  │  ⚠️ Some cloud providers block multiple MACs per port!            │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  IPVLAN: Containers share host MAC, unique IPs                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ Physical Switch: 192.168.1.0/24                                    │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                     │   │
  │  │  │  Host    │   │ Container│   │ Container│                     │   │
  │  │  │MAC: aa:bb│   │MAC: aa:bb│   │MAC: aa:bb│  ← Same MAC!         │   │
  │  │  │IP: .100  │   │IP: .101  │   │IP: .102  │                     │   │
  │  │  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘                     │   │
  │  │  ✅ Works in cloud environments (no MAC restrictions)              │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

15.3 Overlay Networking (Swarm)

Overlay networks connect containers across multiple Docker hosts using VXLAN tunneling. This is the foundation of Docker Swarm's multi-host networking:

TERMINAL
# Initialize Swarm (required for overlay)
$ docker swarm init

# Create an encrypted overlay network
$ docker network create --driver overlay \
    --opt encrypted \
    --subnet 10.0.0.0/24 \
    anihpj-overlay

# Deploy services that communicate across hosts
$ docker service create --name django \
    --network anihpj-overlay \
    --replicas 3 \
    anihpj:v1.0

# Containers on different hosts can now communicate:
# django.1 on node-1 can ping django.2 on node-2
# All service names resolve via Swarm's built-in DNS
Overlay Network — 3 Swarm Nodes
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    ☁️ OVERLAY NETWORK (VXLAN)                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐      │
  │  │   🐝 Manager     │  │   🐝 Worker 1    │  │   🐝 Worker 2    │      │
  │  │   10.0.0.1       │  │   10.0.0.2       │  │   10.0.0.3       │      │
  │  │                  │  │                  │  │                  │      │
  │  │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐  │  │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐  │  │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐  │      │
  │  │  │ C1 │ │ C2 │  │  │  │ C3 │ │ C4 │  │  │  │ C5 │ │ C6 │  │      │
  │  │  │.0.4│ │.0.5│  │  │  │.0.6│ │.0.7│  │  │  │.0.8│ │.0.9│  │      │
  │  │  └────┘ └────┘  │  │  └────┘ └────┘  │  │  └────┘ └────┘  │      │
  │  │                 │  │                 │  │                 │      │
  │  │  VXLAN Tunnel   │  │  VXLAN Tunnel   │  │  VXLAN Tunnel   │      │
  │  └───────┬─────────┘  └───────┬─────────┘  └───────┬─────────┘      │
  │          │                    │                    │                 │
  │          └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘                 │
  │                               │                                      │
  │                    Physical Network (underlay)                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Container C1 on Node-1 pings Container C6 on Node-3:                   │
  │  C1 → VXLAN encapsulate → UDP → Node-3 → VXLAN decapsulate → C6 ✅     │
  │  All containers see each other as if on the same local network!         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

15.4 Troubleshooting Tools

When containers can't communicate, these are your diagnostic tools:

TERMINAL
# 1. Check if containers are on the same network
$ docker inspect container1 | grep -A20 Networks
$ docker inspect container2 | grep -A20 Networks

# 2. Test DNS resolution inside a container
$ docker exec container1 nslookup container2
$ docker exec container1 ping container2

# 3. Check network configuration
$ docker network inspect anihpj-backend

# 4. Test port connectivity
$ docker exec container1 nc -zv container2 5432

# 5. View iptables rules (NAT and port mapping)
$ sudo iptables -t nat -L -n | grep DOCKER

# 6. Run a temporary debug container on the same network
$ docker run --rm -it --network anihpj-backend alpine sh
# Now you can ping, nslookup, curl from within the network

15.5 Network Security Basics

🔒
Use Internal Networks

Create networks with --internal flag to prevent containers from accessing the internet: docker network create --internal secure-net. Containers can talk to each other but NOT to the outside world. Perfect for databases and caches.

📋
Encrypt Overlay Traffic

For Swarm overlay networks, add --opt encrypted to enable IPSec encryption of all container-to-container traffic. Without this, VXLAN traffic between hosts is unencrypted by default.

🚫
Limit Published Ports

Only publish ports that need external access. Never publish database ports (5432, 3306, 27017) to 0.0.0.0. If you must publish, bind to localhost: -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432.

🔍
Network Segmentation

Place services on different networks based on their security zone. Frontend (Nginx) on one network, backend (Django+DB+Redis) on another. Only the application layer bridges them — not the database directly.

📝 Chapter 15 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
When would you use host networking instead of bridge?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

When you need maximum network performance (no NAT overhead) and can accept zero network isolation. Common use cases: high-throughput proxies (HAProxy, Envoy), network monitoring agents, and applications handling millions of packets per second where the slight NAT overhead matters.

EXPLANATION

Host networking bypasses Docker's entire network stack — no docker0 bridge, no iptables NAT rules, no veth pairs. The container's network namespace is the host's. This eliminates ~5-10% overhead from NAT but means: port conflicts are possible, the container sees all host interfaces, and there's no network-level security boundary.

# Network diagnostics:
docker network ls
docker network inspect bridge
docker run --rm --net host alpine ip addr
docker run --rm --net none alpine ping 8.8.8.8  # Fails!
Q2
What's the difference between macvlan and ipvlan?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Macvlan gives each container its own MAC address — it appears as a completely separate physical device on the network. IPvlan shares the host's MAC address but gives containers unique IPs. IPvlan works in cloud environments that restrict MAC addresses per port (AWS, GCP).

EXPLANATION

Macvlan is simpler but many cloud providers block multiple MACs on a single virtual NIC (to prevent MAC spoofing). IPvlan solves this by sharing the host's MAC — the physical switch only sees one MAC with multiple IPs. IPvlan L2 mode behaves like macvlan; IPvlan L3 mode adds routing between subnets.

# Network diagnostics:
docker network ls
docker network inspect bridge
docker run --rm --net host alpine ip addr
docker run --rm --net none alpine ping 8.8.8.8  # Fails!
Q3
How do you enable encryption on a Swarm overlay network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker network create --driver overlay --opt encrypted anihpj-secure. This enables IPSec encryption for all container-to-container traffic across the overlay. Without --opt encrypted, VXLAN traffic between hosts travels in plaintext.

EXPLANATION

IPSec encryption adds CPU overhead (~5-15%) but is essential for production Swarm deployments, especially across untrusted networks (public cloud, WAN). The encryption happens at the VXLAN tunnel level — containers don't need to be aware of it. Keys are automatically rotated by Swarm's manager nodes.

# docker network create --driver overlay --opt encrypted anihpj-secure
# --opt encrypted
Q4
What's the first thing to check when containers on the same custom network can't communicate?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Verify they're actually on the SAME network: docker inspect container1 | grep -A20 Networks and docker inspect container2 | grep -A20 Networks. Then test DNS: docker exec container1 nslookup container2. Then test connectivity: docker exec container1 ping container2.

EXPLANATION

The #1 cause of "can't connect" is containers on different networks. The #2 cause is using the wrong name (container name vs service name vs --network-alias). The #3 cause is firewall/iptables rules blocking traffic. Systematic debugging: check networks → check DNS → check connectivity → check iptables.

# docker inspect container1 | grep -A20 Networks
# docker inspect container2 | grep -A20 Networks
# docker exec container1 nslookup container2
# docker exec container1 ping container2
Q5
What does docker network create --internal do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Creates a network where containers can communicate with each other but CANNOT access the internet or any external network. The network has no gateway to the outside world. Perfect for databases, caches, and any service that should never make outbound connections.

EXPLANATION

An internal network has no default gateway. Containers can resolve each other's names via the embedded DNS, ping each other, and open TCP connections — but any attempt to reach an external IP fails. This is a simple but powerful security control: if your database container is compromised, it can't phone home or exfiltrate data to the internet.

# docker network create --internal
Q6
How do you run a temporary container to debug a network?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --rm -it --network anihpj-backend alpine sh. This creates a temporary Alpine container on the same network, giving you a shell with ping, nslookup, wget, and nc. --rm auto-cleans it up when you exit. Now you can test connectivity from within the network.

EXPLANATION

Alpine is ideal for debug containers — it's 5 MB, has essential network tools, and starts instantly. Other useful debug images: nicolaka/netshoot (pre-loaded with tcpdump, iperf, nmap, curl, dig), busybox (even smaller). The key insight: you can join ANY Docker network with a debug container to test from a neutral vantage point.

# docker run --rm -it --network anihpj-backend alpine sh
# nicolaka/netshoot
Q7
Why would you publish a port to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

-p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 binds the port only to localhost — accessible from the host machine but NOT from the network. This lets you use local tools (pgAdmin, DBeaver) while keeping the database invisible to anyone else on the network. 0.0.0.0 exposes it to ALL network interfaces.

EXPLANATION

This is a critical security practice. Binding to 0.0.0.0 means anyone on your LAN (or the internet, if no firewall) can reach the port. Binding to 127.0.0.1 means only local processes can connect. For databases, always use 127.0.0.1 or, better yet, don't publish at all — use Docker networks for container-to-container communication.

# -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432
# 127.0.0.1
# 127.0.0.1
Q8
What's the purpose of the embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It provides automatic service discovery. When any container on a custom network resolves another container's name, the DNS server at 127.0.0.11 returns the target's IP. This works automatically — no configuration needed. It also handles --network-alias and --link (legacy) resolution.

EXPLANATION

The DNS server is embedded in the Docker daemon (dockerd), not a separate container. Each container's /etc/resolv.conf points to 127.0.0.11. For names it doesn't know (google.com), it forwards to the host's DNS servers. The container registry is updated in real-time as containers start, stop, or change IPs — no stale DNS entries.

# 127.0.0.11
# --network-alias
# /etc/resolv.conf
# 127.0.0.11
Q9
What network security risks does publishing a database port create?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Publishing a database port (-p 5432:5432) exposes it to: (1) brute-force password attacks from the internet, (2) unauthorized access from other machines on the LAN, (3) accidental exposure if the host firewall is misconfigured, (4) network scanners discovering the database. Never publish database ports — use Docker networks for access.

EXPLANATION

Databases are the #1 target for attackers. A published PostgreSQL port on a cloud VM can be discovered by port scanners within minutes. Even with a strong password, you're betting your data against a single authentication mechanism. Keep databases on internal Docker networks and access them through your application layer — never directly.

# -p 5432:5432
Q10
How do you completely isolate a container from all network access?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --network none myimage. The container has only a loopback interface — it can talk to itself on 127.0.0.1 but cannot reach any other container, the host, or the internet. For even stricter isolation, combine with --cap-drop ALL and --read-only.

EXPLANATION

The none network driver creates a container with absolutely no external network interfaces. Only lo exists. This is useful for: batch processing jobs that read from mounted volumes, security-sensitive computations, or any workload where network access is a risk, not a requirement. Combine with --network none + --internal network for defense-in-depth.

# docker run --network none myimage
# --cap-drop ALL
# --read-only
# --network none
# --internal

Chapter 16: Docker Storage Fundamentals

Containers are ephemeral by design — when you delete a container, everything inside it disappears. Storage volumes solve this by separating data from the container lifecycle. Master volumes, and your data survives anything.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours💾 Storage🎯 DCA 15%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand why containers are ephemeral and volumes are essential
  • ✅ Master all 4 Docker storage types
  • ✅ Use Docker volumes — the recommended approach
  • ✅ Manage volumes with docker volume commands

16.1 The Ephemeral Container Problem

Containers are designed to be disposable. docker rm deletes everything — the writable layer, all files, all data. For stateless apps, this is fine. But what about your PostgreSQL database? Your users' uploaded files? That data must survive container deletion.

The Ephemeral Container Problem
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              💾 THE EPHEMERAL CONTAINER PROBLEM                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITHOUT VOLUMES (Data dies with container):                             │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────┐                     │
  │  │ Container: postgres │     │ Container: DELETED  │                     │
  │  │ ┌─────────────────┐ │     │                     │                     │
  │  │ │ /var/lib/       │ │     │  💀 DB GONE!        │                     │
  │  │ │   postgresql/   │ │ ──▶ │  💀 Users GONE!     │                     │
  │  │ │   data/         │ │ rm  │  💀 Orders GONE!    │                     │
  │  │ │   (20 GB DB)    │ │     │  💀 Everything!     │                     │
  │  │ └─────────────────┘ │     └─────────────────────┘                     │
  │  └─────────────────────┘                                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  WITH VOLUMES (Data survives container):                                 │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐                │
  │  │ Container: postgres │         │ Container: DELETED  │                │
  │  │ ┌─────────────────┐ │         │                     │                │
  │  │ │ /var/lib/       │ │         │  Container gone,    │                │
  │  │ │   postgresql/   │ │    ──▶  │  but...             │                │
  │  │ │   data/         │ │   rm    │                     │                │
  │  │ └───────┬─────────┘ │         └─────────────────────┘                │
  │  └─────────┼───────────┘                                               │
  │            │ mount                                                      │
  │            ▼                                                            │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐                │
  │  │ 📦 VOLUME: pg_data  │────────▶│ 📦 VOLUME: pg_data  │                │
  │  │ /var/lib/docker/    │  new    │ STILL HERE! ✅      │                │
  │  │ volumes/pg_data/    │  cont.  │ Mount to new        │                │
  │  │ (20 GB, persistent) │         │ container!          │                │
  │  └─────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────┘                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 "Cattle, Not Pets" — With a Volume Collar

Containers are cattle (disposable), but your data is precious. Volumes are the "collar" that survives the animal. You can delete and recreate containers freely — as long as they reattach to the same volume, the data is safe. This is the fundamental storage pattern of containerized applications.

💀
Level 0
No Persistence

Data lives in container writable layer. docker rm = everything gone.

❌ Data loss guaranteed
📁
Level 1
Bind Mounts

Host directory mounted into container. Survives deletion but host-dependent.

⚠️ Dev only, fragile
📦
Level 2
Named Volumes

Docker-managed, portable, driver plugins. Independent lifecycle.

✅ Production standard
☁️
Level 3
Cloud Drivers

EBS, Azure Disk, NFS. Multi-host, auto-backup, enterprise-grade.

🏆 Enterprise production

16.2 Storage Types Overview

Docker provides 4 ways to persist data. Each has different trade-offs for persistence, performance, and management:

16.3 Docker Volumes — The Recommended Way

Volumes are Docker-managed directories stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes/. They're the recommended way for persistent data because Docker handles: creation, mounting, permissions, backup, and driver plugins. Volumes exist independently of containers:

Volume Lifecycle — Independent of Containers
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🔄 VOLUME LIFECYCLE                                   │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────┐   create    ┌─────────┐   mount    ┌─────────┐            │
  │  │ Nothing │────────────▶│ 📦Volume│──────────▶│Container│            │
  │  │         │             │ (empty) │            │ uses it │            │
  │  └─────────┘             └────┬────┘            └────┬────┘            │
  │                               │                      │                  │
  │                               │   Container writes   │                  │
  │                               │◄─────────────────────┘                  │
  │                               │                                         │
  │                               │   Container deleted 💀                  │
  │                               ▼                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐                  │
  │  │ 📦 Volume STILL EXISTS with all data!            │                  │
  │  │ docker run -v my-volume:/data new-image          │◀── Remount!      │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💡 Volume lifecycle is COMPLETELY separate from container lifecycle!    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

16.4 docker volume Commands

TERMINAL
# List all volumes
$ docker volume ls
DRIVER    VOLUME NAME
local     postgres_data
local     static_volume
local     media_volume

# Create a new volume
$ docker volume create anihpj-logs

# Inspect volume details (mountpoint, driver, labels)
$ docker volume inspect postgres_data
[
    {
        "Name": "postgres_data",
        "Driver": "local",
        "Mountpoint": "/var/lib/docker/volumes/postgres_data/_data"
    }
]

# Remove a volume (must not be in use)
$ docker volume rm anihpj-logs

# Remove all unused volumes
$ docker volume prune

Are you sure? [y/N] y
