Scenario: Backup and Restore a PostgreSQL Volume
  1. Create a named volume: docker volume create pgbackup
  2. Run PostgreSQL with that volume
  3. Create test data
  4. Backup the volume to a tar file
  5. Delete the volume and container
  6. Restore from backup and verify data
Hint: Use an alpine container to tar/untar the volume data

⚠️ Chapter 16 Exam Gotchas

  • Volume backup while container is writing → Stop the container first or use database-native backup tools (pg_dump).
  • docker volume rm on in-use volume → Docker refuses to delete volumes still attached to any container (running or stopped).

📝 Chapter 16 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What happens to data inside a container when you run docker rm?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The writable layer is deleted — ALL data created inside the container is gone permanently. Only data stored in mounted volumes survives. This is by design: containers are disposable, data must be externalized to volumes or bind mounts.

EXPLANATION

Each container has a thin writable layer on top of the image layers. docker rm deletes this writable layer. The image layers (read-only) are unaffected. Volumes, being stored outside the container's filesystem at /var/lib/docker/volumes/, are completely separate from the container lifecycle.

# docker rm
# docker rm
# /var/lib/docker/volumes/
Q2
What are the 4 types of Docker storage mounts?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Volumes (Docker-managed, recommended), Bind mounts (any host directory, dev-friendly), tmpfs (RAM-only, never on disk), and npipe (Windows named pipes, IPC only).

EXPLANATION

Volumes are the production standard — Docker manages them, they work across all platforms, and support driver plugins. Bind mounts are for development (hot reload). tmpfs is for secrets and temp data that should never touch disk. npipe is Windows-specific and rarely used.

# Volume management:
docker volume create appdata
docker volume inspect appdata
docker run -v appdata:/data alpine
docker volume prune
Q3
Why are Docker volumes preferred over bind mounts for production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Volumes are Docker-managed: they work across all OS platforms, can be backed up with Docker commands, support volume driver plugins (NFS, cloud storage), and avoid host filesystem permission issues. Bind mounts depend on the host's directory structure and permissions — fragile across environments.

EXPLANATION

Bind mounts expose your container to host-specific paths and permission models. -v /home/user/data:/data works on your laptop but not in CI or on a colleague's machine. Volumes are portable: -v myvolume:/data works identically everywhere Docker runs.

# -v /home/user/data:/data
# -v myvolume:/data
Q4
Where are Docker volumes stored on the host filesystem?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

/var/lib/docker/volumes/<volume-name>/_data on Linux. On Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows), they're inside the Docker VM. Use docker volume inspect <name> to find the exact Mountpoint.

EXPLANATION

Never manually modify files in /var/lib/docker/volumes/ — Docker manages this directory. If you need to access volume data, use a temporary container: docker run --rm -v myvolume:/data alpine ls /data. This ensures Docker's internal state stays consistent.

# /var/lib/docker/volumes//_data
# docker volume inspect 
# /var/lib/docker/volumes/
# docker run --rm -v myvolume:/data alpine ls /data
Q5
What does docker volume prune do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Removes all local volumes that are not currently mounted by at least one container. This is the volume equivalent of docker image prune. It frees disk space by deleting orphaned volumes. Does NOT delete volumes still in use.

EXPLANATION

Volumes accumulate over time — each docker-compose up may create new anonymous volumes. docker volume prune cleans them up. Warning: this deletes data! Always verify with docker volume ls first. For a complete cleanup: docker system prune -a --volumes removes everything unused.

# docker volume prune
# docker image prune
# docker-compose up
# docker volume prune
# docker volume ls
Q6
What's the difference between a named volume and an anonymous volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Named volumes (-v myname:/data or top-level volumes: in Compose) have a user-defined name and persist across docker compose down. Anonymous volumes (-v /data only) get a random hash name and are removed by docker compose down. Always use named volumes for data you want to keep.

EXPLANATION

Anonymous volumes are created when you specify a container path without a host/volume name: -v /app/data. Docker assigns a random name. These are cleaned up by docker compose down unless you explicitly manage them. Named volumes (-v pg_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data) persist until you explicitly delete them.

# -v myname:/data
# docker compose down
# docker compose down
# -v /app/data
# docker compose down
Q7
What happens to a volume when you delete the last container using it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Nothing — the volume and all its data persist. Volumes have an independent lifecycle. You must explicitly delete a volume with docker volume rm <name> or docker volume prune. Deleting a container never deletes its volumes (unless you use docker rm -v).

EXPLANATION

This is the key insight of Docker storage. Volumes are first-class objects, not children of containers. docker volume ls shows all volumes regardless of container state. docker rm -v only deletes anonymous volumes, not named ones. Named volumes require explicit deletion — this protects your data from accidental removal.

# docker volume rm 
# docker volume prune
# docker rm -v
# docker volume ls
# docker rm -v
Q8
When would you use tmpfs mounts instead of volumes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

When data should NEVER be written to disk: temporary secrets, session tokens, cryptographic material, or high-speed scratch space. tmpfs stores data in RAM — it's extremely fast but disappears when the container stops. Use --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=128m.

EXPLANATION

tmpfs is the only storage type that guarantees data never touches disk. Even if an attacker compromises the container, the data is gone after restart. Use for: API keys at runtime, SSL/TLS ephemeral keys, temporary build artifacts. Combine with --read-only rootfs for defense-in-depth.

# --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=128m
# --read-only
Q9
How do you share data between two containers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Mount the SAME volume into both containers: docker run -v shared:/data container1 and docker run -v shared:/data container2. Both can read and write to the same volume simultaneously. In Compose, declare the volume in the top-level volumes: section and reference it in both services.

EXPLANATION

The anihpj stack uses this pattern: Nginx and Django both mount static_volume — Django writes static files during collectstatic, Nginx reads and serves them. Both containers see the same files on the same volume. This is cleaner than --volumes-from (legacy) which blindly copies all mounts from another container.

# docker run -v shared:/data container1
# docker run -v shared:/data container2
# static_volume
# --volumes-from
Q10
What command shows the mount point of a specific volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker volume inspect postgres_data — the "Mountpoint" field shows the exact host path. Or with format: docker volume inspect -f '{{.Mountpoint}}' postgres_data. On Linux this returns /var/lib/docker/volumes/postgres_data/_data.

EXPLANATION

docker volume inspect also shows: Driver (local, nfs, etc.), Labels, Options, and Scope. This is your go-to command for debugging storage issues — verify the volume exists, see where data is stored, and check which driver is managing it.

# docker volume inspect postgres_data
# docker volume inspect -f '{{.Mountpoint}}' postgres_data
# /var/lib/docker/volumes/postgres_data/_data
# docker volume inspect

Chapter 17: Persistent Data for anihpj

Let's apply storage concepts to the anihpj stack. We'll configure volumes for PostgreSQL data, Django media/uploads, static files, and set up development bind mounts. Plus backup and restore strategies for production.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours💾 Storage🏗️ Hands-On

17.1 What Needs to Persist in anihpj?

🐘
PostgreSQL Data

/var/lib/postgresql/data — The database itself. All your models (Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, Users). This MUST persist — losing it means losing all data.

📸
Django Media Files

/app/media — User-uploaded files (resumes, profile pictures, job attachments). Must persist across deployments.

🎨
Django Static Files

/app/static — CSS, JS, images collected by collectstatic. Shared between Django (writes) and Nginx (reads).

📋
Application Logs

Optional: persist logs to a volume for debugging. Usually sent to stdout for Docker logging, but can be volume-mounted for log aggregation tools.

17.2 Volume Setup for PostgreSQL

compose.yaml (PostgreSQL Volume)
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data  # Named volume = data survives!
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: anihpj
      POSTGRES_USER: anihpj_user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}

volumes:
  postgres_data:    # Top-level declaration = named volume = persists forever
Backup & Restore
# Backup: compress volume contents to a tar.gz on host
$ docker run --rm \
    -v postgres_data:/data \
    -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar czf /backup/postgres_backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).tar.gz -C /data .

# Restore: extract backup into volume
$ docker run --rm \
    -v postgres_data:/data \
    -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar xzf /backup/postgres_backup_20260612.tar.gz -C /data

# Better: pg_dump for database-level backup
$ docker exec anihpj-db pg_dump -U anihpj_user anihpj > backup.sql

17.3 Volume Setup for Django Media & Static

compose.yaml (All Volumes)
services:
  django:
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/app/static     # collectstatic writes here
      - media_volume:/app/media       # User uploads stored here

  nginx:
    volumes:
      - static_volume:/static:ro      # Read-only — Nginx only serves
      - media_volume:/media:ro        # Read-only — Nginx only serves
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro

volumes:
  postgres_data:    # DB data — most critical
  static_volume:    # Shared between Django and Nginx
  media_volume:     # Shared between Django and Nginx

17.4 Bind Mounts for Development

Bind mounts let you mount your source code into the container — edit files on your host, changes reflect instantly. Essential for development, NEVER for production:

compose.override.yaml (Dev Only)
services:
  django:
    volumes:
      - .:/app                      # Bind mount: live code reload!
      - static_volume:/app/static
      - media_volume:/app/media
    command: python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000
⚠️ Bind Mounts: Dev Only

Never use bind mounts in production. They: (1) tie your container to a specific host directory, (2) may expose sensitive files (.git, .env), (3) have host-specific permission models, (4) can't be migrated with the container. Production uses volumes or copies all code into the image at build time.

17.5 tmpfs Mounts — In-Memory Storage

Use CaseCommandWhy
Temp files--tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=128mFaster than disk, auto-cleaned
Secrets at runtime--tmpfs /run/secrets:ro,size=1mNever touches disk — zero trace after stop
Django cache--tmpfs /app/cache:rw,size=256mRAM-speed cache, volatile (use Redis for production)

17.6 Backup & Restore Strategies

TERMINAL
# ─── Strategy 1: Volume-level backup ───
$ docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar czf /backup/all_volumes.tar.gz -C /data .

# ─── Strategy 2: Database-level (pg_dump) ───
$ docker exec anihpj-db pg_dump -U anihpj_user anihpj > backup.sql
$ docker exec -i anihpj-db psql -U anihpj_user anihpj < backup.sql

# ─── Strategy 3: Media files only ───
$ docker run --rm -v media_volume:/media -v $(pwd):/backup \
    alpine tar czf /backup/media.tar.gz -C /media .

# ─── Automated nightly backup (cron on host) ───
# 0 2 * * * docker exec anihpj-db pg_dump -U anihpj_user anihpj > /backups/anihpj_$(date +\%Y\%m\%d).sql

📝 Chapter 17 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Which anihpj data MUST be on a persistent volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

PostgreSQL data (/var/lib/postgresql/data) — without a volume, all database records are lost on container restart. Media files — user uploads must survive deployments. Static files can be regenerated but should be on a volume for Nginx access. Application code does NOT need a volume (baked into image).

EXPLANATION

The hierarchy of persistence needs: Database = critical (can't regenerate), Media = important (can't regenerate), Static = convenient (can regenerate with collectstatic), Code = none (baked into image at build time). Always use named volumes for the first two, consider volumes for static, never for code in production.

# /var/lib/postgresql/data
Q2
Why mount static files as a shared volume between Django and Nginx?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Django's collectstatic gathers all static files (CSS, JS, images) into one directory. Nginx serves these files directly — much faster than Django. The shared volume means both containers see the same files: Django writes during build/deploy, Nginx reads at request time.

EXPLANATION

Without the shared volume, you'd need to copy static files into the Nginx image at build time — coupling the Nginx image to the Django version. With a shared volume, static files can be updated independently. Use :ro on the Nginx side for security — Nginx should never write to the static volume.

# collectstatic
Q3
How do you backup a Docker volume's contents?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Run a temporary container that mounts both the volume and a host backup directory: docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz -C /data .. For databases, use native tools: docker exec db pg_dump > backup.sql.

EXPLANATION

The temporary container pattern is the standard way to access volume data without running the main service. Use alpine (5 MB) for simple tar operations, or the actual database image for native tools. For automated backups, run this as a cron job or scheduled CI/CD pipeline step.

# docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz -C /data .
# docker exec db pg_dump > backup.sql
Q4
Why should you NOT use bind mounts in production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Bind mounts: (1) tie containers to a specific host path — not portable, (2) may expose .git, .env, and other sensitive files, (3) have host-specific file permissions, (4) prevent scaling to multiple hosts. Volumes are Docker-managed, portable, and work with volume drivers for cloud storage.

EXPLANATION

A bind mount like -v /home/dev/anihpj:/app only works on that specific machine. Move to another host or cloud VM — the path doesn't exist. Volumes (-v anihpj_code:/app) work identically everywhere. Bind mounts are excellent for development (hot reload), but production deployments should use volumes or COPY all code into the image.

# -v /home/dev/anihpj:/app
# -v anihpj_code:/app
Q5
What does :ro mean in a volume mount?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Read-Only — the container can read from the volume but cannot write to it. Use for security: Nginx mounts static files as static_volume:/static:ro — it can serve them but can't modify them. If an attacker compromises Nginx, they can't deface your static files.

EXPLANATION

The :ro flag is defense-in-depth. Even if the Nginx process is compromised, the attacker can't write malicious files to the static volume. Combine with --read-only root filesystem for even stronger protection. Only services that need to write (Django for collectstatic, PostgreSQL for data) should have write access.

# static_volume:/static:ro
# --read-only
Q6
How do tmpfs mounts differ from volumes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

tmpfs stores data in RAM — it's the fastest storage type but data disappears when the container stops. Volumes store data on disk — slower but persistent. Use tmpfs for temporary data that should never hit disk (secrets, session tokens); use volumes for data that must survive restarts (database, uploads).

EXPLANATION

tmpfs is ideal for: (1) temporary secrets that should be ephemeral, (2) high-speed scratch space (build caches), (3) directories where the security requirement is "data must never be recoverable from disk." On container stop, tmpfs data is irretrievably gone — even forensics can't recover it from RAM after power loss.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q7
How do you use pg_dump to backup PostgreSQL running in Docker?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker exec anihpj-db pg_dump -U anihpj_user anihpj > backup.sql. This runs pg_dump inside the PostgreSQL container and pipes the SQL output to a file on your host. To restore: docker exec -i anihpj-db psql -U anihpj_user anihpj < backup.sql.

EXPLANATION

pg_dump is preferred over volume-level backup because: (1) it produces a consistent snapshot even while the database is running, (2) the SQL file is portable across PostgreSQL versions, (3) you can selectively restore tables. Volume-level backup (tar) is faster for large databases but may produce inconsistent backups if the database is writing during the tar.

# docker exec anihpj-db pg_dump -U anihpj_user anihpj > backup.sql
# docker exec -i anihpj-db psql -U anihpj_user anihpj < backup.sql
Q8
What's the difference between docker compose down and docker compose down -v regarding volumes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

down stops containers and removes networks — but PRESERVES all named volumes. down -v also DELETES all volumes (named AND anonymous). Your database data survives down; it's wiped by down -v. Use -v only when you want a complete reset.

EXPLANATION

This is the most dangerous Compose flag. docker compose down -v will delete your PostgreSQL data, user uploads, and collected static files — permanently, with no undo. Always double-check before using -v. For safety, list volumes first: docker volume ls, then decide if you really want to delete them.

# docker compose down
# docker compose down -v
# docker compose down -v
# docker volume ls
Q9
How do you migrate Docker volumes to a new host?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) Backup: docker run --rm -v myvol:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/myvol.tar.gz -C /data . (2) Copy tar to new host. (3) Create volume on new host: docker volume create myvol. (4) Restore: docker run --rm -v myvol:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar xzf /backup/myvol.tar.gz -C /data.

EXPLANATION

Volume data is just files in /var/lib/docker/volumes/. You could rsync that directory, but the tar approach is cleaner — it works across Docker versions and OS platforms. For cloud migrations, use volume driver plugins (like EBS or NFS) that handle migration automatically.

# docker run --rm -v myvol:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/myvol.tar.gz -C /data .
# docker volume create myvol
# docker run --rm -v myvol:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar xzf /backup/myvol.tar.gz -C /data
# /var/lib/docker/volumes/
Q10
What volume driver would you use for shared storage across multiple Docker hosts?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

NFS (Network File System) — create with: docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=nfs-server,rw --opt device=:/export/path nfs-volume. Then mount with -v nfs-volume:/data. For cloud: AWS EBS, Azure Disk, or GCE Persistent Disk drivers. For enterprise: Portworx, NetApp Trident.

EXPLANATION

The local driver only works on one host. For multi-host setups (Swarm, or multiple standalone Docker hosts sharing data), you need a network-aware driver. NFS is the simplest — standard protocol, works everywhere. Cloud-specific drivers (like AWS EFS CSI) provide better performance and integration with cloud IAM and backup services.

# docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=nfs-server,rw --opt device=:/export/path nfs-volume
# -v nfs-volume:/data

Chapter 18: Advanced Storage Topics

Beyond basic volumes: understand how Docker manages image layers with storage drivers, use volume plugins for cloud storage, configure NFS volumes for multi-host data sharing, and peek inside the union filesystem that makes Docker images work.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1.5 hours💾 Storage🎯 DCA 5%

18.1 Storage Drivers (Overlay2, aufs, etc.)

A storage driver manages how image layers and the container's writable layer are stored on disk. Docker supports several — overlay2 is the default and recommended for all modern Linux systems:

DriverStatusFilesystemNotes
overlay2✅ Defaultext4, xfsBest performance, recommended for all modern kernels
aufs⚠️ Legacyext4, xfsOriginal Docker driver, deprecated
devicemapper⚠️ Legacydirect-lvmRHEL/CentOS 7 default, replaced by overlay2
btrfs/zfs🔧 Nichebtrfs, zfsAdvanced features (snapshots, compression)
vfs🐌 TestingAnyNo copy-on-write — full copy per layer. Testing only.
TERMINAL
# Check which storage driver is in use
$ docker info | grep "Storage Driver"
Storage Driver: overlay2

18.2 Volume Drivers & Plugins

DriverTypePersistenceBest For
localBuilt-inSingle hostDefault, most applications
NFSBuilt-in (local with opts)Multi-hostShared storage across hosts
AWS EBSCloud pluginAZ-specificEC2 instances, high IOPS
Azure DiskCloud pluginZone-specificAzure VMs, managed disks
GCE Persistent DiskCloud pluginZone-specificGCP instances

18.3 NFS Volumes in Docker

TERMINAL
# Create an NFS volume
$ docker volume create \
    --driver local \
    --opt type=nfs \
    --opt o=addr=192.168.1.100,rw,nfsvers=4 \
    --opt device=:/exports/anihpj_data \
    nfs_shared_volume

# Use it like any other volume
$ docker run -d --name anihpj-app \
    -v nfs_shared_volume:/app/data \
    anihpj:v1.0

# In compose.yaml:
volumes:
  shared_data:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:
      type: nfs
      o: "addr=192.168.1.100,rw,nfsvers=4"
      device: ":/exports/anihpj_data"

18.4 Container Filesystem Internals

The Overlay2 filesystem is how Docker creates the illusion of a single unified filesystem from multiple image layers. Understanding it helps debug storage issues:

Overlay2 — Union Filesystem Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  📚 OVERLAY2 FILESYSTEM — HOW IT WORKS                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │  What the CONTAINER sees:                   What's REALLY on disk:        │
  │  ┌───────────────────────┐                ┌───────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ /app/                 │                │  ┌─────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │ ├── manage.py  (R/W) │                │  │ UpperDir (R/W)       │  │  │
  │  │ ├── anihpj/    (R/W) │                │  │ Container's changes  │  │  │
  │  │ ├── jobpost/   (R/W) │                │  │ (writable layer)     │  │  │
  │  │ ├── bin/python (R/O)│                │  └──────────┬──────────┘  │  │
  │  │ └── lib/       (R/O)│                │             │             │  │
  │  └───────────────────────┘                │  ┌──────────▼──────────┐  │  │
  │                                          │  │ LowerDir (R/O)      │  │  │
  │  The container sees ONE                  │  │ Layer 5: COPY . .   │  │  │
  │  unified filesystem — but                │  │ Layer 4: pip install│  │  │
  │  behind the scenes, Overlay2             │  │ Layer 3: COPY reqs  │  │  │
  │  merges multiple layers                  │  │ Layer 2: WORKDIR    │  │  │
  │  using Copy-on-Write.                    │  │ Layer 1: FROM slim  │  │  │
  │                                          │  └──────────┬──────────┘  │  │
  │  Copy-on-Write:                          │             │             │  │
  │  Write to a file → copy from             │  ┌──────────▼──────────┐  │  │
  │  LowerDir to UpperDir first.             │  │ WorkDir (internal)  │  │  │
  │  Read: if in UpperDir, use it.           │  │ Merge scratch space │  │  │
  │  If not, read from LowerDir.            │  └──────────┬──────────┘  │  │
  │                                          │             │             │  │
  │                                          │  ┌──────────▼──────────┐  │  │
  │                                          │  │ Merged View         │  │  │
  │                                          │  │ (what container     │  │  │
  │                                          │  │  actually sees)     │  │  │
  │                                          │  └─────────────────────┘  │  │
  │                                          └───────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

📝 Chapter 18 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What is the default and recommended Docker storage driver?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

overlay2 — it's the default on all modern Linux distributions. It uses a union filesystem to merge multiple image layers into one view, with copy-on-write for the container's writable layer. Check with docker info | grep "Storage Driver".

EXPLANATION

overlay2 replaced aufs and devicemapper as the universal standard. It's faster, uses less memory, and supports up to 128 layers (vs 42 for aufs). Requires Linux kernel 4.0+ and a filesystem supporting xattr (ext4, xfs). Docker Desktop also uses overlay2 inside its Linux VM.

# docker info | grep "Storage Driver"
Q2
How does Copy-on-Write (CoW) work in Docker's storage?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

When a container wants to MODIFY a file from a lower (read-only) image layer, Docker copies it up to the container's writable layer first, then applies the modification there. The original in the image layer stays unchanged. When READING, Docker checks the writable layer first, then image layers top-down.

EXPLANATION

CoW is why containers start instantly — they don't copy the entire image. Only modified files are copied up. This saves enormous disk space: 10 containers from the same image share most data, each only storing their unique changes. The trade-off: heavy write workloads are slower due to the copy-up overhead.

# Volume management:
docker volume create appdata
docker volume inspect appdata
docker run -v appdata:/data alpine
docker volume prune
Q3
How do you create a Docker volume backed by NFS?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=192.168.1.100,rw --opt device=:/exports/path nfs-vol. Then use it normally: docker run -v nfs-vol:/data myimage. The volume data is stored on the NFS server, accessible from any Docker host that mounts it.

EXPLANATION

NFS volumes are the simplest way to share data across multiple Docker hosts. All hosts mount the same NFS export. Limitations: (1) NFS server becomes a single point of failure unless clustered, (2) database files on NFS can cause locking issues (use PostgreSQL streaming replication instead), (3) performance depends on network speed.

# docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=192.168.1.100,rw --opt device=:/exports/path nfs-vol
# docker run -v nfs-vol:/data myimage
Q4
What's the difference between a storage driver and a volume driver?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Storage driver manages image layers and the container's writable layer (overlay2, aufs). It controls how the container filesystem works. Volume driver manages persistent volumes (local, NFS, cloud plugins). It controls WHERE volume data is stored. Both are pluggable but serve different purposes.

EXPLANATION

Think of the storage driver as "how Docker stores the OS and your app" and the volume driver as "where Docker stores your data." The storage driver is chosen at Docker daemon install time (rarely changed). The volume driver is chosen per-volume and you can mix multiple drivers (local for dev, NFS for shared, EBS for production databases).

# Volume management:
docker volume create appdata
docker volume inspect appdata
docker run -v appdata:/data alpine
docker volume prune
Q5
What command shows the current storage driver?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker info | grep "Storage Driver" or docker info --format '{{.Driver}}'. Also shows the backing filesystem and driver status. This is useful for verifying your Docker installation is using the optimal driver for your OS.

EXPLANATION

docker info provides comprehensive Docker daemon configuration. The Storage Driver line tells you which driver is active. The DCA exam expects you to know that overlay2 is the recommended driver and how to verify it. If you see aufs or devicemapper, the system needs upgrading.

# docker info | grep "Storage Driver"
# docker info --format '{{.Driver}}'
# docker info
Q6
What are the three directories in an Overlay2 filesystem?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

LowerDir — read-only image layers (your Dockerfile instructions). UpperDir — the container's writable layer (changes made at runtime). Merged — the unified view the container sees (LowerDir + UpperDir combined). WorkDir — internal scratch space for atomic operations.

EXPLANATION

You can see these on the host: ls /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<container-id>/ shows diff (UpperDir), merged, and work directories. The LowerDir is referenced via symbolic links. This structure is why docker images shows shared sizes — multiple images can share the same LowerDir layers.

# ls /var/lib/docker/overlay2//
# docker images
Q7
Why might database files on NFS cause problems?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Databases require consistent, low-latency I/O with file locking. NFS adds network latency and has historically had unreliable file locking. PostgreSQL and MySQL explicitly warn against NFS for data directories. Use block storage (EBS, managed disks) or database-native replication instead.

EXPLANATION

PostgreSQL relies on fsync() guarantees — data must be physically on disk before acknowledging a transaction. NFS may cache writes and acknowledge before the server commits them, leading to data corruption on network failure. For production databases: use local volumes + pg_dump backups + replication, not NFS-mounted data directories.

# Volume management:
docker volume create appdata
docker volume inspect appdata
docker run -v appdata:/data alpine
docker volume prune
Q8
What volume driver would you use for high-IOPS database storage on AWS?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

AWS EBS CSI driver — it provisions EBS volumes (gp3/io2) and attaches them to EC2 instances. EBS provides consistent low-latency block storage with provisioned IOPS. For multi-AZ, use EFS (NFS-compatible) for shared files, but EBS for databases.

EXPLANATION

EBS volumes are the cloud equivalent of a physical SSD — block-level, high IOPS, single-AZ. They're ideal for databases because they provide the consistent fsync() guarantees PostgreSQL needs. EFS is NFS-based, good for shared static/media files across AZs, but not recommended for database data directories due to NFS latency and locking issues.

# Volume management:
docker volume create appdata
docker volume inspect appdata
docker run -v appdata:/data alpine
docker volume prune
Q9
What happens to the storage when you run docker system prune?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Removes: stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, and unused build cache. Does NOT remove: volumes (unless --volumes is added), running containers, tagged images. For volumes: docker system prune --volumes also removes all unused volumes.

EXPLANATION

The hierarchy of cleanup: docker system prune (safe, no volumes) → docker system prune -a (removes all unused images too) → docker system prune -a --volumes (nuclear — removes everything unused including volumes). Always run docker system df first to see what will be reclaimed.

# docker system prune
# --volumes
# docker system prune --volumes
# docker system prune
# docker system prune -a
Q10
How does Docker handle file permissions when sharing volumes between containers with different users?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker does NOT translate UIDs between containers. If container A writes a file as UID 1000 (appuser) and container B runs as UID 1001, container B may get "permission denied." Solution: use the same UID across containers (--user 1000:1000), or use chown in an init container, or use :Z SELinux label.

EXPLANATION

This is a common gotcha with shared volumes. The anihpj solution: Django runs as UID 1000 (app), Nginx runs as UID 101 (nginx). Django writes static files as UID 1000. Nginx needs to read them. Fix: either run Nginx as UID 1000 (--user 1000:1000), or set static files to world-readable (chmod -R a+r /app/static) during collectstatic, or use an init container that adjusts permissions.

# --user 1000:1000
# --user 1000:1000
# chmod -R a+r /app/static

Part 6 covers everything you need to persist data beyond the container lifecycle — the difference between ephemeral containers and permanent data:

  • Storage Fundamentals (Ch 16): Containers are ephemeral — volumes are permanent. 4 storage types: volumes (production), bind mounts (dev), tmpfs (RAM-only secrets), npipe (Windows). Volumes have an independent lifecycle — deleting a container never deletes its named volumes.
  • Persistent Data for anihpj (Ch 17): PostgreSQL data MUST be on a volume. Media/static files shared between Django and Nginx via named volumes. Bind mounts ONLY for development. tmpfs for ephemeral secrets. Backup strategies: volume-level tar or database-level pg_dump.
  • Advanced Storage (Ch 18): overlay2 is the default storage driver (union filesystem with Copy-on-Write). Volume drivers enable cloud storage (EBS, Azure Disk, NFS). NFS for multi-host sharing (but not for databases). Understand LowerDir/UpperDir/Merged for debugging.
🔄 Implementation: The Storage Golden Rules

1. Database → named volume, always. 2. Dev → bind mounts for hot reload. 3. Prod → volumes or COPY into image. 4. Backup → pg_dump for databases, tar for volumes. 5. Never use docker compose down -v without checking docker volume ls first. 6. overlay2 is the answer to any "which storage driver" DCA question.

Chapter 19: Container Security Fundamentals

Containers share the host kernel — which means a compromised container can potentially compromise the host. Docker's security model provides multiple layers of defense: namespaces, capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux, and more. Understanding these layers is essential for the DCA exam and production deployments.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🔐 Security🎯 DCA 15%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand why container security requires defense-in-depth
  • ✅ Master Docker's 10-layer security architecture
  • ✅ Run containers as non-root users
  • ✅ Use Linux capabilities to limit process privileges
  • ✅ Harden containers with read-only root filesystems

19.1 Why Container Security Matters

Containers are NOT virtual machines. They share the host kernel — a kernel exploit in a container can affect the ENTIRE host and all other containers. Real-world risks include cryptojacking (stealing CPU for crypto mining), data exfiltration, and container breakout (escaping to the host). Security is not optional — it's the foundation of containerized production.

⚠️
Shared Kernel Risk

Unlike VMs (each has its own kernel), containers share the host kernel. A kernel vulnerability exploited inside a container can compromise the entire host and all other containers.

🔓
Container Breakout

If a process escapes the container's namespace isolation, it gains access to the host. This is the worst-case scenario — full host compromise from inside a container.

📦
Supply Chain Attacks

Pulling a malicious base image from a public registry can give attackers a foothold. Always use trusted images, scan for CVEs, and verify signatures with Docker Content Trust.

🔓
Level 0
Default Container

Runs as root. All capabilities. Writable rootfs. No scanning.

❌ Vulnerable
👤

USER app. --cap-drop ALL. Basic hardening applied.

19.2 Docker Security Architecture — The Onion of Defense

Docker secures containers with multiple independent layers. Even if an attacker bypasses one layer, the next ones still protect the system:

10 Layers of Docker Security
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  🔐 DOCKER SECURITY — ONION OF DEFENSE                     │
  │                                                                          │
  │                           ┌───────────┐                                  │
  │                           │  🐳 Your   │                                 │
  │                           │ Container │                                 │

  │                                 │                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┐    │

  │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │

19.3 Running as Non-Root User

By default, Docker containers run as root (UID 0). If an attacker compromises your app, they have root inside the container — and potentially on the host. Running as non-root is the single most impactful security measure:

Dockerfile (Non-Root User)
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Create a system user (no login, no home directory)
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app

WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=app:app . .

# Switch to non-root user
USER app

CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

# Or override at runtime:
# docker run --user 1000:1000 anihpj:v1
⚠️ Root by Default

Unless you explicitly set USER in your Dockerfile or use --user at runtime, the container process runs as UID 0 (root). This means: (1) the process can modify any file, (2) can bind to privileged ports (<1024), (3) can install packages, (4) can change kernel parameters if capabilities allow it. Always run as non-root.

19.4 Linux Capabilities

Traditionally, root has all power. Linux capabilities split root's power into fine-grained permissions. Docker gives containers a default set — drop ALL and add back only what you need:

CapabilityAllowsRiskWhen Needed
NET_BIND_SERVICEBind to ports < 1024LowWeb servers binding to port 80/443
CHOWNChange file ownershipLowAlmost always needed
SYS_ADMINMount filesystems, many admin ops🔴 Critical — ≈ root!Almost never — avoid!
SYS_PTRACEDebug other processesMediumDebugging tools (strace, gdb)
NET_RAWRaw sockets (ping)MediumNetwork diagnostic tools
TERMINAL
# Run with minimal capabilities
$ docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE --cap-add CHOWN anihpj:v1

# Check current capabilities
$ docker run --rm alpine capsh --print

19.5 Read-Only Root Filesystem

A read-only root filesystem prevents an attacker from modifying binaries, installing malware, or tampering with configuration files. Only explicitly mounted volumes and tmpfs directories are writable:

TERMINAL
# Run with read-only root filesystem
$ docker run --read-only \
    --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid \
    --tmpfs /run:rw,noexec,nosuid \
    -v static_volume:/app/static \
    anihpj:v1

# Django needs writable /tmp for:
# - Gunicorn socket files
# - File uploads temp storage (before moving to media/)
# - Session files (if using file-based sessions)

📝 Chapter 19 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Why are containers less isolated than VMs from a security perspective?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Containers share the host kernel — VMs each have their own kernel. A kernel exploit inside a container can affect the host and all other containers. VMs provide stronger isolation because the hypervisor separates guest kernels from the host. Containers rely on Linux namespaces, which provide process-level — not kernel-level — isolation.

EXPLANATION

This is the fundamental security trade-off: containers are lighter because they share the kernel, but this sharing creates a larger attack surface. Defense-in-depth (namespaces + capabilities + seccomp + AppArmor + read-only rootfs) compensates for this by adding multiple independent security layers.

# Security hardening:
docker run --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp app:v1
docker scout quickview app:v1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
Q2
What are Linux capabilities and why are they important for containers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Capabilities split root's absolute power into fine-grained permissions (CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, CAP_SYS_ADMIN, etc.). Docker gives containers a default set of ~14 capabilities. Dropping ALL (--cap-drop ALL) and adding back only needed ones dramatically reduces what an attacker can do even if they compromise the container.

EXPLANATION

Without capabilities, any root process has unlimited power. With capabilities, you can say "this process can bind to port 80 but cannot mount filesystems, load kernel modules, or change system time." The principle: give containers only what they need. CAP_SYS_ADMIN is the most dangerous — it's essentially root-level power.

# --cap-drop ALL
Q3
How do you run a container as a non-root user?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

In Dockerfile: RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app then USER app. At runtime: docker run --user 1000:1000 anihpj:v1. The --system flag creates a system user (UID < 1000, no login shell, no home directory).

EXPLANATION

The USER instruction in Dockerfile is preferred — it bakes the security policy into the image. The --user flag overrides it at runtime. Note: the user must exist in the container's /etc/passwd, or you can use numeric UIDs. Non-root users can't bind to ports <1024 without CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE.

# RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app
# docker run --user 1000:1000 anihpj:v1
Q4
What does --read-only do for container security?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Makes the container's root filesystem read-only. The container CANNOT write to /, /usr, /bin, or any image layer. This prevents attackers from: modifying binaries (installing backdoors), tampering with config files, or writing malware to disk. Only explicitly mounted volumes and tmpfs directories are writable.

EXPLANATION

Many attacks rely on writing files — dropping a webshell, modifying crontab, creating a new user. --read-only blocks all of these at the filesystem level. You'll need --tmpfs for directories that must be writable (/tmp, /run, /var/run). Gunicorn needs writable /tmp for its socket file.

# --read-only
# --read-only
Q5
What is seccomp and how does Docker use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) filters which system calls a process can make. Docker applies a default seccomp profile that blocks ~60 dangerous syscalls (like mount, reboot, kexec_load) while allowing ~300 safe ones. This prevents a compromised container from making kernel-level attacks.

EXPLANATION

Seccomp operates at the kernel level — before the syscall executes. It's more granular than capabilities: a capability might allow "network operations," while seccomp can say "allow socket() and bind() but block setsockopt()." You can create custom seccomp profiles with --security-opt seccomp=/path/to/profile.json.

# kexec_load
# --security-opt seccomp=/path/to/profile.json
Q6
Why should you never run containers as root in production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Root inside a container has UID 0 — the same UID as host root. While namespaces limit what root can do, kernel vulnerabilities or misconfigured capabilities could allow container escape to the host. Running as non-root limits the damage: even if your app is compromised, the attacker starts with minimal privileges.

EXPLANATION

User namespace remapping (userns-remap) adds another layer: even if a container process thinks it's root (UID 0), the kernel maps it to a high UID on the host (like 100000). This means container root has no actual root privileges on the host. Enable in /etc/docker/daemon.json: {"userns-remap": "default"}.

# userns-remap
# /etc/docker/daemon.json
# {"userns-remap": "default"}
Q7
What are the 10 layers of Docker's security onion?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) User Namespace, (2) Capabilities, (3) Seccomp, (4) AppArmor/SELinux, (5) Cgroups, (6) Read-Only Root FS, (7) Network Isolation, (8) Image Scanning, (9) Content Trust, (10) Host Security. Each layer is independent — bypassing one doesn't compromise the others. This is defense-in-depth.

EXPLANATION

The DCA exam tests your understanding that security is not a single setting — it's layered. Each layer addresses a different attack vector. A container running as non-root (layer 1) with dropped capabilities (layer 2) on a read-only filesystem (layer 6) with scanned images (layer 8) is exponentially harder to compromise than a default root container.

# Security hardening:
docker run --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp app:v1
docker scout quickview app:v1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
Q8
What's the difference between AppArmor and SELinux?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Both are Mandatory Access Control (MAC) systems. AppArmor (Debian/Ubuntu) is path-based — "this process can read /etc/passwd but not /etc/shadow." SELinux (RHEL/CentOS) is label-based — every file and process has a security label and policies define which labels can interact. Both limit what a container can do even if it has root.

EXPLANATION

Docker applies a default AppArmor profile on Ubuntu and a default SELinux policy on RHEL. These profiles prevent common attack patterns: reading host /proc, mounting filesystems, accessing Docker socket. Use --security-opt apparmor=your-profile or --security-opt label=type:container_t to customize.

# --security-opt apparmor=your-profile
# --security-opt label=type:container_t
Q9
What is user namespace remapping (userns-remap)?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It maps container UIDs to different UIDs on the host. A container process running as UID 0 (root) is actually running as a high-numbered UID (like 100000) on the host — with no root privileges. This is the strongest user isolation Docker provides. Enable in daemon.json: {"userns-remap": "default"}.

EXPLANATION

Without userns-remap, container root (UID 0) IS root on the host for any operation not blocked by namespaces. With userns-remap, even if a container process thinks it's root, the kernel sees it as UID 100000 — a completely unprivileged user. Trade-off: some features don't work with userns-remap (like --privileged and host networking).

# {"userns-remap": "default"}
Q10
What command drops all capabilities and adds back only what's needed?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE --cap-add CHOWN anihpj:v1. This removes all capabilities from the container, then adds back only NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind to ports) and CHOWN (change file ownership). The container starts with the absolute minimum privileges.

EXPLANATION

The default Docker capability set includes ~14 capabilities. --cap-drop ALL removes everything, then --cap-add selectively restores. For a Django app, you typically need: NET_BIND_SERVICE (if binding port 80), CHOWN (for startup scripts), and possibly DAC_OVERRIDE (file permission bypass). Test thoroughly after dropping capabilities.

# docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE --cap-add CHOWN anihpj:v1
# --cap-drop ALL
# --cap-add

20.1 Security Hardening Checklist for anihpj

#Security MeasureImplementation
1Specific base image tagFROM python:3.11-slim (not :latest)
2Run as non-rootUSER app after groupadd/adduser --system

20.2 Secrets Management

Environment variables in Dockerfiles and docker inspect are visible to anyone with Docker access. Secrets must be handled differently:

Swarm Secrets (Production)
# Create a secret
$ echo "super-secret-django-key" | docker secret create django_secret_key -

# Use in compose (Swarm mode):
services:
  django:
    secrets:
      - django_secret_key
    environment:
      - SECRET_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/django_secret_key

secrets:
  django_secret_key:
    external: true

# For non-Swarm: use .env file (gitignored!)
# .env:
# DB_PASSWORD=secure_password_here
# SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-xyz

20.3 Securing the Docker Daemon

The Docker daemon runs as root. Its socket (/var/run/docker.sock) is equivalent to root access. Never expose it without TLS:

daemon.json
{
  "icc": false,                  // Disable inter-container communication
  "userns-remap": "default",     // User namespace remapping
  "live-restore": true,          // Keep containers alive during daemon downtime
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "10m",
    "max-file": "3"
  },
  "no-new-privileges": true     // Prevent privilege escalation
}

20.4 Image Signing & Content Trust

Docker Content Trust (DCT) uses Notary to sign and verify images, ensuring you're running exactly what the publisher intended:

TERMINAL
# Enable Content Trust
$ export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1

# Pull only signed images
$ docker pull anihpj:v1         # Fails if unsigned!

# Sign and push (requires signing key)
$ docker trust signer add --key cert.pem alice registry.example.com
$ docker trust sign registry.example.com/anihpj:v1

# Verify image signature
$ docker trust inspect anihpj:v1

20.5 Podman vs Docker — Rootless Containers

AspectDockerPodman
ArchitectureClient-server (dockerd daemon)Daemonless (fork-exec model)
Root required?Daemon runs as rootRootless by default ✅
CLI compatibilitydocker runpodman run (alias docker=podman)
Compose supportdocker compose (built-in)podman-compose (separate)
KubernetesDocker Desktop K8spodman play kube (built-in)
Best forDevelopment, Docker ecosystemSecurity-focused, RHEL environments

📝 Chapter 20 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Why should secrets never be set via ENV in a Dockerfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ENV values are baked into the image and visible to anyone with docker history or docker inspect. They also appear in docker inspect output for running containers. Secrets in ENV are essentially stored in plaintext in the image — accessible to anyone who can pull the image.

EXPLANATION

docker history anihpj:v1 shows EVERY layer's creation command, including ENV values. Even if you delete the Dockerfile, the image itself contains all ENV vars in its config. Solution: inject secrets at runtime via Swarm secrets, Kubernetes Secrets, or mounted .env files. Never set secrets at build time.

# docker history
# docker inspect
# docker inspect
# docker history anihpj:v1
Q2
What is Docker Content Trust and how do you enable it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

DCT uses digital signatures to verify image authenticity and integrity. Enable with export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1. When enabled: docker pull only succeeds for signed images, docker push automatically signs images. This prevents running tampered or unofficial images.

EXPLANATION

DCT is part of Docker's software supply chain security. It uses The Update Framework (TUF) and Notary for key management. Signers hold private keys; the registry holds public metadata. Without DCT, anyone who can push to your registry can replace your image with a malicious one — DCT prevents this by requiring valid signatures.

# export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
# docker pull
# docker push
Q3
Why is the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) dangerous?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The Docker socket gives full control over the Docker daemon — which runs as root. Mounting it into a container (-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock) gives that container root-equivalent access to the host. The container can start privileged containers, access any volume, or escape to the host.

EXPLANATION

Mounting docker.sock is sometimes necessary (CI/CD tools like Jenkins, monitoring agents) but it's extremely dangerous. If that container is compromised, the attacker has root on the host. Mitigations: (1) use Docker's TCP API with TLS instead, (2) use tools that don't need socket access, (3) use rootless Docker or Podman.

# -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
Q4
How do Docker Swarm secrets differ from environment variables?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Swarm secrets are: (1) encrypted at rest (on manager nodes), (2) encrypted in transit (mutual TLS between nodes), (3) mounted as files in /run/secrets/ — not visible in docker inspect or env, (4) only available to services explicitly granted access. ENV vars are plaintext, visible in inspect/history/ps output.

EXPLANATION

Swarm secrets are the production-grade solution for Docker. They're stored in the Raft log (encrypted), transmitted over mTLS, and only mounted into authorized containers as tmpfs files. The container reads /run/secrets/db_password instead of $DB_PASSWORD. This eliminates the entire class of "secret leaked via docker inspect" vulnerabilities.

# /run/secrets/
# docker inspect
# /run/secrets/db_password
# $DB_PASSWORD
Q5
What does userns-remap do in daemon.json?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It remaps container UIDs to different UIDs on the host. Container root (UID 0) becomes UID 100000+ on the host — with zero host privileges. This means even if a container process escapes to the host, it has no root access. It's the strongest user isolation Docker provides.

EXPLANATION

Enable with {"userns-remap": "default"} in /etc/docker/daemon.json, then restart Docker. Creates a dockremap user automatically. Limitations: some features don't work (--privileged, host networking, some volume drivers). Test thoroughly before enabling in production.

# userns-remap
# {"userns-remap": "default"}
# /etc/docker/daemon.json
# dockremap
Q6
What's the difference between Podman and Docker?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker: client-server architecture with dockerd daemon running as root. Podman: daemonless, rootless by default, uses fork-exec model. Podman is CLI-compatible (alias docker=podman), supports pods (Kubernetes-style), and doesn't require a background daemon. Podman is default on RHEL 8+.

EXPLANATION

Podman's rootless design is its biggest security advantage — no root daemon means no root attack surface. However, Docker has a larger ecosystem, better Compose integration, and wider tooling support. The DCA exam focuses on Docker but may mention Podman as an alternative architecture.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q7
What command signs a Docker image with Content Trust?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker trust sign registry.example.com/anihpj:v1 — after adding a signer with docker trust signer add. The image must already be pushed. The sign command creates and pushes trust metadata to the Notary server attached to the registry.

EXPLANATION

Signing workflow: (1) Generate signing keys (docker trust key generate), (2) Add signer to repository (docker trust signer add), (3) Push image (docker push), (4) Sign (docker trust sign). After signing, DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 docker pull will verify the signature before running the image.

# docker trust sign registry.example.com/anihpj:v1
# docker trust signer add
# DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 docker pull
Q8
What setting disables inter-container communication on the default bridge?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

{"icc": false} in /etc/docker/daemon.json. This prevents containers on the default bridge from communicating with each other. They can still communicate via explicitly created networks. Restart Docker daemon after changing.

EXPLANATION

ICC (Inter-Container Communication) is enabled by default on the default bridge. Disabling it adds a network-level security barrier: even if container A is compromised, it can't directly attack container B on the default bridge. Containers on custom bridges are unaffected — this only applies to the default bridge network.

# {"icc": false}
# /etc/docker/daemon.json
Q9
What does --no-new-privileges do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Prevents container processes from gaining additional privileges — even through setuid binaries or SELinux transitions. Once a container starts with a certain privilege level, it cannot escalate. This blocks a common attack vector: exploiting a setuid binary to gain root.

EXPLANATION

Without --no-new-privileges, a non-root user could potentially run a setuid-root binary (like sudo or passwd) to escalate to root. With this flag, the kernel blocks any privilege escalation — the process keeps exactly the privileges it started with. It's set by default in Docker's seccomp profile but can be explicitly enforced.

# --no-new-privileges
# --no-new-privileges
Q10
What's the single most impactful security measure for Docker containers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Running as non-root user. It's simple, has almost zero compatibility impact, and prevents the most common attack escalation path. Combined with --cap-drop ALL and --read-only, you've eliminated the vast majority of container escape vectors. No single measure is perfect — but non-root is the foundation.

EXPLANATION

The hierarchy of security ROI: (1) non-root user = highest impact, lowest effort; (2) capability dropping = high impact, moderate testing; (3) read-only rootfs = high impact, needs tmpfs configuration; (4) image scanning = prevents known vulnerabilities; (5) seccomp/AppArmor = defense-in-depth. Start with #1 and work your way up.

# --cap-drop ALL
# --read-only

Chapter 21: Docker Security Scanning & Compliance

Security isn't just about configuration — it's about continuous verification. Docker Scout, Trivy, Docker Bench Security, and SBOM tools help you find vulnerabilities before attackers do and prove compliance with security standards.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour🔍 Scanning🎯 DCA 10%

21.1 Docker Scout Deep Dive

TERMINAL
# Quick vulnerability summary
$ docker scout quickview anihpj:v1

# Detailed CVE report with severity
$ docker scout cves anihpj:v1

# Get fix recommendations
$ docker scout recommendations anihpj:v1
  → Update base image python:3.11-slim (fixes 12 CVEs)
  → Update package libssl3 (fixes CVE-2024-xxx)

# Compare two images
$ docker scout compare anihpj:v1 anihpj:v2

# CI/CD integration (GitHub Actions)
- uses: docker/scout-action@v1
  with:
    image: anihpj:${{ github.sha }}

21.2 Docker Bench Security

Docker Bench Security runs automated checks against the CIS Docker Benchmark — the industry standard for Docker security configuration:

TERMINAL
$ docker run --rm --pid host --net host --cap-add audit_control \
    -v /var/lib:/var/lib -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
    -v /etc:/etc docker/docker-bench-security

[INFO] 1 - Host Configuration
[PASS] 1.1.1 Ensure a separate partition for containers
[WARN] 1.1.2 Ensure only trusted users control Docker daemon
[PASS] 1.2.1 Ensure auditing is configured for Docker files

[INFO] 2 - Docker Daemon Configuration
[WARN] 2.5 Ensure aufs storage driver is not used
[PASS] 2.11 Ensure authorization for Docker client commands

Score: 23 PASS, 5 WARN, 0 FAIL

21.3 Trivy — Open Source Vulnerability Scanner

TERMINAL
# Scan a Docker image
$ trivy image anihpj:v1

# Scan filesystem (Dockerfile, configs)
$ trivy fs /path/to/project

# Scan with severity filter
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL anihpj:v1

# CI-friendly output (exit 1 if vulns found)
$ trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL anihpj:v1

21.4 SBOM — Software Bill of Materials

An SBOM is a complete inventory of every component in your image — like a nutrition label for containers:

TERMINAL
# Generate SBOM with Docker
$ docker sbom anihpj:v1
NAME                VERSION        TYPE
Django              5.2.0          python
gunicorn            21.2.0         python
psycopg2            2.9.9          python
Pillow              10.3.0         python

# Export in different formats
$ docker sbom --format spdx-json anihpj:v1 > sbom.json
$ docker sbom --format cyclonedx anihpj:v1 > sbom.xml

# Alternative: Syft (Anchore)
$ syft anihpj:v1 -o spdx-json

21.5 CIS Docker Benchmark Overview

CategoryChecksExamples
Host ConfigurationSeparate partition, trusted users, auditingEnsure /var/lib/docker is on separate partition
Docker DaemonNetwork rules, logging, authorizationEnsure swarm mode is not used unless needed
Container ImagesTrusted base images, scanning, minimalUse specific tags, not :latest
Container RuntimeNon-root, read-only, resource limitsContainers should not run as root
Swarm ConfigurationSecrets, encryption, manager nodesEncrypt data exchanged between nodes

📝 Chapter 21 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What command gives a quick vulnerability summary of a Docker image?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker scout quickview anihpj:v1 — shows an overview with CVE counts by severity (Critical, High, Medium, Low), image size, and package count. For detailed CVE information: docker scout cves anihpj:v1.

EXPLANATION

Docker Scout replaced docker scan (which was Snyk-based). Scout generates an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) for the image and checks every package against multiple vulnerability databases. It's available as a CLI command and as a GitHub Action for CI/CD integration.

# docker scout quickview anihpj:v1
# docker scout cves anihpj:v1
# docker scan
Q2
What is Docker Bench Security?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A containerized tool that runs automated checks against the CIS Docker Benchmark — the industry standard for secure Docker configuration. It audits: host configuration, daemon settings, container images, container runtime, and Swarm configuration. Results: PASS, WARN, or FAIL for each check.

EXPLANATION

Docker Bench Security is essentially docker run with specific flags to access the host's Docker daemon, filesystem, and processes. It checks hundreds of CIS benchmark items and produces a scored report. It's the first tool to run when hardening a Docker host — it tells you exactly what needs fixing.

# docker run
Q3
What is Trivy and how does it compare to Docker Scout?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Trivy (Aqua Security) is an open-source vulnerability scanner for containers, filesystems, and Git repositories. Docker Scout is Docker's built-in commercial solution. Trivy is free, supports more targets (K8s, Terraform, config files), and is CI-friendly. Scout is tightly integrated with Docker Hub and provides remediation advice.

EXPLANATION

Both use CVE databases (NVD, GitHub Advisory, etc.) to check packages. Trivy is often preferred in CI/CD because: (1) it's open source (no Docker subscription needed), (2) supports --exit-code 1 for pipeline failure, (3) scans more than just images (IaC files, git repos). Scout's advantage: direct Docker Hub integration and fix recommendations.

# --exit-code 1
Q4
What is an SBOM and why is it important?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Software Bill of Materials — a complete inventory of every component in your image: packages, versions, licenses, and dependencies. It's like a nutrition label for containers. SBOMs are increasingly required for compliance (US Executive Order 14028) and are essential for quickly identifying which images are affected when a new CVE is announced.

EXPLANATION

Without an SBOM, when CVE-2024-XXXX is announced in libssl, you'd need to scan every image to find affected ones. With SBOMs generated at build time and stored in a registry, you can query "which images contain libssl version < 3.2.1?" — and get instant answers. Docker Scout and Syft both generate SBOMs in SPDX or CycloneDX format.

# Security hardening:
docker run --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp app:v1
docker scout quickview app:v1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
Q5
What command generates an SBOM for a Docker image?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker sbom anihpj:v1 — generates a table of all packages. For machine-readable output: docker sbom --format spdx-json anihpj:v1 > sbom.json or --format cyclonedx. Alternative: syft anihpj:v1 (Anchore's open-source SBOM generator).

EXPLANATION

SPDX and CycloneDX are the two standard SBOM formats. SPDX is Linux Foundation's standard; CycloneDX is OWASP's standard. Both are widely supported by vulnerability scanners and compliance tools. The DCA exam expects awareness that SBOMs exist and are a security best practice.

# docker sbom anihpj:v1
# docker sbom --format spdx-json anihpj:v1 > sbom.json
# --format cyclonedx
# syft anihpj:v1
Q6
What are the 5 categories of the CIS Docker Benchmark?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) Host Configuration — filesystem partitioning, trusted users, auditing. (2) Docker Daemon Configuration — network rules, logging level, TLS. (3) Container Images and Build Files — trusted base images, specific tags, Dockerfile best practices. (4) Container Runtime — non-root, read-only, resource limits, seccomp. (5) Docker Swarm Configuration — secrets encryption, manager node count, network encryption.

EXPLANATION

The CIS Benchmark is a 200+ page document with detailed security recommendations. Docker Bench Security automates checking these. The DCA exam may ask about CIS categories — remember the 5 levels: host, daemon, images, runtime, swarm. Each level addresses a different part of the Docker security surface.

# Security hardening:
docker run --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp app:v1
docker scout quickview app:v1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
Q7
How do you integrate vulnerability scanning into CI/CD?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Add a scan step after image build: docker scout cves --exit-code --only-severity critical myimage:$TAG in your CI pipeline. If critical CVEs exist, the pipeline fails — preventing vulnerable images from reaching production. Use --exit-code flag to make the scan command return non-zero on vulnerabilities.

EXPLANATION

The CI/CD security pattern: Build → Scan → Sign (DCT) → Push. If any step fails, the image never reaches the registry. This "shift-left" approach catches vulnerabilities at build time, not in production. Tools: Docker Scout (GitHub Actions), Trivy (any CI), Snyk (any CI). The DCA exam tests the concept of integrating security into the pipeline.

# docker scout cves --exit-code --only-severity critical myimage:$TAG
# --exit-code
Q8
What does trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Scans the image for vulnerabilities and exits with code 1 (failure) if any CRITICAL severity CVEs are found. This makes Trivy ideal for CI/CD pipelines — it blocks deployments that have critical vulnerabilities. Without --exit-code, Trivy always exits 0 (success) even when vulnerabilities exist.

EXPLANATION

The severity hierarchy: CRITICAL > HIGH > MEDIUM > LOW. Most teams set their CI threshold to HIGH (block on HIGH and CRITICAL) or CRITICAL (only block critical). --severity HIGH,CRITICAL blocks on both. You can also ignore specific CVEs with .trivyignore file if they're false positives or accepted risks.

# trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL
# --exit-code
# --severity HIGH,CRITICAL
# .trivyignore
Q9
What compliance requirement is driving SBOM adoption?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

US Executive Order 14028 (2021) — requires federal agencies and their software suppliers to provide SBOMs for all software. This has driven SBOM adoption across the industry. European Cyber Resilience Act is driving similar requirements in the EU. SBOMs are becoming a standard part of software supply chain security.

EXPLANATION

The DCA exam expects awareness that security scanning and SBOMs are not optional extras — they're increasingly mandated by regulation and industry standards. Docker Scout, Syft, and Trivy all support SBOM generation in standard formats (SPDX, CycloneDX) that meet these regulatory requirements.

# Security hardening:
docker run --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp app:v1
docker scout quickview app:v1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
Q10
What's the difference between docker scout and docker bench security?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker Scout scans IMAGES for package vulnerabilities (CVEs) — it checks what's inside your image. Docker Bench Security audits your HOST and DAEMON configuration against CIS benchmarks — it checks how Docker is configured and running. Scout = image-level security; Bench = infrastructure-level security. Use both.

EXPLANATION

Scout answers: "Is there a vulnerable library in my Python image?" Bench answers: "Is the Docker daemon configured securely? Are containers running as root? Are audit logs enabled?" Together they cover both the application layer (what runs inside containers) and the infrastructure layer (how Docker itself is configured).

# Security hardening:
docker run --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp app:v1
docker scout quickview app:v1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1

Part 7 covers the complete Docker security model — from kernel-level isolation to compliance scanning:

  • Security Fundamentals (Ch 19): Containers share the kernel — defense-in-depth is mandatory. 10-layer security onion: user namespaces, capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux, cgroups, read-only rootfs, network isolation, image scanning, content trust, host security. Non-root user is the single most impactful measure. --cap-drop ALL minimizes privileges.
  • Securing anihpj (Ch 20): 10-point hardening checklist. Secrets via Swarm secrets or .env (never in ENV). Docker socket = root access — never expose without TLS. DCT signs and verifies images. Podman offers rootless alternative. userns-remap provides strongest user isolation.
  • Scanning & Compliance (Ch 21): Docker Scout finds CVEs. Docker Bench Security audits against CIS benchmarks. Trivy provides open-source scanning. SBOMs are the industry standard for software transparency. Integrate scanning into CI/CD to block vulnerable images before production.
🔄 Implementation: The Security Golden Rules

1. USER app (never root). 2. --cap-drop ALL. 3. --read-only + tmpfs. 4. Scan images before push. 5. Secrets via Swarm secrets, never ENV. 6. userns-remap in daemon.json. 7. Docker Bench Security for host auditing. 8. DCT for image signing. 9. SBOM for every release. 10. "Shift left" — scan in CI, not just in production.

Chapter 22: Docker in CI/CD Pipelines

CI/CD (Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment) automates building, testing, and deploying your application. Docker is the perfect CI/CD companion — every pipeline step runs in an identical container, eliminating "works on my machine" forever. This chapter covers GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, and Docker Build Cloud.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🚀 CI/CD🎯 DCA 10%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the Docker CI/CD pipeline architecture
  • ✅ Build and push images in GitHub Actions
  • ✅ Configure GitLab CI with Docker-in-Docker
  • ✅ Write Jenkins pipelines with Docker agents
  • ✅ Use Docker Build Cloud for accelerated builds

22.1 Why Docker in CI/CD?

Traditional CI/CD: "It builds on my machine but not on the CI server." With Docker, the CI runner uses the EXACT same image as production. Every step — build, test, scan, deploy — runs in an identical container environment:

Docker CI/CD Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🚀 DOCKER CI/CD PIPELINE                                │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐            │
  │  │ 📝 Code  │──▶│ 🏗️ Build │──▶│ 🧪 Test  │──▶│ 🔍 Scan  │            │
  │  │ Push to  │   │ docker   │   │ docker   │   │ docker   │            │
  │  │ GitHub   │   │ build    │   │ compose  │   │ scout    │            │
  │  └──────────┘   └────┬─────┘   │ run test │   │ quickview│            │
  │                      │         └────┬─────┘   └────┬─────┘            │
  │                      ▼              │              │                   │
  │               ┌──────────┐          ▼              ▼                   │
  │               │ 📦 Push  │   ┌──────────────────────────┐            │
  │               │ docker   │──▶│ ✅ All checks passed?     │            │
  │               │ push     │   │    ▶ YES: Deploy to K8s   │            │
  │               └──────────┘   │    ▶ NO:  Pipeline fails  │            │
  │                              └──────────────────────────┘            │
  │  🔑 EVERY step runs in a Docker container → IDENTICAL environment!    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

22.2 GitHub Actions + Docker

.github/workflows/docker.yml
name: Build and Push anihpj

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ['v*']

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Login to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Docker metadata
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
          tags: |
            type=ref,event=branch
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=sha,prefix=,format=short

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

22.3 GitLab CI + Docker

.gitlab-ci.yml
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - push

variables:
  IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA

build:
  stage: build
  image: docker:latest
  services:
    - docker:dind          # Docker-in-Docker
  script:
    - docker build -t $IMAGE .
    - docker save $IMAGE > image.tar
  artifacts:
    paths: [image.tar]

test:
  stage: test
  image: docker:latest
  services: [docker:dind]
  script:
    - docker load < image.tar
    - docker run --rm $IMAGE python manage.py test

push:
  stage: push
  image: docker:latest
  services: [docker:dind]
  script:
    - docker load < image.tar
    - docker login -u $CI_REGISTRY_USER -p $CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD $CI_REGISTRY
    - docker push $IMAGE

22.4 Jenkins + Docker

Jenkinsfile
pipeline {
    agent any
    environment {
        IMAGE = "ghcr.io/org/anihpj:${GIT_COMMIT.take(7)}"
    }
    stages {
        stage('Build') {
            steps {
                script {
                    docker.build(IMAGE)
                }
            }
        }
        stage('Test') {
            steps {
                script {
                    docker.image(IMAGE).inside {
                        sh 'python manage.py test'
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        stage('Push') {
            steps {
                script {
                    docker.withRegistry('https://ghcr.io', 'github-token') {
                        docker.image(IMAGE).push()
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

22.5 Docker Build Cloud

Docker Build Cloud offloads builds to cloud infrastructure — faster builds, shared cache across your team, and no drain on your local machine:

TERMINAL
# Create a cloud builder
$ docker buildx create --name cloud-builder --use --driver cloud org/builder-name

# Build in the cloud — same syntax!
$ docker buildx build --builder cloud-builder -t anihpj:v1 --push .

# Benefits:
# - Builds run on cloud VMs (faster CPUs, more RAM)
# - Cache shared across your entire team
# - Local machine stays free for coding
