📝 Chapter 22 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Why is Docker ideal for CI/CD pipelines?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker ensures every pipeline step runs in an IDENTICAL environment. The image you build in CI is the exact same image tested and deployed — no "works on my machine" issues. Build once, deploy anywhere: the CI runner, staging, and production all use the same container image.

EXPLANATION

Without Docker, CI/CD pipelines rely on the CI runner's OS, installed tools, and configuration — which may differ from production. With Docker, the pipeline runs inside containers that match production exactly. This eliminates an entire category of deployment failures caused by environment drift.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q2
What GitHub Action builds and pushes Docker images?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker/build-push-action@v5 — builds the image from a Dockerfile and pushes it to a registry. Combine with docker/login-action for authentication and docker/metadata-action for automatic tags and labels.

EXPLANATION

The build-push-action handles: building with BuildKit, multi-platform builds, layer caching (cache-from/cache-to), and pushing to any registry. It's the standard GitHub Action for Docker CI/CD. The metadata-action generates tags from git refs, semver tags, and SHA automatically.

# docker/build-push-action@v5
# docker/login-action
# docker/metadata-action
Q3
What is Docker-in-Docker (dind) and when is it needed?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker-in-Docker runs a Docker daemon INSIDE a container, allowing CI jobs to build and run containers. Needed in GitLab CI when using the docker executor. Specified as a service: services: [docker:dind]. Alternative: mount the host docker socket (less secure but simpler).

EXPLANATION

dind requires --privileged mode (security concern) but provides full isolation — the CI job's Docker daemon is separate from the host's. Socket mounting (-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock) is simpler but shares the host daemon — a compromised CI job could access host containers. GitLab CI uses dind as the recommended approach.

# services: [docker:dind]
# --privileged
# -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
Q4
What is Docker Build Cloud?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker's cloud-based build service. Instead of building images locally, builds run on cloud VMs with more CPU/RAM. Benefits: faster builds, shared team cache, no local resource drain. Use with docker buildx create --driver cloud and build as usual with docker buildx build.

EXPLANATION

Build Cloud is especially valuable for: large monorepos with many images, teams where everyone rebuilds the same layers, CI pipelines that need fast builds, and developers on resource-constrained laptops. The shared cache means if a teammate already built a layer, you get it instantly.

# docker buildx create --driver cloud
# docker buildx build
Q5
How do you cache Docker layers in GitHub Actions?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Use cache-from: type=gha and cache-to: type=gha,mode=max in the build-push-action. This stores layer cache in GitHub Actions' cache storage. Subsequent builds reuse cached layers — dramatically faster. Cache is scoped to the branch by default.

EXPLANATION

GitHub Actions cache (type=gha) is free up to 10 GB per repo. Each layer is stored as a cache entry. On the next build, Docker checks if the cache is still valid (same Dockerfile instruction + same source files) and reuses it. Mode=max caches ALL intermediate layers, not just the final image.

# cache-from: type=gha
# cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
Q6
What's the difference between socket mounting and dind in CI?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Socket mounting (-v /var/run/docker.sock:...): shares the host's Docker daemon — faster, simpler, but less secure. dind (Docker-in-Docker): runs a separate Docker daemon inside a container — more isolated, requires privileged mode, slightly slower startup.

EXPLANATION

Socket mounting: the CI container uses the host's Docker. Pros: fast, no privileged mode needed. Cons: CI container can access/manipulate ALL host containers, images, volumes. dind: the CI container runs its own Docker. Pros: isolated, can't touch host containers. Cons: needs --privileged, overhead of running a second daemon.

# -v /var/run/docker.sock:...
Q7
What does docker/metadata-action do in GitHub Actions?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Generates Docker tags and labels automatically from git context. For a push to main: generates :main tag. For a semver tag v1.2.3: generates :1.2.3, :1.2, :1. For any push: generates :sha-abc1234. Labels include: org.opencontainers.image.source, revision, created date.

EXPLANATION

Without metadata-action, you'd write complex shell scripts to parse git refs and generate tags. This action follows OCI annotation standards and handles edge cases: PRs (generates pr-123 tag), semver (handles pre-release suffixes), and latest tag (only on default branch). It's used in virtually every Docker GitHub Actions workflow.

# :sha-abc1234
Q8
How do you push to multiple registries in one CI pipeline?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Login to each registry, then push with multiple tags. In GitHub Actions: add multiple docker/login-action steps (one per registry). In build-push-action, set tags for all registries: tags: ghcr.io/org/img:v1,docker.io/org/img:v1. Or push sequentially: docker tag img:v1 reg1/img:v1 && docker push reg1/img:v1 && docker push reg2/img:v1.

EXPLANATION

Multi-registry pushes are common: Docker Hub for public, ECR for AWS deployments, GHCR for GitHub integration. The image is the same — just tagged differently. Docker is smart enough to only upload layers once if both registries share a base image. Use docker buildx build --push for efficient multi-registry pushes in one command.

# docker/login-action
# tags: ghcr.io/org/img:v1,docker.io/org/img:v1
# docker tag img:v1 reg1/img:v1 && docker push reg1/img:v1 && docker push reg2/img:v1
# docker buildx build --push
Q9
What are the minimum stages in a Docker CI/CD pipeline?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Build (docker build) → Test (unit/integration tests) → Scan (vulnerability scanning) → Push (docker push to registry). Production pipelines add: Sign (DCT) and Deploy (kubectl apply). The "shift-left" philosophy moves security checks (scanning) earlier in the pipeline.

EXPLANATION

The DCA exam expects you to understand the CI/CD flow: code push triggers pipeline → build image → run tests in that image → scan for CVEs → push to registry → deploy. Each stage gates the next — if tests fail, the image never reaches the registry. This prevents broken or vulnerable code from reaching production.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q10
What is the benefit of using BuildKit in CI/CD?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

BuildKit provides: (1) parallel multi-stage builds, (2) remote cache (critical for CI — cache survives between runs), (3) build secrets (--secret for credentials without baking them into image), (4) SSH forwarding for private repos, (5) better build output for debugging. BuildKit is enabled by default in modern Docker.

EXPLANATION

In CI/CD, remote cache is BuildKit's killer feature. Without it, every CI run starts from scratch (no local cache). With --cache-from type=registry,ref=img:cache and --cache-to type=registry,ref=img:cache,mode=max, layer cache is stored in the registry and reused across pipeline runs — cutting build times from minutes to seconds.

# --cache-from type=registry,ref=img:cache
# --cache-to type=registry,ref=img:cache,mode=max

Chapter 23: Docker Image Versioning & Promotion

Tagging images properly is the difference between organized deployments and chaos. Learn tagging strategies, promotion pipelines, registry strategies, and how to integrate Content Trust into your CI/CD workflow.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour🏷️ Versioning🎯 DCA 5%

23.1 Image Tagging Strategies for CI/CD

StrategyExampleProsCons
Git commit SHAanihpj:abc1234Immutable, traceable to codeNot human-readable
Semantic versionanihpj:1.2.3Human-readable, follows semverManual process or CI automation needed
Branch-basedanihpj:main, :developSimple, automaticMutable — tag moves with each push
Environmentanihpj:staging, :productionClear intentMutable, not tied to specific version
Combinedanihpj:1.2.3-abc1234Best of both — version + traceabilityLongest tag name
🏆 Best Practice

Use multiple tags: anihpj:1.2.3 (semver, mutable for this version), anihpj:abc1234 (git SHA, immutable), anihpj:production (what's currently in prod). The git SHA tag is your "fingerprint" — it uniquely identifies exactly which code produced this image.

23.2 Image Promotion Across Environments

Never rebuild for different environments — promote the EXACT same image:

Image Promotion Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🏷️ IMAGE PROMOTION PIPELINE                              │
  │                                                                          │
  │  Build ONCE → Promote (retag) → Deploy everywhere:                       │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────┐    retag    ┌──────────────┐    retag    ┌──────────┐ │
  │  │ anihpj:abc123│───────────▶│ anihpj:dev   │───────────▶│anihpj:   │ │
  │  │ (immutable)  │    pass     │              │    pass    │ staging  │ │
  │  └──────────────┘    tests    └──────────────┘    scans   └────┬─────┘ │
  │                                                                │       │
  │                                                         retag  │       │
  │                                                                ▼       │
  │                                                         ┌──────────┐  │
  │                                                         │anihpj:   │  │
  │                                                         │production│  │
  │                                                         └──────────┘  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💡 SAME image ID throughout — only the TAG changes!                     │
  │     docker tag anihpj:abc1234 anihpj:production                          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

23.3 Registry Strategies

Organize registries for your deployment topology:

📦
Single Registry, Multiple Repos

One registry (ECR, GHCR) with repos per environment. Simpler to manage. Example: ecr/team/anihpj-dev, ecr/team/anihpj-prod.

🌐
Multi-Registry

Dev images on Docker Hub, production on ECR. Better separation of concerns. Staging registry can mirror production. Adds complexity.

23.4 Docker Content Trust in CI/CD

CI/CD Sign + Verify
# In CI pipeline — after build, before deploy:
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST_REPOSITORY_PASSPHRASE="$SIGNING_KEY_PASSPHRASE"

# Push with signing
docker push ghcr.io/org/anihpj:$TAG   # Auto-signs with DCT enabled

# In deployment — before kubectl apply:
docker pull ghcr.io/org/anihpj:$TAG   # Verifies signature, fails if unsigned!

📝 Chapter 23 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Why should you promote images by retagging instead of rebuilding?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Rebuilding creates a DIFFERENT image — with potentially different packages, different timestamps, different behavior. The image that passed tests in staging is NOT the same image deployed to production. Retagging preserves the exact same image ID — guaranteeing you deploy what you tested.

EXPLANATION

Even with identical Dockerfiles, rebuilding can produce different images: base image may have updated, pip may resolve different versions, timestamps differ. The DCA exam emphasizes: "Build once, deploy many." The image tested is the image deployed — achieved through retagging, never rebuilding.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q2
What's the best tagging strategy for production images?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Combined: git SHA (immutable fingerprint) + semantic version (human-readable). Example: anihpj:1.2.3-abc1234. The SHA traces back to exact code; the semver communicates the release. Avoid mutable tags (latest, production) for anything but convenience pointers.

EXPLANATION

Mutable tags like :latest or :production are useful for convenience (always pull the latest prod image) but dangerous for auditing. If something breaks, you need to know exactly which image was running. The immutable SHA tag gives you that. Use mutable tags as aliases, not as your primary versioning scheme.

# anihpj:1.2.3-abc1234
# :production
Q3
How do you push the same image to multiple registries?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Tag the image with multiple registry prefixes, then push to each: docker tag anihpj:v1 docker.io/user/anihpj:v1 && docker push docker.io/user/anihpj:v1 && docker tag anihpj:v1 ghcr.io/user/anihpj:v1 && docker push ghcr.io/user/anihpj:v1. Or use buildx: docker buildx build --push -t reg1/img:v1 -t reg2/img:v1 .

EXPLANATION

The image is the same — Docker only uploads layers once to each registry. Multi-registry pushes are common when: using Docker Hub for public, ECR for AWS deployments, and GHCR for GitHub integration. Docker Buildx can push to multiple registries in a single build command.

# docker tag anihpj:v1 docker.io/user/anihpj:v1 && docker push docker.io/user/anihpj:v1 && docker tag anihpj:v1 ghcr.io/user/anihpj:v1 && docker push ghcr.io/user/anihpj:v1
# docker buildx build --push -t reg1/img:v1 -t reg2/img:v1 .
Q4
What's the difference between a mutable and immutable tag?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Mutable tags (:latest, :production) can point to different images over time — a new push overwrites the tag. Immutable tags (:abc1234 git SHA, :1.2.3 semver if never retagged) always point to the same image. Use immutable tags for auditing and rollbacks; mutable for convenience pointers.

EXPLANATION

Mutable tags cause "tag drift" — :latest on Monday may be a completely different image than :latest on Tuesday. This makes debugging production issues nearly impossible (which version was actually running?). Immutable tags solve this: the SHA is unique forever. Some registries can enforce immutable tags as a policy.

# :production
Q5
How do you integrate Docker Content Trust into CI/CD?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Set DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 in the CI environment. Push with signing: the CI pipeline holds the signing key (stored as a CI secret). On deploy: the deployment system pulls with DCT enabled — Docker verifies the signature before running. If the image is unsigned or tampered with, the pull fails.

EXPLANATION

The CI pipeline needs the repository signing key (stored securely as a CI secret, not in the repo). The deployment system only needs the root key's public component (to verify, not to sign). This creates a chain of trust: developer pushes code → CI builds and signs → deployment verifies signature before running.

# DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
Q6
What's the promotion pipeline pattern for Docker images?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Build ONCE → tag with SHA → test → retag as :dev → integration tests → retag as :staging → UAT/scanning → retag as :production → deploy. The SAME image (same digest) moves through environments by changing its tag. Gates at each stage: tests, scans, approvals block promotion.

EXPLANATION

This is the "build once, deploy many" pattern. Each environment adds confidence: dev proves it runs, staging proves it works with production-like config, scanning proves it's secure. If any gate fails, the image never reaches production. The key insight: docker tag is instant and doesn't change the image — it just adds a label.

# :production
# docker tag
Q7
What are Docker image retention policies?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Rules that automatically delete old images from a registry. Examples: keep last 10 images per repo, delete images older than 90 days, keep all tagged with semver. Implemented in: Docker Hub (repository settings), AWS ECR (lifecycle policies), GCR/Artifact Registry (cleanup policies).

EXPLANATION

Without retention, registries grow indefinitely — costing money and slowing pulls. ECR lifecycle policies: "untagged images older than 14 days → delete." Docker Hub: "inactive images → move to trash." Always keep production tags and at least the last N builds for rollback capability.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q8
Why shouldn't you use :latest tag in production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

:latest is mutable and unpredictable — it moves to whatever was most recently pushed. Two servers pulling :latest at different times may run different images. If production breaks, you can't determine which version was running. Use specific tags (SHA, semver) for auditability and reproducibility.

EXPLANATION

Kubernetes exacerbates the :latest problem: if imagePullPolicy is Always, every pod restart may pull a different image. This makes rollbacks impossible (there's no previous version to roll back to). The DCA exam considers using :latest in production an anti-pattern. Always pin to a specific tag or digest.

# :latest
# :latest
Q9
What's the difference between image ID and image digest?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Image ID (short SHA like abc1234) is local — different on each machine. Digest (sha256:abc123...) is content-addressable — IDENTICAL everywhere the image exists. Digest is the truly immutable reference. Use digests for guaranteed deployment consistency across all environments.

EXPLANATION

The digest is calculated from the image's content (manifest + layers). Same content = same digest, guaranteed by SHA256. Tags are human-friendly aliases for digests. For the highest deployment fidelity: reference images by digest (anihpj@sha256:abc...) rather than tag — even if someone retags the image, your deployment still pulls the exact version.

# sha256:abc123...
# anihpj@sha256:abc...
Q10
How do you implement image promotion gates in CI/CD?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Each environment promotion requires passing gates: (1) Tests pass → promote to dev, (2) Integration tests pass → promote to staging, (3) Security scan clean + Manual approval → promote to production. Gates are implemented as CI pipeline stages that must succeed before the next retag step executes.

EXPLANATION

In GitHub Actions: separate jobs with needs dependencies and environment protection rules. In GitLab CI: stages with when: manual for approval gates. The image flows: build job → test job → scan job → approval (manual) → retag as production → deploy job. Each failed gate stops the pipeline.

# environment
# when: manual

Chapter 24: Container Testing Strategies

Testing containers requires a layered approach — from unit tests inside the container to full-stack integration tests with real databases. Docker makes it easy to spin up exact replicas of your production environment for testing.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour🧪 Testing🎯 DCA 5%

24.1 Testing Pyramid for Containers

Container Testing Pyramid
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🧪 CONTAINER TESTING PYRAMID                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │                          ┌─────┐                                         │
  │                          │ E2E │  ← docker compose full stack            │
  │                          │     │     Selenium/Cypress tests              │
  │                         ┌┴─────┴┐                                        │
  │                         │ Image  │ ← Container Structure Tests           │
  │                         │ Tests  │    Dockerfile linting (Hadolint)      │
  │                        ┌┴───────┴┐                                       │
  │                        │Integration│ ← docker compose run django test    │
  │                        │  Tests    │    Testcontainers (real DB)         │
  │                       ┌┴──────────┴┐                                    │
  │                       │    Unit     │ ← docker run pytest                │
  │                       │    Tests    │    Fast, isolated, many            │
  │                       └────────────┘                                    │
  │                                                                          │
  │  💡 More tests at bottom (faster, cheaper), fewer at top (slower, E2E)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

24.2 Testing with docker compose run

TERMINAL
# Run Django unit tests (creates a fresh container)
$ docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test

# Run tests for specific Django app
$ docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test jobpost

# Run with pytest
$ docker compose run --rm django pytest --cov=jobpost

# In CI: exit code determines pass/fail
$ docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test --noinput
$ echo $?   # 0 = all passed, 1 = failures

24.3 Testcontainers — Real Database in Tests

Python (Django + Testcontainers)
# conftest.py — Spin up real PostgreSQL for tests
import pytest
from testcontainers.postgres import PostgresContainer

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def postgres_container():
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:15-alpine") as postgres:
        yield postgres

# tests.py — Test against REAL PostgreSQL, not SQLite!
def test_create_jobpost(postgres_container):
    DATABASES['default'] = {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql',
        'HOST': postgres_container.get_container_host_ip(),
        'PORT': postgres_container.get_exposed_port(5432),
        'NAME': 'test',
        'USER': 'test',
        'PASSWORD': 'test',
    }
    # Now test with real PostgreSQL — catches DB-specific bugs!

24.4 Container Structure Tests

tests.yaml
schemaVersion: 2.0.0
metadataTest:
  exposedPorts: ["8000"]
  cmd: ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
  user: "app"               # Must NOT be root!

commandTests:
  - name: "Python version"
    command: "python"
    args: ["--version"]
    expectedOutput: ["Python 3.11"]

  - name: "Django check"
    command: "python"
    args: ["manage.py", "check"]
    expectedOutput: ["System check identified no issues"]

fileExistenceTests:
  - name: "requirements installed"
    path: "/usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages/django"
    shouldExist: true

# Run: container-structure-test test --image anihpj:v1 --config tests.yaml

24.5 Dockerfile Linting

TERMINAL
# Install Hadolint
$ brew install hadolint    # macOS
$ sudo apt install hadolint # Linux

# Lint your Dockerfile
$ hadolint Dockerfile
Dockerfile:1 DL3007 Using latest is prone to errors
Dockerfile:5 DL3008 Pin versions in apt-get install
Dockerfile:8 DL3059 Multiple consecutive RUN instructions

# In CI/CD (GitHub Actions):
- uses: hadolint/hadolint-action@v3
  with:
    dockerfile: Dockerfile

# Fix all warnings and errors before merging!

📝 Chapter 24 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What are the four levels of the container testing pyramid?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Unit tests (fast, isolated, many) → Integration tests (real DB, compose) → Image tests (structure, linting, scanning) → End-to-end tests (full stack, Selenium/Cypress, few). More tests at the bottom (faster, cheaper), fewer at the top (slower, more comprehensive).

EXPLANATION

The pyramid principle: run many fast unit tests on every commit, fewer integration tests on every push, and E2E tests before releases. Docker enables all levels: unit tests in a throwaway container, integration tests with compose + real databases, image tests with structure tests and Hadolint, E2E with the full compose stack.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q2
How do you run Django tests inside a Docker container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test. run creates a fresh container from the service definition — no need to have the service already running. --rm auto-cleans it up after tests complete. The exit code (0=pass, 1=fail) can be used in CI pipelines.

EXPLANATION

docker compose run is preferred over docker compose exec for tests because: (1) it creates a clean container — no state from previous runs, (2) it doesn't require the service to already be running, (3) it respects depends_on — database will be available. For CI, always use --rm to prevent container accumulation.

# docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test
# docker compose run
# docker compose exec
# depends_on
Q3
What is Testcontainers and why use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Testcontainers is a library that spins up REAL database/service containers for integration tests — programmatically, from your test code. Instead of mocking PostgreSQL, your tests run against an actual PostgreSQL container. Available for Python, Java, Node.js, Go, and more.

EXPLANATION

The problem: SQLite for dev, PostgreSQL for production → bugs that only appear in production (different SQL dialects, JSON field handling, transaction behavior). Testcontainers solves this: your tests run against the same database engine as production. The container is created before tests and destroyed after — always a clean state.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q4
What are Container Structure Tests?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Google's framework for testing container images as artifacts. Tests: (1) File existence — is /app/manage.py present? (2) Command output — does "django-admin --version" return expected version? (3) Metadata — is USER set to non-root? Are correct ports exposed? Run: container-structure-test test --image anihpj:v1 --config tests.yaml.

EXPLANATION

Structure tests validate that the image was built correctly — independent of running the application. They catch: missing files, wrong base image version, incorrect USER, missing EXPOSE, wrong CMD. These are essentially unit tests for your Docker image. Integrate in CI: if structure tests fail, the image is rejected before any functional testing.

# container-structure-test test --image anihpj:v1 --config tests.yaml
Q5
What does Hadolint check in Dockerfiles?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Hadolint is a Dockerfile linter. It checks: using :latest tag (DL3007), not pinning apt package versions (DL3008), using ADD instead of COPY (DL3020), multiple consecutive RUN commands (DL3059), not clearing apt lists (DL3009), using root by default (warns on missing USER), and more. Based on Dockerfile best practices.

EXPLANATION

Hadolint has ~50+ rules categorized as error/warning/info. It can be configured via .hadolint.yaml to ignore specific rules. Integrate in CI: if Hadolint fails, the build stops — enforcing Dockerfile quality before images are built. The DCA exam expects awareness that Dockerfile linting is a best practice.

# .hadolint.yaml
Q6
Why run tests inside the container rather than on the host?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The container has the EXACT same Python version, dependencies, OS libraries, and configuration as production. Tests on the host may pass due to different package versions or OS tools that aren't in the container. Running tests inside the container guarantees you're testing what will actually run in production.

EXPLANATION

Classic example: tests pass locally (Python 3.12 with new features) but fail in the container (Python 3.11). Or: a package works locally because a system library is installed, but it's missing from the slim container image. Containerized tests eliminate this entire class of "works on my machine" bugs.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q7
What's the difference between docker compose run and exec for testing?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

run creates a NEW container from the service definition — clean state, no side effects, respects depends_on. exec runs inside an EXISTING running container — may have state from previous operations. Use run for tests (fresh environment), exec for debugging (interactive shell).

EXPLANATION

run is ideal for CI: each test run gets a pristine container, database migrations run from scratch, no leftover test data. exec is faster for local development (container already running, database already migrated) but can have stale state. The DCA exam may ask about this distinction.

# run
# exec
# run
Q8
How do you validate that a Docker image was built correctly before deployment?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Three validation layers: (1) Container Structure Tests — verify files, commands, metadata; (2) Hadolint — lint the Dockerfile before building; (3) docker scout/Trivy — scan for vulnerabilities. All three should run in CI after build and before push to registry.

EXPLANATION

CI pipeline order: (1) Hadolint checks Dockerfile syntax/best practices → (2) docker build → (3) Container Structure Tests verify the built image → (4) docker compose run tests (unit/integration) → (5) docker scout quickview (vulnerability scan) → (6) docker push. Each step gates the next — failures stop the pipeline.

# Production Dockerfile:
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user -r requirements.txt
FROM python:3.11-slim
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY . .
USER 1000
CMD ["python","app.py"]
Q9
Why use Testcontainers instead of SQLite for Django tests?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

SQLite and PostgreSQL have different SQL dialects, feature support, and behavior. Testing on SQLite but deploying on PostgreSQL means bugs can slip through: JSONField queries, case-insensitive text search, transaction isolation, array field operations. Testcontainers gives you the REAL database in tests — catching these differences before production.

EXPLANATION

Django's ORM abstracts SQL but doesn't eliminate all differences. Case/When expressions, distinct() with fields, JSONField key transforms — all behave differently on SQLite vs PostgreSQL. Testcontainers adds ~5 seconds to test startup (container boot) but gives 100% confidence your ORM code works correctly on the target database.

# distinct()
# JSONField
Q10
What's the purpose of Container Structure Test metadata checks?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Metadata checks validate the image CONFIGURATION — not just the files inside. Checks include: exposed ports (are the right ports documented?), CMD/ENTRYPOINT (does it start the right process?), USER (is it non-root?), ENV vars (are required variables set?), WORKDIR (is the working directory correct?). These catch configuration drift before deployment.

EXPLANATION

Metadata tests are like configuration validation for your container. Example: someone accidentally removes USER app from the Dockerfile — the container now runs as root. Without metadata tests, you'd never know until a security audit. With them, the CI pipeline catches the regression immediately: "expected user: app, got: root — FAIL."

# USER app

Chapter 25: Docker → Kubernetes Transition

Docker packages your app; Kubernetes runs it at scale. This chapter bridges the gap — from single-host containers to multi-node clusters. Understand why Kubernetes exists, how Docker concepts map to K8s, and how to take your Dockerized app from compose.yaml to production Kubernetes.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours☸️ K8s🎯 DCA 5%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand why Kubernetes exists and when you need it
  • ✅ Map every Docker concept to its Kubernetes equivalent
  • ✅ Follow the complete Dockerfile → K8s Deployment journey
  • ✅ Convert docker-compose.yml to K8s manifests

25.1 Why Kubernetes After Docker?

Docker excels at running containers on ONE machine. Kubernetes excels at running containers across MANY machines. When your app outgrows a single server — you need auto-scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, and multi-host networking — Kubernetes is the answer:

Docker (Single Host) vs Kubernetes (Cluster)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🐳 DOCKER (Single Host)  vs  ☸️ KUBERNETES (Cluster)           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  DOCKER:                        KUBERNETES:                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │   ONE SERVER     │           │         CLUSTER (Many Servers)        │ │
  │  │                  │           │                                      │ │
  │  │  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ │           │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐│ │
  │  │  │C1│ │C2│ │C3│ │           │  │      🧠 CONTROL PLANE            ││ │
  │  │  └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ │           │  │  API Server | etcd | Scheduler   ││ │
  │  │                  │           │  └──────────────────────────────────┘│ │
  │  │  IF SERVER DIES: │           │                                      │ │
  │  │  💀 Everything   │           │  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐      │ │
  │  │     goes down!   │           │  │ 💪 Node 1  │  │ 💪 Node 2  │      │ │
  │  │                  │           │  │ ┌──┐┌──┐┌──┐│  │ ┌──┐┌──┐┌──┐│      │ │
  │  │  SCALING: Manual │           │  │ │C1││C3││C5││  │ │C2││C4││C6││      │ │
  │  │  NO auto-healing │           │  │ └──┘└──┘└──┘│  │ └──┘└──┘└──┘│      │ │
  │  │  NO rolling upd. │           │  └────────────┘  └────────────┘      │ │
  │  └──────────────────┘           │                                      │ │
  │                                 │  IF NODE DIES: Pods move to Node 2 ✅ │ │
  │                                 │  SCALING: kubectl scale --replicas=10│ │
  │                                 └──────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
DimensionDocker (Standalone)Kubernetes
Multi-Host Cluster❌ No✅ Core feature
Auto-Scaling❌ Manual only✅ HPA + VPA built-in
Self-Healing⚠️ Restart policies✅ Auto-recreates pods

# docker-compose.yml                    # Kubernetes (deployment.yaml)
services:                               apiVersion: apps/v1

    build: .                            metadata:
    ports: ["8000:8000"]                  name: anihpj
    environment:                        spec:
      - DB_HOST=postgres                  replicas: 3
    depends_on: [postgres]                selector:
  postgres:                                 app: anihpj
    image: postgres:15                   template:
    volumes:                               spec:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data     containers:
  redis:                                    - image: ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1
    image: redis:7                             ports: [8000]
volumes:                                       env:
  pgdata:                                      - name: DB_HOST
                                                value: postgres

📝 Chapter 25 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
Why would you use Kubernetes instead of Docker standalone?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

When you need: multi-host deployment, auto-scaling, self-healing, rolling updates with zero downtime, built-in load balancing, and declarative configuration. Docker standalone runs containers on ONE machine — if that machine dies, everything stops. Kubernetes distributes containers across multiple nodes with automatic failover.

EXPLANATION

The threshold question: "Can my app run on a single server?" If yes, Docker + Compose is simpler. If you need high availability (survive server failure), horizontal scaling (handle traffic spikes), or zero-downtime deployments — you need Kubernetes or Docker Swarm. Docker = packaging; Kubernetes = orchestration.

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q2
What is a Kubernetes Pod and how does it differ from a Docker container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in K8s — it wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace (IP, port space) and IPC namespace. A Docker container is a single process. In K8s, you typically run one container per pod, but sidecar patterns (logs, proxies) use multiple containers in one pod.

EXPLANATION

The pod model enables patterns impossible with plain Docker: (1) Sidecar — a logging container shares the pod's filesystem, (2) Ambassador — a proxy container shares the pod's network, (3) Init containers — run before the main container. Containers in a pod can communicate via localhost (same network namespace).

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q3
How do you convert docker-compose.yml to Kubernetes manifests?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Use Kompose: kompose convert -f docker-compose.yml. This generates deployment.yaml, service.yaml, and pvc.yaml files automatically. Alternatively, manually translate: compose services → K8s Deployments, compose ports → K8s Services, compose volumes → K8s PersistentVolumeClaims.

EXPLANATION

Kompose is a conversion tool, not a production solution. It handles 80% of the translation. Manual refinement is usually needed for: health checks, resource limits, ConfigMaps, secrets, and production-specific settings. For production, tools like Helm and Kustomize provide more control than kompose alone.

# kompose convert -f docker-compose.yml
Q4
What Kubernetes resource replaces docker-compose's service definition?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A Deployment manages the pods (replicas, updates, rollbacks). A Service provides stable networking (DNS, load balancing). Together they replace a single Compose service definition. Compose combines deployment + networking in one; K8s separates them for flexibility.

EXPLANATION

In Compose, one service block handles: image, ports, environment, volumes, depends_on, restart. In K8s, these are split: Deployment handles image + replicas + updates, Service handles networking, ConfigMap handles environment, PersistentVolumeClaim handles storage. This separation of concerns is fundamental to K8s' design.

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q5
What is the bridge between Docker and Kubernetes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The container registry. Docker builds and pushes images to a registry (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR). Kubernetes pulls those same images from the registry to create pods. The image is the common artifact — built with Docker, run by Kubernetes. Without a registry, Docker and K8s can't share images.

EXPLANATION

Workflow: (1) Write Dockerfile → (2) docker build → (3) docker push to registry → (4) kubectl apply deployment.yaml (which references the image) → (5) K8s pulls the image from registry → (6) Pods start. The registry is the handoff point between Docker (build) and Kubernetes (run).

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q6
What does kompose convert generate from a compose file?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It generates: deployment.yaml (for each service), service.yaml (for each service with ports), persistentvolumeclaim.yaml (for each named volume), and optionally networkpolicy.yaml and ingress.yaml. These files can be directly applied with kubectl apply -f.

EXPLANATION

Kompose reads your compose.yaml and translates: build: → ignored (image must already be pushed), ports: → Service, volumes: → PVC, environment: → env in Deployment, depends_on: → ignored (K8s handles differently). It's a starting point — production deployments usually need manual refinement.

# kompose convert
# kubectl apply -f
# environment:
# depends_on:
Q7
How does Kubernetes handle what Docker Compose's depends_on does?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Kubernetes does NOT have a direct depends_on equivalent. Instead, containers should be resilient to dependency unavailability — retry connections on startup. K8s provides init containers (run before main container — can wait for dependencies) and readiness probes (don't send traffic until ready).

EXPLANATION

K8s philosophy: services should be self-healing and handle transient failures. Rather than enforcing startup order (fragile), make your app retry database connections with exponential backoff. For hard dependencies, use init containers: they run sequentially and must complete before the main container starts.

# depends_on
Q8
What's the Kubernetes equivalent of a Docker named volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

PersistentVolume (PV) + PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC). The PV is the storage resource (like an EBS volume). The PVC is the request for storage (like "I need 10GB"). The pod references the PVC. This separation lets admins manage storage independently from developers requesting it.

EXPLANATION

Docker volumes are simple: docker volume create myvol. K8s separates provisioning (admin creates PV) from consumption (developer creates PVC). This enables: dynamic provisioning (PVC auto-creates PV via StorageClass), access modes (ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany), and retention policies (delete, retain, recycle).

# docker volume create myvol
Q9
What's the simplest way to deploy anihpj to Kubernetes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) docker build -t ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1 . → (2) docker push ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1 → (3) Write a Deployment YAML referencing that image → (4) kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml → (5) kubectl expose deployment anihpj --port=8000 --type=LoadBalancer. Five commands from Dockerfile to running on K8s.

EXPLANATION

The kubectl expose command creates a Service imperatively (quick but not declarative). For production: write the Service YAML, apply it, and use kubectl apply -f for everything. Always use declarative YAML files in Git for auditability and reproducibility.

# docker build -t ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1 .
# docker push ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1
# kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
# kubectl expose deployment anihpj --port=8000 --type=LoadBalancer
# kubectl expose
Q10
What's the relationship between Docker Swarm and Kubernetes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Both are container orchestrators. Docker Swarm is Docker's built-in orchestrator — simpler, integrated with Docker CLI, good for smaller deployments. Kubernetes is the industry standard — more features, larger ecosystem, steeper learning curve. Docker Desktop includes both. Swarm is easier to start; K8s is where the industry is going.

EXPLANATION

Key differences: Swarm uses docker-compose.yml syntax (familiar), K8s uses its own YAML schemas. Swarm has built-in networking and secrets; K8s has a pluggable ecosystem. Swarm is managed via docker service; K8s via kubectl. The DCA exam covers both: Swarm as Docker's orchestrator, K8s as the broader industry context.

# docker service

Chapter 26: Deploying anihpj to Kubernetes

Let's deploy anihpj to Kubernetes — from building and pushing the image to creating Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and Secrets. This is the complete production deployment walkthrough.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours☸️ K8s🏗️ Hands-On

26.1 Prerequisites for K8s Deployment

☸️
K8s Cluster

Minikube, kind, k3s, or cloud (EKS/GKE/AKS). Verify: kubectl cluster-info.

🔧
kubectl Configured

kubectl version --client. Context set: kubectl config current-context.

🗄️
Registry Access

Image pushed to a registry K8s can pull from. For private: create imagePullSecrets.

🐳
Docker Image Ready

Image built and pushed: docker build -t ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1 . && docker push ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1.

26.2 Building & Pushing the anihpj Image

TERMINAL
$ docker build -t ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0 .
$ docker login ghcr.io -u username
$ docker push ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0

26.3 Creating the Kubernetes Deployment

deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: ghcr.io/username/anihpj:v1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        env:
        - name: DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE
          value: anihpj.settings
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: anihpj-secrets
              key: database-url
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"

26.4 Creating the Kubernetes Service

service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 8000
  type: LoadBalancer  # ClusterIP (internal) | NodePort | LoadBalancer

26.5 ConfigMaps & Secrets for anihpj

configmap.yaml + secret.yaml
# configmap.yaml — Non-sensitive config
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: anihpj-config
data:
  django-settings-module: anihpj.settings
  allowed-hosts: "anihpj.example.com,localhost"
  log-level: "INFO"
---
# secret.yaml — Sensitive data (base64 encoded)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-secrets
type: Opaque
data:
  secret-key: ZGphbmdvLWluc2VjdXJlL...  # echo -n "value" | base64
  database-url: cG9zdGdyZXM6Ly91c2VyOnBhc3NAcG9zdGdyZXM6NTQzMi9hbmlocGo=

26.6 Deploying & Verifying

TERMINAL

📝 Chapter 26 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What does a Kubernetes Deployment do?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A Deployment manages a set of identical pods. It ensures the specified number of replicas are running, handles rolling updates (gradually replacing old pods with new ones), and supports rollbacks. It's the recommended way to run stateless applications on Kubernetes.

EXPLANATION

Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod. The Deployment declares the desired state (3 replicas, image v1.0). The ReplicaSet ensures the right number of pods exist. If a pod dies, the ReplicaSet creates a new one. When you update the image, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and gracefully transitions traffic — zero downtime.

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q2
What's the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ConfigMap: stores non-sensitive configuration (settings module, allowed hosts, log level). Plaintext, visible in kubectl describe. Secret: stores sensitive data (passwords, API keys, tokens). Base64-encoded at rest, can be encrypted with etcd encryption. Secrets are NOT encrypted by default — enable encryption at rest.

EXPLANATION

Both can be mounted as environment variables or files. ConfigMaps are for: Django settings, feature flags, external service URLs, log configurations. Secrets are for: SECRET_KEY, database passwords, API tokens, TLS certificates. Use RBAC to control who can read Secrets — they're more sensitive than ConfigMaps.

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q3
How do you expose a Deployment to external traffic in K8s?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Create a Service with type: LoadBalancer (cloud) or type: NodePort (bare metal). The Service provides a stable IP and DNS name, load-balancing traffic across all pods matching its selector. For HTTP routing, use an Ingress which provides path-based and host-based routing.

EXPLANATION

Service types: ClusterIP (internal only — pods can reach it), NodePort (exposes on each node's IP at a static port 30000-32767), LoadBalancer (provisions a cloud load balancer — AWS ELB, GCP LB). For production: ClusterIP internally + Ingress for external HTTP traffic with TLS termination.

# type: LoadBalancer
# type: NodePort
Q4
What are resource requests and limits in Kubernetes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Requests: minimum guaranteed resources — the scheduler uses this to place pods. Limits: maximum allowed — the container is throttled or killed if exceeded. Set both: resources: requests: memory: "256Mi" cpu: "250m"; limits: memory: "512Mi" cpu: "500m".

EXPLANATION

Without limits, a pod can consume all node resources (noisy neighbor). Without requests, the scheduler can't make good placement decisions. QoS classes: Guaranteed (requests = limits), Burstable (requests < limits), BestEffort (no requests/limits — killed first under memory pressure). Always set both for production.

# resources: requests: memory: "256Mi" cpu: "250m"; limits: memory: "512Mi" cpu: "500m"
Q5
How do you verify a Kubernetes deployment was successful?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) kubectl get pods — all should be Running and Ready. (2) kubectl get deploy anihpj — DESIRED = CURRENT = READY. (3) kubectl logs deployment/anihpj — check for errors. (4) kubectl port-forward svc/anihpj 8000:8000 — test locally. (5) kubectl describe deploy anihpj — check events for issues.

EXPLANATION

The verification sequence: pods running → deployment status healthy → logs clean → port-forward works → external access works. If pods are CrashLoopBackOff: kubectl logs <pod> and kubectl describe pod <pod> are your first debugging tools. ImagePullBackOff usually means wrong image name or registry auth issue.

# kubectl get pods
# kubectl get deploy anihpj
# kubectl logs deployment/anihpj
# kubectl port-forward svc/anihpj 8000:8000
# kubectl describe deploy anihpj
Q6
What is an imagePullSecret and when do you need it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A Kubernetes Secret of type docker-registry that stores credentials for a private container registry. Create: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=you --docker-password=$TOKEN. Reference in pod spec: imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}].

EXPLANATION

Without imagePullSecrets, K8s can only pull from public registries. For private images (GHCR, ECR, private Docker Hub), you must provide credentials. ECR uses a different auth mechanism — the ecr-credential-helper or kubelet IAM role. The token expires (GHCR tokens, ECR 12-hour tokens), so rotate regularly or use credential helpers.

# docker-registry
# kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=you --docker-password=$TOKEN
# imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}]
# ecr-credential-helper
Q7
What command applies all YAML files in a directory?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

kubectl apply -f ./k8s/ — applies all YAML/JSON files in the directory recursively. Or apply specific files: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml,service.yaml,configmap.yaml. Use kubectl apply -k ./k8s/overlays/prod for Kustomize directories.

EXPLANATION

kubectl apply is declarative (desired state) and idempotent (safe to run multiple times). kubectl create is imperative and fails if the resource already exists. Always prefer apply for production. Use kubectl diff -f ./k8s/ to preview changes before applying.

# kubectl apply -f ./k8s/
# kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml,service.yaml,configmap.yaml
# kubectl apply -k ./k8s/overlays/prod
# kubectl apply
# kubectl create
Q8
How does kubectl port-forward work?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It creates a temporary tunnel from your local machine to a pod or service in the cluster: kubectl port-forward svc/anihpj 8000:8000. Traffic to localhost:8000 is forwarded to the service on port 8000. Useful for debugging and local access — not for production traffic.

EXPLANATION

Port-forward uses the K8s API server as a proxy. It's a development tool, not a production solution. For production access, use: LoadBalancer Service, Ingress with TLS, or kubectl proxy (API server proxy). Port-forward requires kubectl access to the cluster and stops when the terminal closes.

# kubectl port-forward svc/anihpj 8000:8000
# kubectl proxy
Q9
Why separate Deployment and Service instead of one resource?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Separation of concerns. The Deployment manages pod lifecycle (which image, how many replicas, update strategy). The Service manages networking (stable IP, DNS, load balancing, port mapping). You can update the Deployment (new image) without touching the Service. You can change the Service type without redeploying pods.

EXPLANATION

This is a fundamental K8s design principle: each resource does one thing well. Compose bundles everything in one service block; K8s separates them. Benefits: independent scaling (Service doesn't scale), independent updates (change Service type without touching Deployment), and cleaner API (each resource has a focused schema).

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q10
What happens when you delete a pod in a Deployment?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The ReplicaSet notices the desired count (3) doesn't match actual (2) — and immediately creates a NEW pod to replace it. This is self-healing: the Deployment guarantees the specified number of replicas are always running. The new pod gets a new name and possibly a new node — but the Service keeps routing traffic correctly.

EXPLANATION

The control loop: Deployment declares "3 replicas" → ReplicaSet ensures 3 pods exist → if a pod dies, ReplicaSet creates a new one → the new pod gets the same labels → the Service selector matches the new pod → traffic resumes automatically. This is why you should never manage pods directly — let the Deployment handle it.

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django

Chapter 27: Kubernetes Deployment Strategies

Production deployments require zero downtime, quick rollbacks, and health monitoring. Kubernetes provides rolling updates, rollbacks, liveness/readiness probes, environment-specific configurations, and resource management — all built into the Deployment resource.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~1 hour☸️ K8s🎯 DCA 5%

27.1 Rolling Updates — Zero Downtime

Rolling Update — Step by Step
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 🔄 ROLLING UPDATE — Step by Step                           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  BEFORE (v1):  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  5 pods running anihpj:v1      │
  │                │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│                                  │
  │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 1:       ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  New v2 pod created        │
  │  (maxSurge=1)  │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v2│  (6 pods total)            │
  │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                             │
  │                                                                          │
  │  STEP 2:       ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  One v1 terminated             │
  │  (maxUnavail=1)│v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v2│  (5 pods total)                │
  │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ...continues one-by-one until...                                         │
  │                                                                          │
  │  AFTER (v2):   ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  All 5 pods running v2!        │
  │                │v2│ │v2│ │v2│ │v2│ │v2│  ZERO DOWNTIME ✅               │
  │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                                  │
  │                                                                          │
  │  KEY CONFIG: maxSurge: 1 (extra pods)  maxUnavailable: 1 (can be down)  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

27.2 Rollback — Undoing a Bad Deploy

TERMINAL
# See rollout history
$ kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj
REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         Initial deploy
2         Update to v2.0
3         Update to v3.0 (BROKEN!)

# Rollback to previous version
$ kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj
# Rollback to specific revision
$ kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj --to-revision=1

# Watch the rollback
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj

27.3 Health Checks — Liveness & Readiness Probes

deployment.yaml (with probes)
spec:
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1
    livenessProbe:           # Is the app still healthy?
      httpGet:               # If fails → restart container
        path: /health/
        port: 8000
      initialDelaySeconds: 30
      periodSeconds: 10
    readinessProbe:          # Is the app ready for traffic?
      httpGet:               # If fails → remove from Service
        path: /ready/
        port: 8000
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 5

27.4 Environment-Specific Deployments

TERMINAL
# Namespace isolation
$ kubectl create namespace dev
$ kubectl create namespace staging
$ kubectl create namespace prod

# Deploy to specific namespace
$ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -n staging

# Kustomize overlays for environment differences
# k8s/overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml:
#   patches: [replicas: 1, image: anihpj:dev]
# k8s/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml:
#   patches: [replicas: 5, image: anihpj:v1.0]

27.5 Resource Management in K8s

deployment.yaml (with resource limits)
resources:
  requests:           # Minimum guaranteed (scheduler uses this)
    memory: "256Mi"
    cpu: "250m"
  limits:             # Maximum allowed (container throttled/killed)
    memory: "512Mi"
    cpu: "500m"

# QoS Classes:
# Guaranteed:  requests == limits  (highest priority)
# Burstable:   requests < limits   (medium priority)
# BestEffort:  no requests/limits  (killed first under memory pressure)

📝 Chapter 27 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
How does a Kubernetes rolling update achieve zero downtime?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

It replaces pods one at a time: creates a new pod (v2), waits until it's ready, then terminates one old pod (v1). maxSurge controls how many extra pods can exist during the update. maxUnavailable controls how many pods can be down. Traffic is always routed to ready pods via the Service.

EXPLANATION

The Service only routes to pods that pass readiness probes. During a rolling update: new pod starts → passes readiness → added to Service → old pod removed from Service → old pod terminated. At every moment, enough pods are serving traffic. With maxSurge=1 and maxUnavailable=0, there's always full capacity during updates.

# maxUnavailable
Q2
How do you rollback a failed Kubernetes deployment?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj — reverts to the previous revision. For specific revision: kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj --to-revision=2. View history: kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj. The rollback creates a new ReplicaSet with the old image — also a rolling update, zero downtime.

EXPLANATION

Kubernetes keeps old ReplicaSets (scaled to 0) for rollback purposes. By default, it keeps the last 10 revisions. The rollback is fast because the old pods' image layers may still be cached on nodes. Use --record flag with kubectl set image to annotate revisions with the change cause.

# kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj
# kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj --to-revision=2
# kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj
# kubectl set image
Q3
What's the difference between liveness and readiness probes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Liveness: "Is the app still alive?" — if it fails, K8s RESTARTS the container. Readiness: "Is the app ready to serve?" — if it fails, K8s removes the pod from the Service (no traffic). Liveness catches deadlocks; readiness handles warmup and overload.

EXPLANATION

Wrong probe choice causes problems: liveness probe on a slow endpoint → container killed unnecessarily → restart loop. Readiness probe too aggressive → pod flapping in/out of Service. Best practice: liveness checks basic health (HTTP 200), readiness checks actual readiness (database connected, cache warmed). Initial delay gives the app time to start.

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q4
How do you deploy different configurations for dev vs production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Use Kustomize overlays: base configuration + environment-specific patches. Or Helm with values files: helm install anihpj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml. Or separate namespaces with environment-specific ConfigMaps: kubectl apply -f configmap-dev.yaml -n dev.

EXPLANATION

Kustomize is built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k). Pattern: base/ (shared config) + overlays/dev/ (patches: 1 replica, debug=true) + overlays/prod/ (patches: 5 replicas, debug=false). Helm uses Go templates with values files. Both avoid duplicating YAML for each environment.

# helm install anihpj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml
# kubectl apply -f configmap-dev.yaml -n dev
# kubectl apply -k
# overlays/dev/
# overlays/prod/
Q5
What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The container is OOMKilled (Out of Memory). Kubernetes terminates it with exit code 137 (SIGKILL). The pod is restarted according to the restart policy. CPU limit: the container is throttled (not killed). Memory is incompressible — you can't throttle memory, so K8s kills the container.

EXPLANATION

Memory limits protect the node from a single container consuming all RAM. When exceeded: kernel OOM killer is invoked → container process killed → K8s records OOMKilled. Best practice: set memory limits slightly above normal usage (to handle spikes), monitor with Prometheus, and set up alerts before limits are hit.

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q6
What QoS class does a pod get with requests=limits?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Guaranteed — the highest priority QoS class. Pods with Guaranteed QoS are the last to be evicted under memory pressure. Requires: (1) memory requests = memory limits, (2) cpu requests = cpu limits, (3) requests and limits set for every container.

EXPLANATION

QoS priority: Guaranteed > Burstable > BestEffort. Under memory pressure, the K8s eviction manager kills BestEffort pods first, then Burstable pods exceeding their requests, then Guaranteed pods (only if absolutely necessary). Production databases and critical services should use Guaranteed QoS.

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q7
How do you update a Deployment to use a new image?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

kubectl set image deployment/anihpj django=ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v2.0 — triggers a rolling update. Or edit the YAML: kubectl edit deployment/anihpj and change the image, then save. Or update the YAML file and kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml. All three trigger the same rolling update mechanism.

EXPLANATION

kubectl set image is the imperative shortcut. Editing the live object is for emergencies. kubectl apply from Git-tracked YAML is the declarative, GitOps approach — preferred for production. Add --record to annotate the change cause: kubectl set image ... --record.

# kubectl set image deployment/anihpj django=ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v2.0
# kubectl edit deployment/anihpj
# kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
# kubectl set image
# kubectl apply
Q8
What does maxSurge and maxUnavailable control?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

maxSurge: maximum number of EXTRA pods allowed during an update (above desired count). maxUnavailable: maximum number of pods that can be UNAVAILABLE during an update. Both can be absolute numbers or percentages. Default: 25% for both.

EXPLANATION

With 10 replicas and defaults: maxSurge=25% (2 extra pods → up to 12 during update), maxUnavailable=25% (2 pods down → at least 8 serving). Aggressive update: maxSurge=50%, maxUnavailable=0% (fast, never below capacity). Conservative: maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0 (slow, always full capacity).

# K8s deployment:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
kubectl logs deployment/django
kubectl rollout status deployment/django
Q9
Why use namespaces for different environments?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Namespaces provide logical isolation: separate dev/staging/prod within the same cluster. Benefits: (1) resource quotas per namespace, (2) RBAC per namespace (devs can't touch prod), (3) network policies per namespace, (4) cost allocation by namespace label. Simpler than maintaining separate clusters for each environment.

EXPLANATION

Namespace is NOT a strong security boundary — it's organizational. For strong isolation (regulated prod), use separate clusters. For most teams, namespaces + RBAC + NetworkPolicies provide sufficient isolation. Use kubens (kubectx tool) to switch namespaces easily. Set default namespace: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=staging.

# kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=staging
Q10
How do you monitor a rolling update in progress?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj — blocks until complete or failed. (2) kubectl get pods -w — watch pods being created and terminated. (3) kubectl describe deployment/anihpj — shows update conditions and events. (4) kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj — check revision state.

EXPLANATION

rollout status is the best for CI/CD — it returns 0 on success, non-zero on failure (pipeline can react). get pods -w is for live debugging — you see each pod transition. If the rollout gets stuck: check pod logs for the new pods (crashing?), check image exists in registry, check resource quotas (can't schedule new pods?).

# kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj
# kubectl get pods -w
# kubectl describe deployment/anihpj
# kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj
# rollout status

Chapter 28: Docker Swarm — Native Orchestration

Docker Swarm is Docker's built-in orchestrator — simpler than Kubernetes, using the same Docker CLI you already know. It turns multiple Docker hosts into a single virtual host, with built-in service discovery, load balancing, and rolling updates. The DCA exam dedicates 25% to orchestration — mostly Swarm.

🔴 Advanced⏱️ ~2 hours🐝 Swarm🎯 DCA 25%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand Swarm architecture (Managers + Workers)
  • ✅ Compare Swarm vs Kubernetes across 20 dimensions
  • ✅ Create and manage a Swarm cluster
  • ✅ Deploy and scale services with docker service
  • ✅ Use Swarm networking, secrets, and configs

28.1 What is Docker Swarm?

Swarm mode turns a group of Docker hosts into a single virtual host. You use docker service commands (similar to docker run) and Swarm distributes containers across nodes, handles failover, and provides built-in load balancing:

Docker Swarm Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     🐝 DOCKER SWARM ARCHITECTURE                            │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
  │  │                     SWARM CLUSTER                                 │    │
  │  │                                                                  │    │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────────┐ │    │
  │  │  │  🧠 MANAGER NODE 1 (Leader)  │  │  🧠 MANAGER NODE 2        │ │    │
  │  │  │  • Maintains cluster state   │  │  (Follower, standby)      │ │    │
  │  │  │  • Raft consensus DB         │  │  • Takes over if Leader   │ │    │
  │  │  │  • Scheduler (assigns tasks) │  │    fails!                 │ │    │
  │  │  │  • API endpoint              │  │                           │ │    │
  │  │  └──────────────┬───────────────┘  └───────────────────────────┘ │    │
  │  │                 │                                                 │    │
  │  │                 ▼  Assign tasks                                   │    │
  │  │  ┌───────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────────┐    │    │
  │  │  │  💪 WORKER NODE 1        │  │  💪 WORKER NODE 2         │    │    │
  │  │  │  anihpj:v1 (replica 1)   │  │  anihpj:v1 (replica 2)   │    │    │
  │  │  │  postgres:15 (replica 1) │  │  postgres:15 (replica 2) │    │    │
  │  │  │  redis:7                 │  │  nginx:latest             │    │    │
  │  │  └───────────────────────────┘  └───────────────────────────┘    │    │
  │  │                                                                  │    │
  │  │  ROUTING MESH: curl ANY_NODE:8000 → routes to container ✅       │    │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
