28.3 Creating a Swarm Cluster

TERMINAL
# On Manager node: initialize swarm
$ docker swarm init --advertise-addr 192.168.1.100
Swarm initialized: current node is now a manager.
To add a worker: docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-1-xxx... 192.168.1.100:2377

# On Worker nodes: join the swarm
$ docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-1-xxx... 192.168.1.100:2377
This node joined a swarm as a worker.

# View cluster nodes
$ docker node ls
ID        HOSTNAME    STATUS    AVAILABILITY   MANAGER STATUS
abc...    manager-1   Ready     Active         Leader
def...    worker-1    Ready     Active
ghi...    worker-2    Ready     Active

28.4 Deploying Services in Swarm

TERMINAL
# Create a service (like docker run, but multi-host)
$ docker service create --name anihpj --replicas 3 -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1

# List services
$ docker service ls
ID        NAME    MODE        REPLICAS  IMAGE
abc...    anihpj  replicated  3/3       ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1

# Scale up
$ docker service scale anihpj=5

# Rolling update to new version
$ docker service update --image ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v2.0 anihpj

# Rollback
$ docker service rollback anihpj

# Deploy a full stack (like docker compose, for Swarm)
$ docker stack deploy -c docker-compose.yml anihpj-stack

28.5 Swarm Networking & Storage

Swarm's routing mesh makes every node in the cluster able to serve any service — even if that node isn't running the container. The overlay network connects containers across hosts transparently. Storage uses volume drivers for multi-host persistence.

💡 Routing Mesh Magic

With Swarm, curl worker-2:8000 works even if worker-2 isn't running an anihpj container. The routing mesh intercepts the request and forwards it to a node that IS running the container. This means you can point your load balancer at ANY Swarm node — built-in high availability.

28.6 Swarm Secrets & Configs

TERMINAL
# Create a secret (encrypted at rest, in transit)
$ echo "super-secret-key" | docker secret create django_secret -

# Create a config (non-sensitive)
$ docker config create nginx_conf nginx.conf

# Use in a service
$ docker service create --secret django_secret --config nginx_conf anihpj

# Secrets mounted as files in /run/secrets/
# Configs mounted as files at / (config name becomes filename)

28.7 Raft Consensus & Swarm Lock/Unlock

Swarm uses the Raft consensus algorithm to maintain cluster state across manager nodes. The Raft log stores ALL cluster state — service definitions, node membership, secrets, and configs. Understanding Raft is critical for the DCA Orchestration domain.

Raft Consensus — Manager Quorum
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              RAFT CONSENSUS IN DOCKER SWARM                 │
  │                                                             │
  │  N managers → tolerates floor((N-1)/2) failures             │
  │                                                             │
  │  1 manager:  0 tolerance (not production)                   │
  │  2 managers: 0 tolerance (even = no quorum if split!)      │
  │  3 managers: 1 failure tolerated ★ minimum prod            │
  │  5 managers: 2 failures tolerated ★ recommended            │
  │  7 managers: 3 failures tolerated ★ large clusters         │
  │                                                             │
  │  Raft requires (N/2)+1 managers for quorum.                 │
  │  NEVER use an even number — wastes resources.               │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔒
Autolock & Swarm Lock

Autolock encrypts the Raft log on disk. When a manager restarts, it requires an unlock key to decrypt and rejoin. Enable: docker swarm init --autolock. Unlock after restart: docker swarm unlock (paste key). View key: docker swarm unlock-key. Rotate key: docker swarm unlock-key --rotate. Without autolock, the Raft log AND all secrets/configs are stored in plaintext on disk.

🔄
Swarm Lock/Unlock Workflow

Enable: docker swarm update --autolock=true. Disable: docker swarm update --autolock=false. After daemon restart: docker swarm unlock ← REQUIRED before any swarm commands work. Store the unlock key safely — if lost, you cannot recover the cluster (must force new cluster).

⚠️ DCA Critical: Autolock

The DCA exam WILL test autolock. Know: (1) it encrypts the Raft log at rest, (2) without it, secrets/configs are plaintext on manager disks, (3) after manager restart, docker swarm unlock is required, (4) rotating the unlock key is docker swarm unlock-key --rotate. This is a top-5 most-tested Swarm topic.

TERMINAL
# Initialize swarm with autolock
$ docker swarm init --autolock
Swarm initialized: current node is now a manager.
To unlock: docker swarm unlock
Unlock key: SWMKEY-1-xxxx...  ← SAVE THIS!

# Enable autolock on existing swarm
$ docker swarm update --autolock=true

# Rotate the unlock key
$ docker swarm unlock-key --rotate

# View current unlock key (if you have it)
$ docker swarm unlock-key

# After manager daemon restart — MUST unlock:
$ docker swarm unlock
Please enter unlock key: [paste key]

# Check autolock status
$ docker info | grep -A2 "Swarm"
  Autolock Managers: true
  Unlock Key: SWMKEY-1-xxxx...

28.8 Advanced Service Update Configuration

docker service update has extensive flags controlling exactly how rolling updates behave. These flags appear frequently on the DCA exam:

FlagDefaultPurposeExample
--update-parallelism1How many replicas to update simultaneously--update-parallelism 2
--update-delay0sWait time between update batches--update-delay 30s
--update-failure-actionpauseWhat to do if an update fails (pause|continue|rollback)--update-failure-action rollback
--update-max-failure-ratio0Max fraction of tasks that can fail (0-1)--update-max-failure-ratio 0.2
--update-monitor5sHow long to monitor new tasks before declaring success--update-monitor 30s
--update-orderstop-firststop-first (stop old then start new) or start-first (start new then stop old)--update-order start-first
stop-first vs start-first Update Order
  stop-first (default):                     start-first:
  ┌──────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Before: [v1][v1][v1]     │              │ Before: [v1][v1][v1]     │
  │ Step 1: [  ][v1][v1] STOP│              │ Step 1: [v2][v1][v1] NEW│
  │ Step 2: [v2][v1][v1] START│             │ Step 2: [v2][  ][v1] STOP│
  │ Capacity drops temporarily│              │ Step 3: [v2][v2][v1] NEW│
  │ ⚠️ 1 less replica during  │              │ Capacity NEVER drops!   │
  └──────────────────────────┘              └──────────────────────────┘
  Use stop-first when resources are         Use start-first when you can''t
  tight and you can''t run extras.           afford any capacity reduction.
TERMINAL
# Aggressive update: fast, parallel, auto-rollback on failure
$ docker service update     --update-parallelism 3     --update-delay 5s     --update-failure-action rollback     --update-order start-first     --image ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v2.0 anihpj

# Conservative update: slow, safe, manual intervention on failure
$ docker service update     --update-parallelism 1     --update-delay 60s     --update-failure-action pause     --update-monitor 30s     --image ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v2.0 anihpj

28.9 Service Rollback Configuration

Rollback is triggered by docker service rollback OR automatically by --update-failure-action rollback. Rollback uses the PREVIOUS service specification — not just the previous image. All configs, secrets, and mounts revert:

FlagDefaultPurpose
--rollback-parallelism1How many tasks to rollback at once
--rollback-delay0sWait time between rollback batches
--rollback-failure-actionpauseWhat to do if rollback itself fails (pause|continue)
--rollback-max-failure-ratio0Max fraction of rollback tasks that can fail
--rollback-monitor5sHow long to monitor rolled-back tasks
--rollback-orderstop-firststop-first or start-first during rollback
TERMINAL
# Manual rollback (instant — uses previous spec)
$ docker service rollback anihpj

# View rollback history
$ docker service ps anihpj
# Look for tasks with "Shutdown" state — shows which version was running

# Configure auto-rollback on failed update
$ docker service update     --update-failure-action rollback     --update-max-failure-ratio 0.3     --update-monitor 15s     anihpj

# Configure rollback behavior itself
$ docker service update     --rollback-parallelism 2     --rollback-delay 10s     --rollback-failure-action pause     anihpj

28.10 Placement Constraints, Preferences & docker_gwbridge

Control WHERE services run with placement constraints and preferences. Understand the Swarm networking internals — ingress and docker_gwbridge:

📍
Placement Constraints

Restrict which nodes can run a service:
--constraint node.labels.ssd==true
--constraint node.role==worker
--constraint node.hostname!=db-server
Add labels: docker node update --label-add ssd=true node1
View labels: docker node inspect node1

📊
Placement Preferences

Spread tasks across labeled nodes:
--placement-pref spread=node.labels.rack
Ensures tasks distribute across racks/zones for HA. Unlike constraints (hard rule), preferences are soft — scheduler tries to satisfy but won''t block scheduling.

Swarm Network Architecture — ingress + docker_gwbridge
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           SWARM NETWORKING INTERNALS                         │
  │                                                             │
  │  EVERY Swarm node has TWO special networks:                 │
  │                                                             │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  ingress (overlay)                                   │   │
  │  │  • Carries published port traffic (routing mesh)     │   │
  │  │  • IPVS load balances across ALL replicas            │   │
  │  │  • Every node joins this automatically               │   │
  │  │  • Subnet: 10.255.0.0/16 (default)                   │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                             │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  docker_gwbridge (bridge)                            │   │
  │  │  • Connects containers to host''s external network    │   │
  │  │  • Provides outbound internet access for tasks       │   │
  │  │  • Every node has one docker_gwbridge                 │   │
  │  │  • Subnet: 172.18.0.0/16 (default)                   │   │
  │  │  • Check: docker network inspect docker_gwbridge     │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                             │
  │  PUBLISHED PORT FLOW:                                      │
  │  Request → ANY_NODE:8000 → ingress → IPVS → Task Container │
  │                                                             │
  │  OUTBOUND FLOW:                                            │
  │  Task Container → docker_gwbridge → Host Network → Internet│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
TERMINAL
# Add node labels for placement
$ docker node update --label-add ssd=true --label-add rack=r1 node1
$ docker node update --label-add ssd=false --label-add rack=r2 node2

# Constrain service to SSD nodes only
$ docker service create --name db     --constraint node.labels.ssd==true     postgres:15

# Spread across racks for HA
$ docker service create --name web     --placement-pref "spread=node.labels.rack"     --replicas 6 nginx

# Inspect special Swarm networks
$ docker network inspect ingress
$ docker network inspect docker_gwbridge

# Customize docker_gwbridge subnet (in daemon.json):
# {"default-address-pools":[{"base":"10.10.0.0/16","size":24}]}

📝 Chapter 28 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What is Docker Swarm and how does it differ from standalone Docker?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Swarm mode turns multiple Docker hosts into a single virtual host. Standalone Docker manages containers on ONE machine. Swarm distributes services across multiple nodes with built-in load balancing, service discovery, rolling updates, and failover. Activate with docker swarm init.

EXPLANATION

Swarm uses Raft consensus for manager nodes (odd number, 3-7 recommended). The routing mesh makes every node able to serve any published port — even if that node isn't running the container. This is the simplest path to multi-host Docker and the foundation of the DCA Orchestration domain (25% of the exam).

# docker swarm init
Q2
How do you initialize a Docker Swarm cluster?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker swarm init --advertise-addr <MANAGER-IP> on the first manager node. This creates the cluster, generates join tokens, and makes the current node the leader. Workers join with: docker swarm join --token <TOKEN> <MANAGER-IP>:2377.

EXPLANATION

--advertise-addr is critical — it tells other nodes how to reach this manager. Without it, multi-network interfaces may cause connectivity issues. Join tokens: manager token (for adding more managers — keep secret!) and worker token (for adding workers). View tokens: docker swarm join-token manager.

# docker swarm init --advertise-addr 
# docker swarm join --token  :2377
# --advertise-addr
# docker swarm join-token manager
Q3
What command creates a service with 5 replicas in Swarm?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service create --name anihpj --replicas 5 -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1. To scale an existing service: docker service scale anihpj=5. To update: docker service update --replicas 5 anihpj.

EXPLANATION

docker service create is like docker run but for Swarm — same flags, multi-host semantics. Swarm's scheduler places replicas across available nodes based on resource availability and constraints. Use docker service ps anihpj to see where each replica is running.

# docker service create --name anihpj --replicas 5 -p 8000:8000 ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v1
# docker service scale anihpj=5
# docker service update --replicas 5 anihpj
# docker service create
# docker run
Q4
How does Swarm's routing mesh work?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Every Swarm node listens on published ports. When a request arrives at ANY node, the routing mesh forwards it to a node running the container. This means you can send traffic to ANY node in the cluster — even workers not running the service. Built-in load balancing distributes requests across all replicas.

EXPLANATION

The routing mesh uses IPVS (IP Virtual Server) for Layer 4 load balancing. Published ports are exposed on ALL nodes (ingress network). This eliminates the need for an external load balancer for basic setups — just point DNS at any Swarm node. For Layer 7 (HTTP) routing, you'd still use a reverse proxy like Traefik or Nginx.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web
Q5
What's the difference between docker service and docker stack?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service manages individual services imperatively. docker stack manages entire application stacks declaratively from a compose file. Stack = Compose for Swarm. Use docker stack deploy -c compose.yml myapp to deploy a multi-service application with one command.

EXPLANATION

Stack files support additional Swarm-specific Compose keys: deploy: (replicas, update_config, restart_policy, resources, placement constraints), secrets:, configs:. A stack deploys all services together and manages them as a unit. docker stack rm myapp removes everything at once.

# docker service
# docker stack
# docker stack deploy -c compose.yml myapp
# docker stack rm myapp
Q6
How do you perform a rolling update in Swarm?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service update --image ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v2.0 anihpj. Swarm gradually replaces old containers with new ones — one at a time by default. Control behavior: --update-parallelism 2 (update 2 at a time), --update-delay 10s (wait 10s between batches), --update-failure-action rollback.

EXPLANATION

Default update: one replica at a time, zero delay. If a new replica fails health checks, the update pauses. --update-failure-action rollback automatically reverts on failure. Check status: docker service ps anihpj (look for "Preparing" or "Running"). This is heavily tested on the DCA exam.

# docker service update --image ghcr.io/you/anihpj:v2.0 anihpj
# --update-parallelism 2
# --update-delay 10s
# --update-failure-action rollback
# --update-failure-action rollback
Q7
How do Docker Swarm secrets differ from environment variables?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Secrets are: encrypted at rest on manager nodes (Raft log), encrypted in transit (mTLS), mounted as tmpfs files in /run/secrets/, and only available to services explicitly granted access. ENV vars are plaintext, visible in docker inspect, and accessible to any process reading /proc.

EXPLANATION

Create: echo "value" | docker secret create name -. Use: docker service create --secret name. The secret appears as a file — your app reads /run/secrets/name instead of $SECRET_NAME. This is the recommended approach for all sensitive data in Swarm. The DCA exam expects you to prefer secrets over ENV for sensitive data.

# /run/secrets/
# docker inspect
# echo "value" | docker secret create name -
# docker service create --secret name
# /run/secrets/name
Q8
What's the difference between Swarm managers and workers?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Managers: maintain cluster state (Raft consensus), schedule tasks, serve the API. Workers: only run containers, report health to managers. Managers CAN also run tasks (like workers) by default. For production: use 3-7 managers (odd number for quorum), and only managers should be manager nodes.

EXPLANATION

Raft consensus requires >50% of managers to be available for the cluster to function. With 3 managers: tolerate 1 failure. With 5: tolerate 2. With 7: tolerate 3. Never use an even number of managers. To dedicate managers to management only: docker node update --availability drain manager-node.

# docker node update --availability drain manager-node
Q9
How do you view the containers (tasks) of a Swarm service?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service ps anihpj — shows every replica (task), which node it's on, its desired state (Running), current state, and error messages if any. This is the Swarm equivalent of kubectl get pods. For detailed info: docker service inspect anihpj.

EXPLANATION

Each replica is a "task" in Swarm terminology. A task is the atomic unit of scheduling — it represents a container + its configuration on a specific node. If a node fails, tasks are rescheduled to healthy nodes. docker service ps shows task history: shutdown tasks, failed tasks, and current running tasks.

# docker service ps anihpj
# kubectl get pods
# docker service inspect anihpj
# docker service ps
Q10
When would you choose Swarm over Kubernetes?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Choose Swarm when: (1) team already knows Docker CLI, (2) 3-10 node cluster, (3) simple deployments without complex scaling, (4) integrated secrets/configs are sufficient, (5) you want single-vendor support (Docker Inc). Swarm's biggest advantage: it's built into Docker — zero additional tooling.

EXPLANATION

Swarm trades features for simplicity. If you need: multi-tenancy (namespaces), RBAC, HPA auto-scaling, service mesh, or cloud-based managed K8s — use Kubernetes. If you want: one command to start clustering, docker-compose.yml compatibility, and don't need K8s' complexity — Swarm is the pragmatic choice.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web

Compose is for development; Kubernetes is for production. This chapter bridges the gap — converting Compose files to K8s manifests, using Helm charts, Kustomize overlays, and understanding when to use which tool.

29.1 Docker Compose for Local, K8s for Prod

Dev → Staging → Production Pipeline
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐   │
  │  │ 💻 DEVELOPMENT    │    │ 🧪 STAGING        │    │ 🚀 PRODUCTION     │   │
  │  │ docker compose up │───▶│ docker compose up │───▶│ kubectl apply    │   │
  │  │ Compose + volumes │    │ Compose + test DB │    │ K8s + Helm       │   │
  │  │ Hot reload        │    │ CI/CD pipeline    │    │ 3+ replicas      │   │
  │  │ DEBUG=True        │    │ DEBUG=False       │    │ Rolling updates  │   │
  │  └──────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                          │

  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

29.4 Helm — The Package Manager for K8s

TERMINAL
# Create a Helm chart
$ helm create anihpj-chart

# Chart structure:
# anihpj-chart/
#   Chart.yaml          # Chart metadata
#   values.yaml         # Default configuration
#   templates/          # K8s manifests (with Go templates)
#     deployment.yaml
#     service.yaml
#     configmap.yaml

# Install with custom values
$ helm install anihpj ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml

29.5 Kustomize — Template-Free Customization

TERMINAL
# Built into kubectl!
$ kubectl apply -k overlays/prod

# Kustomize structure:
# k8s/
#   base/
#     kustomization.yaml   # Shared config
#     deployment.yaml
#     service.yaml
#   overlays/
#     dev/
#       kustomization.yaml # Patches: replicas=1, debug=true
#     prod/
#       kustomization.yaml # Patches: replicas=5, debug=false

# Preview without applying:
$ kubectl kustomize overlays/prod

📝 Chapter 29 — DCA Practice Questions

Q1
What tool automatically converts docker-compose.yml to K8s manifests?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Kompose: kompose convert -f docker-compose.yml. Generates deployment.yaml, service.yaml, and pvc.yaml files. Handles ~80% of the conversion — manual refinement is usually needed for production readiness.

EXPLANATION

Kompose is an official Kubernetes project (part of the Kubernetes GitHub org). It translates: services → Deployments, ports → Services, volumes → PersistentVolumeClaims, environment variables → env in Deployment specs. Limitations: doesn't handle depends_on, health checks, or Swarm-specific Compose keys.

# kompose convert -f docker-compose.yml
Q2
What is Helm and why use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes — like apt/yum for K8s. It bundles K8s manifests into "charts" with parameterized values. Install with helm install myapp ./chart -f values.yaml. Charts can be versioned, shared via repositories, and templated with Go templates.

EXPLANATION

Helm solves the "wall of YAML" problem. Instead of managing 5+ separate YAML files per environment, you have one chart with values files. Example: helm install anihpj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml deploys the same chart with production settings. Helm also manages: release history, rollbacks (helm rollback), and hooks (pre/post install).

# helm install myapp ./chart -f values.yaml
# helm install anihpj ./chart -f values-prod.yaml
# helm rollback
Q3
How does Kustomize differ from Helm?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Helm: uses Go templates (dynamic YAML generation). Kustomize: uses patching (template-free, overlays modify base YAML). Kustomize is built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k). Helm has a richer ecosystem (charts, repos, hooks). Choose Kustomize for simplicity; Helm for ecosystem and complex templating.

EXPLANATION

Kustomize's philosophy: don't template, patch. Your base YAML is valid Kubernetes — overlays modify it declaratively. Helm's philosophy: parameterize everything, generate YAML from templates. Kustomize is simpler for most use cases; Helm is better when you need conditional logic (if/else in templates) or want to publish reusable charts.

# kubectl apply -k
Q4
What's the Kubernetes equivalent of docker compose logs?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

kubectl logs deployment/anihpj — shows logs from all pods in the deployment. For a specific pod: kubectl logs anihpj-5d8f7b9c-abcde. Stream with -f: kubectl logs -f deployment/anihpj. For previous crashed container: kubectl logs --previous.

EXPLANATION

Unlike Compose (which aggregates logs from all services), kubectl logs is per-pod or per-deployment. For multi-pod log aggregation, use: kubetail (third-party), stern (third-party), or a centralized logging stack (Elasticsearch/Fluentd/Kibana or Loki/Promtail/Grafana).

# kubectl logs deployment/anihpj
# kubectl logs anihpj-5d8f7b9c-abcde
# kubectl logs -f deployment/anihpj
# kubectl logs --previous
Q5
What's the Kubernetes equivalent of docker compose exec?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

kubectl exec -it anihpj-5d8f7b9c-abcde -- bash. -it for interactive terminal. Unlike Compose (service name), you must specify the pod name. Find the pod: kubectl get pods. Run a single command: kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- python manage.py migrate.

EXPLANATION

The key difference: Compose uses service names (docker compose exec django bash), K8s uses pod names. Since pods have dynamic names, you often need to find the pod first. Shortcut: kubectl exec -it deploy/anihpj -- bash picks the first pod in the deployment.

# kubectl exec -it anihpj-5d8f7b9c-abcde -- bash
# kubectl get pods
# kubectl exec anihpj-xxx -- python manage.py migrate
# docker compose exec django bash
# kubectl exec -it deploy/anihpj -- bash
Q6
Why use the same Docker image across dev, staging, and production?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

"Build once, deploy many." The image tested in staging is the EXACT same image deployed to production — same binaries, same libraries, same configuration structure (different values via env vars/ConfigMaps). This eliminates "works in staging, broken in production" issues caused by environment drift.

EXPLANATION

The image is the immutable artifact. What changes between environments: (1) Config values — DEBUG, log levels, database URLs (via ConfigMaps/env), (2) Replica count — 1 in dev, 5 in prod, (3) Resource limits — smaller in dev, larger in prod. The image itself is identical — guaranteed by the SHA256 digest.

# compose.yaml:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
Q7
What does kompose NOT handle when converting compose files?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Kompose cannot convert: (1) depends_on (K8s doesn't have direct equivalent — use init containers), (2) healthcheck in compose (need to manually add liveness/readiness probes), (3) Swarm-specific keys (deploy section), (4) build: (image must be pre-built and pushed).

EXPLANATION

After kompose convert, you typically need to: add resource limits, add liveness/readiness probes, replace environment variables with ConfigMaps/Secrets, add Ingress for HTTP routing, and review volume configurations (PV/PVC vs Docker volumes). Kompose gives you 80% — the remaining 20% is production-specific refinement.

# depends_on
# healthcheck
# kompose convert
Q8
What command deploys a Helm chart?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

helm install <release-name> <chart> -f <values-file>. Example: helm install anihpj-prod ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml. Upgrade: helm upgrade anihpj-prod ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml. Rollback: helm rollback anihpj-prod 1.

EXPLANATION

Helm tracks releases (installations) and revisions (versions of a release). Each install/upgrade creates a new revision stored as a Secret. This enables: helm history anihpj-prod (see all versions), helm rollback anihpj-prod 2 (go back to revision 2), helm uninstall anihpj-prod (remove everything).

# helm install   -f 
# helm install anihpj-prod ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml
# helm upgrade anihpj-prod ./anihpj-chart -f values-prod.yaml
# helm rollback anihpj-prod 1
# helm history anihpj-prod
Q9
What's the advantage of Kustomize being built into kubectl?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Zero additional tooling. kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod works on any machine with kubectl — no installation, no server-side component, no templating language to learn. The output is plain YAML (kubectl kustomize shows it) — compatible with any GitOps tool.

EXPLANATION

Kustomize is "server-side apply without a server." It processes overlays locally and sends plain YAML to the API server. This means: (1) no cluster-side controller needed, (2) output is auditable (run kubectl kustomize to see exactly what will be applied), (3) works with ArgoCD/Flux for GitOps.

# kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod
# kubectl kustomize
# kubectl kustomize
Q10
What's the migration path from Docker Compose to production K8s?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) kompose convert to generate initial K8s manifests. (2) Manually refine: add resource limits, probes, ConfigMaps, Secrets. (3) Extract environment-specific configs using Kustomize overlays or Helm values. (4) Set up CI/CD to build image → push → kubectl apply or helm upgrade. (5) Monitor with Prometheus/Grafana.

EXPLANATION

The journey: compose.yaml (dev) → kompose (initial K8s conversion) → manual refinement (production hardening) → Kustomize/Helm (environment management) → CI/CD automation (GitHub Actions → kubectl) → monitoring (production observability). The image stays the same throughout — only the orchestration layer changes.

# kompose convert

30.4 Dockerfile Writing for the Exam

Know every instruction and be able to spot errors in a Dockerfile. The exam will show you broken Dockerfiles and ask what's wrong:

🏆 Exam Dockerfile Checklist

✅ FROM (always first, must be specific tag). ✅ WORKDIR (not RUN cd). ✅ COPY > ADD. ✅ Chain RUN with &&. ✅ CMD vs ENTRYPOINT. ✅ Multi-stage (COPY --from). ✅ EXPOSE is documentation. ✅ ARG vs ENV. ✅ USER for non-root. ✅ HEALTHCHECK for production. ✅ .dockerignore exists. ✅ No secrets in ENV.

30.5 Docker Compose for the Exam

Know the compose.yaml structure and docker compose commands. The exam expects you to understand service configuration, networking, volumes, and environment management:

🏆 Compose Exam Checklist

✅ services → containers. ✅ networks → custom networks. ✅ volumes → named volumes. ✅ depends_on with condition: service_healthy. ✅ environment vs env_file. ✅ ports mapping. ✅ build vs image. ✅ docker compose config (validate). ✅ docker compose up/down/ps/logs/exec.

30.6 Docker Swarm for the Exam

Swarm is 25% of the exam — the single largest domain. Know these commands and concepts:

🏆 Swarm Exam Checklist — 25% of DCA (EXPANDED)

Cluster Management:
✅ swarm init (--advertise-addr, --autolock). ✅ swarm join (manager/worker tokens). ✅ swarm unlock/unlock-key. ✅ swarm leave (--force). ✅ node ls/ps/inspect/update/demote/promote. ✅ node --availability (active/pause/drain). ✅ Manager quorum (NEVER even number: 3,5,7). ✅ Raft consensus basics.

Services:
✅ service create (--name, --replicas, -p, --network, --secret, --config, --constraint, --placement-pref, --restart-condition, --restart-delay, --restart-max-attempts). ✅ service update (--image, --replicas, --update-parallelism, --update-delay, --update-failure-action, --update-order, --update-max-failure-ratio, --update-monitor). ✅ service rollback (--rollback-parallelism, --rollback-delay, --rollback-failure-action, --rollback-order). ✅ service scale. ✅ service ps (task status across nodes). ✅ service logs. ✅ service inspect.

Stacks:
✅ stack deploy (deploy: section: replicas, update_config, rollback_config, restart_policy, placement, resources). ✅ stack ls/ps/services/rm.

Networking:
✅ Routing mesh (ingress network). ✅ docker_gwbridge (outbound connectivity). ✅ Overlay networks (--opt encrypted). ✅ Port publishing (host mode vs ingress mode).

Security:
✅ secrets create/ls/inspect/rm. ✅ configs create/ls/inspect/rm. ✅ Autolock (encrypted Raft log). ✅ MTLS between nodes (automatic in Swarm).

30.7 Exam Strategy & Tips

⏱️
Time Management

55 questions / 90 minutes = ~1.6 min per question. Flag and skip hard ones — return later. Don't spend more than 3 minutes on any question. Answer everything (no penalty for wrong answers).

📖
During the Exam

Docker documentation IS available in the exam! You can access docs.docker.com. Know WHERE to find information quickly — don't memorize everything. Practice navigating the docs.

⚠️
Common Traps

EXPOSE vs -p publishing. CMD vs ENTRYPOINT behavior. depends_on without healthcheck. ENV vs ARG. save vs export. COPY vs ADD. Bridge default vs custom bridge DNS. Swarm manager quorum requirements.

💡
Pro Tips

Read ALL answer choices before selecting. Eliminate obviously wrong answers first. Watch for "NOT", "EXCEPT", "BEST" keywords. Trust your hands-on experience — the exam tests practical knowledge, not trivia.

What is the passing score for the Docker Certified Associate exam?
Show Answer & Explanation

Approximately 65-70%, though Docker does not publish an exact fixed percentage. The exam uses scaled scoring. You need roughly 36-39 correct answers out of 55 questions. The exact threshold varies per exam version.

EXPLANATION

Docker uses psychometric scaling — harder questions are worth more, easier ones less. You don't see a percentage score; you see pass/fail with domain-level feedback. Aim to answer at least 40 questions confidently. The exam allows review of flagged questions before final submission.

Q4
What's the best strategy for time management during the DCA exam?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) First pass: answer all easy questions quickly (~30-40 seconds each). Flag hard ones. (2) Second pass: tackle flagged questions with remaining time. (3) Final pass: review all answers. Never leave a question unanswered — there's no penalty for wrong answers. Target: 1-1.5 minutes per question average.

EXPLANATION

55 questions / 90 minutes. If you spend 5 minutes on one hard question, you've lost time for 3-4 easier ones. The optimal strategy: quick first pass to bank easy points, then use remaining time for harder questions with docs reference. 

  EXAM TIMELINE — 90 minutes, 55 questions:
  
  ┌─ 0 min: START ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  First Pass (50 min):                                │
  │  • Answer all easy Qs (~40s each)                    │
  │  • Flag hard ones (10-15 flags max)                  │
  │  • Target: 35-40 answered                            │
  │                                                      │
  │  Second Pass (30 min):                               │
  │  • Revisit flagged Qs with docs.docker.com           │
  │  • Target: answer remaining 15-20                    │
  │                                                      │
  │  Final Review (10 min):                              │
  │  • Verify ALL answered (no blanks!)                  │
  │  • Quick scan flagged for obvious errors             │
  │  • SUBMIT with confidence                            │
  └─ 90 min: DONE ──────────────────────────────────────┘
Flag liberally — you can unflag after answering. Total flagged should be 10-15 questions max.

Q5
How many manager nodes should a production Swarm cluster have?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

3, 5, or 7 — always an odd number for Raft quorum. 3 managers tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2, 7 tolerate 3. Never use an even number (if you have 2, you need both for quorum — no fault tolerance). For most production deployments, 3 or 5 managers is sufficient.

EXPLANATION

Raft consensus requires (N/2)+1 managers for quorum. With 3 managers: need 2 → tolerate 1 failure. With 2 managers: need 2 → tolerate 0 failures (worse than 3!). 

  SWARM MANAGER QUORUM CALCULATION:
  
  Managers | Quorum (N/2+1) | Tolerates | Recommendation
  ─────────┼────────────────┼───────────┼──────────────
      1    |       1        |   0       | Dev/test only
      2    |       2        |   0       | NEVER use! ❌
      3    |       2        |   1       | Production min ★
      4    |       3        |   1       | No benefit over 3
      5    |       3        |   2       | Recommended ★★
      7    |       4        |   3       | Large clusters
  
  docker node ls                    # Check manager status
  docker node promote worker-1      # Add manager
  docker node demote manager-2      # Remove manager
With 4: need 3 → tolerate 1 (same as 3, one more node for zero benefit). This is a DCA exam favorite — always odd, always 3-7.

Q6
What Docker Compose feature is commonly confused with EXPOSE?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ports: in compose actually PUBLISHES ports (like -p). expose: in compose is documentation only (like Dockerfile EXPOSE). The exam may test this distinction: ports: ["8000:8000"] publishes; expose: ["8000"] is metadata only.

EXPLANATION

In compose.yaml: ports: = docker run -p (actual port mapping, makes container accessible). expose: = EXPOSE in Dockerfile (documentation, no actual publishing). Between services on the same compose network, ports don't need publishing — they can communicate directly. Publishing is only for external access.

# ports: ["8000:8000"]
# expose: ["8000"]
# docker run -p
Q7
What command rolls back a Swarm service to its previous version?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service rollback anihpj. This reverts to the previous service configuration. For specific revision: Swarm doesn't have numbered revisions like K8s — rollback goes to the immediately previous configuration. Check status: docker service ps anihpj.

EXPLANATION

Swarm rollback is simpler than K8s: one level of undo. If you updated v1→v2→v3, rollback goes to v2, not v1. 

# Rollback to previous version:
docker service rollback anihpj

# Configure auto-rollback on failed update:
docker service update     --update-failure-action rollback     --update-max-failure-ratio 0.3     --update-monitor 15s     --update-order start-first     anihpj

# Manual rollback to specific image:
docker service update --image anihpj:v1 anihpj

# Watch rollback progress:
docker service ps anihpj     # See task states
docker service inspect anihpj | grep -A5 Rollback
For deeper rollbacks, you'd need to manually docker service update --image anihpj:v1 anihpj. The --update-failure-action rollback flag automatically rolls back if the update fails health checks.

Q8
What's the most commonly missed Dockerfile best practice on the exam?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Not cleaning up package manager caches after install. RUN apt-get install pkg leaves /var/lib/apt/lists/* in the layer — wasting space. Correct: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*. Same for pip: --no-cache-dir. Also: chaining RUN commands, not just for cleanup but to reduce layers.

EXPLANATION

The exam will show a Dockerfile with: RUN apt-get update, RUN apt-get install pkg (separate lines, no cleanup). 

# ❌ BAD Dockerfile (exam trap):
FROM ubuntu:22.04
RUN apt-get update                     # Separate layer = stale cache
RUN apt-get install -y python3         # No cleanup = bloated image
COPY . /app

# ✅ CORRECT Dockerfile:
FROM ubuntu:22.04
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3     && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*     # Clean + chain = small layer
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
USER 1000                              # Non-root
CMD ["python3", "app.py"]              # Exec form, not shell
Correct answer: chain them with && and clean up. Other common traps: FROM :latest, ADD for local files, CMD in shell form without ENTRYPOINT understanding, and running as root.

Q9
How long is the DCA certification valid?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

2 years from the date you pass the exam. After 2 years, you must recertify by taking the current version of the exam again. Docker may also offer continuing education options for renewal. Check the official Docker certification page for current renewal policies.

EXPLANATION

Docker certifications follow the industry-standard 2-year validity period (same as AWS, Azure, Kubernetes certifications). Technology changes rapidly — 2 years ensures certified professionals stay current. Plan to recertify 3-6 months before expiration to avoid a gap in your certification status.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web
Q10
What should you do in the final 5 minutes of the DCA exam?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

(1) Verify ALL questions are answered — no blanks! (2) Quick review of flagged questions — trust your first instinct unless you're certain of a correction. (3) Verify you haven't accidentally unselected an answer. (4) Take a deep breath and submit. Don't second-guess yourself in the final minutes.

EXPLANATION

The final minutes are for verification, not learning. Changing answers at the last minute is statistically more likely to change a correct answer to wrong than wrong to correct. Use the last 5 minutes to: ensure no unanswered questions, scan flagged questions for obvious mistakes, and confirm your submission. Then celebrate — you've earned it! 🎉

A.1 Container Commands

Commands for managing the complete container lifecycle — create, run, inspect, debug, and destroy.

CommandDescriptionExample

docker stopStop a running container (SIGTERM)docker stop anihpj-app
docker startStart a stopped containerdocker start anihpj-app
docker restartRestart a containerdocker restart anihpj-app

docker createCreate container without startingdocker create --name temp anihpj:v1
💡 DCA Tip: docker stop sends SIGTERM (graceful, 10s timeout then SIGKILL). docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately. docker rm -f does stop + rm in one command. Always prefer docker exec -it CONTAINER sh over docker attach for debugging — attach connects to the main process, exec starts a new one.

📝 Appendix B: Dockerfile Quick Reference

Dockerfile — All Instructions & Templates

Complete reference of every Dockerfile instruction with syntax, plus production-ready templates for Python/Django, Node.js, Go, and static sites. Includes multi-stage patterns and .dockerignore templates.

📝 Reference🎯 DCA Essential

🏗️ FROM

Base image (mandatory)

FROM python:3.11-slim

📁 WORKDIR

Set working directory

WORKDIR /app

📋 COPY

Copy files from context

COPY . /app

⚙️ RUN

Execute build commands

RUN pip install -r req.txt

🚀 CMD

Default runtime command

CMD ["python", "app.py"]

🎯 ENTRYPOINT

Fixed executable

ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"]

🌍 ENV

Runtime env variable

ENV DEBUG=False

🔨 ARG

Build-time variable

ARG VERSION=1.0

📊 Quick visual overview — detailed syntax in the table below

B.1 Complete Instruction Reference

InstructionSyntaxDescription
FROMFROM python:3.11-slim AS builderBase image (MANDATORY, first). Multi-stage: use AS for stage name.
WORKDIRWORKDIR /appSet working directory. Creates if missing. Better than RUN cd.
COPYCOPY requirements.txt .Copy files from build context. Preferred over ADD for local files.
ADDADD https://example.com/file.tar.gz /app/Like COPY + URL download + tar auto-extract. Use COPY when possible.
RUNRUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r req.txtExecute commands during build. Chain with && to reduce layers.
CMDCMD ["gunicorn", "app:application"]Default command (overridable). Exec form preferred.
ENTRYPOINTENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"]Fixed executable (not easily overridden). CMD becomes arguments.
ENVENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=app.settingsSet environment variable (persists at runtime). Visible in history.
ARGARG VERSION=1.0Build-time variable. NOT in final image (unless persisted to ENV).
EXPOSEEXPOSE 8000Document port (metadata only). Use -p to actually publish.
USERUSER appuserSwitch to non-root user. Create first: RUN groupadd && useradd.
VOLUMEVOLUME ["/app/data"]Create mount point. Prefer named volumes in compose/docker run.
HEALTHCHECKHEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost/Container health monitoring. Interval, timeout, retries configurable.
LABELLABEL version="1.0" maintainer="team"Add metadata to image. Visible in docker inspect.
SHELLSHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]Change default shell for RUN commands.
STOPSIGNALSTOPSIGNAL SIGTERMSignal to stop container. Default: SIGTERM.
ONBUILDONBUILD COPY . /app/srcAdd trigger for downstream builds. Executes when image is used as base.
Advanced Dockerfile Features from Official Docs

ONBUILD: registers instructions that execute when your image is used as a base (FROM). Triggers run ONCE in the child build and are cleared afterwards. RUN --mount=type=secret: injects build secrets without baking them into layers. COPY --chown: sets file ownership. COPY --chmod: sets file permissions. Parser directives (# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1): pin Dockerfile syntax version for reproducible builds. Here-Documents: multi-line RUN/COPY without messy backslash escaping.

B.2 Dockerfile Templates (by Language)

Python/Django (anihpj)
FROM python:3.11-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
Node.js
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
Java (Spring Boot)
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/*.jar app.jar
RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
Go (Multi-Stage)
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o server .

FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /app/server /server
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["/server"]
Static HTML (Nginx)
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY ./html /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

B.3 Multi-Stage Dockerfile Template

Multi-Stage Pattern (Generic)
# Stage 1: Build
FROM python:3.11 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Stage 2: Runtime (slim, no build tools)
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY --from=builder /app/static /app/static
COPY . .
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

B.4 Dockerfile for Django (anihpj Full Template)

Complete production-ready Dockerfile for the anihpj/jobpost Django application with all best practices: multi-stage build, non-root user, health check, static collection, and environment hardening.

anihpj/Dockerfile (Production)
# ═══ Stage 1: Builder — installs dependencies & collects static ═══
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput --clear

# ═══ Stage 2: Runtime — minimal production image ═══
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings
# Copy only what's needed from builder
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY --from=builder /app/static /app/static
COPY --from=builder /app/manage.py /app/manage.py
COPY anihpj/ /app/anihpj/
COPY jobpost/ /app/jobpost/
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
# Security: create non-root user
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health/')"
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3", "--timeout", "120"]
Best PracticeImplementationWhy
Pin base imagepython:3.11-slimReproducible builds; slim reduces attack surface
Multi-stageBuilder → RuntimeFinal image has no pip, no build tools
Non-root userUSER appContainer breakout doesn't give host root
Health checkHEALTHCHECK instructionOrchestrators can detect and replace unhealthy pods
Python hardeningPYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1Prevents .pyc files; reduces image size
Workers=3Gunicorn workersRule of thumb: (2 × CPU cores) + 1

RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Stage 2: Runtime
FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ENV DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=anihpj.settings
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
COPY --from=builder /app/static /app/static
COPY . .
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --group app && chown -R app:app /app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health/')"
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "3"]

E.1 namespace.yaml

Creates an isolated anihpj namespace for all application resources. Namespaces provide scope for names, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies.

namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: anihpj
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: jobpost
    environment: production
💡 Tip: Always label namespaces with app.kubernetes.io/* recommended labels for discoverability and tooling support.

E.2 configmap.yaml

Stores non-sensitive configuration: Django settings module, allowed hosts, log level, and database host. Mounted as environment variables in the Deployment.

configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: anihpj-config
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj
    component: config
data:
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "anihpj.settings"
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "anihpj.example.com,localhost"
  LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
  POSTGRES_HOST: "postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
  POSTGRES_PORT: "5432"
  REDIS_HOST: "redis.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
  REDIS_PORT: "6379"
  CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS: "https://anihpj.example.com"
KeyValuePurpose
DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULEanihpj.settingsTells Django which settings file to load
ALLOWED_HOSTSanihpj.example.com,localhostDjango security: blocks host-header attacks
POSTGRES_HOSTpostgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.localK8s internal DNS for the Postgres Service
REDIS_HOSTredis.anihpj.svc.cluster.localK8s internal DNS for Redis cache

E.3 secret.yaml

Stores sensitive data: Django SECRET_KEY, database URL, and email credentials. Base64-encoded at rest; use with RBAC + etcd encryption in production.

secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-secrets
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj
    component: secrets
type: Opaque
stringData:
  SECRET_KEY: "django-insecure-REPLACE-WITH-REAL-SECRET-KEY"
  DATABASE_URL: "postgres://anihpj_user:STRONGpassword123!@postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:5432/anihpj_db"
  EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD: "smtp-password-here"
⚠️ Warning: Never commit stringData to Git! Use kubectl create secret or a sealed-secrets controller in production. This file is for reference only.
🔐 Production Secret Strategy:
1. Use Sealed Secrets or External Secrets Operator
2. Enable etcd encryption at rest
3. Restrict access via RBAC
4. Rotate secrets every 90 days

E.4 deployment.yaml

The core workload resource. Manages a ReplicaSet of 3 Django pods with resource limits, health probes, and rolling updates.

deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj
    tier: backend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
        tier: backend
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: ghcr.io/anihs-canvas/anihpj:v1.0.0
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          name: http
          protocol: TCP
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: anihpj-config
        - secretRef:
            name: anihpj-secrets
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
          timeoutSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 3
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 3
          failureThreshold: 2
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 0
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 12
        volumeMounts:
        - name: static-files
          mountPath: /app/static
        - name: media-files
          mountPath: /app/media
      volumes:
      - name: static-files
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: anihpj-static-pvc
      - name: media-files
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: anihpj-media-pvc
FieldValueWhy
replicas3High availability; survives node failure
strategyRollingUpdateZero-downtime deploys
maxUnavailable0Never drop below desired replica count during update
resources.requests256Mi/250mGuaranteed minimum; informs scheduler
resources.limits512Mi/500mHard cap; prevents noisy-neighbor issues
startupProbe60s windowGives Django time to start before liveness kicks in
terminationGracePeriod30sAllows graceful connection draining
🔄 Rolling Update Sequence
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │        ROLLING UPDATE (zero-downtime)    │
         │                                         │
Step 1:  │ [P1] [P2] [P3]  3 pods serving traffic  │
         │            │                             │
Step 2:  │ [P1] [P2] [P3] [N1]  New pod spawned     │
         │            │              (maxSurge=1)    │
         │                                         │
Step 3:  │ [P1] [P2] [N1]  Old P3 terminated        │
         │            │    (maxUnavailable=0)        │
         │                                         │
Step 4:  │ [N1] [N2] [N3]  All 3 new pods running   │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

E.5 service.yaml

Exposes the Deployment internally via a stable ClusterIP and optionally externally via LoadBalancer. Acts as a virtual IP load-balancing across all 3 pods.

service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: "nlb"
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: anihpj
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
    protocol: TCP
  - name: https
    port: 443
    targetPort: 8000
    protocol: TCP
  sessionAffinity: ClientIP
  sessionAffinityConfig:
    clientIP:
      timeoutSeconds: 10800

    │ (LoadBalancer)│  External:  k8s-anihpj-xxx.elb.amazonaws.com
    └──────┬───────┘
           │ kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS)

    ▼      ▼      ▼

E.6 ingress.yaml

Routes external HTTP/HTTPS traffic to the Service with TLS termination and path-based routing. Requires an Ingress Controller (nginx, traefik, AWS ALB).

ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "10m"
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - anihpj.example.com
    secretName: anihpj-tls
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj
            port:
              number: 80
      - path: /static
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj
            port:
              number: 80
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj
            port:
              number: 80
🌐 Ingress Traffic Routing
     INTERNET
        │
        ▼
  ┌──────────┐
  │  TLS:443  │  cert-manager auto-provisions Let's Encrypt
  │  INGRESS  │
  └────┬─────┘
       │  /         → Service:anihpj:80 → Pods:8000
       │  /static   → Service:anihpj:80 → Pods:8000 (static files)
       │  /api      → Service:anihpj:80 → Pods:8000 (DRF API)

E.7 kustomization.yaml

Kustomize overlays enable environment-specific customization without copying YAML. Supports dev/staging/prod overlays with different replicas, resource limits, and image tags.

base/kustomization.yaml
# base/kustomization.yaml — Common configuration
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: anihpj
resources:
- namespace.yaml
- configmap.yaml
- secret.yaml
- deployment.yaml
- service.yaml
commonLabels:
  app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: kustomize
images:
- name: ghcr.io/anihs-canvas/anihpj
  newTag: v1.0.0
overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
# overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml — Production-specific overrides
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: anihpj
resources:
- ../../base
patches:
- patch: |-
    - op: replace
      path: /spec/replicas
      value: 5
  target:
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj
- patch: |-
    - op: replace
      path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory
      value: "1Gi"
  target:
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj
images:
- name: ghcr.io/anihs-canvas/anihpj
  newTag: v1.2.3
nameSuffix: -prod
commonLabels:
  environment: production
OverlayReplicasMemory LimitImage Tag
dev1256Milatest
staging2512Miv1.2.3-rc1
prod51Giv1.2.3
🚀 Deploy with Kustomize:
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | kubectl apply -f -

E.8 hpa.yaml — HorizontalPodAutoscaler

Automatically scales the Deployment up to 10 pods based on CPU and memory utilization. Requires the Metrics Server installed in the cluster.

hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: anihpj-hpa
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: anihpj
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 50
        periodSeconds: 60
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 100
        periodSeconds: 15
      - type: Pods
        value: 4
        periodSeconds: 15
      selectPolicy: Max
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80
📈 HPA Auto-Scaling Visualization
Pods
 10│                              ╭────
  9│                          ╭───╯
  8│                      ╭───╯
  7│                  ╭───╯
  6│              ╭───╯
  5│          ╭───╯
  4│      ╭───╯
  3│  ╭───╯          ┌─────────────────────┐
  2│──╯──────────────│ minReplicas=2 (floor)│
  1│                 └─────────────────────┘
  0└──────────────────────────────────────────
                    Time →

  CPU > 70% → Scale UP (add pods aggressively)
  CPU < 50% → Scale DOWN (wait 5 min, then reduce 50%)
ParameterValueMeaning
minReplicas2Never drop below 2 pods (HA minimum)
maxReplicas10Never exceed 10 pods (cost control)
cpu target70%Scale up when average CPU exceeds 70% of 250m request
memory target80%Scale up when average memory exceeds 80% of 256Mi
scaleDown stabilization300sWait 5 min before scaling down (prevents flapping)
scaleUp policyMax(100%, 4 pods)Aggressive scale-up; uses whichever adds more pods

F.1 Common Container Errors & Solutions

The most frequent container-level failures — exit codes, OOM kills, permission denials, and port conflicts.

SymptomExit CodeLikely CauseDiagnosticSolution
Container exits immediately0 or 1Wrong CMD, missing file, app crashdocker logs <id>Check CMD/ENTRYPOINT; run docker run -it --entrypoint sh <img>
OOM Killed137Memory limit exceededdocker inspect --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}' <id>Increase --memory limit; check for memory leaks
Permission denied126Non-root user without accessdocker exec <id> whoamiRUN chown -R app:app /app or adjust USER
Port already in useN/A (fails to start)Host port conflictnetstat -tlnp | grep :8000Use different host port -p 8001:8000
Segfault / core dump139Native library incompatibilitydmesg | grep segfaultRebuild for correct arch (amd64 vs arm64)
Connection refusedN/ABinding to 127.0.0.1 not 0.0.0.0docker exec <id> netstat -tlnpUse --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 in Django/Gunicorn
Image pull failsN/AAuth or tag issuedocker pull <img>docker login; verify tag exists on registry
Healthcheck failsunhealthyWrong endpoint or timingdocker inspect --format='{{.State.Health}}' <id>Adjust interval/timeout; verify endpoint
Quick Diagnostic Checklist
# 1. Check container state
docker ps -a --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}"
# 2. Inspect exit reason
docker inspect --format='{{json .State}}' CONTAINER | jq
# 3. View last 50 log lines
docker logs --tail 50 CONTAINER
# 4. Check resource usage
docker stats --no-stream CONTAINER
# 5. Shell into running container
docker exec -it CONTAINER sh

F.2 Network Troubleshooting

DNS resolution failures, inter-container communication, port mapping, and overlay issues.

SymptomDiagnostic CommandLikely CauseSolution
DNS resolution failsdocker exec <id> nslookup postgresContainers on different networksJoin same network: docker network connect net <id>
Cannot reach host portcurl localhost:8000Port not published or wrong interfaceCheck -p HOST:CONTAINER mapping
Intermittent connectivitydocker network inspect bridgeIP address pool exhaustedPrune networks: docker network prune
Swarm overlay brokendocker node lsPort 4789/7946 blockedOpen UDP 4789 (VXLAN), TCP/UDP 7946 (gossip)
Container cannot reach internetdocker exec <id> ping 8.8.8.8iptables rules or IP forwarding disabledsysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
Slow DNS resolutiondocker exec <id> cat /etc/resolv.confDNS server misconfiguredSet --dns 8.8.8.8

   Bridge: docker0 (172.17.0.0/16)       Custom: mynet (172.18.0.0/16)
   ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐           ┌──────────┐
   │ ContainerA│  │ ContainerB│           │ ContainerC│

Network Debug Toolkit
# List all networks and containers on them
docker network ls
docker network inspect bridge --format='{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{.IPv4Address}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'
# Test connectivity from container
docker exec CONTAINER ping -c 3 TARGET_IP
docker exec CONTAINER nslookup TARGET_HOSTNAME
# Check iptables rules
iptables -L DOCKER -n -v
# Inspect DNS
docker exec CONTAINER cat /etc/resolv.conf

Data loss, permission errors, slow I/O, and mount point confusion.

SymptomDiagnosticCauseSolution
Volume appears emptydocker run -v vol:/data ... ls /dataBind mount path does not exist on hostCreate host directory first or use named volume
Permission denied on mountdocker exec <id> ls -la /mntUID/GID mismatch host↔containerdocker run --user $(id -u):$(id -g)
Data lost after container rmdocker volume lsUsed anonymous volume (--rm flag)Always use named volumes in production

Slow volume I/Odocker run --volume-driverWrong storage driver on macOS/WindowsUse :cached or :delegated on bind mounts
Bind mount not reflecting changesdocker exec <id> stat /mnt/fileFile system notification issue (macOS)Use :consistent or switch to named volume

F.4 Build Errors

Dockerfile syntax issues, cache corruption, COPY failures, and multi-stage pitfalls.

Error MessageCauseSolution
COPY failed: file not foundPath relative to build context, not DockerfilePaths are relative to docker build <CONTEXT> directory
returned a non-zero code: 1RUN command failedAdd set -ex at top of script; split long RUN into steps
no such file or directoryMissing dependency or wrong base imageVerify package is available in chosen base image variant
manifest for ... not foundWrong platform/architectureUse --platform linux/amd64 on ARM Macs
Cannot connect to Docker daemonDocker daemon not runningsudo systemctl start docker
Build context huge/slowMissing .dockerignoreCreate .dockerignore; exclude node_modules, .git, venv
exec format errorBinary compiled for wrong architectureUse FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM with BuildKit
Layer cache not usedCOPY/ADD invalidates cacheOrder Dockerfile: install deps FIRST, then COPY source
Build Debug Techniques
# Build with full output (no cache)
docker build --no-cache --progress=plain -t app .
# Inspect a specific layer
docker history IMAGE
docker run -it IMAGE sh  # explore interactively
# Build with BuildKit for better error messages
DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build -t app .
# Check what's in build context
du -sh . && ls -la  # ensure .dockerignore is working

F.5 Docker Daemon Issues

Daemon won't start, disk space exhaustion, API unresponsiveness, and performance degradation.

SymptomDiagnosticSolution
Daemon won't startsudo journalctl -u docker --no-pager -n 50Check daemon.json syntax; verify storage driver
Disk fulldocker system dfdocker system prune -a --volumes (caution!)
API unresponsivedocker info hangssudo systemctl restart docker; check for deadlocks
Too many open filesdocker info | grep -i "file"Increase LimitNOFILE in docker.service
Images won't deletedocker rmi -f IMAGEStop containers using image first; remove child images

Daemon Health Check

sudo journalctl -u docker --since "10 min ago" --no-pager

docker version && docker info

Pod stuck in PendingPendingkubectl describe pod <name>Check resource requests, node capacity, PVC binding
Cannot pull imageImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePullkubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A5 EventsVerify image tag, registry auth (imagePullSecrets)
Container keeps restartingCrashLoopBackOffkubectl logs <pod> --previousFix application error; check CMD in Dockerfile
Probe failingRunning but not Readykubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A10 "Liveness\|Readiness"Adjust probe path, port, initialDelaySeconds
Service not routingPods running but unreachablekubectl get endpoints <svc>Check selector matches pod labels
ConfigMap/Secret not updatingOld config in running podskubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>K8s doesn't auto-restart on ConfigMap change
HPA not scalingLoad high but no new podskubectl top pods -n <ns>Verify Metrics Server is installed and running
Ingress 404/503Request returns errorkubectl describe ingress <name>Check backend service name and port match
K8s Debug Quick Reference
# Pod debugging
kubectl describe pod POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE
kubectl logs POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE --previous  # crash logs
kubectl exec -it POD_NAME -n NAMESPACE -- sh   # shell in
# Deployment debugging
kubectl rollout status deployment/DEPLOY_NAME -n NAMESPACE
kubectl rollout history deployment/DEPLOY_NAME -n NAMESPACE
# Service debugging
kubectl get endpoints SVC_NAME -n NAMESPACE   # are pods registered?
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -O- http://SVC_NAME:PORT
# Events
echo 'kubectl get events -n NAMESPACE --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp'

📋 Appendix F Summary — Troubleshooting Methodology

🔍
Observe
docker ps -a, docker logs, kubectl describe
🧪
Diagnose
Check exit codes, events, resource usage, network isolation
🔧
Fix
Adjust configs, rebuild images, reconnect networks
✅
Verify
Re-run diagnostics, check health, confirm connectivity
🛠️ Golden Rules of Docker Troubleshooting:
1. Always check docker logs first — 80% of answers are in the logs
2. Use docker inspect for structured state (exit codes, mounts, networks)
3. Isolate: run with -it --entrypoint sh to enter a broken container
4. For K8s: describe → logs → exec → events in that order
5. Prune regularly: docker system prune -a prevents disk-full issues

📖 Appendix G: Docker Glossary — A to Z

Every Docker Term You'll Ever Need — Defined Clearly with Context

50+ essential terms organized alphabetically, plus a comprehensive acronym reference. Each definition includes practical context for the DCA exam.

G.1 50+ Docker Terms — A to Z

#TermDefinition
1Bridge NetworkDefault Docker network type. Containers on the same bridge can communicate by IP or container name. Uses NAT (iptables) for external access.
2Build ContextThe directory (and all its contents) sent to the Docker daemon when running docker build. Controlled by .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files.
3BuildKitNext-generation Docker builder supporting parallel builds, secrets injection, remote cache, and advanced Dockerfile syntax. Enabled via DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1.
4CMDDockerfile instruction that sets the default command (and arguments) for a container. Overridable at docker run. If ENTRYPOINT is set, CMD becomes its arguments.
5ContainerA running instance of a Docker image. Has its own writable layer, network namespace, process space (PID), and resource constraints (cgroups).
6Container RuntimeThe low-level software that actually runs containers. Docker uses containerd (which uses runc). Alternatives: CRI-O, gVisor, Firecracker.
7containerdAn industry-standard container runtime managing the complete container lifecycle. Docker donates containerd to CNCF; used by Kubernetes as well.
8Control Groups (cgroups)Linux kernel feature that limits, accounts for, and isolates resource usage (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network) of a collection of processes (containers).
9Copy-on-Write (CoW)Storage optimization: files in read-only image layers are copied to the writable container layer only when modified. Maximizes layer sharing between containers.
10Docker ComposeTool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a YAML file (compose.yaml). Single command: docker compose up.
11Docker Content Trust (DCT)Integrity system that signs Docker images using Notary. Ensures images haven't been tampered with. Enabled via DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1.
12Docker DesktopGUI application for macOS/Windows that packages Docker Engine, CLI, Compose, Kubernetes, and credential helpers into a single install.
13Docker EngineThe core Docker runtime: a client-server application consisting of the Docker daemon (dockerd) and the Docker CLI (docker).
14Docker HubDocker's official public registry. Hosts millions of container images. Free for public repos; paid plans for private repos and vulnerability scanning.
15Docker ScoutBuilt-in image vulnerability scanner that analyzes SBOM, checks against CVE databases, and provides remediation advice. Replaces the older docker scan.
16Docker SwarmDocker's native orchestrator for multi-host container management. Provides service discovery, load balancing, secrets, rolling updates, and self-healing.
17DockerfileText file containing a set of instructions (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD, etc.) that Docker uses to automatically build an image layer by layer.
18ENTRYPOINTDockerfile instruction that defines the fixed executable. Unlike CMD, ENTRYPOINT is not overridden by docker run arguments (unless --entrypoint is used).
19ExposeDockerfile instruction that documents which ports the container listens on. Does NOT publish ports — only -p or ports: in Compose does that.
20HealthcheckDockerfile instruction that defines how Docker tests if a container is still working. Supports CMD, CMD-SHELL, and NONE. Status: starting/healthy/unhealthy.
21Host NetworkNetwork mode (--network host) where the container shares the host's network stack directly — no isolation. Faster but less secure.
22ImageA read-only template composed of stacked layers, built from a Dockerfile. Used as the blueprint to create containers. Identified by name:tag or digest.
23Image DigestContent-addressable SHA256 hash uniquely identifying a specific image version. Immutable — unlike tags which can be moved. Format: sha256:abc123...
24Image LayerEach instruction in a Dockerfile produces a read-only layer. Layers are cached, shared between images, and combined via a union filesystem (Overlay2).
25Init ProcessA lightweight init (tini/dumb-init) that runs as PID 1 to handle zombie processes and signal forwarding. Enabled via docker run --init.
26MACVLANNetwork driver that assigns a MAC address to each container, making it appear as a physical device on the network. Used for legacy applications.
27ManifestA JSON document describing an image's layers, architecture, OS, and digests. Multi-arch images have a manifest list pointing to platform-specific manifests.
28Multi-Stage BuildDockerfile technique using multiple FROM statements. Build dependencies in one stage, copy only the final artifacts to a minimal runtime stage.
29Namespace (Linux)Kernel feature isolating process visibility: PID, NET (network), MNT (mount), IPC, UTS (hostname), USER, CGROUP. Docker uses all 7 namespaces per container.
30OrchestrationAutomated deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications across clusters. Docker Swarm and Kubernetes are the two main orchestrators.
31Overlay NetworkMulti-host Docker network using VXLAN encapsulation (UDP port 4789). Enables containers on different Swarm nodes to communicate securely.
32Overlay2Default Docker storage driver on most Linux distributions. Uses a union mount filesystem with copy-on-write semantics for efficient layer stacking.
33Port MappingPublishing a container port to the host using -p HOST:CONTAINER. Traffic to HOST:PORT is forwarded to CONTAINER:PORT via Docker's proxy.
34Private RegistrySelf-hosted Docker image storage. Can be a simple registry:2 container, or a managed service (AWS ECR, GCR, GHCR, Azure ACR).
35RegistryA stateless, highly scalable server-side application that stores and distributes Docker images. Docker Hub is the default public registry.
36RepositoryA collection of related Docker images with the same name but different tags. Example: python repository contains python:3.11, python:3.12, etc.
37Restart PolicyControls when Docker automatically restarts a container: no, on-failure[:N], always, unless-stopped. Set via --restart flag.
38SBOMSoftware Bill of Materials — a detailed inventory of all packages, libraries, and dependencies inside a container image. Generated by Docker Scout.
39SeccompLinux kernel security feature that filters which system calls a process can make. Docker applies a default seccomp profile blocking ~44 of ~300+ syscalls.
40Service (Swarm)The definition of a desired state for an application in Docker Swarm. A service specifies the image, replicas, ports, networks, and update strategy.
41StackA group of interrelated Swarm services defined in a Compose file and deployed together via docker stack deploy. Stacks span the entire swarm.
42Storage DriverThe plugin that manages how image layers and the container writable layer are stored. Common drivers: overlay2 (default), aufs, devicemapper, btrfs, zfs.
43TagA human-readable label applied to an image (e.g., python:3.11-slim). Tags are mutable — a tag can be moved to a newer image. Use digests for immutability.
44Tmpfs MountA temporary filesystem stored in the host's RAM (not disk). Used for sensitive data that should never hit disk. --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid.
45Union FilesystemFilesystem that allows files from separate filesystems (branches/layers) to be overlaid into a single coherent view. Overlay2 is the Linux union FS Docker uses.
46User NamespaceMaps a container's root user (UID 0) to a non-privileged user on the host. Reduces blast radius of container breakout. --userns-remap.
47VolumeDocker-managed persistent storage that exists outside the container's UnionFS. Survives container deletion. Managed via docker volume commands.
48Volume DriverPlugin enabling Docker volumes to use external storage systems: NFS, AWS EBS, Azure Disk, Ceph, GlusterFS. Specified via --volume-driver.
49Worker NodeA Docker Swarm node that runs containers as scheduled by manager nodes. Workers don't participate in Raft consensus or cluster management.
50Manager NodeA Docker Swarm node that handles cluster management: scheduling, maintaining cluster state, API serving, and Raft consensus. First node is always a manager.
51Docker ContextA configuration that bundles Docker endpoint (daemon) connection details, letting you switch between multiple Docker environments with docker context use.
52Build ArgsBuild-time variables passed via --build-arg or ARG instruction. Unlike ENV, ARGs are NOT persisted in the final image. Use for conditional builds.
53Secrets (Docker)Encrypted blobs (max 500KB) managed by Swarm for sensitive data. Stored in Raft log, mounted as tmpfs into /run/secrets/. Never written to disk.
54Configs (Docker)Non-sensitive configuration data (max 500KB) managed by Swarm. Similar to secrets but not encrypted. Mounted into /<name> in the container.

G.2 Docker Acronyms Explained

Every acronym you'll encounter in Docker documentation, exams, and interviews — expanded and explained.

AcronymExpansionWhat It Means
CI/CDContinuous Integration / Continuous DeliveryAutomated pipeline: build image → test → push → deploy. Docker is the backbone of most CI/CD pipelines.
CNCFCloud Native Computing FoundationLinux Foundation sub-foundation that hosts containerd, Kubernetes, Prometheus, and other cloud-native projects.
CoWCopy-on-WriteStorage strategy: data is copied only when modified. Core to Docker's layer efficiency.
CRIContainer Runtime InterfaceKubernetes API for pluggable container runtimes. containerd implements CRI via the CRI plugin.
CVECommon Vulnerabilities and ExposuresPublicly disclosed security flaws. Docker Scout checks images against CVE databases.
DABDistributed Application Bundle(Deprecated) Early Docker format for multi-service apps. Replaced by Compose files + docker stack deploy.
DCADocker Certified AssociateDocker's official certification exam covering orchestration, image management, networking, security, and storage.
DCTDocker Content TrustImage signing and verification using Notary/TUF. DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1.
OCIOpen Container InitiativeLinux Foundation project creating open standards for containers (image-spec, runtime-spec, distribution-spec).
SBOMSoftware Bill of MaterialsInventory of all software components in an image. Generated via docker scout sbom.
TUFThe Update FrameworkSecure software update specification. Docker Content Trust uses Notary, which implements TUF.
VXLANVirtual Extensible LANEncapsulation protocol (UDP 4789) used by Docker overlay networks for multi-host container communication.
