H.1 Domain 1: Orchestration — 25 Questions

Swarm mode, services, stacks, nodes, rolling updates, and scheduling. 25% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 1 — Orchestration Practice Questions

Q1
What command initializes a Docker Swarm on the current node?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker swarm init. This makes the current node a Swarm manager, generates join tokens, and starts the Raft consensus database.

EXPLANATION

The node becomes the first manager. Swarm uses Raft consensus (an odd number of managers is recommended — 3, 5, or 7). The command outputs docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-... for workers and a separate token for additional managers.

# docker swarm init
# docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-...
Q2
How do you add a worker node to an existing swarm?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

On the manager: docker swarm join-token worker to get the token. On the worker: docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-... MANAGER_IP:2377.

EXPLANATION

Port 2377 is the Swarm management port (TCP). Workers need connectivity to all managers on this port. Join tokens are different for workers vs managers — manager tokens should be guarded carefully as they grant cluster control.

# docker swarm join-token worker
# docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-... MANAGER_IP:2377
Q3
What is the difference between a Swarm service and a Docker container?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A service is a declarative definition of desired state (image, replicas, ports, networks). A container is a single running instance. Services manage containers across the swarm.

EXPLANATION

In Swarm, you don't run containers directly — you create services. The swarm manager ensures the desired number of replicas (containers) are running, rescheduling them if nodes fail. This is the core of orchestration: declaring WHAT you want, letting the system handle HOW.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web
Q4
What command creates a Swarm service running nginx with 5 replicas on port 80?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service create --name web --replicas 5 -p 80:80 nginx

EXPLANATION

The service is automatically load-balanced across all 5 replicas via Swarm's routing mesh. Any node receiving traffic on port 80 will forward it to a healthy replica, even if that node isn't running the container.

# docker service create --name web --replicas 5 -p 80:80 nginx
Q5
How do you perform a rolling update on a Swarm service?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service update --image nginx:1.25 --update-parallelism 2 --update-delay 10s web

EXPLANATION

Swarm performs rolling updates by default. --update-parallelism controls how many replicas update at once; --update-delay adds a pause between batches. Failed updates auto-rollback if --update-failure-action rollback is set.

# docker service update --image nginx:1.25 --update-parallelism 2 --update-delay 10s web
# --update-parallelism
# --update-delay
# --update-failure-action rollback
Q6
What is the Swarm Routing Mesh?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The routing mesh makes every Swarm node listen on published service ports and forward traffic to healthy replicas — even if the receiving node doesn't run that replica. Uses IPVS for load balancing.

EXPLANATION

This means you can hit ANY node on port 80 and reach the nginx service, even if that node has zero nginx containers. The routing mesh forwards to a node that does. This is key for external load balancers — they can point to any swarm node.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web
Q7
How many manager nodes should a production Swarm have, and why?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

3 or 5 manager nodes (odd number). Raft consensus requires (N/2)+1 managers to be available (quorum). With 3 managers, you can lose 1; with 5 managers, you can lose 2.

EXPLANATION

Never use an even number — it wastes capacity with no fault tolerance gain. 4 managers has same fault tolerance as 3 (can lose 1) but requires 3 for quorum vs 2. More managers = slower consensus, so 7+ is rarely needed.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web
Q8
What command deploys a Compose file as a Swarm stack?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker stack deploy -c compose.yaml mystack. This creates services, networks, and secrets defined in the Compose file across the entire swarm.

EXPLANATION

Key difference from docker compose up: stack deploy is Swarm-aware — it respects deploy: section (replicas, update_config, restart_policy, placement constraints). Compose up ignores the deploy: key unless using docker compose --compatibility up.

# docker stack deploy -c compose.yaml mystack
# docker compose up
# docker compose --compatibility up
Q9
How do you scale a Swarm service to 10 replicas?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service scale web=10 or docker service update --replicas 10 web

EXPLANATION

Swarm schedules the additional replicas across available nodes respecting placement constraints and resource availability. If there aren't enough resources, replicas may stay in "pending" state.

# docker service scale web=10
# docker service update --replicas 10 web
Q10
What is a Swarm placement constraint? Give an example.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A rule that restricts which nodes can run a service. Example: docker service create --constraint node.labels.ssd==true --name db postgres ensures the database only runs on nodes with SSD storage.

EXPLANATION

Placement constraints use node labels (docker node update --label-add ssd=true node1). You can also use --placement-pref for spreading across racks/zones. Constraints help with compliance, performance, and licensing requirements.

# docker service create --constraint node.labels.ssd==true --name db postgres
# docker node update --label-add ssd=true node1
# --placement-pref
Q11
How do you drain a Swarm node for maintenance?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker node update --availability drain NODE_NAME. All containers on that node are gracefully stopped and rescheduled to other nodes.

EXPLANATION

Drain prevents new tasks from being scheduled and migrates existing ones. After maintenance: docker node update --availability active NODE_NAME. The node's state preserves; only containers move.

# docker node update --availability drain NODE_NAME
# docker node update --availability active NODE_NAME
Q12
What are the three Swarm node availability states?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Active — normal operation, can receive tasks. Pause — existing containers stay, no new tasks. Drain — all containers moved away, no new tasks.

EXPLANATION

Pause is useful for temporarily suspending a node (troubleshooting without evacuation). Drain is for decommissioning or maintenance. Managers in drain state still participate in Raft but don't run workloads.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web
Q13
What happens to a Swarm service if a worker node fails?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Swarm detects the node failure (after the node becomes unreachable for a configurable period), marks it as Down, and reschedules the failed containers onto healthy nodes to maintain the desired replica count.

EXPLANATION

This is self-healing. The manager monitors heartbeats. If no heartbeat for ~20s, the node is marked Down (~60s for leader election if the manager itself fails). Containers from failed nodes are recreated on healthy nodes automatically.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web
Q14
How do Swarm secrets differ from environment variables for sensitive data?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Secrets are encrypted during transit and at rest in the Raft log, mounted as tmpfs files in /run/secrets/, never exposed in docker inspect or environment variables. Env vars are visible in docker inspect and process lists.

EXPLANATION

Secrets exist only in memory on worker nodes (tmpfs), are encrypted in the Raft database, and are only sent to nodes that need them. Env vars can leak via ps aux, /proc, or logging. Always use secrets for passwords, API keys, certificates.

# /run/secrets/
# docker inspect
# docker inspect
Q15
What command lists all services in a swarm?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker service ls — shows service name, mode (replicated/global), replicas, image, and ports.

EXPLANATION

Add --format for custom output. For detailed inspection: docker service inspect SERVICE_NAME. For task-level view: docker service ps SERVICE_NAME shows each replica's node, state, and error messages.

# docker service ls
# docker service inspect SERVICE_NAME
# docker service ps SERVICE_NAME

H.2 Domain 2: Image Creation & Management — 20 Questions

Dockerfile best practices, multi-stage builds, layer caching, registry operations, and image security. 20% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 2 — Image Management Practice Questions

Q16
What is the purpose of the FROM instruction in a Dockerfile?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

FROM specifies the base image to build upon. Every Dockerfile must start with a FROM instruction (or ARG before FROM). It initializes a new build stage.

EXPLANATION

Multi-stage builds use multiple FROM statements. Always use specific tags (python:3.11-slim) rather than latest for reproducibility. Using FROM scratch creates an empty base (for statically-compiled binaries).

# python:3.11-slim
# FROM scratch
Q17
What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ENTRYPOINT defines the fixed executable — commands after docker run IMAGE become arguments to it. CMD provides default arguments to ENTRYPOINT (or the default command if no ENTRYPOINT). CMD is overridden by docker run IMAGE command.

EXPLANATION

When both are used: ENTRYPOINT ["python"] + CMD ["app.py"] runs python app.py. docker run img test.py overrides CMD, running python test.py. Use ENTRYPOINT for the executable, CMD for default args.

# docker run IMAGE
# docker run IMAGE command
# ENTRYPOINT ["python"]
# CMD ["app.py"]
# python app.py
Q18
Why should you use COPY instead of ADD in Dockerfiles?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

COPY is simpler and predictable — it copies local files/directories. ADD has extra magic (auto-extracting tar archives, fetching remote URLs) that makes builds less deterministic. Docker recommends COPY unless you specifically need tar extraction.

EXPLANATION

ADD's URL fetch doesn't cache well (no cache validation for remote resources) and can be a security risk. For remote files, use RUN curl/wget in a single RUN with cleanup. ADD is only appropriate when you need auto-extraction of local tar files.

# RUN curl/wget
Q19
What is layer caching and how do you optimize it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer. If a layer hasn't changed and all previous layers are cached, Docker reuses it. Optimize by ordering instructions from least to most frequently changed: install dependencies first, COPY source code last.

EXPLANATION

Example: COPY requirements.txt → RUN pip install → COPY . . This way, code changes don't invalidate the pip install cache. If you COPY . . first, any code change forces a full pip reinstall.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web
Q20
What is a multi-stage build and why use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

A Dockerfile with multiple FROM statements. The first stage(s) build/compile the application with full toolchains. The final stage copies only the compiled artifacts, resulting in a much smaller production image without build tools.

EXPLANATION

Example: Stage 1 uses golang:1.21 to compile a Go binary. Stage 2 uses alpine:3.19 and copies just the binary. Result: 10MB image instead of 800MB. This also improves security by removing compilers and dev tools from the final image.

# golang:1.21
# alpine:3.19
Q21
How do you tag an image for a private registry?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker tag myapp:latest registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0 — then docker push registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0. The registry hostname must be part of the tag.

EXPLANATION

The image name format is [HOST[:PORT]/]NAME[:TAG]. Without a host, Docker Hub is assumed. For AWS ECR: 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:v1. Always docker login to the private registry first.

# docker tag myapp:latest registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0
# docker push registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0
# [HOST[:PORT]/]NAME[:TAG]
# 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/myapp:v1
# docker login
Q22
What does docker build -t app . do with the dot?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The dot (.) is the build context — the directory sent to the Docker daemon. All COPY/ADD instructions reference paths relative to this directory. The daemon receives the entire context (minus .dockerignore exclusions).

EXPLANATION

The Dockerfile doesn't have to be in the context root — you can use docker build -f path/to/Dockerfile .. The context is sent as a tar to the daemon, so keep it small with .dockerignore (exclude node_modules, .git, venv).

# docker build -t app .
# docker build -f path/to/Dockerfile .
Q23
How do you reduce Docker image size? List 5 techniques.
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. Use slim/alpine base images
2. Multi-stage builds
3. Combine RUN commands (reduce layers)
4. Remove package caches in same RUN (apt clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*)
5. Use .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files

EXPLANATION

Each layer adds permanent size — even deleting a file in a later layer doesn't reduce the image (the file still exists in the earlier layer). Combine operations: RUN apt update && apt install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* in ONE line.

# apt clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# .dockerignore
# RUN apt update && apt install -y pkg && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
Q24
What is the difference between ENV and ARG in Dockerfiles?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

ENV persists in the final image and is available at runtime. ARG is build-time only — exists only during docker build, not in the final image. ARGs can be passed via --build-arg.

EXPLANATION

Use ARG for build-time configuration (version numbers, build dates). Use ENV for runtime configuration that the container needs. ARG can be used before FROM to dynamically set the base image: ARG PYTHON_VER=3.11 then FROM python:${PYTHON_VER}.

# docker build
# --build-arg
# ARG PYTHON_VER=3.11
# FROM python:${PYTHON_VER}
Q25
What command pushes an image to Docker Hub?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

docker push username/imagename:tag. Requires docker login first. The image must be tagged with the Docker Hub username as prefix.

EXPLANATION

If not logged in: denied: requested access to the resource is denied. For organizations: docker push orgname/imagename:tag. Use docker logout to remove credentials.

# docker push username/imagename:tag
# docker login
# denied: requested access to the resource is denied
# docker push orgname/imagename:tag
# docker logout

H.3 Domain 3: Installation & Configuration — 15 Questions

Docker Engine setup, daemon configuration, logging drivers, storage drivers, and Docker Desktop management. 15% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 3 — Installation & Configuration Practice Questions

Q36
Where is the Docker daemon configuration file located?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

/etc/docker/daemon.json on Linux. Docker Desktop manages this through its Settings UI. The file is JSON and requires a daemon restart (sudo systemctl restart docker) to apply changes.

EXPLANATION

Common daemon.json settings: {"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m"}, "storage-driver": "overlay2", "insecure-registries": ["myreg:5000"], "dns": ["8.8.8.8"]}. Validate JSON syntax before restarting — bad JSON prevents daemon startup.

# /etc/docker/daemon.json
# sudo systemctl restart docker
# {"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m"}, "storage-driver": "overlay2", "insecure-registries": ["myreg:5000"], "dns": ["8.8.8.8"]}
Q37
How do you configure Docker to use a specific logging driver?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

In /etc/docker/daemon.json: {"log-driver": "json-file"} for daemon-wide default. Per-container: docker run --log-driver=syslog --log-opt syslog-address=tcp://....

EXPLANATION

Available drivers: json-file (default), syslog, journald, gelf, fluentd, awslogs, splunk, gcplogs. Set log rotation: {"log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}} to prevent disk exhaustion.

# /etc/docker/daemon.json
# {"log-driver": "json-file"}
# docker run --log-driver=syslog --log-opt syslog-address=tcp://...
# {"log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}}
Q38
What is the default storage driver and how do you change it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Default: overlay2 (on most modern Linux). Change in daemon.json: {"storage-driver": "overlay2"}. Requires daemon restart; existing images/containers are NOT migrated.

EXPLANATION

Supported drivers: overlay2 (recommended), aufs (legacy), devicemapper, btrfs, zfs, vfs (slow, for testing). Check current: docker info | grep "Storage Driver". Changing driver loses all existing data — backup first.

# {"storage-driver": "overlay2"}
# docker info | grep "Storage Driver"
Q39
How do you start/stop/restart the Docker daemon on Linux?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

sudo systemctl start docker, sudo systemctl stop docker, sudo systemctl restart docker. Enable at boot: sudo systemctl enable docker.

EXPLANATION

Check status: sudo systemctl status docker. View logs: sudo journalctl -u docker -f. Docker socket: /var/run/docker.sock (permission group: docker). Add user to docker group: sudo usermod -aG docker $USER.

# sudo systemctl start docker
# sudo systemctl stop docker
# sudo systemctl restart docker
# sudo systemctl enable docker
# sudo systemctl status docker
Q40
What is the difference between Docker CE and Docker EE?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Docker CE (Community Edition) — free, open-source, community-supported. Docker EE (Enterprise Edition, now Mirantis Container Runtime) — paid, with certified plugins, RBAC, image scanning, and support SLAs.

EXPLANATION

For the DCA exam: know that EE includes Docker Trusted Registry (DTR), Universal Control Plane (UCP), and certified infrastructure. CE is sufficient for learning and most production use cases. Mirantis now manages the enterprise Docker products.

# Swarm essentials:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx
docker service update --image nginx:alpine web
docker service rollback web

H.4 Domain 4: Networking — 15 Questions

Bridge, overlay, host, MACVLAN networks; port mapping; DNS resolution; network troubleshooting. 15% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 4 — Networking Practice Questions

Q51
What is the default Docker network type and how does it work?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

The bridge network (docker0). Containers on the same bridge can communicate by IP. The default bridge does NOT support DNS-based service discovery — use custom user-defined bridges for that.

EXPLANATION

Default bridge: containers can only reach each other by IP, not by name. User-defined bridge: automatic DNS resolution between containers. Always create custom networks (docker network create mynet) for production apps.

# docker network create mynet
Q52
How do containers on different networks communicate?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

They cannot communicate directly — Docker networks are isolated. To connect containers across networks, attach a container to both networks: docker network connect net2 container1.

EXPLANATION

Or use port publishing to expose a service on the host, then other containers can reach it via the host IP. In Swarm, overlay networks span nodes and enable cross-host communication via VXLAN tunnels (UDP 4789).

# docker network connect net2 container1
Q53
What is an overlay network and when is it required?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

An overlay network uses VXLAN encapsulation to connect containers across multiple Docker hosts (Swarm nodes). Required for multi-host Swarm services to communicate with each other.

EXPLANATION

Overlay networks encrypt data plane traffic with IPSec (enabled via --opt encrypted). Control plane uses TCP 2377 (Swarm management), data plane uses UDP 4789 (VXLAN) and UDP 7946 (gossip for service discovery).

# --opt encrypted
Q54
What does -p 8080:80 mean in docker run?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Maps host port 8080 to container port 80. Traffic to localhost:8080 is forwarded to port 80 inside the container via Docker's iptables NAT rules.

EXPLANATION

The format is -p HOST:CONTAINER. To bind to a specific interface: -p 192.168.1.100:8080:80. To use a random host port: -p 80 (only container port). Check mappings: docker port CONTAINER.

# -p 8080:80
# localhost:8080
# -p HOST:CONTAINER
# -p 192.168.1.100:8080:80
# docker port CONTAINER
Q55
What is the host network mode and when would you use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

--network host removes network isolation — the container shares the host's network stack directly. Use for maximum network performance or when the container needs to bind to many ports.

EXPLANATION

Tradeoffs: faster (no NAT), but no isolation — port conflicts with host, no network namespace. Only works on Linux. Common use: network monitoring tools, high-throughput proxies. Not recommended for multi-tenant environments.

# --network host

H.5 Domain 5: Security — 15 Questions

Docker Content Trust, secrets management, seccomp profiles, AppArmor, image signing, RBAC, TLS. 15% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 5 — Security Practice Questions

Q66
What is Docker Content Trust (DCT) and how do you enable it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

DCT uses digital signatures (via Notary/TUF) to verify image integrity and publisher identity. Enable: export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1. When enabled, Docker only pulls/pushes signed images.

EXPLANATION

With DCT=1, unsigned images are rejected. Signing keys: repository key (per-repo), root key (offline), timestamp key. DCT prevents supply-chain attacks by ensuring images haven't been tampered with since signing.

# export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
Q67
What is seccomp and how does Docker use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) filters which Linux syscalls a container can make. Docker applies a default seccomp profile that blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls out of 300+, significantly reducing kernel attack surface.

EXPLANATION

You can apply custom profiles: --security-opt seccomp=/path/to/profile.json. Disable (NOT recommended): --security-opt seccomp=unconfined. The default profile is well-tested and suitable for most applications.

# --security-opt seccomp=/path/to/profile.json
# --security-opt seccomp=unconfined
Q68
How do you run a container as a non-root user?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

In Dockerfile: RUN useradd -m app && USER app. At runtime: docker run --user 1000:1000 nginx. Always create the user in the Dockerfile (not at runtime) so file permissions are set during build.

EXPLANATION

Root in container = root on host (unless user namespaces enabled). A container breakout as root gives full host access. The USER instruction should come after permission-critical operations (package installs) and before COPY/CMD.

# RUN useradd -m app && USER app
# docker run --user 1000:1000 nginx
Q69
What are user namespaces and how do they improve security?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

User namespaces remap a container's root user (UID 0) to a non-privileged user on the host (e.g., UID 100000). Enable via {"userns-remap": "default"} in daemon.json. A container breakout as "root" gives only a low-privilege host user.

EXPLANATION

This is a powerful defense-in-depth measure. Tradeoffs: some filesystem operations may need adjustment, and it's incompatible with some volume drivers. Enabled per-daemon, not per-container.

# {"userns-remap": "default"}
Q70
How do Swarm secrets protect sensitive data?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Secrets are encrypted in transit (mutual TLS), encrypted at rest (Raft log encryption), mounted as tmpfs (in-memory only), and only sent to nodes that need them. They're never exposed in environment variables or docker inspect.

EXPLANATION

Create: echo "mypassword" | docker secret create db_pass -. Use in service: docker service create --secret db_pass. Mounted at /run/secrets/db_pass. Max size: 500KB per secret. Use for passwords, API keys, TLS certs.

# echo "mypassword" | docker secret create db_pass -
# docker service create --secret db_pass
# /run/secrets/db_pass

H.6 Domain 6: Storage & Volumes — 10 Questions

Volumes, bind mounts, tmpfs, storage drivers, volume plugins, and data persistence strategies. 10% of the DCA exam.

📝 DCA Domain 6 — Storage & Volumes Practice Questions

Q81
What are the three types of Docker mounts?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

1. Volumes — Docker-managed, stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes/, portable, best for persistence.
2. Bind mounts — Mount any host path, great for development (live code editing).
3. tmpfs — In-memory only (RAM), never written to disk, for sensitive temporary data.

EXPLANATION

Volumes are the recommended production choice: they're managed by Docker, work across OSes, can use volume drivers for cloud storage, and are easy to backup. Bind mounts are path-dependent and can have permission issues on different OSes.

# /var/lib/docker/volumes/
Q82
How do you create and use a named volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Create: docker volume create pgdata. Use: docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres. List: docker volume ls. Inspect: docker volume inspect pgdata.

EXPLANATION

Named volumes survive container deletion. To remove: docker volume rm pgdata (must be unused). Prune all unused: docker volume prune. Backup: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata.tar.gz -C /data .

# docker volume create pgdata
# docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
# docker volume ls
# docker volume inspect pgdata
# docker volume rm pgdata
Q83
What is the difference between a volume and a bind mount?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Volume: Docker-managed location (/var/lib/docker/volumes/), created via docker volume create, portable, recommended for production. Bind mount: any host path (/home/user/data), depends on host directory structure, great for development.

EXPLANATION

Volumes are Docker's recommended approach — they work consistently across all platforms and don't depend on host filesystem structure. Bind mounts can break when moving between macOS, Windows, and Linux due to different path conventions.

# /var/lib/docker/volumes/
# docker volume create
# /home/user/data
Q84
What is a tmpfs mount and when should you use it?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

tmpfs stores data in the host's RAM only — never written to disk. Use: docker run --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid. Best for sensitive data that should never persist (tokens, temp credentials).

EXPLANATION

Unlike volumes/bind mounts, tmpfs data is lost on container stop AND host reboot. It cannot be shared between containers. Swarm secrets use tmpfs internally. Mount options (noexec, nosuid, nodev) add security hardening.

# docker run --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid
Q85
How do you backup a Docker volume?
Show Answer & Explanation
ANSWER

Use a temporary container that mounts both the volume and a backup directory: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/source -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata-backup.tar.gz -C /source .

EXPLANATION

This pattern works for any volume. Restore: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/target -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar xzf /backup/pgdata-backup.tar.gz -C /target. For databases, use native tools (pg_dump, mongodump) instead of raw filesystem backup for consistency.

# docker run --rm -v pgdata:/source -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata-backup.tar.gz -C /source .
# docker run --rm -v pgdata:/target -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar xzf /backup/pgdata-backup.tar.gz -C /target
